title: The PM is promising to fix our everyday annoyances – and I have a list to get him started | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham hopes we’ll forget the big stuff if he sorts out our minor frustrations and low-level gripes. Pothole politics hasn’t won me over yet, but I know some changes that could, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: Andy Burnham hopes we’ll forget the big stuff if he sorts out our minor frustrations and low-level gripes. Pothole politics hasn’t won me over yet, but I know some changes that could, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Hoping for some Mamdani magic? Andy Burnham.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHoping for some Mamdani magic? Andy Burnham.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamThe PM is promising to fix our everyday annoyances – and I have a list to get him startedEmma BeddingtonAndy Burnham hopes we’ll forget the big stuff if he sorts out our minor frustrations and low-level gripes. Pothole politics hasn’t won me over yet, but I know some changes that couldSun 23 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTShareThis is a vulnerable confession, but I spend way too much time on the social media of the New York City mayor,Zohran Mamdani. Whether he is seemingly effortlessly speaking Mandarin, hanging out with kids or charmingly accepting that he should wear a cycle helmet, the man with the million-watt smile is my antidepressant. (Even more vulnerable confession: I believe, irrationally, he is looking after my elder son, who lives there.)This means that I know all about Mamdani’s fight against whatBusiness Insider recently deemed the “annoyance economy”– daily frustrations that make you poorer or drive you slowly, miserably mad. These include the absurd complexity of cancelling subscriptions; hidden fees; getting charged more for something you looked up last week, because of cookies; never being able to find a public toilet; and potholes. He has taken to responding when he gets tagged in people’s “Mamdani, fix this” posts to the point where Britons online are even jokily asking him to take on their problems.He may not need to, because Andy Burnham has started doing something similar with his “everyday fixes” for irritations and unfair expense: bringing forward the ban on auto-renewed subscriptions; tackling betting and vape shops and misleading “sale” prices; andcapping bus fares in England.It’s surely human nature to start by sweating the small stuff – faced with a to-do list, most of us tick off the quick wins first – and would you rather tackle climate breakdown or potholes? More cynically, it also plays well for politicians online. These fixes are visual and easily communicated. As Eric Phillips, who was press secretary for the former New York mayor Bill de Blasio, says: “Theatre is part of the job.” But does Burnham really think fluttering his eyelashes and telling me it will be easier to cancel a Paramount+ subscription I took out in 2021 and then forgot about means I’ll roll over and let him tickle my belly, forgetting all abouthis unconscionable attitude to North Sea drilling?I suppose it’s not impossible. It’s nice to feel as if someone in power understands the low‑level irritations that sap our joy, energy and resources – and will do something about them. And, just possibly, winning public confidence by sorting minor gripes could build goodwill to tackle the big, hard, slow, unpopular stuff.I’m not won over by British pothole politics yet – Burnham doesn’t have Mamdani’s magic. So, having seenthe consumer champion Martin Lewissuggest that the government fix “100 small things that piss people off”, I’ve compiled a list of silly little ways to get me on side.Obviously, start with the scourge of delivery companies claiming you were out when you were in all day, staring out like a lonely dog, waiting for your package. Please also eliminate the headbanging futility of updating “delivery preferences” only for them to be ignored. I could reconcile myself to the surveillance state, I reckon, if the surveillance included a database of everyone’s whereabouts and preferences, so you never had to argue with a bot or retrieve your contact lenses from your mortal enemy at No 114. Perhaps the surveillance state could also remind me where I’ve put my keys?Then there is the “digital annoyance economy”, by which I mean shopping sites that, when you click on an item and then click back, return you to the top of the page, so you have to scroll back down through all the items you’ve already seen: this outrage needs to be stamped out. And if I buy something and the seller signs me up to marketing guff unless I opt out, I want to be able to press a big red button (on my phone, around my neck?) that places the company in administration and bars the entire board from holding corporate office in perpetuity. Please impose the same punishment for having a non-functioning “unsubscribe” option on emails.The CEO of every manufacturer of plastic-film lids needs to demonstrate they can open them effortlessly, using their non-dominant hand, before they can sell them. See also sticky tape – make them prove it unrolls without ripping or the end disappearing. Washing machines should have a built-in tissue sensor; bread should be bio-engineered to fall butter side up and we need free scissor and nail clipper distributors on every street corner. Also, issue everyone with a single, universal sock.Once you’ve fixed all that, @andy.burnham, you might just get my vote.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Terror: Devil in Silver review – this psychiatric hospital horror is scary on so many levels  | Television | The Guardian
description: Expect gory set pieces and jump scares galore in the return of the supernatural anthology series, with Dan Stevens among the many poor souls terrorised by an evil spirit haunting their ward
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Expect gory set pieces and jump scares galore in the return of the supernatural anthology series, with Dan Stevens among the many poor souls terrorised by an evil spirit haunting their ward
Content: Supernaturally charged … Chinaza Uche as Coffee and Dan Stevens as Pepper in The Terror: Devil in Silver.Photograph: Emily V Aragones/AMCView image in fullscreenSupernaturally charged … Chinaza Uche as Coffee and Dan Stevens as Pepper in The Terror: Devil in Silver.Photograph: Emily V Aragones/AMCTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Terror: Devil in Silver review – this psychiatric hospital horror is scary on so many levelsExpect gory set pieces and jump scares galore in the return of the supernatural anthology series, with Dan Stevens among the many poor souls terrorised by an evil spirit haunting their wardLucy ManganSun 23 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThings that go bump in the night? Bad. Things that go bump in the night in a dilapidated psychiatric hospital? Infinitely worse. That, basically, is the premise of Devil in Silver, the latest volume of anthology series The Terror, which began in 2018 with a supernaturally charged tale of a polar expedition to find out what happened to Sir John Franklin’s voyage. Crikey, it does not end well. The next was set during the second world war and was about shapeshifters from Japanese folklore terrorising a Japanese-American community in southern California. A hiatus followed, but now The Terror is back with a double dose of horror: a malevolent spirit moving in and out of the bodies of the patients of New Hyde psychiatric hospital, and the more tangible but no less frightening diabolism of the US mental healthcare system.Pepper (Dan Stevens, still of Downton Abbey fame despite his many varied roles since) is in New Hyde because the three policemen who arrested him after they caught a few punches he was aiming at his girlfriend’s controlling ex threw him in there rather than completing the paperwork the station would have required. There he meets the lost and suffering souls who have ended up in what amounts, due to underfunding and understaffing, to a holding pen rather than a rehabilitative or care facility. Dorry (Judith Light) is the longest-serving resident – put there decades ago by her husband because of her endless crying fits, though her later memories reveal a greater darkness. Kofi (Chinaza Uche) – or Coffee, as he is called by the rest of his companions until it is too late – was a structural engineer in Ghana but now depends on medication to keep himself steady. Loochie (played by non-binary actor b) ended up in the system after a violent incident with a sibling, but at least one member of staff believes her charge is able to cope in the real world and, as the hospital’s evil spirit gathers strength and wrath, gets the chance to prove it.View image in fullscreenLongest-serving resident … Judith Light as Dorry.Photograph: Emily V Aragones/AMC/2025 AMC Film Holdings LLC. All Rights Reserved.Pepper comes to understand from his fellow patients – and some of the staff, none of whom is an out-and-out villain and many of whom are almost as trapped by circumstance as their patients are – that the key to whatever is haunting the hospital lies behind a locked silver door. Beyond it is a single occupancy room that contains the comatose body of a man who has, in one state or other, been at New Hyde even longer than Dorry. Arnold received a transorbital lobotomy after killing a doctor a year after he was sent to the ward.Jump scares, gory set pieces, flickering lights, endless corridors and an extremely unsettling turn from John Benjamin Hickey as the hospital’s founder Dr Walter take care of the required horror element of the show in a fairly rote manner. We have seen it all before, often more punchily done (though the ending does redeem the lack of innovation before). Ditto the idea of monster as metaphor for both mental instability and the systems that are supposedly in place to steady it.You could say that Devil in Silver does not shy away from the latter point. If you were feeling less generous, you could say it labours it. Dorry embodies the effects of misogyny and patriarchalism on the medical profession. The question of racial prejudice permeates the fates of all the patients of colour. None of the patients/prisoners comes from the kind of money that might have protected them – or at least got them placed in a facility that does not require the services of a nurse like Scotch Tape (Hampton Fluker), so called because of his talents for keeping mod cons running with little more than a roll of the stuff and a prayer.It works best as a straightforward drama. The real-life horrors of old-fashioned treatments (as we see when Dorry’s backstory starts to play out), and of contemporary care standards for the forgotten and marginalised masses, are bleaker than any imaginary beastie prowling through psyches and corridors. The ease with which Pepper gets trapped in the system – drugged on arrival, he sleeps through discharge time – the guilt he wrestles with over his abandonment of his young son and how an essentially good man can find a way to redemption: these are all more terrifying and more mesmerising to contemplate than any bogeyman under the bed.The Terror: Devil in Silver aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now. It is available on Stan in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewHorror (TV)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘So many people say things about my appearance – it’s not normal’: Jorja Smith on burnout, body-shaming and finding freedom | Jorja Smith | The Guardian
description: Being recognised by the Brits, Grammys and Drake made the singer one of British music’s most famous names – and also left her exhausted. Now, after decompressing in her home town she returns with a record made for raving
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Being recognised by the Brits, Grammys and Drake made the singer one of British music’s most famous names – and also left her exhausted. Now, after decompressing in her home town she returns with a record made for raving
Content: Jorja Smith … ‘I just love dancing. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m out.’Photograph: Ivor Lawson-AdamahView image in fullscreenJorja Smith … ‘I just love dancing. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m out.’Photograph: Ivor Lawson-AdamahJorja SmithInterview‘So many people say things about my appearance – it’s not normal’: Jorja Smith on burnout, body-shaming and finding freedomEmma LoffhagenBeing recognised by the Brits, Grammys and Drake made the singer one of British music’s most famous names – and also left her exhausted. Now, after decompressing in her home town she returns with a record made for ravingSun 23 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a sticky, sweltering July afternoon, and I have accidentally found myself at a wake withJorja Smith. I’m told that the pub where we have met, in the leafiest part of leafy south-west London, is usually a safe bet for an inconspicuous table. But today, sweaty black suits carrying pints drift between tables, and long queues snake round the bar.Dressed in a simple tank top, bare-faced with her hair scraped back, Smith is waiting for me when I arrive. “I’ve been waiting for my drink for ages,” she says. “But I feel bad saying anything because, you know …”The sombre mood doesn’t last long – in large part because Smith is effortlessly funny. When her alcohol-free sparkling wine finally arrives, she takes one sip, pauses for the waitress to disappear, then winces theatrically. “Oh,” she says. “That’s not good.” Every time we dissolve into laughter, I glance around guiltily, like we’re schoolgirls trying not to get caught talking at the back of assembly.It’s hard to imagine a less appropriate setting in which to discuss an album made for sunburnt block parties and 2am raves. What Are the Odds, the 29-year-old’s third album, released this week, is a certified, old-fashioned ass-shaker. Made with Richard Isong – the London producer better known as P2J, whose credits include Beyoncé, Burna Boy and Tems – and featuring the likes of Wizkid and Devlin, it is a vibrant collage of Black British dance music, weaving together UK garage, funky house, 2-step and Afrobeats, into a 12-track collection that pulsates from top to bottom.double quotation markI went straight to my label and said: ‘I think this is an album, not an EP. This is serious.’ I am so excited about itWhile dance music has always been threaded through Smith’s catalogue, usually in the form of a summer single – On My Mind in 2017, Little Things in 2023 – she is better known for her introspective, soulful R&B, as epitomised by her 2016 breakout single Blue Lights (whichNME praised as“a fantastically introspective and clever piece of songwriting”, and hadcritics declaring her Amy Winehouse’s successor). This is the first time she has committed fully to the dancefloor.“I just love dancing,” Smith shrugs. “I like going out to listen to music, a lot of my friends are DJs. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m outside.”The genesis of this album was different to her previous records. Her Mercury prize-nominated debut album, Lost & Found, emerged because she felt it was time to make an album. Its successor, Falling Or Flying, arrived because she felt she “needed” a second one. What Are the Odds was made almost accidentally, which is perhaps why it feels so light on its feet.After making the effervescent club single Little Things with P2J, the pair initially planned to write a dance EP. But the songs kept coming, and the project outgrew itself. “We went through nine songs in the first two days,” Smith says, her eyes widening again at the memory. “I turned up to the studio and he’d made all this music from our conversations. I left and went straight to my label and said: ‘I think this is an album, not an EP. This is serious.’ I’m so excited about it.”View image in fullscreenOdds on … Jorja Smith.Photograph: Ivor Lawson-AdamahThe album may be created for the dancefloor, but its emotional resonance remains unmistakably Smith. For Life mourns losing a friend to addiction; Young Heart is a love letter to Smith’s younger self; The Way It Was meditates on the end of a friendship. “If you just sang the songs with keys or piano,” she says, “they’d all probably be quite sad.”It is tempting to read What Are the Odds as a comeback album. In the weeks before its release, various headlines have announced Smith’s “return”. When I begin to ask her about this supposed break, she cuts in incredulously. “People keep saying, ‘Oh, you’re back!’ What do you mean, back? I’ve been on tour since 2017. When people say that, I’m like … [you should] check my calendar! People are likely talking about a ‘comeback’,” she says, “because I’m back on social media. I take breaks, and I’m not always out at events and things.”It’s an astute observation, and one that cuts to the heart of Smith’s unconventional relationship with celebrity. Since Blue Lights announced her arrival as an 18-year-old in 2016, she has become one of British music’s defining voices: a Mercury and Grammy nominee, double Brit award winner, and a featured artist capable of surfacing everywhere from Drake’s More Life to Burna Boy’s African Giant. Yet, she has never cultivated the kind of omnipresent celebrity that feels almost compulsory in the social media age, where visibility seems synonymous with existence. There are no carefully choreographed glimpses into her morning routine, no sense that her life exists to be consumed. Smith has clearly never been especially interested in that side of the bargain.“I never wanted to be famous,” she says. “I’ve always been quite private. I just wanted to put music out as a teenager and see what happened. I feel really lucky that I’ve got such an amazing fanbase and people really show me love, but fame was never the goal.”The tension, of course, is that success increasingly lives or dies by the algorithm. The defining British stars of recent years – PinkPantheress, Raye, Lola Young – have all been, in some part, forged in the fires of TikTok. Does Smith ever feel pressure to play that game? “Yeah definitely,” she says. “But, luckily, I’ve got a sick team, and we come up with ideas that we can do that are still me. I don’t want to be here doing trends – you’re not going to catch me doing TikTok dances or any of that stuff.”Her inclination to privacy also stems from growing up under an unusually unforgiving spotlight. Smith first found an audience by uploading covers to YouTube, recorded from her bedroom in Walsall. Aged 15, she signed with a manager, and began making regular trips to London for songwriting sessions. After finishing her A-levels, she moved to the capital full-time, working shifts in a cafe while trying to carve out a career in music.Blue Lights, which hauntingly paired Smith’s mellifluous voice with lyrics about police profiling and urban anxiety, landed on SoundCloud in 2016, instantly establishing her as one of the most compelling new voices in British music. The following year, Drake invited her on to his blockbuster playlist, More Life, exposing her to millions of listeners around the world.Alongside the acclaim, though, came another kind of attention. Almost overnight, Smith became a symbol of a modern beauty ideal, often uncomfortably sexualised before she had properly entered adulthood. For years, the conversation around Jorja Smith the musician existed alongside another conversation entirely, one that Smith had no control over: that of Jorja Smith the face, Jorja Smith the body. “It’s not normal,” she says, reflecting on that time. “Growing up and having so many people having something to say about your appearance.”The internet, as it tends to do, eventually turned. In the run-up to the release of Falling Or Flying in 2023, every online photo or video seemed to invite commentary on her weight. At one point, the phrase “Jorja Smith weight gain” trended on X for two days. It is something she brings up without prompting.View image in fullscreenJorja Smith picks up the Best British female solo artist award at the Brits in 2019.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImage“It was difficult. I’d be reading things like: ‘What happened to her?’ Or, ‘She’s let herself go.’” She trails off. “It really knocks your confidence.”On one occasion, she couldn’t resist replying. “Some blog page”– she waves away the name – “had put two photos side by side, like a before and after. I just commented: ‘What the hell, guys? I’m literally 18 in that picture. Why are you doing that?’” She shrugs. “People are so quick. They love you, then they hate you.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat made that period particularly disorientating, she says, was that the public narrative bore almost no resemblance to reality; at the very moment strangers were dissecting her body online, she felt healthier than ever.“I’d actually started eating properly,” she says. “Before that, I’d be so busy I’d skip meals, wake up late, I was running every day, obsessively. It was the first time I actually felt healthy, and then people wanted to criticise me? It was a proper headfuck because I was thinking: Wait … can I do anything right?”For a while, she stopped wanting to do photoshoots, or even go outside for fear of being photographed. “I sort of went into myself,” she says. “I felt like no one could really understand what I was going through.” Her coping mechanisms, she says, are to go for a walk or to the gym, though she catches herself revealing how fragile that equilibrium can still be.double quotation markI’m feeling the buzz of what London has to offer again, instead of feeling as if I have to wear armour all the timeSometimes she’ll still “see comments … and start thinking: Maybe they’re right?” She stops herself mid-thought. “Oh my God,” she says, laughing in disbelief. “Even me saying that now is crazy. Because they’re just random people!“But I have my days,” she continues. “I was talking to my mum about it the other day, and she was like: ‘At least they’re not saying you sound shit!’”One of the ways she’s protected herself is by stepping away from those online platforms. She no longer runs her own social media – her team posts on Instagram, and she only keeps the app to message artists and friends. She hasn’t been on X in years, and never goes looking for commentary about herself.Part of that self-reclamation meant physically removing herself, too. In 2023, after years in London, she moved back to Walsall – an unusual move for an artist at the height of their career. “I just needed a reset,” she says. “I thought: Let me move back home, touch some grass, see some trees.” London, she says, had become tangled up with the pressures of her career. This City, one of the tracks on What Are the Odds, explores her love-hate relationship with the capital. “Anything negative that happened, I kind of put London as the culprit,” she says. “I was like: ‘I hate this place. I need to get out.’” Distance has since softened London’s hard edges, and today, she divides her time between the West Midlands and the capital: “I’m feeling the buzz of what this place has to offer again, instead of feeling as if I have to wear armour all the time.”She is fiercely protective, too, of the place she comes from. In an industry so often centred on London, she is keen to keep reminding people that remarkable artists also emerge from elsewhere. “People forget I’m not from London,” she laughs. “And I’m not from Birmingham, either!” In September, Smith will return to Walsall for a home town show at Walsall Arena, a school turned community arts space she used to visit as a girl. Part of Spotify’s Hometown Billboard campaign, the bill doubles as a showcase of local talent: childhood friend Wesley Joseph, with whom she released the single July this year, supports, alongside the Blue Lights Choir she founded to create opportunities for young people in the town. “I hope it’s a moment that inspires the next generation to believe that big things really can come from Walsall,” she says.Jorja Smith review – mega-watt charisma powers ambitious new songsRead moreThese days, when she isn’t working, she is trying to build a life that exists beyond music. She walks, cooks and has rediscovered running. “I’ve signed up for the London marathon next year,” she says. “I wanted a goal, and I watched everyone finishing it this year and thought: That’s such a sick thing to do.”Despite her instinct to retreat from the spotlight, Smith is also consciously trying to step back into the world. Recently, she was on the phone with a friend back home when she mentioned turning down an invitation to a Vogue party. Her friend wouldn’t let it slide. “She was like, ‘Go! Not everyone gets invited to these things. You only live once. If you keep turning everything down, you’re going to be 70 and have zero stories of fun nights out because you never went anywhere!’” she laughs.Outside, the heat hasn’t lifted. Mourners are still in the beer garden. As she gets up to leave, Smith pulls a cap low over her face and slides on a pair of oversized sunglasses. Until that moment, it has been surprisingly easy to forget that she is famous at all.“It’s all about finding that balance,” she says, smiling as she stands. “But I’m feeling good. I’m starting to feel like my younger self again.”What Arethe Odds is out nowon FAMM.Jorja Smithperformsat Walsall Arena on 6 September.Explore more on these topicsJorja SmithDance musicR&BPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The kindness of strangers: I was a young, solo tourist when a taxi driver became aggressive – then two men stepped in | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: They relayed to me that the driver wanted more money. I went to grab my wallet, but they told me to put it away
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: They relayed to me that the driver wanted more money. I went to grab my wallet, but they told me to put it away
Content: Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian Desig/AlamyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian Desig/AlamyKindness of strangersAustralian lifestyleThe kindness of strangers: I was a young, solo tourist when a taxi driver became aggressive – then two men stepped inThey relayed to me that the driver wanted more money. I went to grab my wallet, but they told me to put it awayRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesTara Macloughlin, as told toKatie CunninghamSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI travelled alone a lot when I was younger and often got myself into stupid situations. You think you’re immortal when you’re in your 20s.One such occasion happened when I was 25 and travelling solo in Egypt, not long after the turn of the century. I had taken an overnight bus from Cairo to Dahab, which dropped me and my fellow passengers off in the middle of nowhere. I had to get a shared taxi into town at about 3am – one where everyone sat up the back in a ute tray – then find somewhere to stay.I was the only tourist in the taxi and definitely the only woman. When we reached Dahab, things quickly went south. I didn’t speak Arabic, so I couldn’t understand what the driver was saying, but it was quite obvious he was becoming increasingly aggressive toward me.As things got more and more heated, two Egyptian men who were also in the back of the ute stepped in. The taxi driver was gesturing to me and the other guys shouted back at him. They relayed to me that the driver wanted more money. I went to grab my wallet, but they told me to put it away. They paid him off themselves and the driver left. Suddenly I was alone with these two men, in the middle of the night, wondering if I’d gotten myself into an even hairier situation than the one I’d just exited.Kindness of strangers: The day of my mum’s funeral, the saleswoman at the stationery store made me feel less aloneRead moreThe men asked where I was staying and I replied that I hadn’t booked accommodation. So they took me to a hostel, ensured the owner only charged me the locals’ rate, then disappeared without asking anything in return.I woke up the next day determined to find – and thank – those two men. It took me three days of searching the city high and low, but I eventually found them, working in an internet cafe. It turned out they were medical students funding their studies by installing internet all over Egypt. I was a student nurse, so we had a lot in common.They invited me to their home town, where I stayed for a few days and met their wonderful friends, families and future wives. Every time I went out, they escorted me to make sure I was OK. We stayed in contact for years afterwards.You often meet the worst people when travelling alone as a young woman. I have been robbed everywhere, in every language under the sun. But those men were not motivated by anything selfish in helping me. I think they’d have done that for anyone, simply because it was the right thing to do.They started as strangers, but I now regard them as two of the best people I’ve ever met.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: This is how we do it: ‘Since having cancer, I’m more open – before I was straight, now I’m queer’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Following the all-clear, Kevin and Jade found a new openness in discussing sex and intimacy – and also a shared desire for exploring polyamory
Author: Naomi Larsson Piñeda
Headline: Following the all-clear, Kevin and Jade found a new openness in discussing sex and intimacy – and also a shared desire for exploring polyamory
Content: Illustration: Ryan GillettView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan GillettThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘Since having cancer, I’m more open – before I was straight, now I’m queer’Following the all-clear, Kevin and Jade found a new openness in discussing sex and intimacy – and also a shared desire for exploring polyamoryHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toNaomi Larsson PiñedaSun 23 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKevin, 38double quotation markSince the all clear, my relationship with my sexuality has shifted a lotI’ve been in recovery from drug addiction since I was 19, and I had cancer 10 years ago. So there have been points when sex has been important to me, and periods of abstaining and working on myself. Jade and I have been together for 11 years, and the sex was always good – not particularly kinky, just really intimate, nice sex.I got ill after we’d been together less than a year and had to have one of my testicles removed, which put an immediate stop to any sex. Then I was in chemo, and sex wasn’t even on my mind – the whole period was incredibly traumatic. I’m eternally grateful that Jade stuck with me through it. Since then, my relationship with my sexuality has shifted a lot. I’ve become more vulnerable and open.double quotation markAs soon as there was this little bit of spice, maybe even a threat, it gave us a boostWhen Jade came back from a party and said a couple had asked her for a threesome, we were in a really good place. We were having sex multiple times a week, talking a lot, being open. We were actively looking for something fun, exciting and maybe a bit naughty to do. So when she asked how I felt about it, my reaction was, “I feel pretty good.”We started going to parties and clubs together. The first time I saw Jade with a guy, I thought, “Oh, this is actually really nice.” We were instantly more attracted to each other. As soon as there was this little bit of spice, maybe even a threat, it gave us a boost. We found operating as a couple and seeing each other with other people easy. There was an instant uptick in the amount of sex we were having and how exciting it was.I have scarring from the operation – all the lymph nodes were removed from one side of my groin, and there’s a big scar where they removed the testicle on the other side, so that was a massive blow in terms of confidence and self-image. But since exploring polyamory, I’m a far more confident person than I was before. I feel better than I ever have in my life. My relationship to my own sexuality, confidence and body is miles ahead of where it was. If you’d asked me three years ago, I would have said I was straight. I now identify as queer.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreJade, 37double quotation markNow we date and have sex solo. It’s been a very mutual explorationKevin was diagnosed with cancer early on and that obviously shapes things. We had so many challenges that sex wasn’t at the forefront of my mind. But since then we found our feet, and have both been keen to explore new things.We were monogamous for eight years, but decided to open things up three years ago. Some people do it to fix something in their relationship, but we were in a great space and wanted to share that and accelerate it with other people. A few years after Kevin got the all-clear, we were feeling exploratory and I had the opportunity to have a threesome at a party. I didn’t do it, but told Kevin I thought it would be fun, and he immediately said, “Right then, let’s do it.”We started going to sex-positive parties and began playing together in group settings or with a third person. Now we date and have sex with other people solo. I sleep with men, women and everyone in between, and so does Kevin. It’s been a very mutual exploration.double quotation markI’ve had to learn this balance between independence and togetherness between us, and how that looksI’d never really considered non‑monogamy before. There’s this assumed way of being that you accept, and then suddenly you discover all this richness available to you outside monogamy, and what it can bring to your relationship with your primary partner.One of the main challenges is that we do things at different paces. Kevin is really open-hearted and forms quite strong, close relationships with people, which can create a bit of an imbalance. I’ve had to learn this balance between independence and togetherness between us.For me, it feels great when both of our cups are full. We’re both getting meaningful, fun, exciting experiences independently of each other – and then also together.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I love it. It’s hope’: the mysterious self-willed wildflower meadow that seeded itself | Biodiversity | The Guardian
description: Farmer Derek Sayer let a boggy field run wild and just one annual hay-cut has led to remarkable biodiversity
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Farmer Derek Sayer let a boggy field run wild and just one annual hay-cut has led to remarkable biodiversity
Content: ‘Everyone is planting and seeding wildflowers, but sometimes we’re not patient enough,’ said Carl Sayer.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Everyone is planting and seeding wildflowers, but sometimes we’re not patient enough,’ said Carl Sayer.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianBiodiversity‘I love it. It’s hope’: the mysterious self-willed wildflower meadow that seeded itselfFarmer Derek Sayer let a boggy field run wild and just one annual hay-cut has led to remarkable biodiversityPatrick BarkhamSun 23 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTucked away on a country lane, a small field bursts with yellow and pink flowers. Quail and whitethroats call from the thick hedges and the plants, including common centaury, yellow rattle and marsh and common spotted orchids, bounce with hoverflies and butterflies.More than 150 plant species have been recorded on Sayer’s Old Meadow, in north Norfolk, England, which is remarkable when there was just one – oilseed rape – growing there 21 years ago.This transformation has happened without sowing any commercial wildflower mixes or making any other expensive interventions such as deep ploughing or top-soil removal, often undertaken when arable land is “restored” to nature-rich meadow. Instead, the four-acre field was simply cut for hay once every summer, with an abundance of wildflowers naturally – and rather mysteriously – finding their way into the field.View image in fullscreenCommon centaury and orchid species have sprung up in Sayer’s Old Meadow.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianThese findings, published in a scientific paper inRestoration Ecology, could transform the approach to recreating flower-rich meadows. Conservationists and landowners are pushing to revive old meadows because98%in England and Wales have been destroyed over the last century.“Everyone is planting and seeding wildflowers, but sometimes we’re not patient enough,” said Carl Sayer, aprofessor of limnology and freshwater ecology at University College Londonand lead author of the paper. “You don’t always have to reach for that expensive commercial wildflower seed mix. We’ve forgotten that nature has known what to do for quite a long while.”View image in fullscreenCarl Sayer, right, with his father, Derek.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianThe fact that Sayer shares his surname with the meadow is no coincidence: it is owned by his father, farmer Derek Sayer, 86, and has been part of a tiny traditional farm for generations. The land was ploughed and fertilised and sprayed with pesticides as was conventional in postwar farming, but Derek Sayer stopped cultivating it in 2005 because the small field was always “hit and miss” at producing good yields.Springs feeding the Glaven chalk stream rise in the meadow and parts of the field were always boggy. The land was “abandoned” for five years and became a forest of thistles before Carl Sayer began studying its growing diversity, beginning an annual hay-cut in 2011.Fifteen years on, thistles and other arable annual weeds have almost completely disappeared – without any human intervention – to be replaced with a flower-rich perennial sward, which is growing more biodiverse every year.View image in fullscreen‘It looked a bit strange at first’: it took a while for Carl’s father to come round to the idea.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianFor Sayer’s father, watching farmland run wild with “weeds” was challenging but he gradually became more interested in his son’s experiment. “He started off saying: ‘What are you doing, Carl? What a load of rubbish.’ Now he’s like: ‘How many orchids are there this year?’” said Sayer.When Derek Sayer arrived to look at the field during the Guardian’s tour, he still cast a fierce countryman’s gaze over it, checking for “weeds” such as ragwort. “It looked a bit strange at first but I quite like it now,” he said.Each August, a neighbouring farmer cuts and removes the hay, which he feeds to his cattle, grateful for the biodiverse hay crop. “Much more diversity is a tonic to cattle because it’s full of medicinals,” said Carl Sayer. “The monoculture of a rye-grass field may not give them everything they need. The old farmers had it right.”Cutting it each year prevents the meadow becoming an oak woodland. The sward is full of baby oaks and sallow, and a patch of the field which hasn’t been cut regularly is now filled with hummocks of sallow as high as a house: still wildlife-rich habitat but not as rare or much-needed as flower-rich meadows.View image in fullscreenSayer’s Old Meadow was recently mowed to help the more delicate wildflowers develop.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianRemoving the grass growth each year with the hay-cut also reduces the nutrients, enabling more delicate wildflowers to flourish. Several years ago, yellow rattle found its way into the meadow. This is known as “the meadow maker” because it parasitises grass and creates space for other wildflowers, although Sayer said the meadow was thriving without it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Everyone will tell you this approach [not sowing wildflowers] doesn’t work unless you’re close to a seed source. But no one has done a long-term study like this,” he said.View image in fullscreenCarl says people living in the village love the meadow.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianThe surrounding land is intensively farmed and the nearest populations of some of the rare flowers now found in the meadow are at least 3 miles (4.8km) away. One possibility is that seeds have been brought in on the hooves or coats of wild deer that roam the countryside.‘Living proof damaged landscapes can recover’: exploring a vast restored forest in southern SwedenRead more“Everyone’s accused me of bringing it in on my upturned trousers but I don’t wear upturned trousers,” joked Sayer, who was wearing shorts.Sayer’s Old Meadow looks noticeably different from what some conservationists disparagingly call generic “McMeadows” created from popular wildflower mixes which are dominated by white oxeye daisies and purple knapweed. The advantage of “self-willed” meadows is that they are filled with locally-appropriate plants which are likely to be more genetically diverse than those found in commercial seed mixes. This type of meadow creation was also much cheaper, said Sayer.View image in fullscreenAn orchid blooming in the meadow.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianSince last year, barn owls have taken up residence in a field-edge nest box and hunt over the field. The Sayers allow local people to walk in it and an informal path now runs down one side. “Everyone in the village loves it, people walk through it and respect it. It’s working to make people happy as well,” said Sayer. “It’s the thing I’m most proud of in my life. I love it. It’s hope – we can recover things. We just need to do less in the recovery process.”The Guardian’s climate forum 2026: On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts — including ProfAndy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman — for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. title: Burnham to visit Ukraine with promise of boost for Kyiv’s long-range missiles | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: PM will use independence day trip to announce sharing of classified information about Storm Shadow components
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: PM will use independence day trip to announce sharing of classified information about Storm Shadow components
Content: Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelensky talking at HM Naval Base Portsmouth last month. Burnham’s visit to Kyiv on Monday will be his first as prime minister.Photograph: Jason Alden/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelensky talking at HM Naval Base Portsmouth last month. Burnham’s visit to Kyiv on Monday will be his first as prime minister.Photograph: Jason Alden/EPAForeign policyBurnham to visit Ukraine with promise of boost for Kyiv’s long-range missilesPM will use independence day trip to announce sharing of classified information about Storm Shadow componentsKiran Staceyin London andDan Sabbaghin DniproSun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 20.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain will boost Ukraine’s capacity to make its own long-range missiles,Andy Burnhamwill announce on Monday, as he travels to Kyiv for the country’s independence day on his first foreign visit as prime minister.Burnham will arrive in the Ukrainian capital on Monday morning at a crucial time in the war, with Kyiv braced for another wave of Russian missile attacks and the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, facing his most direct domestic challenge.The UK prime minister will use the trip to announce that the UK government will allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to helpUkrainebuild its own version.While the announcement will probably take years to have an impact on the war, it is likely to escalate tensions with Moscow at an already fraught moment in UK-Russian relations.Burnham said in a statement on Sunday night: “On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.“I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security.“The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war. In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine and deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”Burnham will announce in Kyiv that the UK will help France set up assembly lines in Ukraine for long-range missiles, which the French president, Emmanuel Macron, promised last month.Macron spoke to Zelenskyy on Saturday to promise to deliver separate interceptor missiles, which could help counter the recent barrage of high-speed Russian missile attacks on Kyiv.Meanwhile, European leaders have condemnedFriday’s drone attackon a busy shopping centre in central Ukraine, which killed 16 people in Zelenskyy’s home town of Kryvyi Rih.View image in fullscreenRescuers with a dog work at the site of a Russian drone attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih on Saturday.Photograph: Serhii Chalyi/ReutersThe Ukrainian military has run out of US-made Patriot interceptors, and the US president, Donald Trump,recently backtrackedon a promise to let Ukraine build its own.However, Zelenskyy said over the weekend he still wanted to buy more US-made Patriots, adding that Ukraine was happy to pay for them rather than receive them as military aid. “I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package,” he said. “The request from our air force is 360.”He added that he had reached an agreement with France on at least one air-defence system ​this year, and with ‌Germany on the supply of ​about 600 ​interceptors in 2027-28.Macronposted on Xon Saturday: “It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its skies and thwart this aggression … It is essential that all countries with capabilities at their disposal also join this effort.”The British announcement is a small step in a much larger and longer-term project that could lead to Ukraine making its own long-range versions of the Storm Shadow cruise missile in several years’ time.But the move is likely to trigger further criticism from Moscow at a time when tensions between the UK and Russia are already high.Last week, Russiaaccused the UKof deliberately escalating the conflict by allowing Ukraine to launch attacks with British-made drones, warning that the deeper Britain’s involvement, “the higher the price it will pay”.This weekend it emerged that Russia hadwithdrawn its ambassador in Londonwithout naming a replacement, prompting speculation it was downgrading its diplomatic presence in the UK.Burnham has insisted that Russian threats will not weaken British support for Ukraine,saying last week: “We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”The prime minister will on Monday use a meeting of the coalition of the willing, which comprises 34 countries that have promised to help secure Ukraine in the event of a peace deal with Russia, to underline that commitment.Holding election in wartime would risk destroying Ukraine, says ZelenskyyRead moreThe meeting will be co-chaired by Burnham and Macron, who will join remotely via video link. Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, will also take part in the call as the leaders discuss ways to help Ukraine repel the recent wave of long-distance attacks.While there, Burnham will attend independence day events, the details of which are being kept secret amid concerns of a major Russian attack, and receive an award in recognition of the UK’s support for Ukraine.Zelenskyy is facing the most concerted internal political challenge of his presidency after the call for an election by his former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.The Ukrainian president responded to Fedorov’s dramatic announcement for the first time this weekend, telling reporters on Saturday that holding elections, which have been suspended since the war began,risked splitting the country.“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” he said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” he added.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyAndy BurnhamUkraineRussiaLabourEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Government vows to make business rate valuations for pubs and hotels fairer | Business rates | The Guardian
description: Review will look at improving system for English and Welsh hospitality venues before next revaluation date in 2029
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Review will look at improving system for English and Welsh hospitality venues before next revaluation date in 2029
Content: Hospitality venues were hit by higher business rate bills this year after the end of pandemic-era relief and when new revaluations took effect.Photograph: william87/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenHospitality venues were hit by higher business rate bills this year after the end of pandemic-era relief and when new revaluations took effect.Photograph: william87/Getty Images/iStockphotoBusiness ratesGovernment vows to make business rate valuations for pubs and hotels fairerReview will look at improving system for English and Welsh hospitality venues before next revaluation date in 2029Lauren AlmeidaSun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government has promised that business rate valuations will be “made fairer” for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, asAndy Burnhamfaces growing calls to help the UK’s struggling hospitality sector.An independent review forEnglandand Wales will look at improving the system for hospitality venues, which were hit by higher business rate bills this year after the end of pandemic-era relief and when new revaluations took effect.It comes after Burnham announced last month that he would cut business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in Englandby 20%from April next year.The government has faced calls to reduce the tax burden on hospitality businesses, which have also struggled to cope with rising energy and food bills in recent years.The review, which will be led by Jerry Schurder, an independent business rates specialist, will report back to the Treasury by the end of March 2027. It will consider valuations before the next revaluation date in 2029. The rise in valuations this year will not be affected.James Murray, the financial secretary to the Treasury, said: “Pubs and hotels are vital for communities and bringing growth to every postcode,” adding that a “rethink of valuations” would help “build a fairer system for the future”.Allen Simpson, the chief executive of the trade bodyUKHospitality, said it was positive the government was looking seriously at the valuation methodology for pubs and hotels.“Business rates remain a significant burden for hospitality businesses, and the system needs to better reflect the trading realities for the sector,” he said.Emma McClarkin, the chief executive of theBritish Beer & Pub Association, said the review was “sorely needed and hugely welcome” as pubs had for years “paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open”.While cuts have been welcomed by business owners, the industry has repeatedly called for the reform of the whole business rates system. Estimates suggest thattwo pubs are closing a day across Britainthis year, hit by higher taxes, wages, energy and food costs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham is also facing calls to extend the business rates relief aimed at pubs, clubs and live music venues to bookshops. This month 234 independent booksellerssigned an open lettercalling on the prime minister to give bookshops the same consideration as other businesses that play a positive role in their communities.The government has suggested that it will reform business rates, including small business rates relief, at John Healey’s first budget on 28 October.Explore more on these topicsBusiness ratesPubsHotelsHospitality industryAndy BurnhamEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK productivity growing faster than official figures suggest, thinktank finds | Productivity | The Guardian
description: Resolution Foundation suggests economy may finally be emerging from shadow of 2008 financial crisis
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Resolution Foundation suggests economy may finally be emerging from shadow of 2008 financial crisis
Content: Productivity measures the economic output produced by each worker, and is a crucial determinant of growth.Photograph: Matt Crossick/AlamyView image in fullscreenProductivity measures the economic output produced by each worker, and is a crucial determinant of growth.Photograph: Matt Crossick/AlamyProductivityUK productivity growing faster than official figures suggest, thinktank findsResolution Foundation suggests economy may finally be emerging from shadow of 2008 financial crisisHeather StewartEconomics editorSun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProductivity in the UK – a vital measure of economic health – is growing more strongly than official figures suggest, according to analysis from theResolution Foundation.The thinktank suggests the chancellor,John Healey, may have inherited an economy finally starting to emerge from the long shadow of the 2008 global financial crisis.Productivity measures the economic output produced by each worker, and is a crucial determinant of growth.The Resolution Foundation reconsiders the UK’s recent productivity record, using what it argues is a more accurate snapshot of the workforce than the widely criticisedlabour force survey.Simon Pittaway, the thinktank’s principal economist, said: “Britain’s dismal productivity record since the global financial crisis explains a lot of its economic stagnation and weak living standards growth.“But while official figures suggest that the output of workers has worsened further in the mid-2020s, our more accurate productivity measure suggests that it has been improving in recent years.”A positive new report raises the question: was Reeves undermined by dodgy data? | Heather StewartRead moreSome economists have argued the potential uptick in productivity has resulted from job cuts in relatively low-skilled sectors such as hospitality and retail, meaning the average worker has become more productive.However, the thinktank rejects that idea, pointing out that the share of the workforce employed in hospitality is no lower now than it was in the late 2010s, and only just below its post-pandemic peak.It also suggests the uptick cannot just be AI-related, as it is more widespread across different sectors of the UK economy.Pittaway said: “Some have suggested that recent productivity gains have been driven by an early AI boom, and workers leaving low-productivity sectors like retail and hospitality. But nether explanation is borne out by the data. Instead, the UK’s productivity recovery has been achieved by the same workers, doing the same jobs, and working in the same sectors.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Resolution Foundation’s report was the latest to paint a relatively optimistic picture of the economy, after official figures last week showed the UK was the joint fastest-growing economy in the G7 in the first half of 2026.John Van Reenen, Rachel Reeves’s former chief economic adviser,recently published a blogpostpointing to a similar productivity rethink by him and his colleagues at the London School of Economics.Economists at Morgan Stanley said in a recent research note that the UK was now in “an OK place”. In a note titled “The vibes they are a-changin’”, its chief UK economist, Bruna Skarica, pointed out that growth and inflation had been hit less hard than feared by the Iran war, and consumer confidence had reached a two-year high.Explore more on these topicsProductivityResolution FoundationThinktanksJohn HealeyLabourEconomic growth (GDP)EconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ceferin brands Infantino’s failed World Cup plan as ‘even worse than the Super League’ | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Aleksander Ceferin, the Uefa president, has said Gianni Infantino’s attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup was ‘even worse than the Super League’
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Aleksander Ceferin, the Uefa president, has said Gianni Infantino’s attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup was ‘even worse than the Super League’
Content: Aleksander Ceferin (left) is keeping up the pressure on Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenAleksander Ceferin (left) is keeping up the pressure on Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAUefaCeferin brands Infantino’s failed World Cup plan as ‘even worse than the Super League’Fifa president will face opponent if he seeks re-electionCeferin: ‘We stopped another try to steal the sport’Nick AmesSun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has described Gianni Infantino’s doomed attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup as “even worse than the Super League plan” and warned his embattledFifacounterpart that he will face an opponent if he runs for re-election next March.Ceferin has led Uefa’s firm collective stance against the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, which was shelved amid widespread opposition at the start of August. Uefa are pushing for Infantino to quit, also drawing on support from Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, and are yet to drop a threat to boycott Fifa competitions while talks are under way with Concacaf toset up a combined Nations League tournament.Infantino angers Concacaf nations by hijacking meeting in CaribbeanRead moreIn an interview with the podcastThe Rest is Politics: Leading, Ceferin denounced Infantino’s project as more damaging than the breakaway Super League that was shelved in 2021 after large-scale protests. “I think this plan is even worse than the Super League plan,” he said. “In the first case, super-important clubs wanted to do their own league, which is wrong and would destroy football. But in this case, football would be literally sold.“I’m absolutely sure that the [FFE] plan is dead. For me, the most important thing is that we stopped another try to sell the sport. It’s hard to imagine what kind of people would sell the sport that belongs to everyone.”Earlier this month it was reported that Infantino had held talks aboutrunning the Super League under Fifa branding. Ceferin is confident that any revival of that plan would be decades away. “It might happen in 20 years, you never know, but for now we cooperate with everyone in a great way. I’m sure it cannot happen in the next 10 years,” he said.Infantino spent much of the weekendcourting support from Concacaf membersat a meeting in the Dominican Republic, infuriating many of those present. Ceferin, who revealed the pair had not been in contact since the FFE scandal broke, believes the Fifa president’s path to survival is narrowing.“I didn’t speak with him, he didn’t contact me since this happened,” he said. “But there are two options. One option is that he realises that he doesn’t have the support, and that’s not only political support of the ones who vote, but the political support of the football community, the political support of fans, the political support of the players, former players, coaches.“And the second option [is] that he goes to the elections in March, but in that case, I think he will have a candidate against him. I don’t know yet who.” The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, has been tipped as a potential opponent for Infantino if he chooses to run in Rabat.Ceferin has proponents of his own but ruled out making his own bid for the Fifa presidency. “My credibility is much, much, much higher if I’m not interested in the position,” he said. The Slovenian is expected to run unopposed for a fourth term at the helm ofUefa, with the election due next April.Asked whether Infantino had become too close to Donald Trump, with whom he forged a close relationship before the recent World Cup, Ceferin said: “To be honest, I think you are naive if you think that a politician like that, or any politician, is your good friend. The moment you are a problem, you stop being a friend of a politician.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat friendship came under the spotlight last month when Trump said he had called Infantino to ask for a review of the red card given to the US striker Folarin Balogun, whose ban for the last-16 tie against Belgium was later suspended. “That was more than shocking,” Ceferin said. “We have rules and if you don’t respect your own rules, then the game doesn’t make any sense. That’s shocking and, trust me, almost everybody was shocked. Just not everybody dared to speak.”Meanwhile, in a fresh show of European opposition to Infantino, the six Nordic football associations issued a statement saying they had “lost confidence in the Fifa president and have serious concerns about the governance and high-level decision making of the organisation”. They asked for binding assurances that Fifa will never again “open its governance or competitions to private ownership” and called for a full third-party review into the FFE scheme.Earlier in August the Norwegian Football Federation was the first member association tocall directly for Infantino to step down.Infantino travelled straight from the Dominican Republic to Paris on Sunday, attending the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup. Television footage showed him exchanging greetings with the president of France, Emmanuel Macron.Explore more on these topicsUefaFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Families release pictures of police officers killed in A66 crash in which five others died | North Yorkshire | The Guardian
description: Tributes paid to PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough whose vehicle was in a head-on collision with car travelling wrong way
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Tributes paid to PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough whose vehicle was in a head-on collision with car travelling wrong way
Content: PC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades, who died when a car going in the wrong direction hit a police car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.Composite: Cleveland Police/PAView image in fullscreenPC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades, who died when a car going in the wrong direction hit a police car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.Composite: Cleveland Police/PANorth YorkshireFamilies release pictures of police officers killed in A66 crash in which five others diedEmotional tributes paid to PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough whose vehicle was in a head-on collision with car travelling wrong wayMark BrownNorth of England correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 15.55 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCleveland police have published photographs of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough who died when a car travelling the wrong way on the A66 crashed head-on into their police vehicle.Two 17-year-old boys were among the seven people who were killed in the incident on Teesside.Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak died when their Volkswagen Passat, believed to be using cloned plates, collided with a marked armed response vehicle early on Saturday near Middlesbrough.Blades, 37, and Clough, 38, of Cleveland police, who were also killed in the collision, had been driving in the correct direction. Tributes have been paid to the officers, with their chief constable, Victoria Fuller, describing them as “brave officers protecting our communities”.Clough’s family described him as “our hero with a fantastic sense of humour” and someone who “jumped into action whenever needed, and [was] willing to help anyone for any reason”.In a statement issued via Cleveland police, the family said Clough had “proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place. Always on public duty throughout his short life.“We as a family and Tom’s partner would like to express our sincere gratitude for the overwhelming support and condolences from friends, colleagues and the wider community.”Blades’ wife said the pain of losing him is “beyond words” and the family’s lives “will never be the same”.In a statement issued through the force, she said: “No words will ever feel like the right words to honour our Matt – my beloved husband, my best friend, and the most devoted father to our two young boys.“He was an adored son and brother, a perfect son-in-law, and the most fun uncle. He was loved beyond words by all his family and friends, and his loss has left a space that can never be filled.“He gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness.“The pain of losing him is beyond words, and our lives will never be the same. Neither will the love he gave us ever fade.“Our children will grow up knowing what an incredible father he was and will always be, and I will carry his love, his memory and everything we shared with me always.“He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family.”Blades’ wife, who has not been named, also expressed “deepest gratitude and heartfelt thanks” to the police and emergency services and concluded: “Forever loved. Forever missed. Forever our superhero.”A local football club, Seaton Carew FC, said Blades had recently joined as coach and was preparing for the season with the new under-sevens Seahawks team. “He was looking forward to being part of the team and, most importantly, to coaching his own son, who is going to be playing for the Seahawks this season,” the club said on social media.“Matty and his oldest son are much-loved members of our club and our U10 Lions football family. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Matty’s wife, his two boys, and all of his family and friends at this incredibly difficult and heartbreaking time.”View image in fullscreenThe five young people who were killed, clockwise from top left, Jacob Matusiak, Michael Robert Cahill, Makai Saddington, Cole Worthy and Theo Rae.Composite: FacebookView image in fullscreenFlowers left near the scene on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough.Photograph: Richard McCarthy/PAThe Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has opened an investigation into the circumstances leading to the crash at 3.39am in South Bank after a mandatory referral from Cleveland police.On Sunday the IOPC said initial inquiries showed the Passat had been pursued by police for just under seven minutes before it turned on to the A66 against the flow of traffic.At that point the pursuit was aborted, the IOPC said. “Approximately 10 seconds later, the Passat collided with another police vehicle which was not involved in the pursuit but in the area to assist in a search for the Passat believed to be using cloned plates that had activated an ANPR camera.”The IOPC director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, said: “Our thoughts continue to be with the family and friends and all those affected by yesterday’s collision. We recognise the devastating impact the incident has had on those in the force, and the wider policing community, and offer our condolences.”On Sunday, Anna Turley, the Home Office minister and local Redcar MP, said it was “devastating” to think about the grief of the families of everyone who lost their lives on Saturday morning. The whole community was “reeling”, she said.“All of us in the community here are sending our heartfelt thoughts and sympathies to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives so tragically.”“I do want to place on record my tribute to PC Blades and PC Clough. The bravery that we see from our police officers every day, every night is incredible. No one should not come home to their families at the end of their shift.”She also said it was important to thank the emergency service workers who had attended the scene during “a really horrific incident”.Security camera footage from local houses appeared to show the police pursuit moments before the fatal crash on the A66.Security camera footage appears to show police pursuit minutes before fatal A66 crashAndy Burnham said he was “devastated” to hear two police officers had lost their lives on duty, as well as five members of the public. The prime minister said: “My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland police. Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”Fuller said she and her deputy had on Saturday visited the families of the two officers to offer condolences and support.“This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” she said. “This loss is being felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies. These were brave officers, protecting our communities and serving our residents, who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift.”View image in fullscreenCleveland police chief constable Victoria Fuller said it was an ‘incredibly sad day’.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PALauren Somerville, the chair of Cleveland police federation, said the grief among officers was “all-consuming, overwhelming”. She said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland police family are feeling.”The Cleveland police and crime commissioner, Matt Storey, described the force as a “really tight-knit family” and said the deaths “will have a big impact on them”.The young men in the car were named by Cleveland police on Sunday afternoon. The force said family liaison officers were working with the families.This article was amended on 23 August 2026. An earlier version gave the age of Cole Robert Worthy as 16, based on initial information provided by Cleveland police. After publication, Cleveland police corrected this to 17.Explore more on these topicsNorth YorkshireMiddlesbroughNorth of EnglandEnglandPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform says it would put foreign-born UK citizens lower on social housing list | Social housing | The Guardian
description: UK-born married couples under 35 with children would get priority under proposals to be outlined by Farage’s party
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: UK-born married couples under 35 with children would get priority under proposals to be outlined by Farage’s party
Content: Those born while their British parents were temporarily overseas would be exempted from the policy, Reform said.Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamyView image in fullscreenThose born while their British parents were temporarily overseas would be exempted from the policy, Reform said.Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamySocial housingReform says it would put foreign-born UK citizens lower on social housing listUK-born married couples under 35 with children would get priority under proposals to be outlined by Farage’s partyKiran StaceyPolicy editorSun 23 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish citizens who were born abroad would be made to wait longer for social housing under proposals to be announced byReform UKon Monday.Nigel Farage’s party will announce the policy at a press conference in London. Under the policy, people born in the UK and young married couples with children would be given priority for social housing.The party haspreviously saidit would ban foreign nationals from social housing, meaning the new policy specifically prioritises Britons born in the UK over those born overseas.Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, said in a statement: “There are now 1.3 million people waiting for social housing in Britain. The vast majority of them do not have jobs. In terms of the social houses we have, less than half of households are in work and over half a million social homes are currently occupied by foreign nationals.“Meanwhile, young British men and women, who are working hard, can’t afford to move out of their family home, and when they do often find themself sharing a house with strangers, with no realistic prospect of forming a family or getting on.“It is time for us to prioritise young British workers, and that is what our policy is about.”View image in fullscreenFarage had previously proposed to ban foreign nationals from social housing.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe party said some foreign-born Britons would be exempted from the new rules, including those born while their British parents were temporarily overseas. Officials said, however, the new rules would require legislation to avoid breaking existing laws.Under the terms of a previous announcement by Farage, foreign nationals would be barred from social housing, with those already in homes given three months to find private accommodation or face deportation.The new policy would give priority access to British-born people in employment and married couples under 35 with children.Tory plan to ban foreign nationals from social housing condemned as ‘divisive’Read moreThe party said veterans would also be given preferential treatment – though soldiers, veterans and their families are already given priority under existing government policy.Experts have said that prioritising people based on nationality, age and family status could punish some of the most vulnerable in society.Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Designed to stoke division, these plans will only serve to disrupt the lives of thousands of families, tear communities apart, and put even more people at risk of homelessness.“Putting nationality and employment ahead of housing need, and moving away from a system designed to prioritise people who are homeless or at urgent risk of homelessness, could leave even more families trapped in awful temporary accommodation for years on end. Not to mention putting those escaping domestic abuse and violence at serious risk of harm.”A Labour spokesperson said: “Illegal migrants, asylum seekers and migrants on student or work visas are not eligible for social housing. This policy would go after long-term UK residents that have contributed to our country but are not British citizens, including NHS staff.”Reform has also said it would build 50,000 socially affordable homes a year, a significant uplift on the18,000 the government has promised to buildon average each year for a decade.Labour’s plans are being financed by a £39bn affordable housing scheme, 60% of which is due to be allocated to social homes, which are the most heavily subsidised.Reform said its plans would be funded, with no extra borrowing or taxation required to pay for the additional homes. It did not give further details on where the money would come from.Explore more on these topicsSocial housingReform UKHousingCommunitiesHousing benefitImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war | Canada | The Guardian
description: PM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressors
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: PM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressors
