Content: The US president, Donald Trump, and Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, have each blamed the opposite side for the breakdown in negotiations.Photograph: Saul Loeb,dave Chan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US president, Donald Trump, and Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, have each blamed the opposite side for the breakdown in negotiations.Photograph: Saul Loeb,dave Chan/AFP/Getty ImagesCanada‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade warPM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressorsThe lesson from Canada’s collapsed trade talks with the US: negotiation may be futileLauren AlmeidaSun 23 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has hit back at Canada after a breakdown in negotiationsplunged the two countries into a trade war.In his first public comments since negotiations collapsed on Friday in Washington, the US president wrote on social media: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!”“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” he added. “No more!!!”His comments came after the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods, whileMark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar”.The US tariffs came into force on Saturday, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Trade experts have predicted that the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the biggest impact is expected to be political, triggering fresh tension between the neighbours.View image in fullscreenCanadian trade minister Dominic LeBlanc, left, and US trade representative Jamieson Greer speak to reporters in Washington DC on Friday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockBoth sides blamed the other for the breakdown in talks on Friday. Carney told Canadian journalists that the country was “at war” over trade with the US, after Trump “miscalculated” by escalating his tariff attack.“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Ottawa. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”Against the wind: despite Trump’s attacks, unions are fighting for good US clean energy jobsRead moreJamieson Greer, the US trade representative, has said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. He told Fox & Friends Weekend: “We’ve said enough and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.”Dan Kelly, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, estimated that 40% of small Canadian exporters will be directly hit by the US tariffs, and that nearly one-third expect their revenues will drop by 50% or more as a result.The escalation was also met with anger by Democrat lawmakers and governors from US states that border Canada including Minnesota, New York and Washington.New York governor Kathy Hochul posted on X: “Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That’s Trump’s economic policy in a nutshell.”Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar, said the new tariffs meant “higher costs for small businesses, farmers, and all Minnesota families.”She wrote on X: “Canada is Minnesota’s #1 trading partner. Minnesotans are paying for Trump’s chaos.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCarney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England,was elected as Canada’s prime minister last yearafter campaigning to lead a fightback against Trump, who has suggested he wants to make Canada a 51st state with “economic force”.Carney’s “dollar for dollar” tariffs are expected to take effect from 8 September, with new levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The escalation has also called into question the future of the North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico, known as USMCA.The pact, which was signed by Trump during his first term, governs about $2tn annually in goods and services between the three countries. Trumprefused to renew the USMCA this summerafter Canada and Mexico formally requested for it to be renewed for another 16 years.When asked how the US-Canadian collapse in trade talks would affect the USMCA, Carney said it was “certainly not good news”.Increasingly aggressive rhetoric and trade policy from the Trump administration has damaged US-Canadian relations, with tourism also suffering – there was a21% drop in Canadians entering New York state in 2025and 3mn fewer visits compared with the previous year.Furthermore, a petition to expel the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, from the country has gathered around 248,000 signatures since late July, according tothe Associated Press.This year apoll by Globe and Mail newspaperfound that only 9% of Canadians agreed that the US was a “trustworthy ally”, and that 51% of those polled had cancelled American trips in reaction to comments by Trump.Explore more on these topicsCanadaDonald TrumpMark CarneyTariffsUS foreign policyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Landslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government says | Guinea | The Guardian
description: Dump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African state
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African state
Content: Residents and rescuers search for bodies in the dump site in Conakry on 23 August.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenResidents and rescuers search for bodies in the dump site in Conakry on 23 August.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesGuineaLandslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government saysDump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African stateReutersSun 23 Aug 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA ⁠landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to ⁠collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks.The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of WestAfrica.The landslide took ​place at about 2am (3am UK time) ‌in the Gbessia commune ‌of Conakry, according to a government statement.The death toll was 30, with six ‌people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I ‌have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite ​reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a ⁠World Bank report published in April.On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara​, announced ​that the government was closing ​the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to ​be relocated outside Conakry.The prime ‌minister, Amadou Oury ​Bah, visited ​the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.Explore more on these topicsGuineaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham stays away from No 10 North wedding after bride’s plea | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: PM sends video message to newlyweds instead after bride Sarah Burwin asked him not to ‘ruin’ vibe at Heron House
Author: Harry Taylor
Headline: PM sends video message to newlyweds instead after bride Sarah Burwin asked him not to ‘ruin’ vibe at Heron House
Content: Sarah Burwin and her husband watch a message from Andy Burnham on their wedding day.Photograph: TiktokView image in fullscreenSarah Burwin and her husband watch a message from Andy Burnham on their wedding day.Photograph: TiktokAndy BurnhamBurnham stays away from No 10 North wedding after bride’s pleaPM sends video message to newlyweds instead after bride Sarah Burwin asked him not to ‘ruin’ vibe at Heron HouseHarry TaylorSun 23 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham fulfilled a bride’s wishes by not turning up for her wedding after she asked him not to spoil her big day as she got married at the building housing No 10 North.Sarah Burwin had pleaded on TikTok in July for Burnham not to work from the building inManchesterthat day, which hosts the government’s northern headquarters and the city’s register office.Burwin had said she feared the security detail Burnham requires would ruin wedding photographs outside the venue when she got married on Friday.She told the prime minister he would be welcome at her wedding, but told him to give his security detail “an hour off”. She later joked he could DJ the afterparty.Burnham did not turn up, but did send avideo messageto her and her new husband Fred. “Thank you so much for the invite. But sadly, I’m honouring your initial request for me to stay out of the way, as I’m filming this as I’m about to leave No 10 North for the day,” Burnham said.View image in fullscreen‘What a lad!’ The couple watch Burnham’s video reassuring them he was staying away.Photograph: TiktokHe added: “I couldn’t let the day go by without sending you both a message. I hope you have the best day celebrating, and thank you for being such a good sport about No 10 North suddenly being a big part of your big day. The DJ set will have to wait for another time, but I hope you play some good tunes on my behalf, big Manchester bangers.”Burwin could be seen replying: “Oh my God. What a lad. I love him!”Burnhamopened No 10 Northwithin the first few days of becoming prime minister, honouring a pledge he had made before he succeeded Keir Starmer.It falls under hisnew Office of the Prime Minister, which has taken in parts of the Cabinet Office, the Treasury and housing ministry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham to dispatch 100 Whitehall officials to help regional mayorsRead moreIt will, in part, focus on economic growth policy across the country.In her original video onTikTok, which has reached nearly 1.5m views, Burwin had posted: “I saw you set up your new gaff, No 10 North, at Heron House. I saw it on the news; gorgeous, love what you’ve done with the place. But I’m actually getting married there on 21 August, and on the news today, the place was surrounded with police, bollards, all sorts. A lot of stuff that wasn’t there before.“My trouble is, I was planning to get nice photos like after, the register office, outside, and I’m just a bit worried that all of this is kind of ruining the vibe.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamManchesterGreater ManchesterTikTokWeddingsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Drill, Burnham, drill? The oil basin that is a totem for Trump – and a headache for Britain’s new PM | Fossil fuels | The Guardian
description: North Sea oil, once the driving force of the UK economy, may be dwindling but it remains a symbol of prestige and a rich resource for political debate
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: North Sea oil, once the driving force of the UK economy, may be dwindling but it remains a symbol of prestige and a rich resource for political debate
Content: The amount of economically viable oil and gas from the North Sea has declined rapidly since its peak at the turn of the century.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe amount of economically viable oil and gas from the North Sea has declined rapidly since its peak at the turn of the century.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyThe Sunday readFossil fuelsDrill, Burnham, drill? The oil basin that is a totem for Trump – and a headache for Britain’s new PMNorth Sea oil, once the driving force of the UK economy, may be dwindling but it remains a symbol of prestige and a rich resource for political debateMatthew TaylorEnvironment correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.13 EDTShareWhen oil was first discovered off the north-east coast ofScotlandin September 1969, industry folklore has it that the duty superintendent on the rig carefully poured it into a pickle jar commandeered from the canteen and took it back to Amoco’s Great Yarmouth office in Norfolk. There, it was emptied into an ash tray, sniffed and then set alight.From that modest start, North Sea oil – as the huge basin of oil and gas reserves quickly became known – emerged as a driving force of the British economy and a symbol of national power and renewal as the UK emerged from the Opec oil crisis.By 1977, the thenLabourprime minister, Jim Callaghan, declared: “God has given Britain her best opportunity for 100 years in the shape of North Sea oil.” A subsequent white paper said it offered “a unique opportunity for Britain to improve her economic performance, raise her living standards, move forward to full employment, and develop a socially just society”.A decade later, the basin became a central part of Margaret Thatcher’s political project , with its revenues approaching 10% of the UK’s total tax take at times, supporting a programme of tax cuts and privatisation.View image in fullscreenOil rig in the North Sea, 1974.Photograph: Zuma/ShutterstockOutput peaked at the turn of the century, when the basin produced a staggering 4.4m barrels of oil equivalent a day. Aberdeen, chosen over Dundee by the fossil fuel corporations for their onshore headquarters because it had fewer links to bothersome trade unions, was booming, with offshore jobs plentiful and well paid.Ewan Gibbs, a specialist in the history of energy in the UK at the University of Glasgow, said that as the oil began to flow, it was seized upon by politicians and the public as a symbol of British imperial might.“At its peak, oil was associated not only with immense wealth but also with power and international prestige,” said Gibbs. “It came to embody a sense of national renewal.”Now, those boom years are firmly in the past. The amount of economically viable oil and gas has declined rapidly in the past two decades and by 2030 the basin will produce just 15% of its peak output.Many of the biggest oil and gas corporations have left as stocks dwindle –BP was the latest, announcing this summer an end to six decades in the basin. And the jobs are going too. During the boom years, North Sea oil directly employed about 120,000 people and supported hundreds of thousands more jobs indirectly. Data from the Office for National Statistics suggests that figurehas now dropped to about 27,000direct employees.However, although its economic significance has waned, the idea of North Sea oil has retained a disproportionate grip on the national psyche, and – as culture wars over the climate crisis continue to be stoked by politicians and media on the right – it remains a useful symbol of sovereignty and power for some.“Even as it declines, there is still a strong sense for many people that this is Britain’s oil, that it is bountiful and belongs to the country, and that if we don’t exploit it we are turning our back on something important,” said Gibbs.“It is this emotional attachment, this idea that this is our oil that means, even as the area becomes less economically significant, it retains an outsized importance in the country’s imagination.”Culture warsIn the run-up to the 2024 general election, the Labour party announced there would be no new exploratory licences for oil and gas in the North Sea.It was a significant moment in the fight against climate breakdown. In 2021, theInternational Energy Agencyhad said there could be “no new investments in oil, gas and coal” if the world was to avoid the worst impacts of the climate crisis. Now, the government of one of the richest countries in the world was making it clear it was moving away from fossil fuels to focus on renewable energy.It was also a victory for the then energy secretary, Ed Miliband. He had been making the case within Labour that a rapid transition to a cleaner energy systems would not only help tackle the climate crisis but had the potential to make the UK a “clean energy superpower” and unshackle it from the increasingly volatile fossil fuel market, creating jobs and lowering bills.Miliband argued that the transition to a renewable future could also offer a lifeline to communities in north-east Scotland that had seen jobs and wealth disappear as the flow of oil dried up, despite hundreds of new drilling licences being awarded.Graph compares production of and demand for oil over time, from 2000 to the present day, and projected to 2050“In the 20th century through North Sea oil, Britain exported to the world,” Miliband told a speech to the Labour party conference before the 2024 general election. “In the 21st century … Britain will be an energy superpower once again, exporting clean power to the world and controlling our economic destiny. British families and businesses will never again be held to ransom by [the Russian president, Vladimir] Putin.”But fast forward two years, and despite wars in Iran and Ukraine again highlighting the perils of dependence on a volatile fossil fuel market and an escalating climate crisis, those plans are once more at the centre of a political storm.The leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, and the Conservative party leader, Kemi Badenoch, have called for a massive expansion of drilling in the North Sea, claiming they would reverse the ban on new licences if elected.In a speech this year, Farage declared that the UK should be “self-sufficient in gas”. Badenoch followed with the promise of a growing UK oil and gas industry that would “ensure our energy security for generations to come”. .Donald Trump is also a fan of a UK version of“drill, baby, drill”in the North Sea. In one of several interventions on the subject, he claimed the basin was “one of the greatest reserves anywhere in the world … with 500 years of oil and gas reserves left”.Such statements have left climate experts, geologists and energy specialists scratching their heads.Steve Pye, a professor of energy systems and the deputy director of theEnergyInstitute at University College London, said: “The North Sea basin has been in decline since 2000. There are no credible prospects of reversing this.”But in the midst of a cost of living crisis, others are making the case for any intervention, however small, that might ease the burden on households and boost Treasury coffers. Some trade unions and parts of the Labour party are in favour of exploiting the North Sea’s existing licences, arguing they provide some jobs and bring in at least some tax revenue.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband has long advocated a fast transition to renewable energy as a way to shore up Britain’s energy security and reduce bills.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianExperts, however,point outthat energy prices are set globally and there is not enough oil or gas in the North Sea to have any impact, so there would be no reduction in UK bills whatever the country did.Also, the vast majority of what is left in the North Sea is oil that overwhelmingly goes abroad to be refined and then sold on the international markets, meaning it has no impact on the UK’s energy security.More of the gas produced in the North Sea goes to UK homes and businesses but there is less of that left, certainly not enough to make any meaningful impact on our reliance on imports. A recent studyby Carbon Brieffound that even if the government allowed new licences it would only make a fractional difference: gas extraction from the North Sea is forecast to drop 99% by 2050 without new licences, compared with 97% if new licences were awarded.Conversely, the study found that the continued expansion of renewables and low-carbon technologies in the North Sea would reduce reliance on volatile gas imports much faster than allowing new drilling, with energy from new wind and solar from the latest government auction expected to produce six times more electricity by 2030 than new drilling licences would.On employment, the campaign group Uplift points out that the number of jobs supported by the oil and gas industry hasmore than halvedin the last decade – from 441,000 to 214,000 today – despite previous governments issuing hundreds of new licences in six separate licensing rounds.And on tax,criticshave questioned the scale of the benefit once you take into account state subsidies to oil and gas companies, whichglobally run into the hundreds of billionsof pounds.Others question the public appetite for fattening the profit margins of fossil fuel companies, which madea record $93bn in profitin the three months to June, while fossil fuel-driven climate disasters, including wildfires and droughts, hit Europe, the UK experienced five heatwaves this summer, and energy costs continued to rise.View image in fullscreenWildfire rages in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales, after extended dry and hot weather.Photograph: Ethan Fowler/JNA/Zuma Press/ShutterstockIn June last year, when he was still the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham backed the fossil fuel treaty, a proposed international pact on phasing out coal, oil and gas – calling it a “lifeline” that “all governments” should join.In recent weeks, Burnham, now prime minister, has spooked many who want to see this commitment transferred to national government when he said he would take a“pragmatic” approach to oil and gas drillingin the North Sea and that the government could not ignore the potential resources it holds.Miatta Fahnbulleh, who replaced Miliband as energy secretary, has expressed similar views since taking office, although previously she has spoken out about the realities of the climate crisis. With consultations on the Jackdaw and Rosebank field projects now closed, a decision from the government could come at any time.Graph compares production of and demand for North Sea gas over time, from 2000 to the present day, and projected to 2050.Tessa Khan, the director at Uplift, said it was “a dangerous fantasy” to talk up the potential of North Sea oil as a fix for Britain’s problems.“We have seen that, time and again, the arguments put forward by the fossil fuel lobby and their supporters in favour of more drilling have fallen away upon making contact with reality – from falsehoods about lowering bills to exaggerations about improving energy security. After 50 years of drilling, the fact is the UK has burned through most of its gas reserves, while most of what remains is oil that is largely exported.“Politicians know this. Pretending otherwise for political gain, on an issue as serious as energy security, is unedifying and a betrayal of UK energy workers who urgently need a coherent plan to deliver long-term, secure jobs – which will only now come from renewables and other industries – not some pipe dream.”At its core, Khan said, the ongoing debate was the result of an extensive lobbying campaign by the oil and gas industry for lower taxes and greater profits for shareholders and executives.“We shouldn’t fall for it. The lesson of the past five years is clear: the best protection against global energy shocks is accelerating renewables and helping households and businesses switch to clean electricity. This is just common sense in today’s world.”Green jobsIn October last year, the UK government unveiled plans for an extra 400,000 jobs in the burgeoning green economy over the next five years.Making the announcement at the Siemens turbine factory in Hull, Miliband said the government planned to double the number of people working in green industries by 2030, with a particular focus on training those coming from fossil fuel jobs, school leavers, the unemployed, veterans and ex-offenders.The national plan was given a cautious welcome by unions, fromUniteto the GMB, which have long been pushing for a more detailed plan for how people will switch from fossil fuel to clean energy jobs.The green economy is certainly becoming an increasingly significant part of the UK’s future. A recent report from the Confederation of British Industry found it already supported a million jobs and higher wages, with nearly half a trillion pounds of further investment in the pipeline.This rapid growth is visible in the North Sea itself, with huge windfarms springing up across the basin. The electricity they generateaccounts for about 18% of the UK’s total. Overall, in 2025, renewablesprovided 50.4% of the UK’s electricity, compared with 31.8% from fossil fuels.View image in fullscreenRedcar windfarm off the Teesside coast.Photograph: Peter Oliver/AlamyDespite this rapid growth, there are growing concerns that any benefits from these developments are bypassing the workers and communities that need them most.Unite and GMB, the unions representing oil and gas workers, say the transition to renewable energy is not delivering the secure long-term jobs that were promised and – to the dismay of climate activists andothers within the union movement– they have been vocal about their support for more drilling in the North Sea.Others fear the renewables sector is experiencing a repeat of mistakes made during the oil boom, when a big slice of the profits and benefits were taken by private oil companies.Connor Watt, of Platform, which works with current and former oil workers, unions, community groups and climate activists across Scotland, said: “The three main wins from the transition to renewables should be jobs, cheaper energy and income from electricity generation that can be used to bolster public finances, to help local communities. But at the moment, despite huge renewable projects going ahead, none of those three things have materialised and people are beginning to wonder why.”View image in fullscreenFirefighters at the site of wildfires near Dunwich Heath, in Suffolk, in July.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOil and gas workers, unions and community energy groups have organised a campaign to rethink how the government is conducting the “just transition”. They are calling for a greater role for community ownership and nationalisation to stop the profits and benefits bypassing local workers and communities. They are also calling for the government to set up a community wealth fund to ensure the benefits are felt across the country.Watt said North Sea oil had brought some local wealth and jobs but after a decades-long boom there was “no real legacy to speak of.”Many campaigners look to Norway, where the government set up a sovereign wealth fund when it discovered oil and gas in the North Sea. It is used to safeguard the economy and fund future public spending and is now worth more than $2tn – the biggest fund of its kind in the world. Analysts say that if the UK had taken a similar approach, a UK sovereign wealth fundcould be worth about £850bn now.Watt said: “If you compare what has happened here with what Norway did with its sovereign wealth fund, which has had huge benefits for the people of that country, we did something totally different – a market-led approach which has seen the vast majority of the benefit flow into the profits of global corporations rather than local communities.“Once again we are seeing a market-led approach [in the renewables industry], where the vast majority of benefits are simply not going to local communities. People are increasingly disillusioned after decades of economic decline. Life is getting harder and the likes of Reform are exploiting that frustration to deepen division and line the pockets of their industry backers.”The debate about North Sea oil and gas extraction looks set to rumble on, even as its economic significance dwindles.But for many whose lives and livelihoods are entangled with what happens there, it is a distraction from the decisions that will actually shape their future.Watt said: “The real question policymakers and local communities must grapple with now is: can the UK capitalise on the renewable energy revolution? And if it does, will it be the workers and communities across the UK who benefit, or corporate profit margins?”

title: Start your engines! Trump completes fast and furious takeover of Washington with IndyCar race | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president, pushing on with Freedom 250 festivities, makes over nation’s capital for Trump rally on wheels
Author: David Smith
Headline: US president, pushing on with Freedom 250 festivities, makes over nation’s capital for Trump rally on wheels
Content: Donald Trump waves the green flag to start Sunday’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix race in Washington DC, alongside Melania Trump.Photograph: Doug Mills/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump waves the green flag to start Sunday’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix race in Washington DC, alongside Melania Trump.Photograph: Doug Mills/ReutersThe US politics sketchDonald TrumpStart your engines! Trump completes fast and furious takeover of Washington with IndyCar raceUS president, pushing on with Freedom 250 festivities, makes over nation’s capital for Trump rally on wheelsKyle Kirkwood wins Freedom 250 IndyCar race after Trump waves the green flagDavid Smithin WashingtonSun 23 Aug 2026 17.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe got the wrong end of the stick.Donald Trumpcouldn’t figure outhow to hold the green flag until his wife, Melania Trump, and Command Sgt Maj Matt Williams set him right. Then the US presidentwaved the flagfast and furious like an excited schoolboy. Theracewas under way – and his conquest of Washington DC was complete.Since returning to Washington, Trump hasdeployedthe national guard,wreckedthe Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool,demolishedthe East Wing of the White House andrunthe John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts into the ground. His faceadornsthe Department of Justice, and he still has grandplansfor a triumphal arch worthy of a Roman emperor.On Sunday he made the nation’s capital tremble with fast, flashy cars brazenly roaring around a 1.7-mile street circuit in IndyCar’sFreedom ⁠250 Grand Prix, the capstone of his Maga-flavoured celebration of the 250th anniversary of US independence.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump claims IndyCar had been trying to host a race in Washington ‘for 20 years’.Photograph: Allison Robbert/APWashington was not built for a Trump rally on wheels andhad to make accommodations, like a party host bracing for a noisy and obnoxious guest. More than 200 manhole covers were welded down around the course so they would not be sucked up by cars thundering over them. The National Gallery of Art studied how vibrations from the vehicles might affect its exhibits and shielded some outdoor sculptures.Indeed, as the vehicles whizzed by the National Archives, home to America’s desperately fragile founding documents, and the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum, whereNeil Armstrong’s spacesuitrequires constant vigilance, it was not hard to imagine anxious curators twitching at every rattle of crockery or spillage of tea.Controversy and a corporate spectacle under the Claw: Trump’s birthday fight night at the White HouseRead moreNot that the president seemed to be sweating it. While officially the Grand Prix was open to everyone – and DC’s Democratic mayor, Muriel Bowser, declared, “Drivers, to your cars!” – the event had a distinctly Trumpian flavour reminiscent of June’sUltimate Fighting Championship boutson the White House South Lawn.The UFC impresario Dana White,testosteroneavengerPete Hegsethand “human printer”Natalie Harp, who would wait for Trump as ardently as Penelope did for Odysseus, were among the guests. Democratic socialists were less in evidence. IndyCar is neitherWoke 1nor Woke 2.Wearing a dark blue suit, white shirt and red tie, Trump gave fist pumps and shook hands with the IndyCar drivers. They posed for photographers, Trump giving his signature thumbs up, as the sun gleamed off the US Capitol dome beyond.The president gave a perfunctory TV interview to the Fox network. Why was it important for him to bring IndyCars to the streets of DC? The reply was very Trumpian: “Well, Roger [Penske, a billionaire who owns the IndyCar series] told me they’ve beentrying to do it for 20 years, and he’d come down; I think he said he was down 211 times to try and get it done. And when he came to see Trump, it got done in about 15 minutes, and it’s turned out to be much bigger than we ever even thought possible.”View image in fullscreenTrump has inserted himself into UFC fights, the football World Cup final and the Patriot Games in recent months.Photograph: Mike Kropf/Getty ImagesTranslation: every previous administration and mayor thought this plan was madness, and told Penske where to go. Note also the characteristic reference to “Trump” in the third person, and the boast that only he could fix it, and in 15 minutes. (If only ending the Ukraine war were so easy.)A ceremonial trundleTrue to form, the president also bragged about the crowd size and, as he has done since UFC night, insisted that he knows better than the meteorologists. “You know, I was hearing about rain all week long. ‘It’s gonna rain, it’s gonna rain.’ I said: ‘No, it’s not.’ And this is as nice today as I’ve seen in Washington in a long time.”Trump climbed into his armoured limousine, the Beast, mounted with flags and flashing blue and red lights, andtrundled a ceremonial lapof the track. Was that Harp sprinting after him? Or hiding in the trunk? No, but we did get theQatari-gifted planethat Trump has used as Air Force One flying overhead, escorted by four fighter jets.View image in fullscreenMore than 200 manhole covers were welded down around the course in Washington DC.Photograph: Mike Kropf/Getty ImagesThen Christopher Macchio, one of Trump’s favourite singers, performed The Star-Spangled Banner as Trump saluted and Melania, wearing a white blouse, stood with hand on heart in the presidential box, a temporary white, air-conditioned structure with a clear front.A trained bald eagle was released near the start line, swooping and flying overhead before returning to its handler. There were flyovers of military aircraft including a B-2 stealth bomber. Officials paused air traffic at Washington’s Ronald Reagan ​National airport for three hours to ​accommodate them.It fell to another stalwart ally, interior secretary Doug Burgum, sporting sunglasses,to bellow: “Gentlemen, start your engines!”The race began, with drivers completing147 lapscovering roughly 250 miles (400km), and produced an American winner in Kyle Kirkwood.View image in fullscreenTrump’s limousine, mounted with flags and flashing blue and red lights, trundled a ceremonial lap of the track.Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesIt was the latest chapter of a sporting summer in which Trumpinsertedhimself into the UFC fights, thefootball World Cup finaland thePatriot Games, a cross between a game show and athletics meet for high schoolers.Never slow to demonstrate his fealty to Trump, Mike Johnson, the Republican speaker of the House of Representatives, told Fox News that he wants to bring the IndyCar Grand Prix back next year and make it an annual event.By then, one hopes, Trump will have figured out how to hold and wave a green flag. Or as they say inIran, a white flag.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThe US politics sketchIndycarWashington DCUS politicsUS sportsMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: When my husband died in a surfing accident, life as I knew it was destroyed. Ten years on, this is what I’ve learned about grief | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: One crashing wave on one single day changed everything for our family. How would I keep going?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: One crashing wave on one single day changed everything for our family. How would I keep going?
Content: ‘Grief is a sinkhole, opening up where real life once stood’: Hannah Richell at Tamarama beach.Photograph: David Maurice Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Grief is a sinkhole, opening up where real life once stood’: Hannah Richell at Tamarama beach.Photograph: David Maurice Smith/The GuardianAutobiography and memoirWhen my husband died in a surfing accident, life as I knew it was destroyed. Ten years on, this is what I’ve learned about griefOne crashing wave on one single day changed everything for our family. How would I keep going?Hannah RichellSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 17.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore they enter the water, surfers will study the ocean. They consider wind and tide conditions. They analyse currents and patterns, break points and swells. They try to read the waves. I have travelled across oceans and a day to sit here on Tamarama beach in Sydney on a high-tide weekday morning in 2024. A notebook and pen lie beside me on the sand as I, too, attempt to read the waves, to find meaning in their unfathomable churn.These past 10 years, this beach has loomed large in my mind. Even when absent, it’s as if my face has been turned to these waves and I have been buffeted, sometimes staggering, sometimes falling, always bracing for the next set to roll in. For I have learned that all it takes is one ocean, one day, to come along and knock you off your feet.Sydney, 2014It’s an ordinary Wednesday afternoon in Sydney, the first week of July, when two plainclothes police officers knock at our front door. I am not home to greet them. I am a few streets away, buried in my studio, wrestling with the tangled threads of a novel, when I receive a call from my husband’s PA.“I’ve had a call from a Bondi detective,” she tells me. “They were asking for your address. I can’t reach Matt.”I grab my laptop but leave everything else in place and try Matt’s number as I half-run, half-walk up the steep hill to our house. No answer. I call our childminder. “Weird question but has anyone come to the house?”“Yes,” she says. Her voice is different, strained.“Police?”“Yes.”The red front door to our tiny sandstone cottage is shut tight. Through the glass pane I see two figures in dark clothing standing in our living room. I fumble for my keys. The door opens and I cross the threshold.“Hannah Richell?” they ask. I guess I nod, and they introduce themselves as police detectives. One of them, I think, has tears in her eyes.I glance between them, my panic rising, until the more composed of the two comes right out with it. “I’m sorry to tell you your husband has been in a surfing accident.”“Is he OK?” I’m already running through childcare options to make a hospital dash.“I’m afraid he died.”I’m still in my coat and boots. My laptop bag hangs from my shoulder. I look down at the old wooden chest that stands in the front room, doubling as a coffee table, and notice an unfamiliar box of tissues sitting on its surface – a box of tissues I have not bought or placed there. A small part of my brain, one not yet numbed by shock and disbelief, registers that the police must have brought it. I look at the tissues, then back to the police. My bag slides from my shoulder to the floor.On the way to the morgue, I gaze out of the window. He is dead, I keep telling myself. You are going to view his body. But I don’t truly believe it. I will see the body and I will feel only relief, because of course it won’t be him. There is no way it can be him, my warm, vivid, drily funny, thoroughly alive husband. It will be another man, belonging to another family, who are at this very moment unaware of the tragedy that awaits them. I will leave the morgue dizzy with relief and return to the life I should be living.But it is him.And it isn’t.The body in the blue gown lying on the gurney belongs to my husband, but it isn’t my husband as I knew him. What lies before me is a stiff wax model of the man I love.Matt. But not Matt.It is the longest, shortest, most loving, most painful hour of my life. One hour alone, to kiss and caress him. To stroke his stubbled cheek and hold his hand and lay my head upon his chest and weep. Kissing his temples, I see the cuts on his face and a diamond crosshatch line of stitches across the back of his head from the autopsy. The sight of those stitches makes me reel. They have cut open his beautiful skull. The one I absent-mindedly caressed while reading on the sofa, the prickle of his shaved head under my fingers. The one my three-year-old daughter would stroke while high on his shoulders and proclaim “spiky” with a giggle. I try not to think about what else they have had to do to him.From our inauspicious beginning, when Matt joined the London publishing company to steal the promotion I had coveted, to a deep bond forged through travel, marriage and babies, I sit in this closed, quiet morgue and remember words written in my diary as our first new year together had raced towards us. “Don’t let him hurt me,” I had written, imploring an unseen, unknown power. I suppose I knew, even then, that a love like this could break my heart.View image in fullscreenHannah and Matt on their wedding day in 2007.Photograph: Hannah RichellWendy, a counsellor from the forensic science team, enters the room and sits quietly with me. “You’re very affectionate with him,” she says.“I thought his eyes were opening,” I tell her, knowing how crazy I sound for still wishing that they might.“That can happen,” she admits. “Muscles can relax.”“He smells different.”“They will have washed him,” she says.Though not as carefully as they’d intended, perhaps, for when I try to hold his stiff hand, grains of Tamarama sand fall from his palm into mine. They feel like a last gift: a piece of the country he loved so deeply. Precious. I want to scoop the sand up and take it home with me, carry the grains around in a locket, but they slip through my fingers and fall to the floor, disappearing with the sound of my crying and the last kiss I leave on his lips.Itext Adam, the friend who was with Matt when he died. “Hi, this is Hannah, Matt’s wife. Yesterday must have been terrible. Are you OK?” We tread carefully, cautiously polite, until Adam offers to come to our home and talk me through what happened. He is a virtual stranger at my front door, but the moment he steps over the threshold, I am with him. The connection feels instant and real. We sit for a couple of minutes on the sofa in our front room, but the kids are noisy in the background and the house feels claustrophobic and all wrong. “I need to get out of here. Can we get some air?”Adam looks relieved.We walk to the park and sit on the grass. It is strange but, out here, in the sunshine and clean air, I feel calmer. Adam’s presence is comforting, like a blanket, muffling me from the horror of the last few days. Slowly, he begins to tell me about the accident. He talks of their joy paddling out from Bronte beach, two work friends choosing to talk shop on their surfboards rather than over lunch in an overpriced restaurant. “Surely this must be the definition of success?” Adam had said.“Yep,” Matt had replied, and when Adam says it, he delivers it just as Matt would have. In that one word I can see Matt in his wetsuit, straddling his board, salt water in his stubble and a wide grin plastered across his face as he gazes towards the horizon.double quotation markHe must have had hope, until that last wave, rushing at him, pushing him forwards. The cliff rising upAdam tells me of the suddenly shifting tide conditions and of seeing Matt’s board come loose. He describes the rip, pulling Matt dangerously close to the rocky Tamarama headland. I sense his internal struggle as he relives the tragedy, and I sit quietly, listening.Adam’s explanation comes to its end. The swallows are dancing around us, twisting and looping over the grass. I lean back and close my eyes. For the very first time since I arrived home to find the police in my house, I feel my heartbeat begin to slow in my chest. It’s shock – madness – but for a moment it’s as if he is here with us. Three people, not two, Matt’s presence hovering lightly between us.“Have you talked to Wendy?” Adam asks.“Wendy at the morgue?”“She offers counselling. You might want to call her.”My mum appears at the far edge of the park with the kids. They have a soccer ball. I point them out and Adam sprints away to kick the ball back to my son. They play like any others in the park around them – a man and a boy kicking a ball back and forth across the grass – but watching them, I feel a deep pain radiate through my body for all that our children have lost.Grief is a sinkhole, opening up where real life once stood. A cavernous black void swallowing everything I hold dear. Life as we know it has been destroyed in a single day by one crashing wave. The world feels tilted. How to process the enormity of what has happened when everything shifts and moves around me?I visit Wendy for a counselling session. We sit opposite each other in a small windowless room, a box of tissues on a side table at the ready. I am getting used to their subtle placement. I never seem to be far away from a box of tissues these days.Wendy exhales and smiles her greeting. “Hello,” she says. There’s a stillness in the air between us as we regard each other and the threshold we sit upon. Her opening question is to ask how I feel about coming to see her. I think about this carefully, trying to identify the fizzing adrenaline rush inside of me. “Excited,” I reply, then worry she will think me unhinged.“And why is that?” she asks, her face unchanging.“Because this was the last place I saw Matt. It feels like I am returning to him … although I know I’m not,” I add, certain she must think me mad. “I guess I’m excited to talk about him. Glad to be doing something.”I feel that painful ache in my throat, of everything broken held so tightly. “I can’t bear this pain. I need to know how long it will feel like this. I miss him.” That’s all it takes for me to dissolve into tears.There is no judgment from Wendy. No rules. Nothing off limits in our roaming conversations. As I discover in the coming months, sitting in this room with this woman, there is never any judgment, only compassion and a kind ear. Wendy gives me a safe place to explore everything Matt is and was to me, a space where I can crack open the dark chrysalis of grief. I think about her job title. Forensic counsellor. I like that. She allows me to examine the substance of my grief. Not just the macro experience of loss but all the tiny micro details I need to pore over. And afterwards, when I step out through the sliding doors of that building, I feel a lightness in my body that wasn’t there on walking in.Days and months pass in lonely, blunt-edged monotony, a low, breathless panic beating in my chest. I try to return to my novel, but my brain is treacle. I don’t know if it’s single-parent exhaustion or grief, or if there is something physically wrong with me, but the focus required to plot fiction feels beyond me. I have no capacity for creativity or imagination. “No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear,” writes CS Lewis. I am so full of fear. For the future, for my children, that they’ll grow up holding only the faintest outline of their father.A friend tells me about “memory jars”, how they can help grieving children access happy memories and start conversations about their lost parent. We sit down with pens and paper, and begin to talk about the things we love and remember about Matt.View image in fullscreen‘He loved us … and we loved him’: Matt with his daughter, aged three, in May 2014, two months before he died.Photograph: Hannah RichellMy daughter remembers swooping and giggling with her dad on the round saucer swing in the park. My son recalls curling into the crook of Matt’s arm when he read him a bedtime story. I remember the special light that shone in Matt’s eyes whenever he stepped from the waves after an ocean swim. We all remember the unique kind of grumpy he could get when he was hungry. I write each memory down on a slip of paper before placing it into the jar.“Singing Frozen songs at the top of his voice in the car.”“He made the best yorkshire puddings.”“He loved us … and we loved him,” my daughter says.The kids, needing sudden escape from the emotion, race outside. I can hear them squealing and laughing in the courtyard, on the edge of meltdown. It is heartbreaking to reduce the love of your life and the father of your children to fragments of memories scrawled on to pieces of paper, but it feels important. They remind us that he existed and the love was real. I turn the jar under the light, scraps of folded paper trapped in glass. How can it ever be enough?It’s an early spring day when I take the kids to the beach, a gentle bay with a dappled park, a shark net and tapering cliffs that curve to embrace the thin crescent of sand. It has been chosen carefully. No surf. No swell. No obvious signs of danger. We lay our towels on the sand, unpack fruit and water, buckets and spades, before the kids make a break for freedom.“Wait! Sunscreen! Hats!”My son returns grudgingly and allows me to apply the necessary sunscreen, then turns and scampers along the shoreline, lost to the sensory experience of the gently lapping water. I see him stop, then run back. “I’ll put your suncream on, Mummy.” He looks worried, and I hate this new responsibility he bears.Friends arrive. We drink coffee and watch the children dig tunnels in the sand.Go for a swim, Han. It’ll do you good.I hear it just the way Matt used to say it – teasing, goading, slightly exasperated at my reluctance to hurl myself into the cold waves he loved. I study the water, gently undulating, turquoise. I haven’t been into the ocean since his accident, but the water looks enticing, hardly foreboding.Fine, I think. Have it your way.I wade out quickly, eager to get through the chill and minimise the onslaught of emotion before diving under, my body tightening at the sensation of being enveloped. Not thinking. Just doing. Losing myself in movement.A little way out, I stop and float on my back. Blue below me and blue above me. My skin has cooled enough to feel the water like an embrace. I let go and for a moment it’s as if I am not being held by the water but by Matt. I feel him, right there with me, the warmth and pressure of him, and it is the strangest, most unearthly feeling.View image in fullscreen‘I hope he knew we were with him, holding his hand’: with Matt …View image in fullscreen… and their children in 2012. Photographs: Hannah RichellSettled there, I find the perfect, fleeting glimpse of him from another time, another beach. Shaved head, broad shoulders tapering to a slim waist, feet planted in the sand and arms folded. He is sun-speckled and his beard – longer in the holidays – is salt-crusted and scratchy. I notice how, even in this memory, his eyes don’t leave the sea. Whenever I think of Matt by the ocean, it is always like this. Turned away from me, his gaze fixed on the waves he was so drawn to.More and more, I find myself thinking about Matt’s last moments. Not so much the actual sequence of events now, but the experience of them. The sensation. The decision, turning to paddle, feeling the wave lifting his board. The surge of the water. The snap of his leg rope, the surfboard going in one direction as the rip took him in the other. The wash of water. The scrape of rocks.I think he must have had hope; he was a hopeful man. The hope of pulling himself out. The hope of survival, until that last wave, rushing at him, pushing him forwards. The cliff rising up. A churn of salt and sunlight – a final letting go to blackness.I hope it was peaceful.I hope he didn’t know he was about to die.I hope he knew we were with him, holding his hand in that moment, loving him. Always.It is Wendy who tells me, nearly two years later, that an inquest will be held. She explains it is not about pointing fingers or finding fault, but to see if things could be done differently in the future. She adds, gently, that as Matt’s death was so high‑profile and in such a popular beauty spot, it is deemed to be “in the public interest”. Such a jarring phrase for something that feels so intensely private, but I nod. The last thing I could bear is for another family to endure a loss like ours and to know there was a chance it could have been prevented.For two days, over and over, the fast and treacherous chain of events leading to Matt’s death is relayed. The facts are given, all carefully gathered and noted by the coroner, until the last witness steps down from the box and the coroner closes the proceedings and withdraws to consider all the evidence.In the more peaceful days that follow, I retreat to the coast. I find myself thinking more and more about acceptance. The formal procedure seems to have lifted something in my being. I feel calmer and more balanced. I know he is gone. I know my life is transformed.double quotation markI know now that grief will never leave me. It will always be a part of me, just like the love it stems fromView image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Maurice Smith/The GuardianBut can there ever be a final stage to grief? I’m not sure there can. The pendulum keeps swinging back and forth, though with less sickening ferocity. And the pain still rises frequently, as consistently as the tides, the absence of Matt a deep ache. What feels different is how I hold myself, the pain more often tucked away inside, less obvious to others. The grief is a weight I hold almost sacred now, my body developing the muscle to carry it.I realise that I have been looking at the concept of acceptance all wrong. It is not about rightness. There will never be anything right about Matt’s death. No, acceptance is allowing it to be, whatever it is. A letting go of the need for things to be different. Acceptance is seeing a new path open up before you. Not the one you thought you’d be taking. Acceptance is seeing this new path winding ahead of you and finding the strength to put first one foot on it, then the other.Iready the house for sale, our belongings for the move ahead. Sifting through our life’s possessions is not an easy process, but it is the last hours in the house that are most painful. Wandering alone for the very last time, I revisit the empty rooms, my footsteps echoing strangely through the space. I look out at the Japanese maple we planted, new purple-green leaves shimmering in the morning light. I let my hand trail up the polished wooden banister, take the creaking steps to the first floor. It’s all so familiar – so touched by us. I know it almost as well as my own skin.I sit on the floor in my son’s room by the window and let the tears fall. I think of all the moments that have made up our lives here. Big and small. Joyful and painful. Through the windowpane I can see the spire of the church across the road. I remember noticing it the first time Matt and I looked around the house. I think of the number of times we tiptoed into this room to check on our sleeping boy. To retrieve a fallen toy. To tuck his small body beneath a sheet. Time breaks my heart. I wonder what of ourselves we will leave behind. A lost note, fallen down the back of the mantelpiece? A stray marble caught between the cracks of the floorboards? Or perhaps just the lingering of feeling – of lives bound by love and loss – of the simplicity of our everyday, echoing in these empty rooms.Our story here has ended.I thank the house. I lock the door. I leave.Tamarama, Sydney, 2024Golden hour is settling over Tamarama, the sun sliding low on to the hill behind the beach. I’ve been here a while, traversing a decade of grief, honouring and assessing the shifting weight of our loss. With time and patience, I have returned to writing, found solace in books and reading. Slowly, I have relearned the world, restitched my heart.Down at the tideline, I step into the shallows, the water washing the sand from my skin. It’s cold, but my feet are planted. Steady. I can breathe, my chest no longer tight and pained. These waves will not topple me today.‘Grief became my brand’: Freya Bromley on writing about personal tragedyRead moreI know now that grief will never leave me. It will always be a part of me, just like the love it stems from. The shift comes in wanting to embrace it – to own it. And in the embrace, in pulling it close and examining it, the grief has shifted from something ugly and unthinkable to something softer, more akin to love than pain. So when I hear a song on the radio that reminds me of Matt, I can smile now and offer up my silent thank you.The waves still come, yet we carry on, living lives illuminated by wonder and grief, the duet of both. I think of those on the path, a little behind me. Am I brave enough to share my writing in comfort and solidarity?The surfers are still out, straddling their boards as the waves barrel in, occasionally chasing one down to the shore. I know everything has its time and that one day I, too, shall be called upon to take my place in the lineup, but as I stand here in this golden hour, facing the horizon, thinking about this ocean and that day, and all the days that came before, and all the impossible, joyous, wretched, beautiful ones lived since, I feel only gratitude to be here, holding this love and this pain.You will survive your greatest loss.You will be altered, but you will survive.Listen to the breathings of your heart. They will show you the way.This is an edited extract from An Ocean and a Day by Hannah Richell, published by Bedford Square at £16.99 in the UK and by HarperCollins in Australia.
