title: Megasquirt: Fully Loaded review – how to combat existential angst? A comedy rave at an ungodly hour | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Ashley Blair and Drew Reilly send up gen Z anomie with hardcore ditties about awkward dinners, megachurches and centaur boyfriends
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Ashley Blair and Drew Reilly send up gen Z anomie with hardcore ditties about awkward dinners, megachurches and centaur boyfriends
Content: Garnished with silliness … Drew Reilly and Ashley Blair in Fully Loaded.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenGarnished with silliness … Drew Reilly and Ashley Blair in Fully Loaded.Photograph: Alex BrennerEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMegasquirt: Fully Loaded review – how to combat existential angst? A comedy rave at an ungodly hourUnderbelly, Cowgate, EdinburghAshley Blair and Drew Reilly send up gen Z anomie with hardcore ditties about awkward dinners, megachurches and centaur boyfriendsBrian LoganSun 23 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘How to feel whole in an empty world?” There are many possible answers to that question, and Megasquirt’s late-night comedy rave workshops a good few of them. But there’s probably no better way than putting on a banging show and performing it to an adoring audience of your peers – and that’s what Brooklyn imports Ashley Blair and Drew Reilly do in Fully Loaded, turning the Underbelly at some ungodly hour into a pulsating queer(ish) celebration-cum-sendup of gen Z anomie. “Everything is empty / Life is a hole / You gotta fill it up,” they sing, looking like refugees from Warhol’s Factory but delivering comedy that couldn’t be more now.View image in fullscreenCouldn’t be more now … Blair and Reilly in Fully Loaded.Photograph: Alex BrennerThe show starts as if we’re being seconded to a generational revolution, but it’s soon clear that this pair, bothSecond Cityalumni, are threats to nothing but your funny bone. Their premise is that life is void of meaning. We flash back to meet them as alienated schoolkids and one terrific sketch, a silly symphony of clinking cutlery andASMRtuts and sighs, imagines two parents at dinner, struggling to repress their mutual loathing. If this is our hosts’ generational inheritance, whynotlook for a better way of being? Like a romance with an inverted Centaur Boyfriend, the title of one daft ditty, or like forming a megachurch to start replenishing the spiritual chasm.There are first-base satirical sideswipes in that latter sketch, against Christian homophobia and the church’s obsession with sin. But Blair and Reilly’s satire is usually garnished with, or eclipsed by, silliness, as they belt out their songs about being bullied in bakeries, and “gooning in the DJ booth”. So much the funnier that these songs are tightly constructed, lyrically adroit and delivered with hardcore hyperpop attack.Only occasionally does the standard slip: the skit about straight female writers fetishising gay male sex is on point, but soon devolves into so-so smut. That’s not going to fill anyone’s gaping hole – but there’s lots here that will, as Megasquirt minister to our existential angst with whip-smart, high-energy comedy.AtUnderbelly, Cowgate, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)CabaretEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The country of my birth has lost its heart’: Miriam Margolyes on how to fix broken Britain | Miriam Margolyes | The Guardian
description: At 85, the actor has lived through much political upheaval. But, she writes, today’s hostile times feel like ‘the worst yet’. She reflects on her journey from teenage Tory to full-throated leftist – and says there’s still time to save the nation from the bad guys
Author: Miriam Margolyes
Headline: At 85, the actor has lived through much political upheaval. But, she writes, today’s hostile times feel like ‘the worst yet’. She reflects on her journey from teenage Tory to full-throated leftist – and says there’s still time to save the nation from the bad guys
Content: Miriam Margolyes: ‘It feels as though the country of my birth has lost its heart. How did we get here?’Photograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMiriam Margolyes: ‘It feels as though the country of my birth has lost its heart. How did we get here?’Photograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianMiriam Margolyes‘The country of my birth has lost its heart’: Miriam Margolyes on how to fix broken BritainAt 85, the actor has lived through much political upheaval. But, she writes, today’s hostile times feel like ‘the worst yet’. She reflects on her journey from teenage Tory to full-throated leftist – and says there’s still time to save the nation from the bad guysSun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfunny thing happened on the way to 2026: I got old and the world turned nasty. It happened very quickly and it’s to do with politics (the world) and pelvic floor weakness (mine). It’s strange being this old. Sometimes when I look in the mirror, it’s a shock to see wrinkles and grey hair, because inside I am still that naughty Oxford High School girl, risking detention just for the joy of entertaining her friends. People assume that with great age comes great wisdom, but actually we remain who we have always been, only more so, and we need to make our peace with that and with each other.The Britain I grew up in, though – that feels almost unrecognisable, and everyone I speak to says the same thing. The historian Eric Hobsbawm, whom I knew and loved, argued that people invent the past they want for their own purposes – that the real past was quite different: “Today is the great age of historical mythology.” He’s right, but that past is still the safe haven I’d like to return to. People feel adrift, they don’t understand or feel a connection to the place they thought they knew.Now at 85, I look around at my remaining friends and at my unique relationship with a woman of different qualities but luckily the same politics. In many ways I’m having the time of my life: I’ve never been richer or more in demand. And yet my heart is heavy with foreboding …My postwar generation lived through the rise and fall of many things: the Berlin Wall, Winston Churchill, the European Union, the NHS, the Beatles, Profumo, Elizabeth II, the Great Train Robbery, the pill, the IRA, Margaret Thatcher, the Falklands war, Black Monday and Grenfell, heart transplants, driverless cars, Brexit, the Covid-19 pandemic. But this feels the worst time yet.The things we took for granted – free speech, the Post Office, our local bank, even the home telephone – are disappearing. The US is an enemy. Evil oligarchs and their influence stalk the world, my world, your world. In recent times, thearchbishop of Canterbury resignedand north London Jews are afraid to wear a Magen David (Shield or Star of David) necklace outside their homes for fear of being attacked. You’re brave to open your mouth these days. Indeed, many have demanded I keep mine shut. But I can’t. The present has become threatening, hostile and unwelcoming to us – much as our shores must feel to asylum seekers, as they scramble for a foothold in our United Kingdom. It also feels as though the country of my birth has lost its heart. How did we get here?Now, I’m not usually one to tell jokes. Like my farts, my humour is largely unscripted. I love making people laugh, but at heart I’m a serious person, not just a funny little wobbly thing. I’m not a fan of jokes at the expense of others, those that are trite and mean and racist. But I’ve discovered that, in terms of the relationships and tensions between our nations, sometimes jokes go straight to the jugular.An Englishman is driving down a country road in Wales and realises he’s lost his way. He spots a localand pulls up alongside.“Dai! Dai!” he calls out in a lordly English accent,“which way is it to Cardiff ?” The Welshman eyes him up and down:“Just a minute now, how did you know my name was Dai?” The Englishman says,“I guessed, man! I guessed!”“Well, better guess your way to bloody Cardiff then, hadn’t you!”An Irishman, a Scotsman, a Welshman and an Englishman are on a plane which is going down and there is only one parachute. The Scotsman says,“Scotland will remember me,” and jumps out to his death. The Welshman says,“Wales will remember me,” and jumpsto his death. The Irishman says,“Ireland will remember me,” and pushes the Englishman out of the plane.I don’t think the English understand why their Welsh, Scottish and Irish neighbours loathe them so much. Like the Englishman in the first joke, they’re rather baffled by the hostility, while prolonging it with their arrogant attitudes. This behaviour is, of course, not isolated to them. It turns out that we Brits are even less popular abroad than we are with each other. The history of the British Isles is full of painful moments and terrible decisions. And we need to face those. It’s much easier to look away from bad things that happened and, as with a fart, hope no one noticed. (Spoiler: everyone noticed.) Like every multinational corporation, Great Britain plc has done a lot of harm in its long life. The choice of red to represent the British empire on the global map feels entirely apt. Take these unloving nicknames that zoom in on our annoyingness, inability to wear suncream and/or stop swearing:BrittunculiThis one’s the oldest: it was found on a tablet at the Roman fort of Vindolanda on Hadrian’s Wall, a Latin term showing exasperation and meaning “wretched little Brits”.PomsThis is what the Australians and New Zealanders call us. There are various theories: the late journalist Alan Whicker said “Pom” was short for pomegranate, the bright red colour a new arrival turns in the sun down under. Others claim that Pommie is really “POME”, which stands for prisoner of mother England, and thus the British convicts who were transported to Botany Bay.Rooinekor“redneck”The Boer nickname for the pale Brits, dangerously sunburnt again. Afrikaners of old had a ruder nickname for us, though –soutpiel(“salty penis”) – meaning that the Brits had one foot back home, the other in South Africa, so their penises were left to dangle in the salty ocean.LimeysThe American term, originating in the 1850s as “lime-juicer”, from the Royal Navy practice of adding lemon or lime juice to British sailors’ daily ration to ward off the scurvy that made all their teeth fall out.InselaffenTranslating as “island monkeys”, this is the Germans’ contemptuous nickname, supposedly dating back to Darwin’s theories of evolution.Les rosbifs“Roast beefs”; this French take is based on our fondness for a traditional Sunday roast. Historically they also called us “les goddams”, which originated in the hundred years war, referring to the typically potty-mouthed English soldiers. (So that’s where I got it from!) More recently, British tourists have been called “les fuckoffs”. Très charmant!My point is, history has always been the propaganda of the victors, but it can lead you astray. So why not try listening to the other side of the story? Don’t fall for your own hype. It all seems heroic if you turn it into a monologue about why you were right all along, instead of facing the painful bits from which there’s no way you can come out well.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jay Brooks/The Guardiandouble quotation markIt’s that rule of polite society again: one mustn’t rock the boat, ruffle feathers or put anyone’s nose out of joint. How absurd. Facts are factsOur British history needs to reflect our mother tongue, which is a patchwork of words gathered from the different tribes and peoples who’ve made these islands home. There’s room for everyone: we all bring something to the table, whether invader or inhabitant. The French word for a fanlight or transom window is vasistas and comes from the seven years war, when the German soldiers were baffled by the newfangled windows they saw in French houses and kept asking “Was ist das?” The French word is a joke, a snooty echo of the German reactions, but it stuck.People are always trying to fix language, but it remains on the move. The Normans tried to make England French; the English tried to ban the native Irish, Welsh and Scottish languages for “the greater common good” and then later to replace regional dialect and accents with received pronunciation. What idiots! Not only did they not succeed, but our shared language has ended up all the richer. If you can’t beat ’em, join ’em.Now I know many of my opinions – particularly those on politics, Palestine and Potter (Harry) – have provoked outrage. But I can’t help it – I believe in telling the truth, even if it’s my truth. In this, again, I realise I do not fit the English stereotype. The English excel at obfuscation, you see; they are masters at avoiding the truth. It’s that rule of polite society again: one mustn’t rock the boat, ruffle feathers or put anyone’s nose out of joint. How absurd. Facts are facts.My advice? If you believe someone is a liar, stay away from them. All around us, our politicians, news outlets and the media – the very people we are supposed to trust – are caught up in a relentless and divisive campaign of fearmongering and misinformation. Now it feels more crucial than ever to think for ourselves, debunk the deceits and sort the sheep from the goats.Mummy used to say “speak as you find”, and I think that’s an excellent way of sorting out decent folk from the vile. What unites us is far greater than what divides. Don’t be afraid to learn from everything wrong in our past – and there is a lot wrong in our past – let’s just do it better in the future.Ibet you didn’t know I was once a Tory candidate. But unlike most of the former Conservatives who have swelled the ranks of the current Deform party, I have grown into maturity and swung left. My campaign was in May 1955: I was 14 and in the upper fourth at Oxford High School. A general election was being held in the country, and we decided to hold one at school. Of course I was a Conservative: my parents had always been Tories – it was all I knew. They both worshipped Winston Churchill and credited him with having saved the United Kingdom from the Nazis. For Mummy, being Tory was a key part of her upwardly mobile climb, and so it was for my father, who, despite being a passionate supporter of the newly created NHS, could not imagine following Labour. They were delighted to hear I was the Tory candidate. We don’t remember who dared to stand against me in our form, or what my policies and promises were at the hustings – I was an old-school Tory and definitely pro capital punishment, so I dread to think – but I carried the day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLawrence Turner, the Tory who won the Oxford constituency when I won the upper fourth, went on to vote in favour of the Suez invasion, spend more than he earned and finally go bankrupt. Rather sweetly, one of his last parliamentary activities was presenting a petition to preserve the copyright of the words of WS Gilbert, one half of the prolific theatrical partnership Gilbert and Sullivan who created the comic operas that were the ironic soundtrack to the burgeoning British empire. Turner proved ineffectual again: he was not “the very model of a modern major-general” or even of a modern member of parliament, and copyright expired in 1961.Right seemed self-evidently right until I was assailed on two respectable fronts. After my election success, the father of my best chum from those days, Biddy Peppin, insisted I was invited to tea. He was that unusual thing, a leftwing bank manager, and his chosen task was to turn my path into a socialist future. And then another friend, Liz Hodgkin, also invited me for dinner. The Hodgkins were academic royalty – Liz’s mother Dorothy was later to win a Nobel prize – but they were committed socialists, too. You know how sometimes you can fall in love with a whole family? Well, I did. Their dinner guests were all communists and convinced Marxists (oh, that I had the courage to be a Marxist now, but that Putin, he puts me right off) and were winsome, hugely entertaining and great storytellers. Previously I had thought of communists as grim and humourless but boy, was I wrong. And so, eventually, this lady was for turning. I made a U-turn in the direction of sanity and humanity, and have never looked back. My parents were surprised and shocked by my new politics. But had they lived to experience the full horror of the last 14 years of Conservative reign under Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss and finally Sunak, I hope they, too, would have seen the light and embraced the left.The rise of the far right in Britain today can be traced back to a daft dyke. It depresses me to share that one of my fellow lesbians could be so silly, but the truth must be faced, and in 1923, Rotha Lintorn-Orman founded the first British fascist movement. In 1895 she was born in Kensington (where else?!) into enormous wealth. Obviously liking uniforms and women – and women in uniforms – she and a close chum originally wanted to join the Boy Scouts, but the Scouts wouldn’t have them. When the first world war broke out, she served as an ambulance driver, and was decorated for valour.After the war, Lintorn-Orman, a passionate admirer of Mussolini, formed the British Fascisti. But other, more extreme fascist societies proliferated and soon Lintorn-Orman and her cronies were outflanked. She descended into alcoholism and drug addiction, indulging in “drunken orgies and undesirable practices”, and her organisation died. But fascism would live on – from Oswald Mosley and his Blackshirts right through to Tommy Robinson.View image in fullscreenSet design: Victoria Twyman. Hair and makeup: Alice Theobald at Arlington Artists using Charlotte Tilbury and Living Proof. Stylist: Charlotte Gornall. All clothes, Margolyes’ own.Photograph: Jay Brooks/The Guardiandouble quotation markWhile the bad guys seem to be winning everywhere, I’m not giving up – and neither should youNow I’m old, I understand that older people like things “the way they were”. Me, too: I hate upgrades – be it in computers, in phones, in style, in my neighbours. I want what I had. And so, change (which the politicians tell us we want), I actively don’t want. Change makes me feel powerless and then I get angry and look for someone to blame. At least I know enough not to blame immigrants and asylum seekers. The mess the country’s in has got nothing to do with them, but too many of us have been bamboozled into thinking it has.I grew up knowing I’d receive a fine education and would get a job when I left university (which was free in 1963). Fascism had had its day, we thought. More than 70 million people had died to secure our freedom. But now racism was impossible to ignore, as one by one the last vestiges of the Empire started claiming their independence. The Windrush generation came to Britain – at the government of the time’s invitation – to staff our new welfare state, believing they were wanted and would be appreciated for leaving their homes and families, but finding the promised motherland felt harsh, hostile and unwelcoming.Taking advantage of this highly charged political climate, a new British fascist party – the National Front – was born in early 1967. The next year Enoch Powell, Conservative MP for Wolverhampton South West, made his “Rivers of Blood” speech. He posed as a brave visionary; perhaps he even believed that he was giving voice to the displaced white community of the Midlands who felt crowded out by Black and Asian immigrants.I knew straight away what Powell wanted to achieve with the speech: to fan the flames of public dissent. His Oxford education, classical training and powers of oratory served him well. He saw the race card as the way to obtain power. It still is.Today, a nasty little turd is floating about in our polluted waters. It has many names; one sticks out more than the others. A public schoolboy, posing as “one of the lads”; someone who thought it was funny to hiss at Jewish boys just after the second world war; someone who was given £5m to keep himself safe; someone who got German citizenship legally for his sons (his ex-wife is German) so Brexit disadvantages don’t inconvenience those close to him. There is a widespread fear that Farage (AKA the Odious Niggle) could succeed to the leadership; the kingdom is teetering on the brink of annihilation. But it’s not too late. After all, it is not the lie that passeth through the mind but the lie that sinketh in and settleth in it that doth the hurt. (Thanks, Francis Bacon.) While the bad guys seem to be winning everywhere, I’m not giving up – and neither should you.Exhausted by but addicted to doomscrolling, sliding from one terrifying headline to another, it’s easy to forget we are all in the same unsteady boat, north or south, young or old, lower, middle and even upper class, ignoring the culprits hiding in plain sight. It’snotthe foreigners, legal or illegal, who are pissing on us; it’s the billionaires who own the media and the internet and can pay the debts of the political parties they want to control, and fuck the rest of us. Well, I’m not putting up with it any longer. And neither need you. Let’s have a laugh. It’s the antidote (and all the ammunition) we need to those arseholes who forget that Britain was great before they were born – we can see right through them.Never forget that laughter is a good medicine, ridicule and satire can change minds, and there’s always sex. Mind you, it’s a while since I enjoyed the full-throated variety, but I know it’s out there.I refuse to be cut off from the wealth of possibilities that Britain and Ireland offer. Let’s live, have fun, learn new tastes, new words, new mastications. Build bridges, cross chasms. And before we go to the moon again, let’s reap the benefits strangers in our midst offer. It’s not their fault that things are tough. It’s ours. This is my middle finger to naysayers, Nigel Farage and everyone who says “whatever”. It’s time to be Great Britain again – or at least Better Britain. Steady the Buffs andonwards!This is an edited extract from Miriam’s Full English by Miriam Margolyes, published by John Murray on 3 September at £25. title: Dining across the divide: ‘I thought he was going to be quite “stop the boats, bring up the drawbridge”’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A Green party member and a Labour-voting Brexiter didn’t agree on the EU, but what about renewable energy and the NHS?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: A Green party member and a Labour-voting Brexiter didn’t agree on the EU, but what about renewable energy and the NHS?
Content: Joe (left) and Keith. All photographs: Jane MacNeil/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJoe (left) and Keith. All photographs: Jane MacNeil/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘I thought he was going to be quite “stop the boats, bring up the drawbridge”’A Green party member and a Labour-voting Brexiter didn’t agree on the EU, but what about renewable energy and the NHS?Want to meet someone from across the divide? Clickhereto find out howZoe WilliamsSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe, 41, Trafford, Greater ManchesterView image in fullscreenOccupationPress officer at a universityVoting recordHistorically, under Jeremy Corbyn, Labour; is a Green member now but was planning to vote Labour in the mayoral electionAmuse boucheLong-distance cycle touring is Joe’s big thing: he has been all over Europe solo, staying with families, trying to speak the languages, embedding himself with local peopleKeith, 89, CheshireView image in fullscreenOccupationRetired – used to be a journalist, moved to Liverpool to edit a shipping newspaper and ended up owning itVoting recordKeith normally votes Labour. There was one occasion when he voted Conservative, for Margaret ThatcherAmuse boucheKeith once went to Rio de Janeiro for the day. He was producing a magazine for British Airways Cargo and they wanted to promote the route to São PauloFor startersJoeI’d formed a view of what his character might be but he was really warm and friendly. It was like two old friends. It was just so comfortable.KeithThe first thing he said was, “Are you as nervous as I am?” I said I wasn’t nervous at all. I’m used to talking to people and it didn’t bother me.JoeI had the prosciutto and melon, then chicken in breadcrumbs.KeithI started with calamari, then gnocchi with prawns.View image in fullscreenThe big beefJoeHe was very set on the idea that the EU is anti-democratic. The arguments I had about the damage that leaving the EU has done to the British economy – how it has destroyed exports and left us isolated – he agreed with. But none of it mattered to him. He was a Brexiter from quite a leftwing perspective. I thought he was going to be quite “stop the boats, bring up the drawbridge”, but he wasn’t like that at all.Dining across the divide: ‘She’s got a real downer on Nigel Farage – I think he’s a charismatic guy’Read moreKeithI voted for Brexit for independence, not for the economy, although the economy could have been handled better by the prime ministers since. You had Theresa May – who was, I believe, a remainer at heart – trying to cobble together some sort of deal that looked like Brexit but wasn’t. Both she and Boris Johnson should share the blame because they let it drag on for so long. You should never be governed by people you can’t vote out of office.JoeHe said Nigel Farage sometimes says things that he agrees with – principally stuff about the European superstate. When he was talking about that, you couldn’t put a cigarette paper between him and Farage. But at the same time, he’s really anti-Trump, and really anti the rightwing position on migrants.KeithThere are 4,000 different edicts in the EU that we should have got rid of. I don’t feel we’ve taken advantage economically of the opportunities. Joe sort of saw that, but he believes too many small companies have lost business. I did point out that traders should have looked elsewhere for business. We were the sixth largest trading nation in the world before and we still are.View image in fullscreenSharing plateJoeOn the NHS, I don’t think we were miles apart. I’ve worked in the NHS in the past; the right wing dresses up overspending as back office stuff and equality and diversity, but all of that is a tiny drop in the ocean compared with PFI.KeithHe saw how the NHS is paying hundreds of millions in interest on PFI payments. PFI has been a bit of a disaster, but I’d be very open to other ways of bringing in private money.View image in fullscreenFor aftersJoeDrilling in the North Sea won’t make us more resilient as a country because it has all got to be sold on the international markets anyway. Is there any point doing damage to the environment when it won’t benefit British consumers? We could be spending that money and energy building renewable capacity.KeithI’m all for going to renewables, I’m all for cutting pollution. I agree with all that, but I just don’t think we need to do it as quickly as people like Ed Miliband want us to. It’s impoverishing the country, we’re losing industry.View image in fullscreenTakeawaysJoeAs I was driving away, I did think I should have taken his email address, so we could have kept in touch.KeithThe only problem I was left with was that I’m never going to see him or hear from him again. He’s a long way away to go out for a casual drink.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeJoe and Keith ate atLa Cantinain Ellesmere Port, CheshireWant to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Walking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of England | John Harris | The Guardian
description: The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we should, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we should, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionHostelsWalking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of EnglandJohn HarrisThe landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we shouldSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.06 EDTShareAfortnight or so ago, my two teenage kids and I set out on a three-night visit to the Peak District where temperatures were hovering at a comparatively tepid 28C. We stayed at a youth hostel – more of which in a moment – and began the trip with the 20-minute ascent ofMam Tor, a modest peak that pulls in both dedicated ramblers who then yomp along the ridge beyond, and newbies who mostly want to get to the top and immerse themselves in the jaw-dropping view.The next bit might sound self-parodically Guardian-esque, but what the hell: in its own way, the most striking sight was the diversity of the scores of people rambling up, down and along. Women in their 20s wearing hijabs picnicked on giant rocks, while multiracial gaggles of young men attempted to race to the top; solo and shirtless white fitness freaks and retirement-age dog walkers took their places alongside them. With plenty of justification, country walking has long been typified as one of the most monoculturally white pursuits there is. But here – presumably because of the relatively close proximity of Manchester and Sheffield – things looked different.The scenes didn’t quite suggest Britain in microcosm, but they weren’t far off. I began to wonder, in fact, whether I was witnessing the (extremely) belated next emancipatory phase of a story that began with themass trespassat the nearby Kinder Scout in 1932, led by the Jewish anti-fascist Benny Rothman: the protest in which hundreds of men and women defied the law to walk on privately owned Derbyshire hills and moorland. Five of them received prison sentences, but the way was thereby opened to the creation of the UK’s first national parks.The latter-day people and organisations working tomake walking more inclusive– in response to national statistics that remain depressing, and often in the face of straight-up prejudice – surely deserve as much praise as Rothman and his comrades.Black Girls Hikewas founded in 2019 by the brilliant Mancunian Rhiane Fatinikun, aimed at creating “a safe space for Black women to explore the outdoors … challenging the status quo”. Soon after, the Coventry-based rambler Haroon Mota startedMuslim Hikers, and began group walks just over a year later. In the same city, Cherelle Harding createdSteppers UK, intended to “normalise black and brown faces in outdoor spaces and create a community of outdoor enthusiasts”.All this reflects aspects of our culture and politics that can be fascinating and inspiring – and, on the other side of some modern political and cultural divides, very unsettling. If he were to visit the Peak District, Nigel Farage would presumably get no further than his chosen pub. But his vision of bucolic England is symbolised by the outfit he tends to wear when he wants to accuse the supposed metropolitan elite of neglecting the countryside, usually by turning up at one of those faux – or not so faux –fox hunts. We all know the drill: flat cap, Barbour jacket, wellies, fag and pint. The cosplay is replete with meaning, and not just in its embodiment of what a cultural-studies specialist might call white rurality. Look, for example, at the terrible twist Farage and his political allies got their collective knickers in over theNational Trust’s driveto be open about some of its properties’ links to colonialism and slavery, and the same organisation’scampaigning to protect the environment.Further to the right, somewhere in the heart of every nativist lurk darkly romanticised visions of the British landscape – think of what is meant by that toxic phrase “blood and soil”. Last year, news broke about two wooded stretches of land in mid-Walesbeing bought by the Woodlander Initiative, a scheme led by the far-right activist Simon Birkett. He has links to Patriotic Alternative, reckoned to be the UK’s largest fascist organisation. The people involved were never going to be interested in urban land: to the fascist mind, the countryside, as opposed to the cosmopolitan and decadent stereotypical city (think about the far right’s constant demonisation of London), represents notions of racial purity and noble simplicity. From some far-right activists, there was sympathetic talk in response about “indigenous heartlands – places for our people”.The upshot of all this is obvious: the UK’s rural expanses can be as toxified and contested as any other aspect of our national life, and without wanting to sound too dour – walking is meant to be fun, after all – we need to actively promote the idea that the countryside belongs to all of us. To do so is to deprive the assortment of opportunists and hate-mongers who span the hard and far right of any idea that the British landscape and its romance and mythology might be theirs to monopolise.There is another, much more benign and everyday obstacle to maximising access to green spaces. In many places, hotels and hospitality increasingly embody a different kind of exclusivity: the upgrading of pubs and hotels to boutique, gastro-centric establishments with sky-high prices. Those charged on such platforms as Airbnb are part of the same problem. So if your ambitions extend further than a day trip and such luxury is beyond your budget, where can you stay?Part of the answer lies with the Youth Hostels Association (YHA) of England and Wales (the equivalent north of the border is Hostelling Scotland) and its network of places to eat, sleep and socialise. But the pandemic caused the YHA an incomeloss of £40min the first year alone, and in March last year, it said that its energy costs had quadrupled. In 2023, it had about 150 hostels; to date, it has announced the sale or closure of 29. Eight are now run as hostels thanks to a YHA franchising scheme, and there are similar hopes for at least one of my threatened favourites: Bellever on Dartmoor, one of the most idyllic places I have ever spent the night.But here is the crucial point: the YHA runsa programmethat provides fully or “partly funded stays at youth hostels for young people and families facing significant challenges” (including young carers, and those involved in refugee and migrant groups), and a scheme calledNo Child Left Behindthat helps to ensure that financial hardship does not stop kids going on residential school trips. It is an organisation that should be expanding, not shrinking.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving come down off Mam Tor, I drove the half hour back to where we were staying: Hartington Hall, a 17th-century manor house owned and run by the YHA. As we were having dinner, I noticeda plaquefixed to the wall, presumably dating from the distant days (the YHA was founded in 1930) when guests were obliged to muck in with the chores rather than sample the £14 burger-and-beer meal deal. “This youth hostel,” it said, “is one of many, both in this country and abroad, where young people, regardless of race or creed, may spend the night. The buildings are diverse in character but they have a common purpose: to help all, especially young people of limited means, to a greater knowledge, love and care for the countryside.”How, then, to preserve as many hostels as possible, bring in more young people and make those words real? An injection of cash from big-spending philanthropists? A modest tourist tax on hotels and short-let accommodation? Or the kind of relative loose change that could presumably be found by the departments for Food and Rural Affairs, Education, Culture, Media and Sport, or all three? Some parts of the British landscape are starting to undergo what seems to be an overdue and very welcome social change, but it needs the kind of support that comes in the form of bunk-beds and brickwork. In a country whose divisions are constantly inflamed and hyped up by demagogic chancers, that challenge is a lot more urgent than it might seem.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHostelsOpinionPeak District holidaysWalkingHobbiesHealth & wellbeingRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: Jumpy bond markets make it clear: Trump risks driving US into debt crisis | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm bond markets is a sign of weakness not strength
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm bond markets is a sign of weakness not strength
Content: Donald Trump and Scott Bessent.  Bessent’s panicky intervention last week smacked of rising anxiety about how markets now view the US fiscal position.Photograph: Al Drago/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Scott Bessent.  Bessent’s panicky intervention last week smacked of rising anxiety about how markets now view the US fiscal position.Photograph: Al Drago/EPAEconomics viewpointUS economyJumpy bond markets make it clear: Trump risks driving US into debt crisisHeather StewartTreasury secretary Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm bond markets is a sign of weakness not strengthSun 23 Aug 2026 06.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTShare“Look, there’s nothing magic about that $40tn number,” the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, told CNBC insouciantly last week, as the country’s debt mountain surpassed another bleak record.Yet Bessent’s decision to intervene in government bond markets in an effort to combat soaring yields belied his studied calm in TV interviews – and reignited fears the US may be on the road to a debt crisis.Half a lifetime ago, in 1992, Bessent cut his teeth in markets shorting the pound alongside George Soros in the chaos that led up to Black Wednesday, when the UK plunged out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.Why is the Trump administration causing turmoil in the bond markets? | Richard PartingtonRead moreToday he is on the other side of the tussle between policymakers and markets. When the US Treasury intervened tohelp prop up the Japanese yenearlier this month – crucially by selling euros, not the US dollar – it was widely read as a sign of weakness.Japan is a mega holder of US treasuries, and it looked as though theTrump administrationwas fretting that Tokyo might be preparing to dump a chunk of them to buy yen – potentially pushing up the yield, or interest rate.The US Treasury’s announcement that Japan would in future be able to use a little-known facility called the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility, effectively to borrow against its treasury holdings without having to sell them, was read as another sign of concern.As the economist Barry Eichengreenwrote in the FT at the time: “The bottom line is that Washington, fearing the consequences for US financial markets, is reluctant to see foreign central banks use their dollar reserves. This is telling us that the dollar is not the attractive reserve currency it once was.”In last week’s fresh intervention Bessent promised todouble the rateat which the Treasury woul buy up the longest-dated bonds – hoping to massage the yield downwards.It was the clearest sign yet of anxiety in Washington about a sell-off that has pushed up yields on 30-year government bonds to levels last seen before the global financial crisis in 2008.There are several, overlapping reasons for the bond market sell-off. One is inflation. Treasuries, which pay a fixed amount each year, are in part a bet on the future value of money – with higher inflation eroding the real value of those payments.With the Iran conflict slipping towards a forever war, keeping oil prices elevated, and amid concerns about the newFederal Reservechair Kevin Warsh’s willingness to raise interest rates, investors are fretting more about future inflation.Another reason lies in the extraordinary AI investment boom. Tech giants have been funding the buildout of vast datacentres by issuing a wall of corporate debt.Debt issuance by the “hyperscaler” AI companies is already $219bn (£160.5bn) so far this year,according to analysis by JP Morgan– potentially offering investors an alternative to treasuries and crowding out public debt.Third, and most worrying, is the gnawing sense that despite continued robust economic growth, the US is not the rock-solid creditor it once was.US public debt has exploded in recent years, smashing through every forecast. It lurched higher after the financial crisis and took another leg up during the Covid pandemic. It has continued to surge in Donald Trump’s second term, as tax cuts have been unmatched either by tariff revenue – some of which is now being repaid – or by spending cuts from Elon Musk’s short-lived Department of Government Efficiency.Without radical policy change, for which there seems little appetite on Capitol Hill, the independent Congressional Budget Office expects US government debt to rise from 100% of GDP today to 175% in 30 years’ time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, with his unwinnable war in the Middle East, capricious tariff regime andpenchant for self-enrichment on an epic scale, Trump is turning the US into an increasingly unpredictable player in the global economy. Instead of the guarantor of rules-based markets and open global trade routes, the US has become a source of uncertainty and chaos.As Adam Posen of the Peterson Institute for InternationalEconomicsput it in a recent piece: “The entire world is now doing business, investing, and trying to make a living in the post-American world economy.”Chart which forecasts US government debt rising to 175.1% by 2056The withdrawal was largely a deliberate decision by Trump’s Maga crew, who felt the US was shouldering too many of the running costs of the geopolitical order.Yet it was partly this role as the anchor of the global economy, with treasuries the quintessential safe haven asset, that prevented the logic of runaway deficits and spiralling debt from hitting home.By contrast, Bessent’s panicky intervention last week smacked of rising anxiety about how markets now view the US fiscal position.Far from drawing a line under the bond rout, 30-year yields were rising again by Friday afternoon, while at the same time the dollar was sliding fast – a cursed correlation more often associated with emerging economies.Bessent seemed to be signalling a willingness to step in again, if 30-year yields are pulled too far above 5%. As the financial commentator Stephen Innes put it: “Once traders think they have identified a policy pain threshold, they tend to come back and test whether it is real.”Warsh will have his moment in the spotlight at the Jackson Hole central bankers’ conference this week, but the risks are clearly growing of a self-inflicted bond market crisis – with consequences that would ripple out far beyond the US.Explore more on these topicsUS economyEconomics viewpointBondsEconomicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationGlobal economyFederal ReservecommentShareReuse this content

title: When I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinised | Sanghmitra Singh | The Guardian
description: The city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendliness, says human rights lawyer and farmer Sanghmitra Singh
Author: Sanghmitra Singh
Headline: The city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendliness, says human rights lawyer and farmer Sanghmitra Singh
Content: An anti-racism demonstration in Glasgow, 13 June 2026.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn anti-racism demonstration in Glasgow, 13 June 2026.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionScotlandWhen I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinisedSanghmitra SinghThe city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendlinessSun 23 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 05.11 EDTShareScottish people have always been known for their friendliness. “We’re not like the south of us,” they say, referring to England. The official slogan of Scotland’s largest city, “People make Glasgow”, appears everywhere – on T-shirts, buildings, bus stops and mugs. And when I first moved to Scotland from India in 2018, I was immediately welcomed by kind strangers and helpful neighbours. People showed curiosity, rather than intrusiveness. They respected queues; told me I fit right in. Music, art and cultural events were considered inclusive spaces in the city, with calls for diversity, creativity, inclusion – all the good things.As an outsider, this was a dream come true: to be myself, to be alone, to have brotherhood and a community. It was life-changing. I could do whatever I wanted, wear whatever I wanted, walk by myself at night, even. That is a luxury, especially for a woman. But something has changed, particularly after Covid, a global recession and years of austerity. Now, I watch the steady rise of far-right, fringe violence and I feel a special scrutiny upon me.In June, we saw disorder and racists assaults in Glasgow as hundreds of masked protesters marched through the streets. Asian business owners were harassed and people were attacked – according to the police – “because of the colour of their skin”. Later that month, a man wascharged with attempted murderafter allegedly attacking men leaving a mosque in Edinburgh. A video appeared to show him shouting that he was “protecting the country”. In July, a delivery driverwas assaultedafter anti-immigration protesters, many of them masked, some shouting racist abuse, once again “rampaged” through Glasgow. We have seenmosques defacedwith “hate graffiti” – one is attacked in Britainevery five days, according to new data. We’ve heard a speaker at a protest outside an asylum hotel in Falkirk calling for a crowd to “keep Britain white”. There have been activists outside the Scottish parliamentstaging fascist-style demonstrations. It goes to show top-down propaganda funnels to real-life incidents.I feel this increasing hostility personally, too. Strangers point-blank question me about my nationality, accent, religion or clothes. A stranger once told me that my accent was weird. Anacquaintance said immigrants were taking away jobs from locals, after I told them I was struggling to find work despite being qualified. People jump queues and are quickly confrontational. The “outsiders” that Glasgow loved and accepted have seemingly become the subject of derision and suspicion.I find people staring at me, head to toe, for an uncomfortably long time. A customer in a Govan pub casually remarked aloud that immigrants are criminals and that we “need to go back”. An old lady on a bus interrupted me and my very white, very British husband to tell us to stop talking the way we were talking. Was it because we’re clearly an interracial couple? Is it because we categorically don’t sound like the locals? I’ll never know, but it’s gnawing now at the back of my mind when it never would have a few short years ago.Colleagues who have been here since the 1980s and earlier tell me that racist violence has happened inScotlandbefore, but this time it feels different. We’re afraid to step out now. There’s a clear, marked shift in our levels of nervousness. It is certainly more imminent, more immediate – closer to home.I blame a combination of factors for this unsettling change: the high cost of living, the worsening climate crisis and the rightwing agenda of some of the mainstream media have all increased resentment and suspicion of one’s neighbours. Then, during the Covid-19 pandemic, many people felt that they had been left alone. That the state wasn’t taking care of them as a democracy is supposed to do.Even a global health emergency, it seemed, couldn’t make for a better world. Instead of a fairer, more equal or accessible society, we haveextreme wealth inequalitythat is persistent and increasing. And it doesn’t help thatinflammatory posts are favouredby social-media algorithms. All of this creates a tinderbox in which people of colour understandably feel afraid.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform’s toxic thinking has infected Scottish politics – this week’s Holyrood elections will tell us how badly | Jasmeen KanwalRead moreMany places, including Leith and Glasgow, held anti-racist, pro-immigrant, pro-humanity rallies days after the racist incidents occurred. People carried signs reading: “Racism is weird, have you tried hobbies?”; “Migrants make the NHS”; “Hate has no home”. They made passionate speeches about standing up to bigotry. But is that enough? While it was heartwarming to see thousands of people come out, uniting for diversity, inclusion and multiculturalism, it won’t stop agrowing hatred and fearof people like me. And so every time I’m out in public now, my stress levels go up. Am I safe alone? What is my exit strategy? Can I even afford to be angry? Others feel it, too.I understand why many British people feel overlooked and badly done by – it’s true thatBritain is unequaland unfair. But I wish that the media would not validate people’s inherent biases and misconceptions, nor politicians legitimise their worst sentiments by calling for reactions like “pure, cold rage”. It is easy to whip up hatred between neighbours, but systematic hatred and divisiveness can take decades to undo. The only individuals who benefit from scapegoating are the powerful.We have to say “no” to this normalisation of bigotry, violence and othering. We have to focus on the living conditions and inequality we all share. We need to remember we have more in common with each other than with any billionaire. We must remember that the real blame lies with the system that wants us divided. Talk to real people who look and sound different from you. You’ll realise we’re all humans. We can do better than this.Sanghmitra Singh is a human rights lawyer and a writerThis article is published as part of a partnership with Pass the Mic, which works to amplify the expertise of women of colourDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Is there a pending AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0 | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: Fears of a datacenter buildout debt crisis are exaggerated. The risks are different than in the past and they are recoverable
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: Fears of a datacenter buildout debt crisis are exaggerated. The risks are different than in the past and they are recoverable
Content: The Stargate AI datacenter in Abilene, Texas, on 24 September 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Stargate AI datacenter in Abilene, Texas, on 24 September 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Is there a pending AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0Gene MarksFears of a datacenter buildout debt crisis are exaggerated. The risks are different than in the past and they are recoverableSun 23 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTShareSome experts are warning of a looming “debt bomb” crisis because bigdatacenterbuilders such asMeta,Oracle,xAIandCoreWeaveare not only raising billions to construct these facilities but are also not recognizing these long-term debt obligations on their balance sheets.Should we be concerned? No. I know because I’ve seen this movie before.It works like this: Meta wants to build a datacenter to accommodate its growingAIand cloud computing needs. It forms a separate entity that’s not consolidated in its financials, which builds the datacenter. To fund this, the entity raises money from investors, banks and other financial firms (including some from Meta) that own the majority of the entity. There is a contract by which Meta has exclusive and full use of the datacenter once built. This way Meta gets its datacenter but most of the debt incurred to build it is not shown as a liability on its books.Gen Z calls it ‘loud budgeting’ – small business owners have been doing it for decades | Gene MarksRead moreThe worry comes from the enormous sums of money being plowed into these entities. TheFinancial Timesreported in December 2025 that tech companies had shifted more than $120bn of AI datacenter spending off their balance sheets through special-purpose vehicles and similar financing structures.Goldman Sachsestimates that hyperscalers could spend $5.3tn on AI and datacenters through 2030 and expects private markets to play an increasingly important role in financing that buildout.Skeptics are worried that these tech guys are pulling the wool over the public’s eyes and not properly disclosing the long-term impact of all this debt. They point toEnron, the energy firm that spectacularly failed in 2001, causing tens of billions of dollars of losses to its shareholders and contributing to a historic market meltdown.Fine. Scrutinize them. Read the footnotes. Argue about consolidation. But don’t call them Enron. Enron caused the Enron crash. It’s highly unlikely that fraud at that level is being perpetuated now by these companies.When I first started out in accounting back in the mid-1980s, my biggest client was a publicly held biotechnology firm calledCentocor, which, at the time, was developing drugs using a technology based on monoclonal-antibody treatment for various purposes including sepsis. To raise money, Centocor also did off-balance-sheet financing. The company formed limited partnerships in which it held a minority interest but the entity issued debt and took in investments from limited partners in order to fund the development of various drugs, which Centocor then had the exclusive right to use.In the 1980s and early 1990s, hundreds of millions of dollars were plowed into these partnerships. This was common practice in the biotechnology during that time.Did some of the drugs fail in clinical testing? Yes. But did this cause a stock market panic? No. Like with today’s datacenters, the risks were spread. During that time – before the Internet, SEC disclosures and 24/7 media scrutiny – the public little knew of these vehicles. The good news is that the accounting has evolved, although the economic idea has stayed the same – no debt was shown on Centocor’s balance sheet. Ultimately, this financing vehicle became more expensive and less popular because it was easier and more affordable to raise money other ways.The off-balance-sheet financing strategies today that are being used by big tech firms have different risks than what the biotech companies were doing when I was younger. Today, the disclosures required by companies doing this are significant. The scrutiny is intense. The investing public is smarter. Today’s risks are different and arguably more recoverable.In the 90s Centocor,Genentech,Amgen,Biogenand other companies like them were raising millions in partnerships that were developing products with a high probability of failure during clinical testing.Today’s investors are financing land, buildings, electrical infrastructure and computing equipment. A datacenter can disappoint financially, but it doesn’t disappear because a clinical trial fails. It’s whyJeff Bezoscalls AI an “industrial bubble”. Industrial bubbles leave things behind. Railways. Fiber-optic cable. Factories. And this time, datacenters.If this is a glut, it’s a strange one: developers increased North American capacity by 36% last year and vacancy still fell to a record 1.4%. According toCBRE’s North America Data Center Trends H2 2025 report, demand is outpacing supply in nearly every major market. Unlike the drug companies hoping for success, there’s a legitimate market need today for datacenters. AI isn’t going away.Microsoftestimates that only 17.8% of the world’s working-age population currently uses generative AI. If that’s anywhere near correct, we’re still much closer to the beginning of adoption than the end.Some of these investments will fail. Some lenders will lose money. Some datacenters will be worth less than their owners paid for them. But that’s exactly why these financing structures exist: to spread enormous capital requirements and risk among investors willing to take it. The obligations are disclosed, the assets are real and demand for computing capacity remains strong. That’s why I’m not losing sleep over big tech’s off-balance-sheet debt. I see financial engineering, yes. I don’t see a debt bomb.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Datacenters – USMetaAmazonJeff BezoscommentShareReuse this content

title: Is a French Sunday the secret to a healthier, happier life? | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: The idea of being deliberately unproductive is certainly tempting. The only concern is that you might enjoy it too much, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: The idea of being deliberately unproductive is certainly tempting. The only concern is that you might enjoy it too much, writes Polly Hudson
Content: Hats off … a French Sunday in action.Photograph: Posed by model; swissmediavision/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHats off … a French Sunday in action.Photograph: Posed by model; swissmediavision/Getty ImagesOpinionFranceIs a French Sunday the secret to a healthier, happier life?Polly HudsonThe idea of being deliberately unproductive is certainly tempting. The only concern is that you might enjoy it too much ...Sun 23 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 10.20 EDTShareThey know what they’re doing when it comes to kissing, toast and horns, so get ready for a French Sunday. A new theory suggests that embracing this intriguing-sounding strategy might just be the secret to life, and, more importantly, to dreading Monday less.Apparently inFrancethe Sabbath really is a complete day of rest; not for the French any running of errands, cleaning or batch cooking. Rather than trying to do everything, they do nothing. And the hypothesis is that the French Sunday – orle dimanche français, as nobody is calling it – is transformative, and stamps out the Sunday Scaries for good.The idea of being deliberately unproductive is certainly tempting. It feels bold and controversial because it’s the antithesis of the modern way of life, where we cram as much as we can into every single second, all aiming to become the most efficient, effective, prolific versions of ourselves. Sacré bleu, exhausting! No wonder we’re not looking forward to climbing back on the hamster wheel on Monday; we haven’t given ourselves a break, in either sense.A French Sunday is not a waste of a day, you’re not being slothful, you are staving off burnout and recharging. Instead of running yourself ragged trying to wring the most out of the weekend, you’re sleeping in, vegging out, relaxing, lolling, pottering, while thinking chic thoughts, or whatever. Perhaps reading a bit, although holding a book takes a lot of energy, so caution is advised.The only potential pitfall with the French Sunday is enjoying it too much, climbing too enthusiastically on board and trying to extend it. Can’t imagine many bosses would approve a proposal to introduce a company-wide French Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, but, you know, God loves a trier. Bonne chance with that.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
