title: Stores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaning | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Capitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spice
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Capitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spice
Content: ‘Our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionHalloweenStores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaningDave SchillingCapitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spiceSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTShareHappy spooky season, everyone! Get those jack-o’-lanterns out, becauseHalloweenis just around the corner!Just kidding, no, it’s not.It’s August, for God’s sake. Every day, I wake up to 90F weather – my skin moist with sweat and my eyelids stuck together. I can’t drink coffee on my porch without being consumed by an army of voracious mosquitoes that seem to find my blood to be the most delicious of all.And it’s not just Los Angeles that’s withering under a summer of discontent. Theeast coast heatwavesare piling up, sending millions of young people to the absolute last place they want to be:an air-conditioned movie theater. But you want to tell me it’s fine to be putting out Halloween decorations? If I don’t store my giant bag of fun-size Twix in a standup freezer, the whole damn thing will melt into chocolate soup. (Don’t even get me started on recent claims you shouldeat soup when it’s hotoutside. It’d rather slurp up my own sweat from a bowl.)Halloween is no ungodly American import – just ask the medieval monks and nuns who marketed it | Michael CarterRead moreWhy am I fuming about this? Even though I love Halloween, I’m mad because our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun. In August. I find all of that unacceptable. It feels like a violation of the natural order, a realignment of one of the few glorious constants left in the world. I yearn to go back to the tidy order of holidays, where no two ever cross paths. At most, Halloween celebrations should start in late September. Not a month after Independence Day. I fear those days are done, that our world has irrevocably changed and I need to start getting ready to give in to the new normal.I first became aware of Halloween’s creep into the summer during a recent sundries run at Target. There arecostumes, life-size skeletons, treats and various decorationson offer in-store. I’ve seen massive candy bags positioned to move at CVS. There’s even a smattering of greeting cards, which I find doubly frustrating, as I’ve never in my life considered buying someone a card for Halloween, a holiday that most adults spend binge drinking or squeezing into provocative outfits. What does a Halloween greeting card even say? “I Boo-lieve You Should Get an Uber Home”? “Have a Spooktacular One-Night Stand With Your Marginally Attractive Co-Worker”?On that Target outing, my friend Halle (an admitted Halloween pervert) bought a miniature cauldron from the growing, metastasizing spooky section. I asked what she expected to do with such a trivial piece of merchandise. “Maybe I can put my keys or some change in here.” For two months? Then what? Do you sayBack to the closet with youand wait another nine months before getting your coin cauldron out again?double quotation markIf the data says we want Halloween in the heat, then data shall be respected and worshipped. Who am I to argue with hard numbers?I know there are people with boxes and boxes of festive decorations who swap them out season after season. Christmas ends, but Easter is just around the corner. Once that’s done, you chuck the bunny rabbits and start bedazzling your home with American flags to prep for the Fourth of July. Now I’m seeing the insidious truth: we aren’t far off from that Fourth-to-Halloween corridor shrinking even further. I see a world in which witches, demons and vampires slowly start bleeding into our patriotic revelries. It’ll get to the point where some of us might start thinking Frankenstein’s monster fought at the battle of Yorktown.One day, we’ll all just celebrate whichever holidays we want, whenever we feel like it. As the climate crisis renders the idea of distinct seasons and unique weather conditions a relic of a bygone era, why wouldn’t we just all live our own little celebratory truths? Even if my local store isn’t carrying Halloween decorations, I could feasibly buy them year-round on Amazon – my mailbox jammed up with boxes of plastic fangs, fake blood and green grease paint. If it never gets cold again, then Halloween can be whenever. Though I suppose the lifestyle I’m describing already has a name and it’s “being goth”.It could be that our society is naturally evolving to be unbound by passé limitations such as “calendars” and “nature”. Instead of using holidays to mark the phases of the harvest or cycles of the moon (boring), they can be dictated by big data (chill and modern). Surely retailers around the country have statistics that point to consumers having a hankering for Halloween by August. Otherwise, why would Target be hawking rubber bats or decorative ghosts right now? We’re giving ourselves over to analytics in almost every other sector of our lives. Why not holidays?From bone-dry to soaked to the bone, welcome to the age of climate whiplash | Aditya ChakraborttyRead moreIf the data says we want Halloween in the heat, then data shall be respected and worshipped. Who am I to argue with hard numbers? If the sun’s always shining, the grass is consistently brown and the acrid bite of wildfire smoke is clogging our lungs, the average human being might not be able to differentiate between the phases of our natural world. The only way for me to not continue to rage against this phenomenon is to surrender to capitalism completely. Instead of putting my finger out and seeing which way the wind blows, I just have to pop into Target to know what season it is.The cognitive dissonance I might feel carrying my friend’s cauldron to my car in August is something my son might never feel. Time passes under the pall of climate control and fluorescent lighting. Our lives are measured by the movement of currency undulating and cresting like waves in the ocean. As this existentially crippling revelation washes over me, I take comfort in one thing:Soon, sooner than you think, it will be pumpkin spice season.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsHalloweenOpinionClimate crisisUS weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s foreign policy: work in progress | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The prime minister has focused on domestic affairs since coming to office. But at a time of global disruption, he will need to define Britain’s place in the world
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The prime minister has focused on domestic affairs since coming to office. But at a time of global disruption, he will need to define Britain’s place in the world
Content: ‘Where Washington is concerned, Andy Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump.’Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Where Washington is concerned, Andy Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump.’Photograph: ReutersOpinionForeign policyThe Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s foreign policy: work in progressEditorialThe prime minister has focused on domestic affairs since coming to office. But at a time of global disruption, he will need to define Britain’s place in the worldSun 23 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.16 EDTShareArun of volatility in domestic British politics in recent years has tracked a period of global turbulence, and yet foreign policy over the same period has been an area of relative stability. What little is known about Andy Burnham’s approach to international relations expresses more continuity with Sir Keir Starmer’s administration than deviation. In negotiations with the EU, the red lines that prohibit membership of the single market or customs unionstill stand. Where Washington is concerned, Mr Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump, but his predecessor had already swapped that approach for a cooler pragmatic tone by the end of his tenure.The new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has opened a gooddialogue with Marco Rubio, his US counterpart. Such is the density of integration in defence and security matters that incoming UK prime ministers, regardless of ideology, have little choice but to invest time in cultivating a bond with whoever sits in the White House. Anyone hoping for a spectacular transatlantic rupture and sudden clinch with Brussels will be disappointed.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband and Marco Rubio.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPASome patterns of consistency date back beyond the recent transfer of power within the Labour party to the previous Conservative administrations. Support for Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression was one of the few creditable positionstaken by Boris Johnson, and that line has held through four transfers of power in Downing Street.The process of rebuilding functional relations with European neighbours predated the 2024 general election. Rishi Sunak negotiated theWindsor frameworkfor Northern Ireland. He also ditched a bill that threatened chaos for businesses by vaporising retained EU laws without a timetable to replace them.The business secretary who executed that U-turn in defiance of the Tories’ fanatical Eurosceptic tendency wasKemi Badenoch. It was not a choice she highlighted in her subsequent bid to become Conservative leader. By then the party, relieved of the burden of governing responsibility, was in no mood to consider the merits of pragmatism where Europe was concerned.Having withdrawn to an ideological comfort zone, the Tories still cannot pretend that Brexit has been a success. Sir Keir became gradually more confident in attributing Britain’s economic woes to the terms of departure from the EU. But the shift was largely rhetorical because he was locked into a manifesto commitment that precluded a substantial change of direction. Mr Burnham hasaccepted the same constraintas a condition of his hand-me-down electoral mandate.Having accepted the parameters of Boris Johnson’s hardBrexitand acknowledged Britain’s security dependency on Washington, the prime minister doesn’t have much room to innovate in foreign policy. Nor has he shown much interest, focusing instead on domestic issues that are much more salient to voters than geopolitics.That is a rational priority for a new leader hoping to win over sceptical voters. But with no sign of global volatility abating, an international crisis will force itself on to Mr Burnham’s agenda soon enough. Global strife, especially when it whips up economic headwinds, quickly manifests itself as pressure to act in domestic politics. The prime minister has proved adept at connecting with an audience close to home. That advantage will be degraded if he cannot also connect his domestic agenda to a coherent strategy for engagement with the wider world.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyOpinionAndy BurnhamKeir StarmerLabourEd MilibandMarco RubioDonald TrumpeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at pace | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: As a Brussels deadline looms with over €10bn at stake, Péter Magyar’s first three months have been transformative in addressing a corrupt legacy
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: As a Brussels deadline looms with over €10bn at stake, Péter Magyar’s first three months have been transformative in addressing a corrupt legacy
Content: Péter Magyar speaks during a ceremony in Budapest marking the country's national day.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPéter Magyar speaks during a ceremony in Budapest marking the country's national day.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionPéter MagyarThe Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at paceEditorialAs a Brussels deadline looms with over €10bn at stake, Péter Magyar’s first three months have been transformative in addressing a corrupt legacySun 23 Aug 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.06 EDTShareSome elections are more important than others. Since taking office in May, Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has embarked upon the country’s most far-reaching and dramatic programme of transformation since the fall of communism in 1989. Mr Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orbán,establisheda soft autocracy which thrived on corruption and, over 16 years, exerted its grip on most areas of Hungarian life, from religion to culture and the media. It is being dismantled at extraordinary pace.Last week, a newly appointed presidenttook officefollowing thesackingof Tamás Sulyok, accused by Mr Magyar of having rubber-stamped the erosion of the rule of law in the country. In stark contrast, András Baka is a former president of Hungary’s supreme court, a role he was removed from by the Orbán regime in an actionjudgedunlawful by the European court of human rights.On Hungary’s national day last Thursday, news bulletins returned to the main state television channel, having beenshut downfor six weeks. In July, viewers had encountered a blank screen along with the message: “Public media should not lie. We are sorry for doing it for so long.” Ending naked bias on state TV was one of Mr Magyar’s key pledges, in a campaign that saw him buck an electoral system weighted in favour of Mr Orbán and win alandslide.The tempo has been equally relentless when it comes to attacking networks of corruption and clientelism built up over a decade and a half. Well over €100bn in public funds, including billions of euros of EU money, is believed to have been siphoned off during the Orbán years. Investigators have beenempoweredto go after it via a new National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Mr Magyar has also confirmed Hungarianparticipationin the European public prosecutor’s office, enabling the EU to better protect itself from financial crime in the country.It will take time forHungaryto feel like a normal pluralist European democracy again. For now, Mr Magyar is functioning as a one-man political whirlwind, heading what amounts to a national unity government elected by voters across the political spectrum. Concerns have been raised over constitutional manoeuvring to ensure many MPs in Mr Orbán’s Fidesz party cannot stand again, and Mr Baka has warned against appearing to take revenge on the former prime minister’s supporters. But a root-and-branch approach to de-Orbánising Hungary was what was needed, and continues to be rewarded by record levels of popularity in polls.The next major threshold is likely to be crossed in the autumn. Brussels hasgivenHungary’s new government until the end of this month to demonstrate that enough is being done on corruption to warrant the release of over €10bn in frozen funds. If, as seems likely, the vast majority of the funds are disbursed, it will seal the ongoing rapprochement between the EU and its former rogue member state.In May, Mr Magyar relocated the prime minister’s office away from a controversially cordoned-off former Carmelite monastery used by Mr Orbán, opening the building up to the public. “I was not elected simply to change the government, but to change the regime,” he hadtoldinterviewers soon after taking power. Three months on, the symbolism is being supplemented by a peaceful political revolution.Explore more on these topicsPéter MagyarOpinionViktor OrbánHungaryEuropean UnionEuropeeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The far right is steering the EU’s response on migration | European Union | The Guardian
description: Letter: Positions once associated with the radical right have travelled well beyond it, says Giuseppe Martinico
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Positions once associated with the radical right have travelled well beyond it, says Giuseppe Martinico
Content: A rally in Madrid calling for changes to EU migration policies. The banner says “Borders Kill”.Photograph: Edu León/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA rally in Madrid calling for changes to EU migration policies. The banner says “Borders Kill”.Photograph: Edu León/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockEuropean UnionLettersThe far right is steering the EU’s response on migrationPositions once associated with the radical right have travelled well beyond it, saysGiuseppe MartinicoSun 23 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 12.58 EDTShareI agree with much of Alberto Alemanno’s analysis (How the far right is tightening its grip over the EU – from the inside, 18 August), but I wonder whether framing this primarily as the far right tightening its grip on the EU risks missing an even more troubling development.What we are witnessing is not simply the success of the far right. It is a broader cultural shift within the European political mainstream.Migrationis perhaps the clearest example. The convergence between governments as politically different as those of Denmark and Italy suggests that positions once associated with the radical right have travelled well beyond it. Parts of the centre-left and centre-right have progressively abandoned a rights-based understanding of migration. More fundamentally, migrants increasingly disappear from the European political conversation aspersons– as bearers of rights whose dignity should constitute a limit to what political majorities may legitimately do.This cultural transformation has been facilitated by an increasingly weak European Commission. The secondUrsula von der Leyencommission was born under the auspices of a strong presidency, but that political authority seems to have progressively evaporated. The response to the Ceuta crisis is revealing. Neither the commission’s president, Von der Leyen, nor its European commissioner for internal affairs and migration,Magnus Brunner, has provided the kind of strong political signal that might counterbalance the competitive hardening of national positions.The problem, therefore, may be deeper than the collapse of the traditional firewall around the far right. The firewall becomes almost irrelevant once much of the mainstream has internalised the assumptions that it was originally supposed to contain.The real question is no longer simply whether mainstream parties cooperate with the far right, but how much of the far right’s understanding of migration, rights and belonging has already become mainstream European common sense.Giuseppe MartinicoProfessor of comparative public law, Dirpolis Institute, Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Pisa, ItalyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: It’s unwise to end local scrutiny of NHS trusts  | Health | The Guardian
description: Letters: Abolishing the role of statutory governors is ill-advised, says Jean Flanagan. Plus a letter from Jonathan Phillips on the abolition of Healthwatch
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Abolishing the role of statutory governors is ill-advised, says Jean Flanagan. Plus a letter from Jonathan Phillips on the abolition of Healthwatch
Content: ‘Local scrutiny by informed practitioners seems an essential check on the powers of a centralising Department of Health and health minister.’Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Local scrutiny by informed practitioners seems an essential check on the powers of a centralising Department of Health and health minister.’Photograph: PA Images/AlamyHealthLettersIt’s unwise to end local scrutiny of NHS trustsAbolishing the role of statutory governors is ill-advised, saysJean Flanagan.Plus a letter fromJonathan Phillipson the abolition of HealthwatchSun 23 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.07 EDTShareI wonder how many members of the public are aware that the latesthealth plan for England, due to be ratified by parliament this autumn, abolishes the role of statutory governors on all of its constituent health trusts?For a number of years I have volunteered to act as a governor at two hospital trusts inYorkshire. As a former health professional and principal nursing educator, I have brought years of experience to the role, for which I have been elected locally. For any organisation to wilfully remove hundreds of such skilled and committed activists from their supportive scrutiny seems ill-advised.Local scrutiny by informed practitioners seems an essential check on the powers of a centralising Department ofHealthand health minister. I suspect that their newspeak of replacement by “more dynamic stakeholders” is shorthand for health industry shareholders. For a Labour government to be proposing such bureaucratic butchery seems strange indeed. I hope a concerned public can prevent this centralisation of hospital oversight.Jean FlanaganScarborough, North YorkshireYour article (21 August) about concerns raised by Healthwatch Rotherham that an AI telephone receptionist used by GP practices could not understand broad Yorkshire accents was amusing, but with serious undertones. Access to GP services is an issue that Healthwatch has highlighted all over the country. Here in Leeds, our work has led to welcome improvement.And what’s happening to Healthwatch? The government is abolishing it, so local people will no longer have a trusted independent organisation to which they can refer problems such as these failings in an AI receptionist.It’s not over yet – the health bill is still being debated. Let’s hope the government sees sense so that the experience of people using health and care is still heard loud and clear. That’s how things get better.Jonathan PhillipsCo-chair, Healthwatch LeedsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: To end homelessness, look to the root causes | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Andy Burnham’s pledge to get all rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Andy Burnham’s pledge to get all rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas
Content: Tents housing rough sleepers line Euston Road in London.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTents housing rough sleepers line Euston Road in London.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockHomelessnessLettersTo end homelessness, look to the root causesReaders respond to Andy Burnham’s pledge to get all rough sleepers off the streets by ChristmasSun 23 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.02 EDTShareAs a vulnerable teenage girl carrying my life in a rucksack, I have been the person Andy Burnham describes people walking past in his article (I won’t abandon anyone to sleep rough on our streets. That’s my £442m promise, 19 August). That experience taught me that homelessness is far more complex than rough sleeping alone, and that ending it takes more than getting people off the streets.Getting everyone in for Christmas is an important ambition. But lasting success means preventing people from reaching crisis point and giving those who do the practical support and opportunities they need. I was lucky. Public sector work gave me structure, stability, and someone willing to believe in my potential.Housing must sit alongside education, healthcare, employment and social mobility, giving people not just somewhere to live, but a genuine route to stability, independence and opportunity.This is why charities and initiatives such asHomewards, with a collaborative, prevention-first approach, are so important. Solving homelessness takes joined-up support, earlier intervention, and a belief that people need routes into housing, work, health, safety and belonging. As Mr Burnham rightly says, homelessness is a problem to solve, not step around. Prevention must be at the heart of that solution.Dr Sabrina Cohen-HattonChief fire officer, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue ServiceThe prime minister’s pledge to end rough sleeping is admirable, and he’s right about the importance of catching people “long before they hit the pavement”. But to succeed, the he must confront the Home Office’s role in creating homelessness. Last year, around 21,000 households in England needed homelessness help after eviction from Home Office accommodation.Research by the Refugee Council and others has highlighted how delayed documentation, inadequate support and too little time to find accommodation leave refugees facing homelessness and destitution within weeks of a being given leave to stay in the UK.Current plans making refugee status more precarious, putting refugees in thousands of pounds of debt and further restricting asylum support will only worsen this. Until the Home Office stops pushing refugees on to the streets, ending rough sleeping will be out of reach.Imran HussainRefugee CouncilAs a psychiatrist, I have seen an increasing number of patients with severe mental health difficulties ending up homeless, and the local council concluding that it doesn’t have a duty to house them as they have made themselves “intentionally homeless” by failing to stick to the rules.This is usually because the patient has used drugs on the premises and they are evicted from their temporary accommodation. They are then expected to demonstrate three months of abstinence while being street homeless before they can try again for accommodation – with no understanding that housing will aid their ability to get off drugs.While I have some sympathy for the local authority’s position, we need to have a system that thinks housing first, with recognition the reducing drug use takes time and requires wraparound support from mental health and drug services.Until that happens, I fear Andy Burnham’s new initiative will result in accommodation being found, but the patient quickly falling foul of the rules, and the local authorities washing their hands of them again.Dr Charles DixonExeterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Is this why close encounters with intelligent aliens have so far eluded us? | Alien life | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers offer their explanations for the absence of hard evidence for extraterrestrial civilisations, in response to an article by Adam Kirsch
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers offer their explanations for the absence of hard evidence for extraterrestrial civilisations, in response to an article by Adam Kirsch
Content: Radio telescope dishes near Socorro,  New Mexico.Photograph: Wim Wiskerke/AlamyView image in fullscreenRadio telescope dishes near Socorro,  New Mexico.Photograph: Wim Wiskerke/AlamyAlien lifeLettersIs this why close encounters with intelligent aliens have so far eluded us?Readers offer their explanations for the absence of hard evidence for extraterrestrial civilisations, in response to an article by Adam KirschSun 23 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.02 EDTShareWhen thinking about why we have not encountered intelligent aliens yet, as Adam Kirsch does (The long read, 11 August), it seems to me that one factor gets neglected: fossil fuels. Alien life could develop intelligence on myriad planets, but to develop advanced technology that would enable them to get off‑world, they need to go through an equivalent of the Industrial Revolution, and that needed first coal, then oil and gas.There could be many intelligent alien races out there, but on planets without an easily accessible fossil fuel equivalent, they’d never get past a 17th-century level of development.Even if we can eventually detect life on planets outside our solar system, we’d never know these civilisations existed, as their signature from afar would be indistinguishable from that of a planet with just plant-like life and a fire ecology.It is entirely probable, as a result, that almost all alien races, if they exist, are living in an eternal equivalent of Game of Thrones’s Westeros, not Iain M Banks’s Culture, doomed never to be detected from afar.Ian SimmonsWestcliff-on-Sea, EssexAdam Kirsch’s article misses one possibility: that any advanced civilisation might simply be keeping its distance. Humans have long imagined such watchers. The Kayapó people of Brazil, for example, tell of Bep Kororoti, a visitor who shared knowledge and helped their ancestors build a stable and sustainable society.It’s easy to imagine a similar conversation among distant observers today. A younger voice might look at our atomic weapons and shake its head, predicting that we’ll finish ourselves off. An older voice might reply that humans have a habit of rebuilding, and that societies like the Kayapó show we can live with balance when we choose. Their verdict might be to wait a while, and see whether we can keep our civilisation going, before attempting contact. Given our history, who could blame them?Miland JoshiBirminghamGiven the age of the universe, estimated at 13.8bn years, it is quite possible that many forms of life and civilisations have arisen, flourished, declined and disappeared (just as humanity seems likely to). The notion that two such phenomena might occur at the same time and thus permit mutual communication would be a mind-boggling cosmic coincidence. So one response to Fermi’s question “Where is everybody?” might be “they all left before we got here” or “they haven’t arrived yet, and we’ll be gone by the time they do”.David WalkerSheffieldMaybe aliens have arrived, but were too small for us to notice? Perhaps they fell down a drain, were eaten by seagulls, or ended up in an ants’ nest?Sheila PrestonShoreham-by-Sea, West SussexHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Newcastle and Liverpool crank up entertainment in fitting Keegan tribute | Newcastle United | The Guardian
description: While the teams produced more promise than polish, this thrilling encounter gave an emotional send-off to a legend of both clubs
Author: Sam Dalling
Headline: While the teams produced more promise than polish, this thrilling encounter gave an emotional send-off to a legend of both clubs
Content: Newcastle supporters display a banner in memory of club favourite Kevin Keegan.Photograph: Newcastle United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNewcastle supporters display a banner in memory of club favourite Kevin Keegan.Photograph: Newcastle United/Getty ImagesNewcastle UnitedAnalysisNewcastle and Liverpool crank up entertainment in fitting Keegan tributeSam Dallingat St James' ParkWhile the teams produced more promise than polish, this thrilling encounter gave an emotional send-off to a legend of both clubsSun 23 Aug 2026 16.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTShareIt’s 4.35pm on Tyneside. William Osula sets Anthony Elanga away, slightly right of centre and just short of 50,000 draw collective breaths. Pace is no issue; Elanga has no shortage of that, and Milos Kerkez won’t catch him.But Newcastle fans have seen this clip before and remember the ending. Muscles tighten, cheeks clench, as they brace themselves for it to start again like it carried on before. (Yet) another memeable‑moment inbound.Iraola ‘wouldn’t have signed up for this result’ but relieved for Liverpool to earn pointRead moreA tiny part of each of them, though, thinks: “Wait, hang on, this is a new season, a fresh start.” The slate is not just clean but has been entirely replaced and is now AI-operated.Elanga takes a touch, a tad heavier ideal but it pushes the ball away from Alisson. A moment of composure follows and Newcastle lead. An entirely goalless league season passed after Elanga’s £55m transfer from Nottingham Forest and now, within five minutes of a new one, his drought is broken.Elanga missed a much easier opportunity against Aston Villa on the 2025-26 opening day, and his confidence never recovered. Can you walk back through a sliding door?Nearly two hours later, there remain just a few precious seconds for Liverpool to salvage something. Victor Muñoz is brought down clumsily by Lewis Hall.Dominik Szoboszlai converts the resulting penalty. 2-2.Muñoz apparently gave Newcastle positive noises about joining them during summer. Then, in a flexing of financial muscle,Liverpoolmet the Osasuna forward’s release clause and to Anfield he went. What was that about sliding doors?View image in fullscreenLiverpool’s Víctor Muñoz – a summer target for Newcastle – is brought down by Lewis Hall to hand the visitors a late penalty.Photograph: Ian Hodgson/APThose two goals bookended an afternoon that was, if you want to do go down that road, a fitting tribute to the recently departed Kevin Keegan. Entertaining but flawed.As a term, legend is so chronically overused now that it is meaningless. ButKeegan is a prime example of the word’s proper application. Shortly before kick-off everyone present paid an emotional tribute to him. Legend. Hero. King. All subjective labels essentially turned objective.With Liverpool, Keegan’s seven trophies in six years – including three titles and the European Cup – set the club up to be the behemoth they now are. Across three spells at Newcastle, he jabbed syringes of hope into a flailing, helpless shell.St James’ Park is not quite the house that Keegan built, but it is no stretch to say it is the house built because of him. Without his steering Newcastle to Second Division safety in 1992 as manager, the club in its current guise might not exist.So, why does Keegan remain so adored? He is in effect a symbol of what football once was and should still be, can be even. Maybe.Forget spreadsheets, financial acronyms and PR-doused messaging. Ignore expected this and that, low blocks and cancelling each other out. Find the joy. Forget perfect; take a risk. Failure and fallibility? Both absolutely OK.Those are sentiments Andoni Iraola and Matthias Jaissle would do well to remember as they look to settle themselves into new gigs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe former, with Liverpool being champions two seasons ago, will be under the greater pressure. A repeat of his start at Bournemouth, where he won only at the 10th time of asking, would be difficult to tolerate.There were promising signs for Iraola, sure. Jérémy Jacquet grew into his debut. Cody Gakpo had only just whipped a strike narrowly off target before his fine equaliser just after half-time. Rio Ngumoha was quiet but that he has impressed sufficiently to start the season opener is itself a plus.View image in fullscreenFlorian Wirtz (centre) and former Newcastle man Alexander Isak again both struggled to make an impact for Liverpool.Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesBut there were familiar failings, too. The full-backs looked shaky and Iraola needs more (much, much more) from both the sums and the whole of the £241m Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak combo.Isak is about as popular in Newcastle as government-mandated balaclava wearing in a heatwave would be, but the stick-cum-abuse he received didn’t seem to bother him. However, what should keep Isak up at night is how he can and must refind the level that rightly saw him tagged one of the Premier League’s best forwards not so long ago. A skied left-footed effort was the closest he came to silencing the heckles.Jaissle is likely to get more slack. Everyone is aware of what Newcastle have, where they are and, most pertinent, what they have lost.Something fresh was absolutely needed but that requires time and patience. There are, and will continue to be, warts, imperfections, things that Bruno Guimarães might have done.A midfield pair sold for north of £180m were replaced on Sunday by a double pivot with a combined aged of 38 and less than 50 league starts. Lewis Miley and Sean Steur looked the part but made mistakes. That they did so seeking the positive option will only endear them to fans. As will more similar performances from Yoane Wissa. A player who last season looked sluggish and largely static, was suddenly full of everything in the No 10 role.A decent start. Room for improvement. Apply that to both sides.Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UnitedLiverpoolanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘Call his agent’: Emery feels Watkins should explain absence from Villa’s rout by Brighton | Aston Villa | The Guardian
description: With Ollie Watkins considering a move to  Al-Hilal and not in the squad in Sunday’s heavy defeat at Brighton, Unai Emery said: ‘This question is for him’
Author: David Hytner
Headline: With Ollie Watkins considering a move to Al-Hilal and not in the squad in Sunday’s heavy defeat at Brighton, Unai Emery said: ‘This question is for him’
Content: Unai Emery fielded Emiliano Buendía up front at Brighton given absences and injuries.Photograph: Steve Bardens/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUnai Emery fielded Emiliano Buendía up front at Brighton given absences and injuries.Photograph: Steve Bardens/AMA/Getty ImagesAston Villa‘Call his agent’: Emery feels Watkins should explain absence from Villa’s rout by BrightonEngland forward is considering move to Al-Hilal‘This question is for him … I answer only with silence’David Hytnerat the Amex StadiumSun 23 Aug 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnai Emery did nothing to deny that Ollie Watkins had refused to play for Aston Villa in their sobering4-0 defeat by Brightonat the Amex on Sunday. The head coach had a selection crisis up front with Brian Madjo and Tammy Abraham injured. However, he did not include Watkins in the matchday squad as the England striker considers a move to Al-Hilal in Saudi Arabia.Emery was forced to rely on the attacking midfielder Emiliano Buendía as an emergency striker and his team disappeared without trace on the south coast. They were 4-0 down after 31 minutes and had their new signing João Gomes sent off on his debut in the 40th minute. Gomes kicked up and out at the Brighton striker Georginio Rutter after being dispossessed by him.Brighton hammer Aston Villa and João Gomes red adds to Unai Emery’s painRead moreAl-Hilal have made a number of bids for Watkins, all of which have been rejected. It is understood the 30-year-old is open to the move and Emery talked on Friday like a manager who was realistic about the sale happening. Villa would plainly like to replace Watkins should he depart as they approach the end of another difficult summer window. They have already sold Ezri Konsa, Morgan Rogers, Lucas Digne and Youri Tielemans, while they are expected to move on Emiliano Martínez.Emery was asked why he had not picked Watkins against Brighton. “This question is for him,” he said. “I can answer only with my silence.” Emery was then asked if Watkins had refused to play, to which he said: “I think you can call him and you can call his agent and he can respond.”The Guardian have contacted Watkins’s agent for comment.“He [Watkins] can only explain his answer, I can’t,” Emery added, after being asked if he felt let down by Watkins.Emery reported that Madjo would be out for “two weeks more … more or less” while attacking midfielder Johan Manzambi – who has been the club’s marquee summer signing – would “need maybe some days more [than that]”. He was unclear about a timeframe for Abraham’s return.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Emery talked up the resistance of his players in the second half against Brighton and said he was optimistic about finding solutions for the season ahead. But he returned to the difficult preparations for the opening fixture, noting that: “Two strikers are injured and another striker gives his answer.”The head coach added: “This problem [with the transfer market] … we had every season and every season we overcame it. It’s something we have to accept and always we reacted, especially the players. This is something hard for us every year but we are calm. With this result, it’s more difficult to explain but calm, work, be positive and find solutions for the next week and after the transfer window.”Explore more on these topicsAston VillaUnai EmeryBrighton & Hove AlbionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maresca concedes Manchester City ‘a work in progress’ after hair-raising escape | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Enzo Maresca admitted his Manchester City team were a ‘work in progress’ after they beat Bournemouth in their opening game
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Enzo Maresca admitted his Manchester City team were a ‘work in progress’ after they beat Bournemouth in their opening game
Content: Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca talks to the newly-shorn Erling Haaland after their late win against Bournemouth.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APView image in fullscreenManchester City head coach Enzo Maresca talks to the newly-shorn Erling Haaland after their late win against Bournemouth.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APManchester CityMaresca concedes Manchester City ‘a work in progress’ after hair-raising escapeGvardiol’s stoppage-time strike gives City points‘I’m looking for solutions. When you win games it helps’Jamie Jacksonat the Etihad StadiumSun 23 Aug 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca said Manchester City remain a “work in progress” after Sunday’slast-gasp win over Bournemouthat the Etihad Stadium.Marc Guéhi’s 85th-minute equaliser and Josko Gvardiol’s 91st-minute winner gave City’s new manager victory in his first game, after Marcus Tavernier’s first-half strike for the visitors.Guéhi and Gvardiol late show earns Manchester City dramatic win against BournemouthRead moreMaresca thought his side performed similarly to last Sunday’s3-0 Community Shield lossto Arsenal. “I feel in the same position as after Arsenal,” the Italian said. “It’s normal you judge after results but I don’t see big changes. Unfortunately, this is a work in progress and I’m looking for solutions. For sure when you win games it helps.“If you think of the Premier League – it won’t happen that you will concede nothing. The goal we conceded was their first shot. They had two or three dangerous moments but it’s how you react. We’ve still got [Erling] Haaland, Elliot [Anderson], Marc [Guéhi], Nico O’Reilly [who all started], who are in pre-season still. It’s a huge difference in terms of physicality and we are going to get better and better.”Before the game City unfurled a huge tifo bearing his image that said: “Welcome back Enzo.” He said: “It is the perfect day. I was very pleased to see the banner when the game started. We gave them [fans] the joy at the end. It was quite emotional. The spirit was fantastic. It’s a game we deserved to win [but] you don’t need to wait for the last five minutes. We missed chances, then they scored and it became more complicated.”Maresca fielded Guéhi in an unfamiliar midfield role. “I know Marc from [ Crystal] Palace and I always thought he could play as a midfielder because he is very good,” the manager said. “So we tried it for a few days and I think he was quite good. He gives us a solution for the future,.”In his first game managingBournemouth, Marco Rose came close to leading them to a first away win against City. “We’re competitors, we came here to win for the first time,” said the German. “We were in a good way to do so. But we did many good things. We have a lot of things to improve. At the end, how the game went was quite unlucky to lose that way. We had two situations – one corner kick and one attacking [move] – when we defended too passively.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We need to defend the corner better and the second goal was just too passive. We always try to push up – we want to defend higher. Here you need to find the right triggers and it’s hard to press. We did it really well until the end.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityEnzo MarescaBournemouthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brydon Carse handcuffed by police outside nightclub prompting ECB investigation | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: A social media video showed the England and Durham bowler being apprehended by police outside a Derby nightclub, but he was released without charge
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: A social media video showed the England and Durham bowler being apprehended by police outside a Derby nightclub, but he was released without charge
Content: Brydon Carse took part in England nets before the first Test but was released and played for Durham in their win against Derbyshire.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrydon Carse took part in England nets before the first Test but was released and played for Durham in their win against Derbyshire.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamBrydon Carse handcuffed by police outside nightclub prompting ECB investigationEngland fast bowler released without chargeIncident happened in Derby as Durham celebrated winTanya AldredSun 23 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrydon Carse has become the latest England cricketer involved in a late-night incident after footage emerged of the fast bowler in police handcuffs outside a bar in Derby.The England and WalesCricketBoard has confirmed it is investigating the incident, which occurred after Durham, the Division Two leaders, completed a three-day thrashing of Derbyshire in the County Championship on Saturday. Matthew Potts and Ben Stokes can also briefly be seen in the footage.“We are aware of an incident, which is reported to have taken place in Derby last night, and are currently investigating,” read the ECB statement. “We will provide a further update when possible.”According to reports, Carse was released without charge.Trescothick keen on England role under incoming Fleming: ‘It’s a wonderful place to be’Read moreThe incident comes after a spate of bad publicity off the field for England and just five days after Joe Root, the returning England captain, spoke of his desire for his players to be “really good role models, good human beings”.England’s winter tour of Australia was rocked by various off-field incidents, includingthe infamous boozy week in Noosaduring a mid-Ashes break andthe hushed-up accountof Harry Brook being punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington last November, the night before leading England out in a one-day international against New Zealand. Then this summer, Stokes and Gus Atkinson were suspended for the second Test against New Zealand afterbreaking the team’s newly imposed midnight curfewfollowing the first Test win – an incident that was the catalyst forStokes’s shock retirementfrom international cricket.Stokes himself has said cricket has a drinking culture. This month, he told the For the Love of Cricket Podcast: “We are in 2026 now, where the game has gone more professional over the years, and one thing that has stayed within cricket is its relationship with alcohol – from club cricket it works its way up.”Carse was England’s leading wicket-taker during the Ashes series but injury has kept him on the sidelines this season. He was picked in the super-sized squad for the Headingley Test against Pakistan but released to play forDurham. He is in the squad for the second Test at Lord’s.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe was not on England duty at the time of the incident but is centrally contracted. He serveda three-month banin 2024 for historic betting offences between 2017 and 2019.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamDurhamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arthur Fils wins first Masters title after beating Frances Tiafoe in Cincinnati final | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Arthur Fils, the 22-year-old Frenchman, beat Francis Tiafoe 6-3, 1-6, 6-0 in the final of the Cincinnati Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Arthur Fils, the 22-year-old Frenchman, beat Francis Tiafoe 6-3, 1-6, 6-0 in the final of the Cincinnati Open
Content: Arthur Fils holds aloft the Rookwood Cup after defeating Francis Tiafoe in the Cincinnati Open final.Photograph: Matthew Stockman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArthur Fils holds aloft the Rookwood Cup after defeating Francis Tiafoe in the Cincinnati Open final.Photograph: Matthew Stockman/Getty ImagesTennisArthur Fils wins first Masters title after beating Frances Tiafoe in Cincinnati final22-year-old wins 6-3, 1-6, 6-0Fils now ranked No 11 in worldTumaini Carayolat the Lindner Family Tennis CenterSun 23 Aug 2026 18.59 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArthur Fils has always believed he was on the path to the very top of his chosen sport. Even when others considered him too young, too green or far too self-confident, he has entered the biggest tournaments in the world with the intention of winning them, ambitions he did not hesitate to express.On a historic afternoon in Mason, Ohio, Fils took an huge step forward in pursuit of those massive goals as the 22-year-old became a Masters 1000 champion for the first time in his young career. His greatest achievement was secured with a supreme mental effort under pressure as the Frenchman dragged himself back into contention after a desperate second set, recovering to defeat Frances Tiafoe 6-3, 1-6, 6-0 and win the Cincinnati Open.Jannik Sinner and Jack Draper out of US Open as injuries take their tollRead moreEven before a ball was struck, this was a historic moment: the first ATP Masters 1000 final played between two black players. The pair have built such a great rapport that before this match, the biggest final of their careers, they cracked jokes together as they departed the practice courts side-by-side. After taking a customary picture with the guest invited on-court to deliver the coin toss, Fils insisted on taking a picture with Tiafoe alone to mark the occasion.However, they were far more conscious of the enormous opportunity before them. One winnable match stood between each man and their first ever Masters 1000 title. That shared tension is perhaps what made for a disjointed battle, with sharp momentum swings and minimal rhythm. In the end, it was Fils who managed his emotions at the beginning of the final set and willed his best tennis to the surface when it mattered most.This victory hopefully marks the end of a cruel period in Fils’s career and the ascension of a special talent capable of remaining at the top for many years. He has long been one of the best young players on the tour and until last year he was steadily rising. His momentum was broken by a series of injuries, starting with a stress fracture in his back that essentially sidelined him for nine months until this February. He then endured an injury to his hip and back area that forced him to miss the French Open this year. Fils has finished only one grand slam tournament without an injury, Wimbledon this year, since the 2024 US Open.Between those injuries, however, Fils has been comfortably one of the best players in the world and this result is merely reflective of that. Despite his injury layoffs, he now sits at No 5 in the ATP race and at a career high ranking of No 11. With Jannik Sinner absent and Carlos Alcaraz only just returning from his four month wrist injury layoff, he heads into the US Open as part of the top group of contenders competing for their first grand slam title.View image in fullscreenArthur Fils (right) embraces Frances Tiafoe after their three-set final.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesAs was the case for much of this week, Fils burst into the match serving at an incredible level from the start, with five aces in his first three service games.With Tiafoe struggling to land his first serve, Fils broke serve in his opening return game and he followed up his supreme serving by relentlessly attacking his forehand as he rolled through the first set.Tiafoe had been so mentally tough all week and he immediately reset after being outplayed in the first set. After being handed a break from Fils at the beginning of set two with a loose, erratic service game, Tiafoe began to find rhythm behind his first serve and it freed up his groundstrokes in turn. He spent the remainder of the set striking the ball so cleanly and rushing Fils with his early shotmaking and he eased through to level the match. Just 54 minutes into the encounter, they were in a deciding set.While Tiafoe soared, Fils’s entire game had been in freefall throughout the second set. After a brief bathroom break, Fils immediately trailed 0-30 on his serve at the beginning of set three. He responded with ample first serves and relentless aggression off both wings, recovering to seal an essential hold at the start of the decider. Having halted the momentum against him, Fils resumed his serving dominance and took control of the baseline as he dominated an erratic Tiafoe.Fils leaves Cincinnati having provided another supreme exhibition of his talent, and more evidence in favour of the increasingly popular belief that he could be the player to challenge Sinner and Alcaraz once they are both healthy and at full strength again.His forehand, with all its monstrous pace and spin, is the biggest groundstroke on the tour, and his excellent backhand means there is no safe place on the court against him once the ball is in play. He is serving better than he ever has and very few players move as well as him.Most importantly, though, he has full belief in his capacity to achieve great things on the court, and he continues to move in the direction of those objectives.Explore more on these topicsTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Frustrated Lewis Hamilton claims Ferrari strategy cost him F1 Dutch GP podium | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Britain’s Lewis Hamilton said talks were needed at Ferrari as to why they delayed bringing teammate Charles Leclerc into the pits at the Dutch Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Britain’s Lewis Hamilton said talks were needed at Ferrari as to why they delayed bringing teammate Charles Leclerc into the pits at the Dutch Grand Prix
Content: Fourth-placed Lewis Hamilton reckoned he could have improved his finishing position if Ferrari had been more decisive.Photograph: Antonin Vincent/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFourth-placed Lewis Hamilton reckoned he could have improved his finishing position if Ferrari had been more decisive.Photograph: Antonin Vincent/DPPI/ShutterstockFormula One 2026Frustrated Lewis Hamilton claims Ferrari strategy cost him F1 Dutch GP podiumBriton says team too slow to pit Charles Leclerc‘It’s something that we need to discuss offline’Giles Richardsat ZandvoortSun 23 Aug 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has told his Ferrari team that they must up their game if he is to remain in the Formula One world championship fight after the British driver was angry with strategy calls atthe Dutch Grand Prix, comparing them unfavourably with the decisive way his former team ­Mercedes had acted.The race was won by McLaren’s Lando Norris from Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and George Russell. Hamilton was fourth but believed he might have had a shot of a podium hadFerrarimoved Charles Leclerc aside sooner when Hamilton, on a different tyre strategy, was quicker than his teammate.Lando Norris denies Antonelli in F1 Dutch GP after Verstappen crashes out of home raceRead more“Great way of wasting time, good job,” was his unusually blunt admonishment when Ferrari finally pitted Leclerc. In contrast Russell had been given swift instruction to move over for Antonelli in the final stages of the race when the Italian was similarly on much faster rubber.“I think what’s clear is I’m looking ahead and seeing Mercedes execute like that,” Hamilton said. “They’ve got the car, they’re fighting for the championship, in the lead and they did it straight away. Here, I’m sitting back, losing seconds. It’s something that we need to discuss offline.”Despite Antonelli finishing second he has extended his lead over Russell and Hamilton, who are now 59 points behind the Italian, and Hamilton was adamant that his team could not afford to drop any points.“Today was definitely frustrating for me,” he added. “I’m here to win and I really believe that this team can win. To win championships you have to pick up every point. The last few races have been difficult with penalties and today I lost several seconds behind Charles which I think ultimately would have made the difference at the end.“My goal is to try and lead this team to the championship and we’ve got some work to do for sure.”Mercedes’ quick intervention with team orders was questioned, not least by Russell at the time given he is also vying for the title, but the British driver accepted it had been the right call.“We’ve always said as a team, when we’re on different strategies, we’re never going to fight, that’s always just been our sort of rules,” he said. “Kimi was ahead of me anyway, so he deserved to finish ahead. When you’re in the race, you want to fight for every single position but with the pace, with a new tyre, he would have overtaken anyway. So it’s the right decision.”Toto Wolff maintained it had been a straightforward on the pit wall. “Team orders are always harsh from one drivers’ perspective but it is what we always discussed,” the Mercedes team principal said. “We are not losing time with each other if there are competitors breathing down our neck. Today wasn’t a difficult call.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026FerrariLewis HamiltonFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Le Court claims Tour of Britain glory despite Wiebes’ fourth stage win in five | Tour of Britain Women | The Guardian
description: Mauritian claims landmark victory at Leamington Spa while Wiebes finishes second overall after claiming her 137th career stage victory
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Mauritian claims landmark victory at Leamington Spa while Wiebes finishes second overall after claiming her 137th career stage victory
Content: Kim Le Court lifts her bike aloft after completing her Tour of Britain Women victory at Leamington Spa.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKim Le Court lifts her bike aloft after completing her Tour of Britain Women victory at Leamington Spa.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockTour of Britain WomenLe Court claims Tour of Britain glory despite Wiebes’ fourth stage win in fiveMauritian claims landmark victory at Leamington SpaWiebes finishes second after 137th career stage winJeremy WhittleSun 23 Aug 2026 10.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 18.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKim Le Court sealed overall victory in theTour of Britain Womenin Royal Leamington Spa, as Lorena Wiebes took her fourth sprint win in this year’s race and the 11th stage victory of her career.Wiebes has surpassed Mark Cavendish’s career mark of 10 stage wins and now has the most victories of any rider competing in either the men’s or women’s Tour of Britain. Le Court, who won a stage and finished ninth overall in the Tour de France Femmes earlier this month, based her success on a solo victory in Friday’s uphill finish to the Great Orme, overlooking Llandudno. It was the most significant race victory of the Mauritian rider’s career.Vuelta a España: Britain’s Matt Brennan leaves Pogacar in wake to win stage twoRead more“This win is really special,” she said. “This is my first general classification win and it is a first GC win for me in a team.“People had questioned if I am a GC rider or not, and it is good to know that the mental state is still quite high and I’m glad I could achieve that for me and the team,” the AG Insurance Soudal rider said.The 30-year-old has had a chequered past in the British race, but this year proved the strongest of the overall contenders.“I had a bad experience last year and I just wanted to redeem myself after that,” she said of her 2025 Tour of Britain, when she won the first stage, only to crash out of the race on day two.“In 2015 I came here and I was dead last, so I didn’t have a good experience of the Tour of Britain in the past. I think the challenge is not to carry the form [from the Tour de France Femmes] but to carry the recovery process and make sure you are recovering mentally and physically, so you don’t burn out.”If Le Court was the best overall rider, then Wiebes’s four stage wins allied to second place overall – a matter of days after she won two stages in the Tour de France Femmes – were evidence of her status as the fastest sprinter in the Women’s World Tour.“It feels pretty good because last year we expected way more from the Tour of Britain, but this year it was really successful,” the Dutch rider said. “I’m happy to finish this week off with four victories, and the team worked hard for it.”Wiebes, who is quickly becoming more than simply a fast finisher, admitted that the overall classification was not her ambition but added: “When I crossed the finish line on stage three and was still third on GC, I knew we could fight for second.”View image in fullscreenLorena Wiebes powers to a fourth stage win and second place overall in the Tour of Britain.Photograph: Pete Goding/GodingImages/ShutterstockLe Court, who was placed in an induced coma as a child due to malaria, is one of cycling’s great survivors and has shown immense resilience to become one of the world’s top riders.She has now worn the yellow jersey in the Tour de France Femmes, won stages in both the Tour and Giro d’Italia, the coveted classic Liège-Bastogne-Liège and has now added the overall title in the Tour of Britain to her résumé. The final stage was characterised by a resilient three-rider breakaway that built a lead approaching two-and-a-half minutes until the climbs of Sun Rising Hill and Burton Dassett took their toll and the chasing field picked up speed.Sara Martín, of Movistar, British rider Alice Towers and Eva van Agt, teammate to the 2026 Tour de France Femmes winner, Demi Vollering, at FDJ United-Suez, slipped clear with 110km to race and worked well to distance the peloton.However, in a frenzied final 20km, their advantage was steadily eroded as the peloton accelerated on the approach to the Warwickshire spa town. Even with under 5km remaining the trio still led by half a minute but they were finally reeled in with barely a kilometre to race, as Wiebes once again moved ahead of her peers to claim another success.Explore more on these topicsTour of Britain WomenCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 3: Birmingham City | Birmingham City Women | The Guardian
description: Returning to the top flight after four seasons, Amy Merricks’ side have added WSL experience in a bid to consolidate
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Returning to the top flight after four seasons, Amy Merricks’ side have added WSL experience in a bid to consolidate
Content: Birmingham secured promotion to the WSL on the final day of last season. Photograph: Leila Coker/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesBack in the top flight after four seasons, Amy Merricks’ side have added WSL experience in a bid to consolidateByTom GarrySun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:12th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:1st (WSL2)ProspectsFounding members of the Women’s Super League when it launched in 2011, Birmingham are back in the top flight after four years in the second tier, having won promotion as WSL2 champions on the final day of last season. After a decent summer transfer window, Birmingham look to have a fighting chance of staying up, and perhaps even surprising a few teams, while off the pitch they are the best-equipped of the three promoted sides to cement themselves in the top division.Forwards Lily Crosthwaite and Wilma Leidhammar and defender Neve Herron, are all 23-years-old and likely to continue improving. Birmingham have also added players with WSL experience, such as the former Brighton goalkeeper Sophie Baggaley and the centre-back Millie Turner.Inconsistency was nearly their downfall last season; they won the most games in WSL2, but also lost six times. They delivered under pressure, boosted by the performances of Leidhammar after her club-record arrival in January, ensuring they avoided a repeat of the heartbreak of 12 months earlier when they missed out on promotion on the final day. Nonetheless, Birmingham are still a long way off from the days when they were runners-up in the top tier and their first two away fixtures are against Manchester City and Chelsea. They also host fellow promoted sides Crystal Palace and Charlton relatively early in the campaign and those home fixtures could be key to building confidence.BFCOff-field pictureBirmingham’s women’s team were sold to the club’s ownership group in February, with Shelby Companies Limited – an affiliate of Knighthead Capital Management – owning 97%. The remaining 3% was purchased by investors including the former England midfielder Karen Carney and the four-time grand slam tennis champion Kim Clijsters. The club appear to be in a relatively healthy position with ambitious owners determined to reestablish the 2012 FA Cup winners as a regular, competitive presence in the WSL. They train at the recently renovated Knighthead Performance Centre, on the same site as the men’s team’s former Wast Hills training base, with a new gym among other extensive refurbishments.The managerAmy Merricks has been in charge since April 2024 She holds a Uefa Pro Licence and was 30 years old when she was appointed by Birmingham. She has previously coached within the England youth setup as well as at Gillingham, Millwall and Brighton, where was stepped up to be interim manager three times.Star signingView image in fullscreenLisa Naalsund arrives from Manchester United to boost Birmingham’s midfield.Photograph: DeFodi Images/Getty ImagesBirmingham have recruited players with international experience, including the Canada defender Marie Levasseur from Montpellier, but their two most eyebrow-raising additions are Turner and Lisa Naalsund from Manchester United. They were starting members ofUnited’s FA Cup-winning side of 2024and played in a Women’s Champions League quarter-final as recently as April. Naalsund will be an influential force in the midfield – she has won 39 caps and was part of Norway’s squad at last year’s Euros.Stat attackBirmingham topped WSL2 last season despite not scoring the most goals or conceding the fewest. One stat they led was big chances, Opta’s metric for opportunities where it is reasonable to expect the attacker to score. While their tally will be much harder to repeat in the top flight, their attacking process looks in good order.BFCSet for a breakthroughThere is plenty of excitement at Birmingham about another of their new signings, the 19-year-old France youth forward Chancelle Effa Effa, who arrived from Le Havre for a fee understood to be about €120,000 (£100,000) this month. She broke into Le Havre’s first team at the age of 15 and scored 17 times in 28 games for France’s Under-17 and Under-19 teams, having helped France win 2023’s Under-17 Euros.What they say …“We know it’s going to be a massive challenge, but it’s a challenge that, as players, you thrive upon.As long as we can take that togetherness, that relentlessness, into the games, I’m sure we’re going to be just fine”– Chelsea Cornet.Where are they playing their home games?Birmingham play their home fixtures at St Andrew’s, which has been the women’s team’s home since 2021. They set a club record attendance for a women’s game there on the final day of the 2024-25 season – 8,749. Long-term, the club have announced plans to build a new women’s team stadium as part of the ‘Sports Quarter’, which also includes the proposed 62,000-seater men’s team Powerhouse Stadium as well as an indoor arena, training ground facilities and a new railway station.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Birmingham City WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: European football: Torres double rescues PSG point after Rennes threaten shock win | European club football | The Guardian
description: Julián Alvarez was booed by Atlético Madrid fans during the 2-2 draw with Villarreal while Mohamed Salah scored his first goals for Trabzonspor in their 2-1 win against Istanbul Basaksehir
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Julián Alvarez was booed by Atlético Madrid fans during the 2-2 draw with Villarreal while Mohamed Salah scored his first goals for Trabzonspor in their 2-1 win against Istanbul Basaksehir
Content: Ferran Torres (in white strip) scores Paris Saint-Germain’s equaliser at Rennes.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersView image in fullscreenFerran Torres (in white strip) scores Paris Saint-Germain’s equaliser at Rennes.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersEuropean club footballEuropean football: Torres double rescues PSG point after Rennes threaten shock winAtlético’s Alvarez booed by own fans in home drawSalah scores first goals in Trabzonspor victoryGuardian sportand agenciesSun 23 Aug 2026 17.48 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 10.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFerran Torres came off the bench to score a late double ⁠on his debut asParis Saint-Germainrallied from two goals down to draw ⁠2-2 with ⁠hosts Rennes in their Ligue 1 season opener on Sunday. Sebastian Szymanski and Esteban Lepaul gave ⁠the home side a 2-0 lead at half-time but PSG piled on the pressure in ⁠the second period and were rewarded with a point.Rennes led ​inside nine minutes as ‌Szymanski’s shot went ‌in off the post to provide the perfect start ‌to the season for the hosts. Désiré Doué thought he had levelled for PSG, but his effort was ruled out for offside, and the home side made it 2-0 seven minutes before the break. Przemyslaw Frankowski found space ‌on the right wing and his low cross into the box was turned into the ​net by Lepaul.José Mourinho marks Real Madrid return with late drama and touch of humilityRead morePSG pulled a goal back with 19 minutes remaining as Torres’ clever run beat the offside trap and he collected a Fabián ⁠Ruiz pass and scored his first goal for the ​club since ​his move fromBarcelona. Torres ​then levelled the scores in the 83rd ​minute, and again ‌Ruiz was ​the provider ​with a cross from the left, as the Spanish duo dragged their side back into the contest but could not help them find a winner.Atlético Madridsalvaged a 2-2 draw againstVillarrealin La Liga despite having defender Robin Le Normand sent off. Giuliano Simeone grabbed his team a draw after penalties from Gerard Moreno and Georges Mikautadze putVillarrealin front following Marc Pubill’s 59th-minute opener for the hosts.The Atlético head coach, Diego Simeone, brought Julián Álvarez on as a second-half substitute to a chorus of boos from home supporters. The forward walked down the tunnel alone at the end, while his teammates were thanking the Atlético supporters.View image in fullscreenJulián Alvarez leaves the pitch at the end of the game after Atlético Madrid fans booed him during the 2-2 draw with Villarreal.Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty ImagesBarcelonabegan their title defence ⁠and bid for a third successive crown with ⁠a 5-0 victory ⁠at ​Elcheas Raphinha and Fermín López ⁠scored twice each.Mohamed Salah scored his first goals forTrabzonsporwith a brace in their 2-1 win overIstanbul Basaksehir. The former Liverpool forwardjoined the Super Lig sideon a two-year deal at the start of August and made his debut for the club from the bench in their 1-1 draw at Kasimpasa last week. Salah was named in the starting lineup for the clash with Basaksehir and made an instant impact, opening the scoring in the eighth minute.Basaksehir levelled in the 19th minute when Eldor Shomurodov slotted home from the penalty spot, but Salah restored his side’s lead just three minutes into the second half. His brace was enough to clinch victory forTrabzonspor, who return to Super Lig action on 31 August against Amed SK.In Serie A,Ruben Amorimstarted hisMilanreign with a 2-1 victory atTorino. The second-half substitute Adrien Rabiot set up Alphadjo Cissè’s 64th-minute opener and then scored himself three minutes later. Ché Adams scored a stunning consolation deep in stoppage time for Torino.View image in fullscreenAdrien Rabiot scores Milan’s second goal against Torino.Photograph: Valerio Pennicino/Getty ImagesJuventussecured a 1-0 away win against newly promotedFrosinone, but failed to impress in their opening match of the season.Juve, who finished sixth last season, secured all three points thanks to Gleison Bremer’s 22nd-minute header. Luciano Spalletti’s side went on to dominate but failed to put the game beyond doubt. The goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario, on loan from Tottenham, picked up a leg injury and had to be substituted late on, which nearly cost Juve as Frosinone pressed hard in stoppage time, hitting the crossbar.Another of the newly promoted teams,Monza, were thrashed 4-1 by the champions,Inter, on Saturday in the season opener.Leccemade a strong start to the season against the third promoted side,Venezia, on Sunday as they defeated their hosts 2-0 courtesy of second-half goals from Olaf Gorter and Tiago Gabriel.TheBayern Munichstriker Harry Kane was voted the 2026 player of the year in Germany by an association of sports journalists on Sunday, finishing ahead of teammate Michael Olise. Kicker magazine revealed the results of its yearly polls of members of the Association of German Sports Journalists. Kane, the England captain, won the award after a stellar season in which he won the Bundesliga and German Cup while Bayern also reached the Champions League semi-finals. Bayern’s Vincent Kompany was named coach of the year, while their women’s captain, Giulia Gwinn, won the award for best female player.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballParis Saint-GermainRennesLigue 1La LigaAtlético MadridVillarrealnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mateta’s Palace dispute deepens after losing appeals to end contract early | Crystal Palace | The Guardian
description: Jean-Philippe Mateta wants to leave Crystal Palace and failed in an attempt to have the last year of his contract ruled invalid by a tribunal and Fifa
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Jean-Philippe Mateta wants to leave Crystal Palace and failed in an attempt to have the last year of his contract ruled invalid by a tribunal and Fifa
Content: Jean-Philippe Mateta played in Crystal Palace’s 2-0 defeat at Everton on Saturday.Photograph: Craig Galloway/ProSports/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJean-Philippe Mateta played in Crystal Palace’s 2-0 defeat at Everton on Saturday.Photograph: Craig Galloway/ProSports/ShutterstockCrystal PalaceMateta’s Palace dispute deepens after losing appeals to end contract earlyStriker wants move and said final year of deal was invalid29-year-old took his case to tribunal and Fifa but lostEd AaronsSun 23 Aug 2026 06.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 06.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJean-Philippe Mateta is in dispute withCrystal Palaceover the final year of his contract but failed in an attempt to have it ruled invalid by an independent Premier League tribunal and Fifa. The France striker signed a four-and-a-half-year contract when he joined permanently from Mainz in January 2022 after an initial loan, in a deal that also included the option of a 12-month extension. That was activated by Palace in 2024, with Mateta’s contract now due to expire at the end of this season.But it is understood the 29-year-old and his representatives have disputed whether that extension was valid and took the case to an independent tribunal under Premier League regulations last season. Official confirmation of the outcome has not been disclosed, although Palace insist Mateta’s contract remains binding and he played intheir defeat at Evertonon Saturday. Fifa also rejected his claim after ruling it did not have jurisdiction over the dispute. Mateta’s representative has been approached for comment.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Mateta has been trying to force through a move from Selhurst Park for some time and it is understood he has interest from Aston Villa, who are considering whether to sell Ollie Watkins to the Saudi Arabian side Al-Hilal. Mateta failed a medical with Milan in January because of a knee problem after the Italian side had agreed a fee of around £30m and spent two months on the sidelines before returning to help Palace win the Conference League. Mateta was booed by some sections of supporters at first and is likely to get another frosty reception when Manchester City visit south London on Friday night in their first home match of the new campaign.View image in fullscreenJean-Philippe Mateta had a shot hit a post during Crystal Palace’s defeat at Everton.Photograph: Paul Currie/ShutterstockMeanwhile, Pierre Sage has insisted that Ismaïla Sarr will remain at the club despite strong interest from Galatasaray. The Senegal forward missed the 2-0 defeat at Everton due to what Sage described as a “pain in his groin” and Palace’s new manager dismissed reports that the 28-year-old had refused to travel to Merseyside because he wants to leave.“We took the decision before the session with the doctor, the player, and me, to let him get treatment and do an individual session, and he will be back on Monday with us,” he said. “For the moment, we don’t want him to leave.
