He is under contract with us with three years to go and he will be with us on Monday.”Palace are also braced for more interest this week in Adam Wharton and Daniel Muñoz, who has entered the final two years of his contract and has been linked with Everton, Nottingham Forest and Tottenham. They have already agreed a loan move for Chelsea’s Axel Disasi but may be forced into signing another centre back before the deadline if fears over Chadi Riad’s knee injury are proved correct.The Moroccan, who was out for more than a year after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament injury on his second appearance for the club after joining in 2024, was carried off on a stretcher after attempting to block a cross in the second half against Everton. “I hope it will be better than we think,” said Sage. “We await the medical tests.”Explore more on these topicsCrystal PalaceTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Hull punished United defence in victory but Carrick’s attack is bigger area of concern  | Hull City | The Guardian
description: Manchester United again struggled against a back five as the promoted hosts exploited a set-piece weakness
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: Manchester United again struggled against a back five as the promoted hosts exploited a set-piece weakness
Content: A dejected Matheus Cunha (right) of Manchester United during their defeat at Hull.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA dejected Matheus Cunha (right) of Manchester United during their defeat at Hull.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesHull CityAnalysisHull punished United defence in victory but Carrick’s attack is bigger area of concernAndrew BeasleyManchester United again struggled against a back five as the promoted hosts exploited a set-piece weaknessSun 23 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 14.21 EDTShareHull scored nine league goals from set plays last season, the joint-fewest in the Championship. Yet two in 21 minutes earned them avictory over Manchester Unitedon Saturday.It was a disastrous start to the campaign for the visitors. While Michael Carrick said before the gameit would not be easy, he would not have expected victory being so straightforward for Hull. It was a match United simply had to win given the gulf in resources and expectation. Opta rated their chance of victory at 68.9% before kick-off.Carrick tells Manchester United to keep calm and carry on after Hull humblingRead moreUnited’s inability to deal with Oli McBurnie as the target man was painful to watch. Their slack defending on the set pieces from which Hull scored will also draw focus. Their attacking should be the greatest concern, though.A glance at expected goal numbers can paint a false impression. Hull generated 1.01 expected goals to United’s 1.83, so did the visitors deserve to win? The issue is the breakdown of chances that contributed to the total. United had 21 shots, 16 of which were worth less than 0.1 expected goals.This was a theme last season, albeit less obvious when they performed well under Carrick. United’s open-play shots were worth an average of 0.104 expected goals in 2025-26, the third worst rate among teams that finished in the top half of the Premier League. Against Hull, this figure was just 0.087.Not until the 78th minute did a notable opportunity fall to a player they would hope to have one, as Bryan Mbeumo received a through ball from Matheus Cunha. Before that, their highest-value chances fell to Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui. The former has experience as a winger, and started in the attacking midfield trio in United’s 4-2-3-1 formation, but the duo have just 16 top-flight goals between them. They are not reliable chance converters.Chart showing the worst 10 teams for expected goals per open play shot in the 2025-26 Premier LeagueMarcus Rashford is far stronger. He should take Dorgu’s berth in the long term, assuming he remains with the club. His natural attacking instincts may have aided in the creation of better chances in the first half. Regardless, it was alarming how hard United found it to fashion valuable opportunities against a club that conceded the second-most expected goals in the 2025-26 Championship.Hull’s manager, Sergej Jakirovic, used a back five. He deployed three centre-backs on 10 occasions last season, notably in victories in the playoff semi-final second leg against Millwall and the final against Middlesbrough.Chart showing the expected goal value of shots in Hull 2‑0 Manchester UnitedIt worked against United, with the extra bodies at the back able to crowd out attackers. Opta’s shot map showed Hull conceded eight efforts in the “danger zone” – the centre of the penalty area that covers the width of the six-yard box out to the 18-yard line. Five of the eight were headers, which are harder to convert, leaving little else of note. Space in the most valuable real estate came at a premium at the MKM Stadium and United were unable to penetrate it.This structure has caused United problems before. They have now won only one of their last six league matches against teams that started with a back three or five. Leeds won 2-1 at Old Trafford in April with a 3-4-3 formation and used the same system to draw 1-1 two weeks ago in a pre-season friendly. Milan employed the same framework when beating United 4-2 in their final warm-up game.“We got beat, we’re hurt and it’s not a nice feeling. It doesn’t mean it’s going to change the whole direction of how we’re going as a team or as a football club,”Carrick said. As sensible a long-term approach as that may be, United’s attack needs work.Explore more on these topicsHull CityManchester UnitedanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s continued distrust in election integrity has experts eyeing his next move | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: President’s speech, declassification of documents and heightened claims of noncitizen voting have experts concerned
Author: George Chidi
Headline: President’s speech, declassification of documents and heightened claims of noncitizen voting have experts concerned
Content: Donald Trump arrives to deliver remarks in Garden City, New York, on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump arrives to deliver remarks in Garden City, New York, on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026Trump’s continued distrust in election integrity has experts eyeing his next movePresident’s speech, declassification of documents and heightened claims of noncitizen voting have experts concernedGeorge ChidiSun 23 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA series of moves byDonald Trump’s administration to sow doubt in the integrity of US elections has intensified concern among voting experts – and sparked hope among election deniers – that it could declare a national emergency.The White House and US federal agencies have released a string of documents this summer – including disputed analyses of alleged voting by noncitzens and historical intelligence memos – stoking expectations that the US president could move to exert greater control over November’s US midterm elections.Trump used aprimetime television address in Julyto claim – again – that US elections were vulnerable to foreign manipulation, and repeat the lie that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was stolen.Trump’s speech prompted Steve Bannon, his former political strategist, to predict the US president will declare a state of emergency on national security grounds to “protect” elections.“Take your No 2 pencil out,” Bannon, a rightwing commentator,saidon his War Room video podcast on 29 July. “It’s coming. It’s coming. Just block the last week of August out. It’s coming.”While Trump and his allies could try to use a national emergency declaration to delegitimize results of November’s results, experts say such a declaration would not supersede the constitutional restrictions on executive power on election administration. No president has ever attempted to invoke an emergency to assert control over voting.Asked earlier this month by Wayne Allyn Root, a rightwing broadcaster, if he would “declare a national security emergency for elections”, Trump notably did not shoot down the idea.“Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?” the president told Real America’s Voice, a rightwing cable channel. “I’ll leave it at that.”The administration is “trying to lay the groundwork to declare some sort of emergency to nationalize elections”, said Aria Branch, a partner at the Elias Law Group, who led a lawsuit blocking Trump’s previous executive orders on election administration. “I think the president is looking for any opportunity to do that.”‘We need to be prepared for everything’“I mean, listen, I think it is quite obvious that the man is losing his grip in reality, so I think we need to be prepared for everything,” said Santiago Mayer, president of Voters of Tomorrow, a gen Z-led voter advocacy organization. “We have spent a long time thinking and preparing for any eventuality and anything that he might attempt. I think our focus at the end of the day is to turn out enough voters where, no matter what he pulls, it won’t succeed.”Democratic members of US congress have beenwargaming strategiesto respond to executive provocations in recent months, considering scenarios such as AI-generated disinformation videos and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents being dispatched to polls. Progressive organizations in the democracy space have also been preparing for something to happen before the election.Top Democrats simulate election threats as Trump continues assault on votingRead moreThe presence of Tulsi Gabbard, Trump’s former director of national intelligence, at an FBI raid in Fulton county, Georgia,raised questions earlier this year. Gabbard later testified before Congress that she had been leading an investigation into claims of foreign interference in US elections. Gabbard’s team was involved in the seizure and examination of voting equipment in Puerto Rico, and spent months scrutinizing potential vulnerabilities in voting machines and the possibility of foreign interference.When Gabbardresigned on 30 June, Trump named his longstanding ally Bill Pulte as her acting replacement, a widely criticized move by members of both parties, who pointed to Pulte’s lack of intelligence experience. While Jay Clayton later took up the post permanently, Pulte is said to have pushed the election interference narrative in a less-visible role.“This is why Pulte is so important,” Bannon said in July. “So, ah, Jay has got to – Clayton – has big shoes to fill. Every day we’re going to be dogging him on, like, where’s the next release on this.”On the night of Trump’s July address, BannontextedCNN: “We need a National Security Emergency about the midterm elections immediately – this is a powerful predicate for that.”Ty Cobb, a former White House attorney, now a sharp Trump critic, warned of the same whilespeakingto PBS following the president’s July TV address. “Well, I think tonight’s speech is intended to add the predicate that he needs to declare an emergency at or about the time of the elections,” he said.ICE agents at polls is “a virtual certainty”, said Cobb, who questioned whether National Guard officers would also be presented. “Anything to intimidate minority voters, particularly immigrant voters, and also I think anything that allows them to try to seize voting machines, as Trump wanted to do in 2020, but [then-attorney general] Bill Barr explained to him there was just no basis for it.”‘Noncitizen voting … is just not a widespread problem’After Trump’s TV address, a White House “Government Transparency Task Force” – composed of members of the office of the director of national intelligence, the National Security Agency, the Central Intelligence Agency and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) – began releasing declassified “election integrity” documents on the White Housewebsite.The first tranche included declassified intelligence memos which described electronic voting machine vulnerabilities, foreign access to state voter registration data and foreign digital manipulation strategies. Much of the material was already known to the public and amounted to a US intelligence assessment that found no evidence Beijing altered the 2020 vote, which Trump lost.A week later, Trump and his allies quickly seized on an announcement from Mikie Sherrill, the New Jersey governor, that 6,600 non-citizens had registered to vote because of a software error. While fewer than 400 of them voted, the disclosure was used to escalate false claims that there are scores of noncitizens on the voter rolls.On 31 July, DHS released a public notice arguing that New Jersey’s administrative errors demonstrated a need for standardized federal oversight.The taskforce also declassified documents in a Michigan case where the FBI investigated suspected fraudulent voter registrations by a get-out-the-vote organization, in which no criminal charges were filed, and investigative material related to a data scrape of voter information in Maricopa county, Arizona.The pace of releases has been accelerating.On Monday, the taskforce declassified and released investigative files related to an investigation into Chinese intelligence, which disclosed how disgraced former Democratic US representative Eric Swalwell had told FBI agents how he had “occasionally hooked up” with Christine Fang, a Chinese national allegedly engaged in a political influence campaign.On Tuesday, the US Census Bureau released a brief claiming it had identified 24,000 noncitizens voting in the 2020 election in a preliminary match of 128m records. It did not reveal its methodology and was sharply criticized by democracy advocates.“This alleged analysis based on census data fails the laugh test,” said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research. “The administration does not provide a sufficient explanation of how it arrived at these numbers – and for good reason.”Branch, of Elias Law Group, suggested theTrump administrationis “searching for” the legal basis for an executive order. “I think they believe there may be one. I think such a document just doesn’t exist, because the fact is our elections are secure,” she said. “Noncitizen voting in our elections is just not a widespread problem … All of the fear and narrative around that issue is just completely unfounded, and it’s really just to stoke fear and lay the groundwork for future action.”In July, DHS also released an analysis arguing that 278,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in federal elections. It did not reveal its methodology for identifying the noncitizens, either, or disclose how confident its officials were in their assessment. The tool it used to flag noncitizens on voter rollsis knowntobe inaccurate.‘The founders recognized the risk of centralizing power’Asked about the possibility of an executive order declaring a national emergency on elections, the White House did not rule it out, refusing to comment on hypotheticals.“Extreme liberal Democrats are keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections by refusing to vote for the Save America Act,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, referring to legislation that would enforce a crackdown on voting. “The American people overwhelmingly support this commonsense legislation that ensures Americans, and Americans only, decide our elections. President Trump is absolutely right: we fix this now, or we lose our country.”The Save America Act would require states to submit their voter rolls to federal inspection, effectively give DHS the power to de-register anyone it deemed ineligible to vote. The act would also sharply curtail mail-in voting – a practice Trump repeatedly criticized, but has reportedly done himselfas recently as in this week’s Florida Republican primary– and require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and a narrow set of photo IDs to cast a ballot.“I mean, we’ve been closely monitoring what the administration is saying,” said Branch, who sees the rhetoric itself as an act of intimidation.“The constitution is extremely clear on this, and the founders recognized the risk of centralizing power over elections in the executive branch,” she added. “Very helpful, in terms of litigation to push back on these types of efforts.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026Donald TrumpUS politicsRepublicansTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spying device detectors may give domestic abuse victims false sense of security, study finds | Domestic violence | The Guardian
description: Many tools fail to help victims find hidden cameras, microphones and trackers, leaving them at risk of ongoing surveillance
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Many tools fail to help victims find hidden cameras, microphones and trackers, leaving them at risk of ongoing surveillance
Content: Surveillance devices are often marketed as home security or pet tracking tools, but can be misused for spying.Photograph: Pau Barrena/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSurveillance devices are often marketed as home security or pet tracking tools, but can be misused for spying.Photograph: Pau Barrena/AFP/Getty ImagesDomestic violenceSpying device detectors may give domestic abuse victims false sense of security, study findsMany tools fail to help victims find hidden cameras, microphones and trackers, leaving them at risk of ongoing surveillancePriya BharadiaSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCommercial detectors intended to help domestic abuse victims find hidden spying devices may actually give them a false sense of security, a study has found.The consumer detection tools claim to identify hidden cameras, microphones or trackers through methods such as signal-strength readings, infrared lens detection and scanning for wifi or Bluetooth devices.However, researchers at University College London’s computer science department found that many detectorsfail to adequately help users identify hidden surveillance devices, giving them a false sense of security.“There’s quite a great disparity in the capabilities of the [spying] devices themselves and the tools that are available for detecting them,” said the lead author, Akhil Polamarasetty.The researchers said that if the detectors failed to find surveillance devices it meant victims continued to be spied on in their homes unaware.The researchers identified approximately 1,000 covert surveillance products and 500 detection tools sold in the UK through mainstream online platforms, such as Amazon, AliExpress and eBay.Hidden surveillance devices included small cameras or microphones concealed inside everyday household items such as USB chargers, plush toys and clocks.Often marketed as home security or pet tracking tools, the researchers and campaigners said the devices could be misused for spying and abuse.“These devices are so small, it doesn’t actually make sense for them to be used for home security purposes,” said Polamarasetty. “[They’re] essentially designed for spying on people.”The researchers asked 34 study participants to search for hidden surveillance devices on their own inside a simulated living room, and then to do the same again using detection tools. The latter showed only a marginal improvement: participants missed 67% of the hidden devices when searching on their own, compared with a 59% miss rate when using a detector.During the experiment, many participants reported difficulties in interpreting a detector’s readings. Other tools gave out false positives, causing anxiety in the participants, or missed surveillance objects entirely.“Most of the detectors on the market are not designed with the typical consumer in mind,” said Polamarasetty. “Many people do not necessarily understand the limitations of such detectors and risk misinterpreting the results.”He said many of the detection products were not built with at-risk users in mind, often emitting loud sounds that could alert the person spying on them. “They’re absolutely not safe to be used when you’re living with the perpetrator. The devices are not discreet enough.”The researchers made several recommendations for manufacturers of detection devices, including making user guidance clearer and communicating inconclusive readings.However, the authors noted these recommendations alone could not prevent tech-facilitated abuse, and the only real solution was to stop the sale of hidden spy devices.The co-author Dr Leonie Tanczer said: “Most technology is dual-use, and companies have a responsibility to think about how their products can be misused – at the design stage, rather than after the harms emerge.She added: “A camera in things like a showerhead or a plug – I just cannot really see a legitimate reason for that without the intention to monitor someone without their consent.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDomestic abuse law fails to recognise danger of tech abuse, Lords committee toldRead moreThe UK domestic abuse charity Refuge said it had seen a “notable rise” in victims reporting finding hidden microphones or cameras inside their homes. Its policy manager, Bo Bottomley, said: “What is especially worrying is how accessible and affordable these devices are, allowing more perpetrators to weaponise them as a form of control.“We urge the government to review how these products are designed, safety tested, marketed and sold, and to take swift regulatory action to mitigate the risk they pose to survivors,” Bottomley said.Amazon declined to comment. A spokesperson from eBay said the platform “prohibits the sale of many products that are used to transmit or receive signals or for covert surveillance, and all sellers are required to comply with our policies and applicable UK law.“After investigation, we’ve removed two of the three listings shared and we are committed to maintaining a safe and trusted marketplace for our buyers and sellers.”A spokesperson for the Home Office said: “We will not tolerate covert filming or the harassment of victims.“The government has committed to updating controlling and coercive behaviour guidance to reflect clearer recognition of technology-facilitated abuse and we’re making it an offence to take intimate images without consent, including by installing equipment such as cameras to enable people to do so.”AliExpress has been contacted for comment.In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsDomestic violenceSurveillancePrivacynewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to face pressure at Labour conference to recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide | Labour | The Guardian
description: Grassroots groups to urge PM to break with Starmer policy and impose full arms embargo on Israel
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Grassroots groups to urge PM to break with Starmer policy and impose full arms embargo on Israel
Content: Groups want Burnham to accept findings of UN commission of inquiry that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.Photograph: Hassan al-Jedi/APAImages/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGroups want Burnham to accept findings of UN commission of inquiry that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.Photograph: Hassan al-Jedi/APAImages/ShutterstockLabourBurnham to face pressure at Labour conference to recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocideGrassroots groups to urge PM to break with Starmer policy and impose full arms embargo on IsraelAletha AduPolitical correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 07.26 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrassroots Labour groups are gearing up for a conference showdown withAndy Burnhamover Gaza, as the party’s members seek to force the prime minister to recognise Israel’s actions as a genocide and impose a full arms embargo.Momentum, Labour & Palestine, the Campaign for Labour Party Democracy and Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) plan to ramp up pressure on Burnham before his firstLabour conferenceas prime minister next month.The groups are circulating a model motion for Labour members to submit to conference, demanding the government accepts the findings of a UN commission of inquiry thatIsraelhas committed genocide in Gaza, and to impose “comprehensive sanctions”, including a full arms embargo.The motion also demands that ministers impose comprehensive sanctions and ban trade that “aids or assists” Israel’s military actions in Gaza or its unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territories, including trade withIsraeli settlements.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has apologised for Labour’s handling of Gaza under Starmer.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBurnham’s refusal to use the term genocide has caused frustration among manyLabourMPs, not just those on the left of the party. Several MPs told the Guardian they welcomed Burnham’s apology, but wanted him to go further and explicitly “acknowledge Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide”.The prime minister hasapologised for the party’s handling of Gaza under Starmer’s leadership, saying Labour had “not got it right”.Weeks before he became prime minister,Burnham told the Guardian: “We’ve got to do more to put pressure on the Israeli government … let’s be honest, the UK was too slow to call for a ceasefire. And we must now do more to strengthen our approach.” But he stopped short of describing what was happening on the ground in Gaza as a genocide, saying that while there was “increasing evidence” of war crimes, it was for the international courts to make that ruling.The UK government has signalled that further measures against Israel could be coming. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said ministers would set out a “comprehensive set of measures” after Israel moved ahead with its controversial E1 settlement plans in the occupiedWest Bank.In the run-up to the 2025 party conference, Labour sought to rule out motions onPalestinebeing debated at the conference, which triggered accusations that the party was trying to stifle debate. About 30 motions about Palestine from local parties were struck off last September.But conference went against the then leadership and backed an emergency motionproposed bythe Unison union that the Labour government should “employ all means reasonably available to it to prevent the commission of genocide in Gaza” and “fully suspend the arms trade withIsraeland the UK-Israel trade and partnership agreement”.The Labour groups are seeking to force the issue back on the conference floor this year, presenting it as an early test of Burnham’s promise not to “stifle debate” within Labour. Momentum is launching a petition aimed at current and former Labour members and voters, urging the prime minister to stick to the position backed by delegates last year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenActivists protest against Israel’s actions in Gaza.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianHe is facing growing pressure beyond Labour’s left after more than 100 British and French former diplomatswrote to Burnham and Emmanuel Macron urging tough action against Israel, including suspending arms transfers and taking further trade measures. Emily Thornberry this week said Britain should ban imports from the occupied West Bank amid growing concern over Israeli settlement expansion.It comes as Labour is hoping to win back progressive voters who deserted the party under Starmer. Polling commissioned by PSC and Friends of the Earth this summer found 67% of voters who switched from Labour to the Greens citedPalestineas a factor in their decision to leave Labour.Sasha Das Gupta, co-chair of Momentum, said: “Burnham must not allow the same failures that alienated voters under Starmer to continue. He must listen to the majority of the labour movement and take decisive action onGaza.”Dan Iley-Williamson, a political organiser at the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, said: “Burnham’s apology for Labour’s previous stance on Palestine will mean nothing if his government doesn’t decisively break with Keir Starmer’s complicity in Israel’s crimes.“Burnham could use this Labour conference to show the country he will make this break with Starmer. If he doesn’t, he risks the same fate: plummeting support and a legacy of infamy.”Explore more on these topicsLabourAndy BurnhamLabour conferenceIsraelGazaPalestineWest BanknewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran-linked hackers blamed for cyber-attack that shut down UK power plant | Iran | The Guardian
description: Incident marks apparent escalation by Tehran in its in retaliation against UK over allowing US to use British bases
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Incident marks apparent escalation by Tehran in its in retaliation against UK over allowing US to use British bases
Content: Richard Horne of the National Cyber Security Centre, who has said the systems behind the UK’s key services are increasingly being targeted.Photograph: CyberUK/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRichard Horne of the National Cyber Security Centre, who has said the systems behind the UK’s key services are increasingly being targeted.Photograph: CyberUK/Getty ImagesIranIran-linked hackers blamed for cyber-attack that shut down UK power plantIncident marks apparent escalation by Tehran in its in retaliation against UK over allowing US to use British basesBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 10.46 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 05.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHackers linked toIranhave been blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down.The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government, which said that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system.However, it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran after the UK said it had given permission for the US to launch “defensive” operations against Tehran from British bases.‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacksRead moreThe power plant was shut down for four days as a result of the attack last month, accordingto the Sunday Telegraph, which first reported it.A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This story refers to an incident impacting a small-scale energy generator, and at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system. The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards.”The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, is understood not to have received any reported outages from regulated operators of power stations.The Conservatives said the incident reflected a “new kind of warfare”, which meant Britain needed to prioritise “cheap, reliable energy”. “The world is getting more dangerous, which is why we need to prioritise our energy security,” said Claire Coutinho, the Conservative spokesperson on energy.“Leaving ourselves reliant on imports of gas and electricity and failing to build enough reliable gas or nuclear plants for backup at home, all leaves us more vulnerable.”Hostile states such as Russia, China and Iran are increasingly targeting systems behind the UK’s key services, according to a warning this year from Richard Horne, the NCSC’s chief executive.The government said last month the UK was “ready to defend itself” after Iran’s military warnedany bases being used by the US were “legitimate targets”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK ‘ready to defend itself’ after Iranian threat over US basesRead moreThe UK has allowed the US to launch so-called defensive operations from British bases hosting American planes since the start of its war on Iran but has refused to help in offensive operations. That policy has not been altered by the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who was notified last week that a decision had been made to extend the agreement with the US.Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said last month that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.Iran has been accused for years of carrying out cyber-attacks on various countries, including in relation to a massivepower outage in Turkey in 2015and several possible breaches of Israeli government websites in 2022.US government security agencies issued a warning earlier this year of cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure by hackers linked to the IRGC.The US has alleged that an Iran-affiliated group known as “CyberAv3ngers” carried out a campaign against it in 2023 that compromised at least 75 devices in multiple infrastructure sectors.Get in touchContact Ben Quinn about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Ben using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. When asked to choose a recipient please switch to the Journalists list and select Ben Quinn.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailben.quinn@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsIranCyberwarHackingMiddle East and north AfricaForeign policyMilitaryEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Eight-year-old dies after contracting rare brain-eating amoeba in Louisiana | Louisiana | The Guardian
description: Lillian Smart of Ruston infected with fatal Naegleria fowleri, likely after swimming in Lake Claiborne, health officials say
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Lillian Smart of Ruston infected with fatal Naegleria fowleri, likely after swimming in Lake Claiborne, health officials say
Content: Lillian Smart, an eight-year-old girl from Ruston, Louisiana.Photograph: Love for Lillian Smart/FacebookView image in fullscreenLillian Smart, an eight-year-old girl from Ruston, Louisiana.Photograph: Love for Lillian Smart/FacebookLouisianaEight-year-old dies after contracting rare brain-eating amoeba in LouisianaLillian Smart of Ruston infected with fatalNaegleria fowleri, likely after swimming in Lake Claiborne, health officials sayMarina DunbarSun 23 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn eight-year-oldLouisianagirl has died after contracting a rare, typically fatal brain-eating amoeba after a swim in Lake Claiborne.Lillian Smart, of Ruston, died on Saturday, one day after celebrating her birthday, her family announced in a public Facebook post on the “Love for Lillian”page.“Last night Lillian ran from our arms to the arms of Jesus,” her family said in the post. “The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from. Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?”The Louisiana department of healthconfirmedon 19 August that a state resident had been infected withNaegleria fowleriand said the exposure most likely occurred while the person was swimming in Lake Claiborne in Claiborne parish. Family friends later identified Lillian as the infected resident, according to reports from several local media outlets.View image in fullscreenNaegleria fowleriinfections are extremely rare.Photograph: CDC/ReutersNaegleria fowleriinfections are almost always fatal.Lillian had been hospitalized since 15 August,KNOEreported. As her family faced the crisis, more than two dozen businesses in Ruston showed support and donated a portion of sales to the Smart family, according to the Facebook page.Naegleria fowleriinfections are extremely rare, with only a handful occurring inLouisianasince 2011.The amoeba flourishes in warm water and is most commonly found in southern states during the summer. Only about 180 cases have been identified in the US since 1937,according tothe Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.In 2023, an Arkansas child died aftercontractingNaegleria fowlerifrom a country club splash pad in the state capital of Little Rock.Naegleria fowlerican be found in warm freshwater across the country, including lakes, rivers and ponds. It is not found in salt water or in swimming pools that are properly maintained and chlorinated.Experts say the climate crisis iscausingthe amoeba to pop up in parts of the US where it isn’t typical, such as the north and west. It is likely to cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis, a brain infection that can develop when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain.People cannot become infected just by swallowing water containingNaegleria fowleri, and the infection does not spread from one person to another.Explore more on these topicsLouisianaInfectious diseasesChildrenHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s marine parks protect ‘places no one goes’ rather than fragile waters near the mainland, scientists say | Environment | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of experts write to environment minister calling for stronger protections for ‘unique and distinct’ marine ecosystems
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: Hundreds of experts write to environment minister calling for stronger protections for ‘unique and distinct’ marine ecosystems
Content: A weedy sea dragon in Port Botany off Sydney’s coast. A group of scientists are calling for Australia’s coastal marine ecosystems to be better protected, saying many highly protected zones are concentrated in remote waters.Photograph: DaveBluck/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenA weedy sea dragon in Port Botany off Sydney’s coast. A group of scientists are calling for Australia’s coastal marine ecosystems to be better protected, saying many highly protected zones are concentrated in remote waters.Photograph: DaveBluck/Getty Images/iStockphotoAustralian climate and environmental reportingEnvironmentAustralia’s marine parks protect ‘places no one goes’ rather than fragile waters near the mainland, scientists sayHundreds of experts write to environment minister calling for stronger protections for ‘unique and distinct’ marine ecosystemsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian government has been accused of leaving waters near the mainland largely unprotected by establishing the bulk of highly protected marine parks in remote areas.More than 270 leading marine scientists from 84 research institutes have written to the environment minister, Murray Watt, urging stronger protections for marine ecosystems, as aonce-in-a-decadereview of marine parks gets under way.The oceans and seas surrounding Australia and its territories areglobally remarkable, with tropical reefs to icy Antarctic shores, six Unesco world heritage areas and at least 33,000 marine species. But they also face compounding pressures due to climate-driven ocean warming, fishing and extractive industries, and expanding use.Fears of ‘catastrophic’ decline of giant Australian cuttlefish after only 44 counted in dive surveyRead moreProf Jessica Meeuwig, director of the Marine Futures Lab at the University of Western Australia and an author of the statement sent to Watt, said many species found in Australian waters existed nowhere else on the planet. “If we don’t protect them here, it’s not like we can expect somebody else to do the job, they’re lost for ever.”About a quarter of Australian waters are currently highly protected. But these “no take zones” were concentrated in remote offshore and territorial waters, with minimal coverage in the waters surrounding mainland Australia, the statement said.It called for “at least 30%” of every marine bioregion to be highly protected, with bans on industrial trawling, long lining and mining across all marine parks. The scientists said no current protections should be wound back.“In some of our regions, there’s only 1% to 7% of the oceans that are highly protected, and the rest is open slather,” Meeuwig said. These included marine regions off New South Wales, south-east Queensland, Western Australia, western South Australia and the Northern Territory.View image in fullscreenA cock-eyed squid (Histioteuthis miranda) at the Bremer marine park on the south coast of Western Australia.Photograph: Marine Futures LabProf David Booth, a marine ecologist at the University of Technology Sydney, said the temperate east region – one of five regions up for review – is “incredibly biodiverse”.“For instance, around Sydney, we’ve got six to seven hundred species of fish, which is way more than we should have based on our latitude, and a mix of tropical and temperate species,” he said.The region, which stretches from the Great Barrier Reef’s southern border to Bermagui on the south coast of NSW, features the East Australian Current and underwater seamounts and canyons.It is also a “hot spot” for climate-driven changes, he said, with temperate fish species – including many that people liked to eat –moving south, and added pressure from urbanisation, industry and fishing. “It’s an area of rapid change, with very little protection at the moment,” he said.Watt said the government was “well on the way to meeting the Albanese government’s commitment to highly protect 30% of Australia’s ocean by 2030”, and the proposed expansion of marine parks around Lord Howe and Norfolk islands would achieve the target ahead of time.The marine parks review would provide “further opportunities to better protect key ocean habitats”, he said, “while allowing for sustainable use and conservation”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAssociate professor Carissa Klein, director of the Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Science at the University of Queensland, said the current locations of highly protected areas were “biased towards places that no one goes”.“We’re not actually protecting the diversity of life that we have in the ocean,” she said. “Every bioregion is unique and distinct, and has different animals and plants. We want them to get to 30% of every one.“We want a representative network of protected areas all around Australia.”That would benefit fishers too, as well as boosting tourism and the environment, Meeuwig said. For example, 80% of the coral trout caught in areas open to fishing on the Great Barrier Reef were born in highly protected areas.The review was a “tremendous opportunity”, she said. “When Australia leads, it keeps the bar high. When we set the bar low, it gives permission to everybody else to do a bad job.“If Australia flounders at this opportunity, it will have ramifications across other places.”This article was updated on 24 August, 2026, to remove reference to coastal waters. Commonwealth waters start 6km offshore.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentAustralian climate and environmental reportingOceansMarine lifenewsShareReuse this content

title: London’s low emission zone is working – so why are cities around the world so cautious about clean air? | Low emission zones | The Guardian
description: Similar initiatives have been launched from Barcelona to Bogotá, but they have misinformation, political pressure and vested interests stacked against them
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Similar initiatives have been launched from Barcelona to Bogotá, but they have misinformation, political pressure and vested interests stacked against them
Content: Vehicles pass by a sign indicating the new boundary of the LEZ and ULEZ expansion on August 29, 2023 in London, UK.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVehicles pass by a sign indicating the new boundary of the LEZ and ULEZ expansion on August 29, 2023 in London, UK.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesLow emission zonesLondon’s low emission zone is working – so why are cities around the world so cautious about clean air?Similar initiatives have been launched from Barcelona to Bogotá, but they have misinformation, political pressure and vested interests stacked against themFiona HarveyEnvironment editorSun 23 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 08.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen years ago, Alastair Harper was an advocate for young people’s health sitting in a stuffy meeting room inLondonplanning an air pollution campaign. “My phone started buzzing,” he said. “I took the call, and then told the room I needed to leave immediately.“I had to get to UCLH [one of London’s major hospitals]. My own child was headed there in a blue-lit ambulance because she was struggling to breathe London’s toxic air.”Hundreds of thousands of parents across the UK capital had similar experiences in those years. Between about 6,000 and 8,000 people were dying prematurely each year in London in the late 2010s. In 2020, an inquest found that the death of Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah in 2013 had been a direct result of air pollution,the first time it had been listed as a cause of death in the UK.View image in fullscreenCommuters cross London Bridge on a smoggy morning in 2012.Photograph: Barry Lewis/Corbis/Getty ImagesThis week, astudyfrom Queen Mary University London (QMUL) showed a significant reversal. Children’s lungs had grown bigger and stronger since the most polluting vehicles have been restricted on the capital’s roads, scientists found. The ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) – introduced by London’s mayor Sadiq Khan in 2019 and expanded in 2021 and 2023 – charges £12.50 a day for more polluting vehicles that do not meet stringent standards. It has drastically cut levels of nitrogen dioxide, a harmful pollutant.To Harper, who later worked for Khan as an environmental adviser, and now works independently, relief at his own child’s recovery has been supplemented by the satisfaction of knowing that far fewer parents will experience such dread. “To know now that same air is so much safer for the kids that breathe it because of the political choice of one man makes me feel proud of this city,” he said.Nick Hopkinson, a professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London, said the QMUL study was not a surprise. “There is anabsolute wealth of evidencethat air pollution is amajor cause of ill health and premature deathacross the planet,” he said. Air pollution kills 7 million people a year globally, according to the World Health Organization.Poor air not only causes respiratory difficulties and the stunting of children’s lungs, but also heart disease and stroke. It is associated with some forms of cancer, dementia, autism and cognitive difficulties in children too. New studies are adding to our knowledge, but we have known for decades of the basic dangers of dirty air. So why is there so much opposition to curbs on air pollution, which are clearly sound public health measures?This opposition, culture war even, is central for all cities hoping to follow Khan’s lead. The leading causes of air pollution vary around the world –coal use in power stations in China and India, agricultural burning in south-east Asia, waste burning in many of the poorest countries anddust and local industry in others– but road traffic is a constant.View image in fullscreenThe Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, speaks to the driver of a van taking part in a protest against London’s Ulez.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesThe technology to cut all of these types of air pollution already exists, says a former social development minister of Ecuador and now executive director of the Breathe Cities initiative, whose supporters include the Clean Air Fund and C40, a global coalition of mayors and leaders of nearly 100 major cities. “We know that we have the means to make a difference, and we are sharing knowledge and success stories so they can be replicated with impactful policies,” she said.In the case of coal, the alternatives are renewable energy. Halting the burning of forests and peatlands would also combat the climate crisis. The alternatives to polluting traffic arepublic transport, electric vehicles, the redesign of cities and encouragement of active transport – walking and cycling. Trees are also important everywhere.Paris and Barcelona haveshown what is possible within a few yearswhen mayors embrace the joys of cycling, following the lead long ago taken in Denmark and the Netherlands. New York’s Zohran Mamdani,now wearing a cycle helmet, hopes to do the same. But elsewhere in car-dominated America, infamously poorpublic transportprovision, anintractable SUV cultureand a president in Donald Trump intent on rolling back environmental protections mean widespread change is unlikely.Other cities are working to make a difference. Bogotá is about to embark on its second Zuma, aclean air zone that involves expanding cycle lanes and footpaths, paving roads to suppress dust and planting trees. The Colombian capital won last year’s global Earthshot prize for its first Zuma. The city’s environment secretary, Adriana Soto, said: “Residents helped shape the design, particularly how the works would maintain access to their homes and respond to local mobility needs.” Hundreds of cities around the world now have clean air zones of varying sizes.View image in fullscreenRush-hour traffic in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, in July.Photograph: Tony Karumba/AFP/Getty ImagesAnother is Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, which passed an air quality act in 2022 that requires harmful emissions to be halved by 2035 and has installed a network of 50 low-cost monitoring stations as a first step. Imports of vehicles more than eight years old are banned, and the city is consulting on establishing clean air zones. The lead for the C40 Breathe Cities project in Nairobi, Victor Indasi, said: “More remains to be done, but Nairobi is firmly on the right trajectory.”Bulgaria’s capital, Sofia, is saddled with old-fashioned heating systems dependent on coal and wood burning. These are being phased out and replaced with cleaner heat pumps, subsidised for those on low incomes, as part of a city-wide introduction – the first in south-east Europe – of low-emissions zones for transport and heating. Recent results show a 22% reduction in the average concentration of PM10 particulate matter, and a halving of days that exceed air quality guidance levels. Poland isalso cutting its reliance on solid fuels.View image in fullscreenA tram runs along a boulevard in Sofia.Photograph: Hristo Rusev/Getty ImagesIn Australia, Melbourne’s mayor was inspired by a speech Khan gave last year before Brazil’s Cop30 climate summit. The first step was discovering that state-level monitoring was telling the city little about the real quality of its air at a neighbourhood level. “It was surprising to us that this wasn’t being measured,” a spokesperson said. With the new monitoring data coming in, the mayor has yet to decide what actions will be taken, whether a clean air zone or other restrictions, or carrots in the form of scrappage schemes and improved public transport. “We are still at the beginning of this journey,” the spokesperson said.London’s low emission zone might not have happened if Khan had notstaked his reputation on it. When he launched the scheme in 2019, he faced fierce opposition from political opponents and large groups of voters, and even his own party. The plan waschallenged in the courts,businesses complainedof the supposedly crippling costs, and Khan received personal threats and shouts of “Nazi” at public appearances. One survey found 60% of Londoners who replied to a consultation were against it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPeople protest outside Downing Street after the low emission zone was expanded in 2023.Photograph: Anadolu Agency/Getty ImagesIn 2023, the resurgent Labour party under its new leader Keir Starmer faced an important byelection in Uxbridge, on the outer edge of London. The Ulez was a key issue for voters and Labour lost by a small margin,leadingStarmer’s advisers to blame the zone and demand row-backs in London and elsewhere. Andy Burnham, then the mayor of Greater Manchester, who took over from Starmer as prime minister this summer,abandoned plansfor a Ulez after Uxbridge.In all of these cities there is a sense of caution, even hesitancy, and none are moving fast enough. In London, the successes of the Ulez arethreatened by the ballooning number of wood-burning stoves, a fashion accessory rather than a necessity for most of their urban owners. These are now a bigger source of particle pollution than traffic. More than 110,000 children were admitted to hospital with breathing difficulties in London in 2024.Monitoring is a vital first step, but what is done with the data is what counts. That will involve tough measures. “There is always a price. You have to change people’s behaviour, you have to change the transport, the heating, the energy generation,” said Hopkinson. “The way things are in cities is the way they have developed over long periods, and changing all that is difficult.”The pollution is often invisible. As Vaca Jones put it: “Air is not a tangible public good that people can feel and see. That means it is not a priority on the political agenda.”Vested interests also intervene. Though studies show thatair pollution takes an economic as well as a physical toll, businesses often complain – with little evidence – that curbs on driving will hurt them.There is also the fact that the people driving the cars and operating the polluting factories are often not the same people whose children are being admitted to hospital. “Those who are suffering are those who have done least to cause the pollution,” said Chris Griffiths, a professor of primary care at Oxford University.When Khan embarked on London’s Ulez, hysterical misinformation quickly spread online, suggesting the mayor intended to shut down London for his own ends. His deputy, Mete Coban, recalls the shock. “The personal abuse Sadiq got on the back of it was incredible,” he said. “I think it’s this, the misinformation, that is the number one thing that puts off other countries from doing this.”View image in fullscreenPeople protest against the expansion of London’s low emission zone in 2023.Photograph: Guy Bell/ShutterstockHopkinson said: “There is a kind of madness about it. “Disinformation, which is lying to people, is confusing them. They are trying to persuade people that air pollution is not bad for them, and climate change is not real.“They are spreading wild conspiracy theories [for instancethat 15-minute cities, where all amenities can be accessed within a small area, are devices of government control] and the far right are exploiting this and generating grievance.”With the latest study adding to a growing pool of evidence of the Ulez’s success, proponents of cleaner urban air hope to be able to cut through the madness with facts that speak loudly to parents and responsible people everywhere.As Hopkinson put it: “The question for pro-pollution campaigners is ‘why do you hate children?’”Explore more on these topicsLow emission zonesAir pollutionLondonHealthPollutionRoad transportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pine-cone grenades and planet-baking carbon: the French fires 170 years in the making – a visual guide | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: An 1857 decree to drain swamps and plant a monoculture, detritus from the trees and global heating combined to produce the conditions for the Gironde inferno
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: An 1857 decree to drain swamps and plant a monoculture, detritus from the trees and global heating combined to produce the conditions for the Gironde inferno
Content: An image of a firefighting vehicle taking part in efforts to contain the Gironde fire, overlain with a map of the area burned. Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / EPA / Getty ImagesAn 1857 decree to drain swamps and plant a monoculture, detritus from the trees and global heating combined to produce the conditions for the Gironde infernoByAjit Niranjanwith graphics byLucy Swan,Harvey SymonsandPaul ScrutonSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ruinous fires that overran parts ofFrancethis summer have burned more land than ever recorded, forced more people from their homes than at any point since the second world war and caused what scientists suspect is the country’s first firestorm thundercloud. The smoke from France’s biggest inferno in nearly 80 years choked Limoges, a city 125 miles (200km) from the flames, with more toxic dust than Delhi residents inhaled on the city’s worst day of smog last year.The blaze that tore through forests outsideBordeauxin late July took just a few weeks to reforge France’s relationship with fire, but the conditions behind it were centuries in the making.In the 18th century, the coastal wetlands of south-western France were so swampy that shepherds used stilts to cross them in winter. When an 1857 decree from Napoleon III forced landowners to drain the marsh and populate it with maritime pines, the water-logged landscape was converted into Europe’s largest human-made forest. It has since become a regional economic engine running on timber that employs 30,000 people.Map of Landes de GascogneIt is also a firefighter’s nightmare. The pines that make up 90% of the trees in the Landes forest hold resin that burns like petrol, needles that carpet the ground with flammable material and cones that whiz in the wind like grenades, spreading flames across breaks in vegetation that should act as barriers. Without the diversity offered by broad-leafed species, which retain more moisture and have shady canopies that stop vegetation from drying, the dense monoculture can burn with fury when sparks catch.View image in fullscreenPine trees burn near Marcheprime outside  Bordeaux on 26 July.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APThat is what happened in 1949, when a blaze that began in a saw mill burned 50,000 hectares. Gorging on plentiful fuel and with few breaks to impede their spread, the flames killed 82 people, most of them volunteers racing to put out the fire. It remains Europe’s deadliest wildfire.Firefighting capacity has vastly improved since, but the potential for disaster has continued to increase. Humanity has fouled the atmosphere with 1.85tn tonnes of planet-baking carbon since the 1857 decree,warming Europeby 2.4C and increasing the risk of hot and dry extremes that were once unthinkable.Astrikingly wet winterin western Europe this year helped plants grow tall, only for relentless heatwaves to later strip them of moisture, creating a large fuel surplus for fires to devour. By mid-July, temperatures across France had reached record highs and soil moisture had fallen to record lows, setting the stage for the Gironde inferno.Chart showing record breaking heat and drought conditions in FranceNot long after noon on 22 July, after three straight weeks of more than 30C heat, smoke rose from the tightly packed pine stands near Saumos, a village 20 miles west of Bordeaux. The source of ignition is under investigation, but workers contracted by Enedis, a utility company that manages France’s electricity distribution, were active in the area and reported having sparked a fire with a faulty machine. The Bordeaux public prosecutor, which has identified the machine as its leading line of inquiry, did not respond to requests for comment. Enedis declined to answer specific questions because of the continuing investigation.‘We stared into an abyss’: the men and women battling France’s megafireRead moreMost wildfires are started by humans through actions such as dropping cigarette butts, failing to properly extinguish campfires or dispose of barbecues. Public awareness campaigns to discourage reckless behaviour are thought to have contributed to a fall in the number of fires in southern Europe since the 1980s but preventing arson is much harder. French police havearrestednearly 500 people on suspicion of starting fires since the start of the summer, about 70% of which are thought to have been deliberate.Once a fire has begun, it is weather and geography that dictate whether it will quickly wither or morph into a hellish blaze. Outside Saumos, it was immediately clear that firefighters were facing the latter. The fire engulfed several hundreds of hectares in a matter of hours and reached the outskirts of La Porge, which would lose one in 10 homes to the flames in the days that followed. Within 24 hours of the initial spark, southerly winds had pushed the fire’s southern front to Cap Ferret, an upmarket peninsula known as the Hamptons of France, nine miles away.mapHelping the fire’s rapid spread was its location in an area that had been flattened by a powerful storm in 1999 and then swiftly replanted, resulting in a uniform tree height that created a continuous fuel load. But the response in those crucial early hours has also been criticised. Local forestry workers told Le Monde that firefighters had rejected their recommendation to quickly set a controlled burn, while residents of La Porge claim resources were taken from their village to protect the wealthier Cap Ferret. The Gironde fire service, which did not respond to requests for comment, has said it had done all it could to stop the fire and rejected allegations that it abandoned La Porge.Bruno Lafon, the head of the regional forest fire prevention service, an association of forestry workers who work with firefighters to prevent blazes, said he could understand that volunteers who saw their livelihoods go up in flames wanted more help to have come. But, he said, the powerful combination of drought, heat and wind made the initial spread extremely hard to stop. “The men on the ground did what they could, though I think it would have taken a greater number of planes from the beginning,” he said. The French government has also been criticised because maintenance work meant only seven of its 12 water-bombing planes were available at the peak of the fire.View image in fullscreenWildfires evacuees at an exhibition centre in Bordeaux.Photograph: Alain Jocard/AFP/Getty ImagesAs the fire torched more land, authorities acted quickly to get people to safety. The firstevacuationsbegan on the afternoon of 22 July, when 100 residents of the north-eastern quarter of La Porge were taken to shelter in a community hall. Overnight, that number rose to more than 10,000, and just a few days later it had reached nearly 220,000. Across France and neighbouring Spain, which was also battling extreme wildfires, evacuation orders covered more than 300,000 people, a peacetime displacement unprecedented in Europe.Some residents returned to charred possessions, burnt-out homes and shells of cars, but the evacuations proved hugely successful. Not a single person died as a direct result of the Gironde fire, though four firefighters lost their lives tackling separate blazes across the country last month.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA resident of Le Porge inspects damage caused by the fire.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesAmong the evacuees was Hervé Jactel, a forest scientist at INRAE, a public research institute, who was forced to flee twice in two days. Watching Nasa maps with apprehension as the fire drew near, he lost a 20-year experiment investigating the diversity of forest trees as a result of burning biomass that jumped a cornfield. He said the fire had not come as a surprise.“From an ecological and forest management point of view, everything was in place to increase the risk of a very large fire,” he said. “Not only because of the climate, but because of the amount and homogeneity of the fuel.”Scientists suspect those conditions resulted in the extreme levels of energy that generated a firecloud, a powerful chimney of smoke stretching into the atmosphere that creates its own weather system. Known as apyrocumulonimbus cloud, it can spit lightning, and rain down burning embers that spark new blazes and spread the fire further. Nasa has described them as fire-breathing dragons.The true danger, however, lay not in the apocalyptic fire cloud but in the pollutants that it dispersed.mapStudies have foundwildfire smoketo be responsible for 1.5 million deaths around the world each year, making it one of the deadliest environmental threats to human health. Initially, much of the smoke blew straight out over the Atlantic Ocean, but a shift in wind direction caused it to choke Bordeaux, which was nervously watching the approaching inferno, before drifting over Angoulême and Limoges.It clogged the air with so much soot and ash that daily concentrations of airway-inflaming particles hit highs rarely seen, even in cities as polluted as Delhi.graphA shift in the weather helped firefighters halt the advance of the blaze at 42,000 hectares of burned area at the end of July. In the days since, they have continued to put out small flare-ups and smouldering “zombie fires” underground that they say could continue to return for months.Scientists fear for the forest’s short-term recovery. Fire can trigger outbreaks of bark beetles, which attack damaged trees and increase the fuel load for the next fire – a vicious cycle already well documented in California. The burned wood also attracts the invasive pine nematode, a microscopic worm that had arrived in south-west France in November. It blocks the flow of sap in trees, causing them to wilt and die within months.The greatest threats to the forest, however, are yet to come.Fire weatheris projected to become increasingly severe across Europe as carbon pollution continues to heat the planet. Without action to improve fire management, the burned area in Europeis predicted to rise by 39%even in a best-scenario scenario for cutting pollution. In a worst-case scenario, it could nearly triple.Experts have called for rapid cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and better management of the land, such as breaking up continuous tracts of forest and diversifying tree species.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceExtreme heatExtreme weatherAir pollutionPollutionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Onshore windfarm applications hit 10-year high in England | Wind power | The Guardian
description: Surge in proposals follows Labour’s lifting of de facto ban, with about 45 plans submitted in the year to March
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Surge in proposals follows Labour’s lifting of de facto ban, with about 45 plans submitted in the year to March
Content: Little Cheyne Court windfarm near Rye, East Sussex.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/GettyView image in fullscreenLittle Cheyne Court windfarm near Rye, East Sussex.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/GettyWind powerOnshore windfarm applications hit 10-year high in EnglandSurge in proposals follows Labour’s lifting of de facto ban, with about 45 plans submitted in the year to MarchJillian AmbroseandAlex ClarkSun 23 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlans for new onshore windfarms inEnglandhave reached their highest annual level in a decade, after the government overturned the Conservatives’ de facto ban in 2015.About 45 applications for new onshore windfarms were submitted in the year to March,according to a Guardian analysis of government data.Onshore wind power capacity entering the planning system has more than tripled since Labour dropped the blocks on onshore developments within days of coming to power just over two years ago, the analysis revealed.Before the party’s election victory, applications for about 9 megawatts of onshore wind were submitted in England each month on a 12-month rolling average basis. But by the beginning of this year that rate reached about 36MW a month, according to the data, as renewable energy developers began to return to England.The onshore wind resurgence is even greater when compared with the nadir of onshore wind in England in the months before September 2023, when Conservative ministers first began to loosen the regulatory red tape on onshore wind developments.Chart showing applications for onshore windfarms in England have surged since the ban was liftedThen, onshore wind applications averaged about 1MW a month. At the time, the Guardian revealed thatUkraine was completing more onshore windfarmsthan England, even as it was occupied by Russian soldiers.A government spokesperson said: “For too long, a de facto ban held back onshore wind in England, despite its potential to strengthen our energy security, grow the economy and get bills down for good.“That is why we lifted the ban, backed the largest onshore windfarm in England in a decade through our flagship renewables auction, and made it easier for farms and factories to install a single small turbine – no bigger than an oak tree – without needing planning permission.”UK backs biggest English onshore windfarm in a decade among 190 green energy projectsRead moreThe Imerys project, near St Austell, Cornwall, became the largest onshore windfarm in England to secure a government subsidy since the ban was lifted earlier this year. The 20MW project is dwarfed by many Scottish onshore windfarms, and underlines the trend for smaller windfarms in England since the ban was lifted.The Guardian’s analysis shows that since the onshore ban was lifted, the average onshore windfarm proposed in England had just two turbines, delivering 8MW of renewable power capacity. In Scotland, the average onshore windfarm proposed over the same period had nine turbines, with 59MW of capacity.Only one windfarm with a capacity above 100MW has been proposed in England since the onshore ban was lifted. Meanwhile, there have been 18 onshore windfarms with a capacity greater than 100MW proposed in Scotland over the same period.In total, England’s onshore wind proposals since the ban was lifted have climbed to 438MW, compared with applications totalling 490MW in Wales and 5,280MW in Scotland over the same period.Chart showing onshore wind application are at a decade high in England, but still far below ScotlandTara Singh, CEO of RenewableUK, welcomed the return of onshore wind to England.“Onshore wind is one of the UK’s cheapest sources of new electricity, generating power at around half the cost of new gas-fired generation,” she said. “What’s more, new projects can be built quickly, strengthening our energy security and reducing our exposure to volatile global gas prices at a critical time for the country.“With the new prime minister focusing on driving growth across every part of the UK, onshore wind can make an immediate contribution by delivering investment, skilled jobs and lower energy bills for households and businesses.“The benefits are being felt locally too. Community benefit funds worth £5,000 a year for every megawatt of onshore wind capacity installed across England are helping local people invest in the priorities that matter most to them – and we have nearly 3,000MW fully operational in England so far. For every £1 in post-tax profit a developer makes, around 37p is typically invested back into the local community.”The UK’s onshore wind supply chain could add up to £56bn to the economy by 2050 by increasing the manufacturing of high-value components such as blades, towers and cables, according to data from Renewable UK. About 70% of developers’ life cycle spending takes place in the UK, the trade group added.Explore more on these topicsWind powerEnergyRenewable energyEnglandPlanning policyGreenhouse gas emissionsEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Manuscript fragments hiding in plain sight shed light on medieval Guernsey’s literary life | Guernsey | The Guardian
description: Researchers say texts from 12th to 15th centuries ‘hint at a culture which has not even been imagined’
Author: Dalya Alberge
Headline: Researchers say texts from 12th to 15th centuries ‘hint at a culture which has not even been imagined’
Content: The fragments were identified by Island Archives staff working alongside two outside experts.Photograph: Max Rhydwen-Jones/States of Guernsey.View image in fullscreenThe fragments were identified by Island Archives staff working alongside two outside experts.Photograph: Max Rhydwen-Jones/States of Guernsey.GuernseyManuscript fragments hiding in plain sight shed light on medieval Guernsey’s literary lifeResearchers say texts from 12th to 15th centuries ‘hint at a culture which has not even been imagined’Dalya AlbergeSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnprecedented insights into the literary and intellectual life on the island ofGuernseyduring the middle ages have been revealed through the discovery of 17 medieval manuscript fragments.Dating from between the 12th and 15th centuries, they offer evidence of wide-ranging reading tastes, with everything from an extract from a play and an Ovid poem to passages from the Bible and a travel text.Until now, medieval Guernsey’s literary culture had been a blank page in the history books. Little was known about its books and libraries, let alone whether the islanders read for pleasure.These sizeable fragments are significant evidence of volumes that were once found on the Channel island, a British crown dependency 30 miles west of Normandy.They reveal that Guernsey’s medieval citizens had broad literary tastes and that when they read for pleasure, they did so not in English but in French – a clue to where their intellectual interests lay at that time.The fragments had been hiding in plain sight, having been cut up and recycled into practical bindings for rent books and other administrative records during the 16th and 17th centuries. Whoever recycled them could never have imagined their historical value today. But their make-do-and-mend approach ensured that the fragments were preserved for centuries.View image in fullscreen‘There are many more non-religious fragments in this collection than you would expect,’ one expert said.Photograph: Max Rhydwen-Jones/States of GuernseyThey are held in the public collections of theIsland ArchivesandHis Majesty’s greffier’s strongroom. They were identified by Island Archives staff working alongside Dr David Rundle, a manuscript expert at the University of Kent’s Centre for Medieval and Early Modern Studies, and Prof Tamara Atkin, a book historian at the University of Oxford.Rundle told the Guardian: “Why Guernsey is exciting is [that] nobody’s known of anything here. Elsewhere, the Reformation in England, the dissolution of the monasteries, often involved the breaking up of manuscripts. Quite a lot of those manuscripts were liturgical. There are many more non-religious fragments in this Guernsey collection than you would expect.”He added: “Although French was available in England throughout the middle ages as a literary language, it was declining at the end of the middle ages. But it looks to be continuing to be significant on Guernsey.”Fragments from French literature include a dramatic poem fromL’Estoire de Griseldis, a secular play that is thought to have been written around 1395 by Philippe de Mézières. The poem reworks the story of Griselda, first told by the Italian writer Giovanni Boccaccio in The Decameron in 1353.The Griselda story was a medieval blockbuster across Europe but this version is exceptionally rare. Crucially, this fragment reveals that the manuscript play was being read beyond the French royal court circles, where it probably first circulated.The Bible fragments include one in Latin that dates from the late 12th century and that bears an early 15th-century annotation, possibly by a priest.View image in fullscreenThe academics believe further fragments are waiting to be found.Photograph: Max Rhydwen-Jones/States of GuernseyResearch by Callum Tostevin-Hall, an archives assistant at Island Archives, led to these discoveries. He said: “This first began when I was asked to track down a 16th-century copy of Edward III’s 1331 Extente of Guernsey and I noticed that the shelf mark contained reference to a vellum cover with Latin text that had been removed from the notebook in a previous round of conservation. I checked this cover and was astonished to find that it was clearly a reused bifolium from a medieval manuscript.“The project has been a real baby of mine and seeing it finally come to fruition, as well as being able to lay claim to the discovery of several of these manuscript fragments, is both an honour and a privilege.”Rundle said: “This collection is exciting in its variety, of subjects and of dates, and hint at a culture which has not even been imagined.”The academics believe further fragments are waiting to be found in the Guernsey archives and elsewhere.Island Archives will host an academic study day on 10 September, supported by the University of Kent, involving academics from the UK and France. Tickets will be available through Eventbrite.Explore more on these topicsGuernseyHeritageManuscripts and lettersnewsShareReuse this content

title: CrossCountry cancels almost all rail services after power cut hits control centre | Rail industry | The Guardian
description: Transport secretary asks ‘publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible’
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Transport secretary asks ‘publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible’
