Content: CrossCountry says: ‘We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption.’Photograph: James Gill/Danehouse/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCrossCountry says: ‘We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption.’Photograph: James Gill/Danehouse/Getty ImagesRail industryCrossCountry cancels almost all rail services after power cut hits control centreTransport secretary asks ‘publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible’Lauren AlmeidaSun 23 Aug 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCrossCountry cancelled almost all of its train services in Great Britain on Sunday after a power cut in Birmingham hit its control centre.Most services were cancelled until further notice, including routes from Glasgow to Edinburgh, Manchester to Birmingham, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Newcastle to Edinburgh.The train operator said it expected a “near normal service” between Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted Airport, while a planned rail replacement bus service was running between Leicester and Peterborough.CrossCountry said a “very limited” number of trains would run from around 6pm on Sunday, with a return to normal service expected on Monday.The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told the Press Association: “I am concerned to hear about a power outage affecting CrossCountry rail services today, which I know will be very frustrating to passengers.“The service between Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted is still running.“I’ve asked publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible. We’ve also sent Network Rail power teams who are on site and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible.”CrossCountry told customers that tickets for its services on Sunday could be used with other train operators on the same route, and that they would remain valid on CrossCountry services until Wednesday 26 August.Chiltern Railways said it had added services between Birmingham Moor Street and Oxford, and that it would accept all CrossCountry tickets “via any reasonable route”. LNER also said it would accept CrossCountry tickets “to help get affected customers to their destination”.Customers are entitled todelay repaycompensation if their train is delayed by 30 minutes or more. Those who choose not to travel can claim a refund.It is the latest in a series of delays and cancellations on CrossCountry services, with the passenger watchdog warning the train operator this year that it needed toimprove its performance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn June,TransportFocus urged CrossCountry to improve its passenger information during disruption and tackle overcrowding on its trains. Its survey found that while overall 87% of rail customers were satisfied with their experience on a train, that fell to 79% for CrossCountry customers, who were most dissatisfied with how the train operator had dealt with delays.A spokesperson for CrossCountry said: “While we will run as many trains as possible, passengers should expect significant reductions to services and cancellations across almost all CrossCountry routes throughout the day.“We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption. We are working closely with relevant partners and will provide further updates as soon as possible.”Explore more on these topicsRail industryRail transportEnergy industryTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: First Bus bans under-16s in Stoke-on-Trent travelling alone after 6pm after disorder | Bus fares | The Guardian
description: Company says decision comes after spate of antisocial behaviour since free travel scheme was introduced
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Company says decision comes after spate of antisocial behaviour since free travel scheme was introduced
Content: One incident involved more than 100 young people acting in an ‘intimidating and aggressive way’ at Hanley bus station in the city centre.Photograph: TC/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne incident involved more than 100 young people acting in an ‘intimidating and aggressive way’ at Hanley bus station in the city centre.Photograph: TC/AlamyBus faresFirst Bus bans under-16s in Stoke-on-Trent travelling alone after 6pm after disorderCompany says decision comes after spate of antisocial behaviour since free travel scheme was introducedDonna FergusonSun 23 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor some, it is a quotidian nuisance that inevitably occurs when you are in the vicinity of teenagers. For others, it is an expression of modern-day lawlessness among young people.Whatever view you take, antisocial behaviour on public transport has become a hot debate – and with the introduction of free bus travel for kids aged 5 to 15 across England during August, matters have come to a head inStaffordshire.On Friday, the bus company First Bus banned all passengers aged 15 and under travelling without an adult after 6pm inStoke-on-Trentuntil further notice.The company said multiple incidents of antisocial behaviour had occurred since the government’s “cost of living-busting” flagship free travel scheme was introduced on 1 August, including one involving more than 100 young people acting in an “intimidating and aggressive way” at Hanley bus station in the city centre.“Police had to be called,” local First Bus regional director Simon Mathieson told a journalist on BBC Radio Stoke. “Lots of my drivers, who want to do a good job, [were] feeling very unsafe; lots of passengers, trying to get home, [were] feeling very unsafe.”He revealed the company had seen a large uptake of the free travel offer by children in the area, describing it as a brilliant scheme to get people using buses. But he added that one driver had since reported children had been swinging on strap handles on the handrails of his bus and running up and down the vehicle while it was in motion.“That’s not really helping people feel like they can travel in safety and comfort,” Mathieson said. “Unfortunately – and very regretfully – because of the antisocial behaviour … We’ve made the decision to protect staff and other customers on the buses.”Last year, the Liberal Democrats called for tougher action to be taken to tackle “headphone dodgers” who play loud music on buses and trains, including fines of up to £1,000.The Scottish government is planning to bring in legislation that will allow it to force people who benefit from its free bus travel scheme – including young people aged 5 to 21 – to abide by aforthcoming code of conduct, or have their right to concessionary travel withdrawn or suspended.But others say policies to prevent antisocial behaviour in public places are already disproportionate and can result in hefty fines.For example, one passenger at Waterloo station who put a coffee cup in a rubbish bag next to a “completely full” bin was recentlyfined £500by a Lambeth council enforcement officer who had been standing at a distance, watching the bin.An 86-year-old pensioner wasfined £250in Skegness, Lincolnshire, last year for spitting out a leaf after it blew into his mouth.Cllr Finlay Gordon-McCusker, the cabinet minister for transport at Stoke-on-Trent council, said it was disappointing that First Bus had decided to ban all unaccompanied under-16s in the evenings. “Sadly, the children paying the price are overwhelmingly the ones who did nothing wrong.”He said that during his discussions with the company, he had questioned why more transport safety officers could not have been deployed to monitor the routes that were affected instead. “It’s a real shame that First Bus felt that this was their only option … It’s certainly not the option I would have liked to see put in place.”He and his fellow councillors had welcomed the government’s free bus travel scheme in August, he said. “But clearly it’s presented an opportunity for some kids to travel across the city and cause trouble, which is what they’ve done in this situation.”That doesn’t mean there is anything wrong with the policy, he added. “Teenagers with nothing to do in August isn’t a new phenomenon. The scheme didn’t create the behaviour. It changed its geography.”He added: “What the free travel did, possibly, was move it [the antisocial behaviour] from the estates where it’s dispersed and largely unreported to the bus station where it’s concentrated, it’s visible and it lands in an incident log.”He disagrees that banning unaccompanied children from buses in evenings is the right way to tackle antisocial behaviour in Stoke-on-Trent. A better solution might have been greater police presence at the bus station, he said, so that young people could have continued to benefit from the freedom of having unlimited free bus travel during the summer holidays.“It’s certainly not fair,” he said. “I think it’s a crying shame that that freedom [to travel] has been taken away because of the unacceptable behaviour of a very small minority of young people.”First Bus declined to be interviewed by the Guardian but said in a statement the decision had been approved by the Department forTransport(DfT) and has the full support of the council.Drivers will continue to be able to exercise their discretion to provide free travel for unaccompanied children and young people if they are vulnerable or to ensure their safety.A government spokesperson said: “Our Great British Summer Savings scheme allows kids under 15 to travel for free on participating services, to give families room to breathe and enjoy days out throughout August.“The scheme rightly offers all local operators flexibilities to deal with issues like anti-social behaviour, such as the right to refuse travel or localised time restrictions.”Explore more on these topicsBus faresPublic transportStoke-on-TrentTransport policyTransportEnglandStaffordshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nine out of 10 unsolved murders in London linked to minority ethnic victims | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Analysis risks deepening perception of ‘unequal protection under the law’, say campaigners
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Exclusive: Analysis risks deepening perception of ‘unequal protection under the law’, say campaigners
Content: Police officers in forensic suits at the scene of a fatal shooting this month in Clapham, south London.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenPolice officers in forensic suits at the scene of a fatal shooting this month in Clapham, south London.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAUK criminal justiceNine out of 10 unsolved murders in London linked to minority ethnic victimsExclusive: Analysis risks deepening perception of ‘unequal protection under the law’, say campaignersVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKillers who take the lives of black people have a greater chance of getting away with their crimes than those who target white people, new research shows.Analysis of unsolved homicides inLondonbetween 2019 to 2023 reveals a stark disparity: minority ethnic British people represented 61.7% of reported homicide victims, but 92.9% of all unsolved murder victims.Also between 2019 and 2023, black people were victims in 40% of all homicides and represented 73% of all unsolved murder cases during that period. Black victims made up 83.7%, 36 victims, of unsolved shootings and 73.5%, 39 victims, of unsolved stabbings.TheMetropolitan policesay the racial disparity is due in part to black people having lower trust in the police, which they say they are trying to improve.The Met’s head of homicide, commander Paul Brogden, told the Guardian: “We know serious violence disproportionately affects certain communities, particularly young black men, who have the lowest trust in policing. This means sadly victims or witnesses are less likely to come forward and trust us.”The study, conducted byAction on Armed Violence, also found that deaths by shooting were more likely to be unsolved than those by stabbing. Between 2019 and 2023, London averaged 124.6 homicides a year, with stabbings accounting for 65.3% of all killings and shootings 8.7%.Yet among the 41 murders from this period that remain unsolved, shootings made up 38%, more than four times their share of overall homicide total.Brogden said: “As this report outlines, that is an added complexity following shootings or stabbings on the streets, where identifying suspects requires more detailed investigative work, particularly when compared to domestic murders.“While we use every tool at our disposal such as CCTV and forensics, often it’s witness evidence which can prove vital in securing convictions.”DCI Alex Gammampila, a senior Scotland Yard homicide detective, said: “There tends to be more planning and thought to it [a shooting], rather than a spontaneous pick up of a knife and stabbing thrust.“All this makes firearms offences more challenging to solve.”The average age of homicide victims in London is about 36. However, for unsolved cases, the average victim’s age drops significantly to 28, indicating a notable skew toward younger victims.Iain Overton, of Action on Armed Violence, said of the findings: “Our data suggest that London’s unsolved murders are not evenly distributed. Instead, they are concentrated among young Black men and in cases involving firearm violence.“While there are many reasons for why such murder investigations are especially difficult, the result must seem often clear to the victims’ families: those communities most affected by deadly violence are often the least likely to see those responsible brought to justice. This in itself risks deepening existing mistrust and creating the perception of unequal protection under the law. And that can’t be a good thing.”The Met has a high clear-up rate for homicides, running at nine out of 10 killings resulting in justice.Last year the Met recorded 97 homicides in London,down from 153 in 2019, and the lowest in a decade.The study says between 2015 and 2024 there were 110 unsolved homicides, 9%, of 1,222 killings in that period.Explore more on these topicsUK criminal justiceRaceCrimeLondonMetropolitan policePolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Fast-moving wildfire in Reno, Nevada, forces tens of thousands to evacuate homes | US wildfires | The Guardian
description: Human-caused Hawk fire covers more than 13,000 acres as blaze approaches University of Nevada campus in Reno
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Human-caused Hawk fire covers more than 13,000 acres as blaze approaches University of Nevada campus in Reno
Content: Hawk wildfire in Nevada forces evacuations and road closuresUS wildfiresFast-moving wildfire in Reno, Nevada, forces tens of thousands to evacuate homesHuman-caused Hawk fire covers more than 15,000 acres as blaze approaches University of Nevada campus in RenoMarina Dunbarand agenciesSun 23 Aug 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fast-movingNevadawildfireexploded to more than 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares) on Sunday, pushing from the Sierra foothills toward the center of Reno and urging nearly 90,000 residents to evacuate as flames threatened neighborhoods and reached the edge of the University of Nevada campus.The Hawk fire’s “GO NOW” evacuation zone had expanded to the edge of the university campus as strong, gusty winds, low humidity and dry vegetation fueled the blaze, according to Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue in Reno. Of those urged to evacuate, 42,000 were under strict orders. An additional 45,000 people were in the evacuation warning zone, and encouraged to leave now and be prepared to stay away for several days to clear the roads for first-responders.“If you have been told to evacuate, please don’t wait!” Hillary Schieve, Reno’s mayor, said in astatementposted on social media on Saturday night. “Structures have already been burned in this fire and your life is more important than a building. Evacuating before the fire arrives also allows our firefighters to focus their efforts on battling the blaze.”Firefighters sound alarm as US faces critical staffing shortage: ‘We don’t have enough people’Read moreAuthorities confirmed three civilians and three first responders had been injured in the fire and several structures have been destroyed. Officials said the fire was human-caused but did not provide additional details on how the fire was started, saying it was under investigation.Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe county and mobilized theNevadanational guard. Two helicopter crews were deployed to support aerial firefighting operations, while 60 troops were assigned to help police safeguard evacuated neighborhoods. However winds were whipping the flames, complicating the fight.“It was extremely confusing,” said Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff, describing how changing winds sent the flames in different directions.The fire had already proved to be a challenge on Saturday night, moving exceptionally fast, jumping over fire trucks and making it difficult for responders to get to hotspots while residents were trying to get out, Balaam said.The fire was so small on Saturday morning that it wasn’t even a concern, said Tyler Duvall, who went camping over the weekend. By the next day, his house was in the evacuation zone.“The wind really blew it up,” Duvall said.“Approximately 400 personnel are currently working on the incident, with resources coming together from local, state and federal agencies, including ground crews and air resources,” the Truckee Meadowsstatementsaid.The rapidly expanding fire was surrounded by neighborhoods, and nearly 10,000 homes and businesses in Washoe county were without power on Sunday. Portions of US Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed because of the fire.Reno has a population of more than 280,000 residents.View image in fullscreenFire crews and local agencies respond to a fast-moving wildfire on the dry hillsides outside Reno, Nevada, on Saturday.Photograph: Hale Irwin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockDavid Barb returned from a weekend hunting trip to find the fire had leveled his taxidermy shop, but his house nearby appeared to have been spared thanks to workers with a landscaping company who cut a fire break, he said. His wife was home when the fire started on the other side of the mountain and later evacuated to a friend’s house.“I’m kind of devastated, but thank God everyone’s safe,” he said on Sunday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWashoe county emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees, but said pets could not be brought there. Small and large animals were instead to be left at two other locations. Casinos in Reno offered discounts on hotel rooms to evacuees.At least 20road closureswere in effect as of Sunday afternoon.The University of Nevada’s Reno campus remained just outside the evacuation zone on Sunday morning. The university, which had an enrollment of about 24,000 students in fall 2025, said officials hadestablishedan emergency response plan should conditions change. The first day of classes at the university is 24 August. However, students who are new to the university were allowed to move in as early as 13 August.The Reno-Tahoe international airport also remained outside the evacuation zone, and commercial flights were unaffected on Sunday. The smaller Reno-Stead airport was closed to general aviation traffic because of the Hawk fire but remained open to firefighting aircraft.Authorities were also closely watching a county detention facility located several blocks from the outer edge of the evacuation warning area.“We have those inmates in mind and we are making sure that we have plans in place in case we may have to evacuate the facility,” said Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff.The Hawk fire comes just weeks after three wildfires fueled by dry and windy conditions north of Reno forced more than 13,000 residents from their homes earlier this month, according to the Nevada national guard.Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsUS wildfiresNevadaUS weatherWildfiresnewsShareReuse this content

title: The ‘ordinary’ woman accused of assassinating a Russian commander in Crimea  | Russia | The Guardian
description: Friends close to Margarita Reutt are shocked she could allegedly plant bomb that killed Ukrainian defector Robert Shageev, while others recall a stubborn grit to see any plan through
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Friends close to Margarita Reutt are shocked she could allegedly plant bomb that killed Ukrainian defector Robert Shageev, while others recall a stubborn grit to see any plan through
Content: Margarita Reutt posted frequently online about health and animal rights.Photograph: VkontakteView image in fullscreenMargarita Reutt posted frequently online about health and animal rights.Photograph: VkontakteRussiaThe ‘ordinary’ woman accused of assassinating a Russian commander in CrimeaFriends close to Margarita Reutt are shocked she could allegedly plant bomb that killed Ukrainian defector Robert Shageev, while others recall a stubborn grit to see any plan throughPjotr SauerSun 23 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was just after dawn in Sevastopol when a powerful explosion tore through a quiet square in a residential district of the Russian-occupied Crimean port city.Hidden inside a rubbish bin, a bomb containing the equivalent of about 500g of TNT detonated on 13 August as Robert Shageev, the deputy commander of a Russian Black Sea fleet submarine brigade, walked past in naval uniform. He was killed on the spot.Within hours, investigators had a suspect. Police detained Margarita Reutt, a 32-year-old resident of Sochi, the Russian resort city about 300 miles across the Black Sea from Sevastopol.During a search, investigators said they had found a remote control they believed was used to detonate the bomb that killed Shageev, a former commander of Ukraine’s only submarine who switched allegiance to Russia in 2014 when Moscow annexed Crimea.According to the security service, she confessed to the attack and said that a handler linked to Ukrainian intelligence had promised her a large payment in cryptocurrency and documents that would allow her to leave Russia afterwards.View image in fullscreenFriends remember Margarita Reutt as warm and sociable, but also unusually drawn to adventure and risk.Photograph: VkontakteThe FSB also said Reutt showed no remorse.Those assertions could not be independently verified, and Russian security agencies have previously publicised purported confessions from detainees before their cases have reached court. But several people previously accused by Russia of carrying out similar attacks against military figures were later found by reporters to have been involved in the operations Moscow had accused them of conducting.What exactly drove Reutt to allegedly embark on such an audacious mission remains unclear. As with other cases involving accused Ukrainian intelligence operations, her trial is likely to take place behind closed doors, offering little opportunity for her to give her own account publicly.But interviews with a dozen friends and acquaintances, combined with an examination of years of her social media activity, offer a portrait of a determined and adventurous woman whose attitude towards her country appears to have hardened gradually, with signs of a more striking change emerging in the months leading up to the attack.“Rita believed that the country was going in the wrong direction,” said a longtime friend, using the diminutive form of her name. “But I am still shocked she went so far,” the friend added.View image in fullscreenAn examination of Margarita Reutt’s social media activity offers a portrait of a determined woman whose attitude towards her country appears to have gradually hardened.Photograph: VkontakteRussia quickly accused Reutt of carrying out the attack on the orders of Ukrainian intelligence. Kyiv has not commented on the bombing or Reutt’s alleged role in it.Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have been linked to a string of assassinations and attempted killings of senior Russian military officers whom Kyiv has accused of involvement in the invasion. Ukrainian officials have occasionally acknowledged involvement in such operations, but more often have remained silent.The attacks have involved an array of methods and recruits, from committed anti-Kremlin saboteurs to Russians promised large sums of money. In other cases, unsuspecting couriers and delivery workers have effectively been used as mules.Usually, little is known about those accused of carrying out such attacks or how they prepared for them. Some have managed to escape, or were never publicly identified by Russian authorities, while others were killed carrying out their operations.The swift capture and naming of Reutt, however, offers a rare opportunity to examine the journey of a Russian citizen accused of turning against her own country.Reutt, born Margarita Yakovleva, grew up in Yaroslavl, a city north-east of Moscow, where she took the surname of the grandmother who largely raised her after her parents divorced. Friends recalled a largely unremarkable childhood, remembering her as warm and sociable, but also unusually drawn to adventure and risk.“Margarita was fearless. She would climb trees, jump off cars, do things most boys were scared of,” recalled one friend from her childhood.That streak followed her to Novosibirsk, thousands of miles to the east, where she studied management and threw herself into university life. Reutt became a regular at a local parachuting club, with photographs showing her jumping from Soviet-era aircraft, often the only woman among groups of men in camouflage gear.She also won prizes in amateur go-karting competitions and took up water polo, becoming goalkeeper for the university team and quickly distinguishing herself despite being new to the sport. “Margarita was so talented and never afraid of the ball,” recalled her water polo coach at the time.There was little then to suggest hostility towards the Kremlin. In Novosibirsk, Reutt became a well-liked member of a patriotic volunteer group that searched for the remains of Soviet soldiers killed during the second world war, part of a nationwide movement dedicated to recovering and reburying the war dead.After graduating, Reutt moved south to Sochi, the Black Sea resort that became her home. She briefly tried her hand at running a travel agency before joining Vitauct in the early 2020s, an alternative medicine company specialising in longevity.“She was the most ordinary person,” said Gennadiy Garbuzov, the company’s founder, who struggled to reconcile the woman he knew with the allegations now facing her. “There was nothing to indicate she would do this. She must have fallen under someone’s influence.”On the surface, her online life was similarly unremarkable. She posted frequently about health and animal rights and took to Telegram forums to discuss alternative medicine.Reutt also travelled widely. Leaked records from travel databases seen by the Guardian and photographs posted online show frequent trips abroad, including to Turkey, Thailand and Sri Lanka, where she often shared photographs of herself in bikinis at beach resorts.View image in fullscreenMargarita Reutt on one of her frequent trips abroad in a picture shared online.Photograph: Vkontakte“Margarita just seemed to be living her life and had lots of plans for the future,” said another colleague at Vitauct.“She was good-looking and popular,” the colleague added.In October 2025, Reutt travelled to Minsk for her sister’s wedding. Photographs from the celebration show her smiling among relatives and catching the bridal bouquet. To one friend she painted an idyllic picture of her life in Sochi, traversing mountains, waterfalls and canyons. “You can explore endlessly here, everything is lush and green,” she wrote to the friend.But beneath that outwardly happy life, another side of Reutt was becoming visible. She increasingly expressed concerns about environmental problems plaguing Sochi, and started to become involved in local volunteer initiatives, friends said.After a large oil spill in the Black Sea in December 2024, whentwo Russian tankers were wreckedin a storm, Reutt travelled to Anapa to join volunteers cleaning mazut, a heavy fuel oil, from contaminated beaches.Exactly when dissatisfaction with her surroundings hardened into something more political is difficult to establish. Friends described a growing estrangement from Russia that deepened after the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.“The war came as a shock,” said one friend, who recalled Reutt becoming increasingly outspoken in public about the fighting in Ukraine. “I told her once to keep quiet, otherwise she would get us both into trouble,” the friend said.By July 2025, her anti-war feelings had spilt into public view. While travelling on a Samara-Adler train, Reutt was fined under Russia’s sweeping law against “discrediting” the armed forces after reportedly shouting “Serves you right, Russians!” when news broke of a Ukrainian drone strike on a railway station in the Rostov region.The following February, Reutt posted the results of a genetic test showing she was 98% Russian, adding a hashtag declaring that she was “ashamed to be Russian”.Yet to friends and acquaintances, Reutt appeared to carry on much as before. She picked up occasional jobs, appeared in video clips made by friends and continued to travel. As recently as March, photographs from a trip to Cuba showed her drinking from a coconut.View image in fullscreenMargarita Reutt on a beach in Cuba.Photograph: VkontakteIt was only in late spring, several people who knew her said, that her behaviour began to change in ways they struggled to understand at the time. “She became more withdrawn,” recalled one friend.Around the same time, a group of friends began planning a trip together for the autumn. Reutt declined to join them without much explanation – an unusual response from someone friends said could be counted on to say yes to a new adventure.Another friend remembered Reutt suddenly acquiring a second phone. “She bought this second phone in the spring. She explained that she needed it for work, but it didn’t really make sense to me at the time.”“Margarita was hiding something,” the friend added. “I thought maybe she had a new boyfriend.”By the summer, Reutt had begun spending more time in Crimea, the place where she would eventually be arrested. One acquaintance said she explained the trips to Crimea by saying she was scouting possible locations for video shoots, having recently begun appearing more frequently in music clips.What she was actually doing in Crimea – and when, if at all, she came into contact with Ukrainian intelligence – remains unknown.If Russia’s allegations that she was recruited by Ukraine are true, Reutt would join a growing group of Russian citizens accused of being enlisted by Ukrainian intelligence to carry out sabotage and assassinations deep behind the frontlines.Such recruits offer obvious advantages: they can move around Russia more freely, and attract less scrutiny than Ukrainian operatives, and they can reach targets far from the frontline without putting trained agents at risk. Women have featured prominently in several of the most high-profile operations, potentially attracting even less suspicion.For those close to Reutt, there is no easy explanation for how the woman they remember ended up accused of carrying out an assassination. But a friend of two decades recalled a stubborn determination to follow through on whatever she decided to do.“If she had a plan in mind, she would do it,” the friend said. “Even if it was something like this.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaCrimeaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iryna Zarutska’s family sues North Carolina city over her murder | Charlotte | The Guardian
description: Relatives of woman fatally stabbed on public transit allege death was preventable and Charlotte knew of violent crime issue
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Relatives of woman fatally stabbed on public transit allege death was preventable and Charlotte knew of violent crime issue
Content: A memorial dedicated to Iryna Zarutska at the East/West Blvd light rail station in Charlotte, North Carolina, on 11 September 2025.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA memorial dedicated to Iryna Zarutska at the East/West Blvd light rail station in Charlotte, North Carolina, on 11 September 2025.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesCharlotteIryna Zarutska’s family sues North Carolina city over her murderRelatives of woman fatally stabbed on public transit allege death was preventable and Charlotte knew of violent crime issueMarina DunbarSun 23 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family ofIryna Zarutskais suingCharlotteand a security company one year after the Ukrainian refugee was fatally stabbed onboard a light rail train in theNorth Carolinacity.A lawsuit filed on Friday in Charlotte’s Mecklenburg county superior court alleges Zarutska’s death was preventable. It also claims the city and the company that provides security for theCharlotteArea Transit System failed to put adequate protections in place despite knowing about violent crime on and around the municipal light rail line.Frank Scott Haskell, Zarutska’s uncle, filed the lawsuit, which alleges the defendants knew about safety and crime concerns involving Charlotte’s public transit system before the deadly attack.US judge finds man accused of killing woman on Charlotte train incompetent to stand trialRead moreThe city and Professional Security Services “were responsible for protecting lawful passengers from known and foreseeable danger”, the lawsuit states, according to theCharlotte Observer. It adds: “Their failures caused the fatal stabbing.”The lawsuit points to what it describes as inadequate fare enforcement and security staffing. It contends that simple measures such as fare enforcement, turnstiles or proper security staffing, which it says the city had the money for, could have prevented Zarutska’s death.Her family is seeking monetary damages and says it hopes the legal action will lead to security changes across Charlotte’s light rail system.The lawsuit came one year after Zarutska was killed while riding a light rail train home from work in Charlotte. Decarlos Brown Jr waschargedin her death. In June, a judge ruled Brownincompetentto stand trial due to mental illness.Zarutska had come to the US after living in a bomb shelter in Ukraine, according to relatives. She fled the war in hopes of finding safety in the US, and family members described her as determined to build a safer life.Zarutska’s killing became a flashpoint in abroader public debateover violent crime, mental illness and public transit safety, including questions about whether cities such as Charlotte are doing enough to address those issues.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Trump administration and its Republican allies seized on the case, claiming the killing demonstrated how local leaders, judges and policies in Democratic-led cities were failing to protect residents from violent crime.In September, North CarolinapassedIryna’s Law, which redefined certain violent offenses, imposed bail limits for people charged with violent offenses and ended cashless bond releases in certain circumstances.Explore more on these topicsCharlotteUS crimeNorth CarolinaUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey | Artemis II | The Guardian
description: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen broke record for farthest distance traveled from Earth
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen broke record for farthest distance traveled from Earth
Content: Jeremy Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman at Ellington Field Joint Reserve Base in Houston, Texas, on 11 April 2026.Photograph: Lexi Parra/ReutersView image in fullscreenJeremy Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman at Ellington Field Joint Reserve Base in Houston, Texas, on 11 April 2026.Photograph: Lexi Parra/ReutersArtemis IIArtemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journeyReid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen broke record for farthest distance traveled from EarthRamon Antonio VargasSun 23 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 18.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe crew of the historicArtemis IIlunar flyby mission have earned the US’s top space medal, officials have announced.Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August, the US space agency Nasasaid.Nasa’s website indicates that only 30 astronauts have gained the honor – among them Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and John Glenn, who was the first American to orbit Earth and then served four terms in the US Senate.Trump hosts crew of historic Artemis mission: ‘I would have had no trouble making it’Read moreWiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen were selected for the medal, despite its name, by Donald Trump after the Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, recommended them to the president.TheArtemis IIcrew broke Apollo 13’s record for farthest distance traveled from Earth during their 10-day mission, which began on 1 April. They reached 252,756 miles (406,771km) as they swung above the lunar surface, surpassing the 1970 record of 248,655 miles as part of US plans to again land on the moon – then eventually reach Mars.Furthermore, Hansen – who is from Canada – became the first non-US citizen to fly to the moon.“This was not easy,” Wiseman said to reporters after the Artemis II mission safely ended with a textbook splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. “Before you launch, it feels like it’s the greatest dream on Earth. And when you’re out there, you just want to get back to your families and your friends. It’s a special thing to be a human, and it’s a special thing to be on planet Earth.”The medal ceremony scheduled for Wiseman and his colleagues at the JohnsonSpaceCenter in Houston comes four months after Trump hosted the Artemis II crew at the White House. The occasion was marked in part by the president, who turned 80 in June, telling the astronauts: “I would have had no trouble making it – I’m physically very, very good.”Nasa listed an 11am Eastern start time for the ceremony, with a video live stream of the event available atwww.nasa.gov/live.Trump has sought to embrace the Artemis II crew’s achievements despite his administration’sproposalto cut Nasa’s budget by 23%, including a 46% reduction for space science initiatives, for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October. A House commerce, justice and science subcommittee led by Trump’s Republican partyrespondedby advancing its own Nasa budget proposal that would maintain the science projects the president has been aiming to eliminate.Beside Armstrong and Glenn, previous Congressional Space Medal of Honor recipients include astronauts who were killed in the Apollo I fire as well as the explosions of the Challenger and Columbia space shuttles.Douglas Hurley and Robert Behnken were the last astronauts to have been chosen for the medal before the Artemis II crew. Hurley and Behnken in 2020 became the first to launch into orbit on a commercial spacecraft, and they accepted the medal in 2023 during Joe Biden’s presidency.This article was amended on 23 August 2026. John Glenn was the first American to orbit the Earth, but not the first person as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsArtemis IISpaceNasanewsShareReuse this content

title: UK orders reviews of franchising sector after Vodafone allegations | Vodafone | The Guardian
description: Two studies will be used to shape government policy amid claims about a former franchisee who took his own life
Author: Simon Goodley
Headline: Two studies will be used to shape government policy amid claims about a former franchisee who took his own life
Content: A group of 62 former Vodafone franchisees brought a high court claim  against the company in 2024.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenA group of 62 former Vodafone franchisees brought a high court claim  against the company in 2024.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAVodafoneUK orders reviews of franchising sector after Vodafone allegationsTwo studies will be used to shape government policy amid claims about a former franchisee who took his own lifeSimon GoodleySun 23 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters have commissioned a pair of in-depth reports into how franchising businesses are policed in the UK, as the government considers introducing new laws after high-profile allegations about conduct in the sector.The action followsa Guardian investigation last December, which revealed claims that Adrian Howe, a former Vodafone employee who had agreed to start a franchise in 2018, had taken his own life after pressure from the FTSE 100 telecoms group.The Department for Business and Trade is understood to be working with the British Franchise Association on a study of the domestic market, while it has also engaged the Centre for Economic Policy Research to analyse different models in operation internationally.Vodafone settles legal claim brought by 62 former franchisees after Guardian investigationRead moreBoth studies will feed into the government’s assessment of the legal framework required to “ensure franchisees are properly protected, while avoiding unnecessary burdens on small businesses”.The developments come as the department said that Lord Leong, who was named in July asminister for small business and enterprise, has been handed franchising as part of his portfolio.His appointment follows a pledge in January by Keir Starmer toreview laws governing franchising agreements, as part of the official response to the Howe case. The former Vodafone store manager was found drowned days before his new franchise was due to open its doors when his relatives said he had become convinced his deal with the multinational company would prove financially disastrous.December’s Guardian investigation also spoke to two formerVodafonefranchisees who recounted that commission cuts by the company in 2020 had caused their franchising companies to run up huge debts, which they each said contributed to them making attempts on their own lives.They were among a group of 62 former Vodafone franchisees who brought ahigh court claimin 2024, alleging the company “unjustly enriched” itself and whichMPs have comparedto the Post Office Horizon IT scandal.In July, Vodafonesettled the 19-month-old court claimvia a confidential agreement “without any admission of liability”. Howe was not included in that claim, which was launched after his death, but his family has since said they will continue to press the government tointroduce an “Adrian’s law”to incorporate new regulations to govern the franchising sector.Campaigners have argued that franchisees are uniquely exposed under the current UK system as the law treats their small companies as equals to huge corporations – even though there are often large imbalances in power formalised within the franchise agreements that govern the relationship between both parties.During an adjournment debate on franchising in July 2025, theformer Conservative minister John Hayes told MPs: “Franchising can be used as a method to exaggerate the power of the business at the heart of the franchise and to weaken the position of franchisees. My assertion is that is common and is particular in the case of Vodafone.”A Vodafone UK spokesperson said: “While we are sorry if any partners have had a difficult experience, we reject any suggestion that our franchisees were put under undue pressure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We continue to run a successful franchise operation of over 350 stores, and many of our existing franchisees have expanded their business with us by taking on additional stores. We encourage everyone to raise issues, and we will always seek to resolve them.”The company said last year it “wholly rejects” any suggestion that it had “knowingly or recklessly or negligently” put anybody involved with its franchise stores under unreasonable pressure.Mental health experts emphasise that suicide is usually complex and can often involve many triggers.The company has added that comparisons to the Post Office scandal are “wholly inappropriate”.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsVodafoneCorporate governanceTelecommunications industryMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chineke!/ Heyward/ Angel Blue review – belated premiere for forgotten Black composer | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: A suite of reconstructed dance pieces from 1918 by Edmund Thornton Jenkins made a moving start to Chineke!’s Prom, where soprano Angel Blue sang Barber’s nostalgic Knoxville and Dvořák’s Symphony No 8 made a breathless finale
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: A suite of reconstructed dance pieces from 1918 by Edmund Thornton Jenkins made a moving start to Chineke!’s Prom, where soprano Angel Blue sang Barber’s nostalgic Knoxville and Dvořák’s Symphony No 8 made a breathless finale
Content: Gleaming tone … Angel Blue performs alongside conductor Jonathon Heyward and Chineke! Orchestra.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCView image in fullscreenGleaming tone … Angel Blue performs alongside conductor Jonathon Heyward and Chineke! Orchestra.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCProms 2026ReviewChineke!/ Heyward/ Angel Blue review – belated premiere for forgotten Black composerRoyal Albert Hall, LondonA suite of reconstructed dance pieces from 1918 by Edmund Thornton Jenkins made a moving start to Chineke!’s Prom, where soprano Angel Blue sang Barber’s nostalgic Knoxville and Dvořák’s Symphony No 8 made a breathless finaleErica JealSun 23 Aug 2026 09.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSlowly but surely, our perceptions of what a composer looked like in the early 20th century are widening.Chineke!’s ongoing mission to unearth music by forgotten Black composers here brought about the belated premiere of Ballet by Edmund Thornton Jenkins, its incomplete manuscript parts reconstructed by his great-nephewTuffus Zimbabwe.Growing up in Charleston, South Carolina, Jenkins died in Paris aged only 32, having made a name for himself as a rising composer and band leader. In between he studied at the Royal Academy of Music in London, where in 1918 he wrote his three-movement Ballet. It sounded persuasive here, as conducted by Jonathon Heyward. A substantial opening Processional, ominous then light-footed, gives way to a second movement beginning with a bubbling flute duet and a florid viola solo; together, these repeatedly show a gift for weaving together melody and countermelody. The flaw is in the finale, where the waltz that dominates the movement sounds unavoidably slender and staid next to the trumpet fanfare that announces it. Still, Jenkins rounds things off with an exuberant, uptempo ending.That was where the discoveries ended in this Prom – it was a pity that a song by Margaret Bonds had been quietly dropped from the programme. The rest of the first half was a showcase for the US soprano Angel Blue. In Barber’s Knoxville: Summer of 1915, the words of the poet James Agee didn’t always make it across the hall, but her gleaming tone, the childish innocence of her character and the music’s atmosphere of intense nostalgia certainly did.A change of frock later Blue returned to the stage, microphone in hand, and powered rather self-indulgently through four Great American Songbook standards. She relied a lot on charm, singing My Funny Valentine directly to the front rows, but these songs didn’t all get the vocal polish they deserve: in Puttin’ On the Ritz the high point was Richard Kelley’s trumpet solo.The whole orchestra, not least its versatile and superbly blended brass section, was on form in Dvořák’s Symphony No 8. Heyward shaped a performance full of momentum, setting electric tempos and driving the finale to its close with breathless excitement.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicChineke! OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content

title: A supreme being, the nearly naked show and politics with paws: Edinburgh fringe pick’n’mix | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: From Taiwanese steampunk dance to Australian climate comedy, here are 13 quick-fire fringe reviews
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: From Taiwanese steampunk dance to Australian climate comedy, here are 13 quick-fire fringe reviews
Content: What on earth … Anna Leong Brophy: Born Sexy Yesterday.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWhat on earth … Anna Leong Brophy: Born Sexy Yesterday.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026A supreme being, the nearly naked show and politics with paws: Edinburgh fringe pick’n’mixFrom Taiwanese steampunk dance to Australian climate comedy, here are 13 quick-fire fringe reviewsAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsBrian Logan,Lyndsey Winship,Arifa Akbar,Kate Wyver,Tim JonzeandChris WiegandSun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 04.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnna Leong Brophy: Born Sexy YesterdayFor new perspective on the strange ways we behave, we all know the thought experiment “if a visitor from space arrived on Earth, what would they think?” In Born Sexy Yesterday, Anna Leong Brophy plays a supreme being implanted into a grown woman’s body to experience life for the first time. Presenting like some sci-fi sex robot with the soul of a naive child, Brophy duly marries a man on the front row and settles down to a life of domestic drudgery. Until she discovers she has other settings, other brands of femininity available for her to try out … Thus begins a potent hour, not always hilarious but undeniably persuasive, protesting against the strictly circumscribed roles that women are allowed to play – particularly in the movies, as Brophy sardonically demonstrates. The supreme-being conceit dilutes a bit – but our host’s righteous indignation and strong performing chops make this a compelling hour.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustTaiwan Season: Under MaskSome of the best dancers I have seen at the fringe are from Mailantia Dance Company, led by choreographer Lai Yun-Chi, who has danced with Hofesh Shechter’s junior company in London. It is worth singling out Huang Hsiao-Wen, who moves with incredible flow and compelling presence. Under Mask is a quartet for dancers dressed in steampunk-style masks and painted faces – the theme of identity, masks and the roles we play don’t come through much more meaningfully than that, but the way they move with swagger and mystery is enough. The piece is inspired by Taiwanese temple rituals and has that feel of something ancient, mythical or spiritual, even when the movement recalls commercial pop. It also draws on martial arts, hip-hop and contemporary dance, and you can see hints of Indian classical dance, maybe even flamenco at one point. A choreographer to watch out for.LWAtAssembly @ Dance Baseuntil 30 AugustView image in fullscreenGreat fun … Lauryn Jenkins in Big Dog.Photograph: Danny KaanBig DogPromising young writer-actor Izzy Radford’s debut play, Seating Plan, was a romcom set at a birthday party. Now she has penned an exuberant satire about a group of true-crime podcasters. Directed by Zoë Templeman-Young, Radford stars alongside Lauryn Jenkins as a fellow podcaster and Tumba Katanda as a journalist and office newbie, with Eleanor Cross as a disgruntled listener. There are energetic performances across the board, but it verges on the chaotic at times and is overstuffed with ideas, wavering somewhere between a true-crime parody and a dark comedy in the vein ofSeverance, for its observations on managerial-level, white-collar tyranny and conformist office behaviour. Great fun to watch, even if it feels underdeveloped in this current state.AAAtGilded Balloon Patter Houseuntil 31 AugustRosalie Minnitt: Clementine 2“A single baguette is worth 1,000 francs – and a married one far more!” Inher smash-hit maiden show, Rosalie Minnitt’s Regency-era alter ego Clementine tried to find a husband. In its follow-up (and in a bid, jokes Minnitt, to pass the Bechdel test), our heroine makes for the big city, to get caught up in a revolution with a distinctly French flavour. And taking to the streets amid popular revolt could scarcely be more disorientating than Clementine 2, an absolute blizzard of character-comedy that confirms Minnitt as a writer/performer in the vanguard. Does it pack quite the punch of its predecessor? Perhaps the satirical bite of Clementine 1.0 is lacking. Is its plot throwaway bordering on incomprehensible? It is. But this adventure in self-realisation for our bumptious, puppyish heroine (befriending Dickensian pickpockets; orchestrating the regicide of the king; flirting shamelessly with the audience) makes up for that abundantly in chaos, silliness, smarts and Minnitt’s full-pelt approach to comic performance.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustView image in fullscreenFolky celebration … The Palestinian Circus: Step and a Half.Photograph: UnderbellyThe Palestinian Circus: Step and a Half“Hope is a daily choice,” says a voice at the opening of the Palestinian Circus’s Step and a Half. “As long as the heart continues to beat, we keep on moving.” The Palestinian Circus has been running for 20 years, teaching children across the region and spawning this collective of artists. Not all the acts are at the technical level you become accustomed to at the fringe, but that’s not to say there isn’t some great work on the trapeze, straps and silks, taking nosedives from the ceiling. There’s a street performer feel, with fire poi and one guy who seems a very average juggler and then turns out to be a demon on the diabolo. It’s all enveloped in a folky, celebratory atmosphere, with traditional dabke dancing, too. “Joy itself is an act of resistance,” they say. It’s an easy show to feel warm towards.LWAtUnderbelly’s Circus Hub on the Meadowsuntil 29 AugustAhir Shah: Golden“Three hundred people looking one way, and one person looking the other. How do I justify that?” So asks comedianAhir Shah, and his answer is: honesty, about where he’s at in his life right now. That’s a laudable principle, but the result in Golden suggests honesty isn’t always the best policy – or at least, not in this dosage. The show finds Shah 35 and married, so overworked and anxious about money he develops a severe allergic reaction to his own life. Pile on depression, autism, a fire in his parents’ house and the expounding of his pessimistic view of midlife stasis with no further possibility of personal growth, and you get a show that no amount of decent jokes (of which there aren’t quite enough) can jollify. What’s left is an hour with a man grappling with his own mordant worldview, towards a sunnier conclusion – and probably towards a show striking a better balance as it develops between dark humour and despondency.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustView image in fullscreen‘What my mum thinks all fringe theatre looks like’ … Fanny Bleach: The Nearly Naked Show.Photograph: Ray MaloneFanny Bleach: The Nearly Naked ShowThis is what my mum thinks all fringe theatre looks like. A skulking performer dressed as a many-eyed Ikea bag hag emerges from an overflowing bin to lip-sync with toothy aggression, before stripping down several layers and unhinging her jaw to scream into a microphone. From geordie clown Emma Crowley-Bennett, this is an irreverent cabaret “freak show” – but everyone else in the lineup has tapped out, leaving only nervous work experience kid Daniel to man the stage. Crowley-Bennett’s energy is high and her costumes and characters are inventively grotesque, with Ms One-Tit flashing us her single massive nipple, and a Prawn Star pulling out its dark vein to appease Daniel’s fishy fetish. But what might work as a subversive short slot in a more populated cabaret is dragged out, with not enough dramatic muscle to confidently pull us through. A show that’s yet to find its hairy green feet.KWAtAssembly Roxyuntil 30 AugustRosco McClelland: The BonesIt’s never a great sign when a comedian airs their difficulties deciding what their show should be about. Rosco McClelland settles on “pathological demand avoidance”, his own brand of stubbornness that resists anyone making demands on him. It provides a very tenuous frame for what is, in effect, several club-comedy routines strung together by the Glaswegian. When that’s the case – when your show isn’t really about anything – you’ve got to hit big joke-to-joke, and happily McClelland lands a few comic haymakers here. There’s some palate-cleansing material about Scotland’s World Cup (mis)adventure, and a dopey anecdote about “ladling piss from a dog”. Later, an argument with his wife about a picture posted on Facebook (and this oneisabout demand avoidance) ends with a very satisfying punchline, and his shaggy-dog story about a supposed cyborg nemesis stacks laugh upon ridiculous laugh.BLAtMonkey Barrel Comedy(Cabaret Voltaire)until 30 AugustView image in fullscreenTrapped in a novelty news story … Meet Mayor MaxMeet Mayor MaxFirstly: awwwww! If you love puppy pics – and what kind of heartless fringegoer doesn’t? – then Alex Robins will quickly have you eating out of the palm of his paw. When Robins is dressed in dog ears and yapping away, a PowerPoint presentation is always on hand to bring coos of affection. This one-man play tells the true story of Max, a golden retriever who becomes the mayor of the sleepy California town of Idyllwild. So beloved is Max to this community of artists and hippies that, when he dies, a second Max is installed, and then a third (Maximus Mighty-Dog Mueller III currently serves there with a lifetime term). The play is billed as a story of hope but it can feel like you’re trapped inside a novelty news story. Robins is an engaging performer with an unsettlingly messianic edge, but we’re left with too many unanswered questions: what happens after Idyllwild’s citizens start voting for Trump? How exactly did Robins extract himself from scientology? The ending – no doubt like lovely Max himself – needs a sharper bite.TJAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 31 AugustCrushHadsan Mohamud’s debut play, longlisted for the 2025 Tony Craze award, oozes charm. It is a kooky kind of meet-cute in a mental health clinic for people with eating disorders where two British Somali teenagers become friends. When Najma (played by Mohamud) spots Zak (Mohamed Hashi), she finds him pretentious. But they are drawn closer, slowly opening up to each other, in Alena Sahota’s production. Although full of painful truths and culture-specific reflections, it plays out haltingly and rather statically. The couple are sweet although the romance seems contrived. But it captures the insidious and insistent nature of eating disorders and we fear for the outcome of these teenagers in their rocky journeys towards healing.AAAtUnderbelly, Bristo Squareuntil 30 AugustView image in fullscreenToo hot to handle … Alex Hines and Sarah Stafford in BirdsBirdsJust sit back and enjoy the heat?Richard Tice should try telling that to this pair.House of Oz’s apocalyptic two-hander, created by Alex Hines and Sarah Stafford, opens with two toweringly beehived ladies of leisure, Shayna and Beverley, on deckchairs beneath the punishing sun. As the booze from the cooler slips down, they watch the birds above whose cackling cries and sharp talons they share – along with the instinct to beak into each other’s business. It can feel like a cheeky camp spin on Caryl Churchill’s Escaped Alone and the flights of fancy build in terrible rage until a rat-a-tat finale delivered almost at the pace of Beckett’s Not I. As their skin begins to peel and houses collapse into the ocean, in a luridly painted show that feels a little over-extended, you may need to lie down in a shady spot yourself.CWAtAssembly George Squareuntil 30 AugustBurger and a Pint: Treats for the SoulSketch duo Burger and a Pint (AKA James Trickey and Ted Milligan) won the Leicester Square Sketch Off in 2024 and arrive promising to explore “expectations of masculinity” in their debut fringe show. That promise is not fulfilled by a conventional and fairly slapdash offering with nothing to say about masculinity whatsoever – unless there’s deeper meaning sublimated in that Indiana Jones-alike sketch about having to amputate your penis to enter an ancient temple. That’s blokey par for the course in a show that reaches its nadir with a sketch in which a puppeteer must repeatedly insist that he doesn’t have sex with his puppets. There’s better stuff elsewhere: a choice Mastermind sketch; Dickens’ Fagin on Diary of a CEO. The between-scene banter, and the relationship it reveals, is unsurprising. Even allowing for tech difficulties at the performance I saw, it all feels a little underworked.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustJonathan Oldfield: Exquisite CorpseOldfield makes his solo debut this year but he’s been an unseen presence in recent hits, includingLorna Rose Treen’s workandJoe Kent-Walters’ debut as Frankie Monroe. This character-comedy effort is a real eye-catcher, similar to Treen’s in its array of apropos-of-nothing oddballs, yet with a flavour entirely its own. It derives from the kids’ doodling game sometimes called exquisite corpse, in which legs, torso and head, all drawn by different people, are united to create unlikely bodies. Oldfield plays it with his audience here, and feeds the results into his gallery of eccentric creations: an allotment gardener with a sideline in erotic dancing; a Blockbuster video clerk pining for a son. The linking narrative about Oldfield breaking his arm seven times, and how that led to an ambivalent relationship with his body, can feel tenuous – but this is a captivating hour on corporeal fragmentation and reassembly.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsIn the UK,Beatcan be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In the US, theNational Eating Disorders Associationis on 800-931-2237. In Australia, theButterfly Foundationis at 1800 33 4673. Other international helplines can be found atEating Disorder Hope.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalDanceCircusfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a hit jumpy horror series returns with Dan Stevens  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Terror is a terrifying drama anthology. Plus, tissues at the ready for a super emotional finale of The Piano. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The Terror is a terrifying drama anthology. Plus, tissues at the ready for a super emotional finale of The Piano. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: The ambient hum of horror … The Terror: Devil in Silver on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Emily V Aragones/AMC/2025 AMC Film Holdings LLC. All Rights Reserved.View image in fullscreenThe ambient hum of horror … The Terror: Devil in Silver on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Emily V Aragones/AMC/2025 AMC Film Holdings LLC. All Rights Reserved.TV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a hit jumpy horror series returns with Dan StevensThe Terror is a terrifying drama anthology. Plus, tissues at the ready for a super emotional finale of The Piano. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Graeme Virtue,Hannah VerdierandSimon WardellSun 23 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Terror: Devil in Silver9pm, Sky Atlantic“We all got our demons, don’t we?” We certainly do, though it’s rare to see them manifest so vividly in a drama. This third standalone story in The Terror anthology series is set in an understaffed, underfunded and quite possibly cursed psychiatric hospital. Dan Stevens stars as Peter “Pepper” Coffin, who has been wrongfully committed to the institution and is forced to reckon with its tatty malevolence. We meet the patients in their past and present lives and connect them via the sinister Dr Walter (John Benjamin Hickey) who may just be the key to the whole mystery. It doesn’t lack jump-scares but also generates a subtler, more genuinely unsettling ambient hum of horror.Phil HarrisonViolent Earth6pm, Sky Nature“It was chewing up everything in its path!” So begins the first episode – about terrifying tornadoes – in an intense new series about the science behind natural disasters. It’s presented by actor Liev Schreiber, for reasons unknown, and features first-hand footage taken across the world, along with eyewitness accounts.Hollie RichardsonForce of Nature7pm, ITV1Extreme heat is tackled in this instalment of the series dramatising how the climate crisis affects animals, from increased drought to the rise of wildfires around the globe. That means a wombat in Australia, a leopard in Zambia and a kangaroo rat in Arizona all abruptly find themselves starring in their own mini disaster movies.Graeme VirtueMozart at the Proms8pm, BBC FourA pair of Wolfie’s crowd-pleasers for your delectation: the Third Horn Concerto, featuring star soloist Felix Klieser; plus his exuberant Symphony No 35, AKA the “Haffner”, whose first movement, Amadeus advised, should be “played with fire”. Also, pieces by Elgar, Britten and, making its Proms debut, Thea Musgrave’s Out of the Darkness concerto for bassoon.Ali CatterallThe Piano9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenShow time! … The Piano on Channel 4.Photograph: Channel 4 / Nic Serpell RandJamie asked Claudia to sing a few notes, which he then improvised from when he first played in the competition. Will he need her help again in the final? He plays on stage along with Grace, who lost all her fingers after meningitis, Harri, with his song inspired by his grandad, wildcard teen Sophie and “piano-breaker” Gabby.HROne Dollar11.20pm, ITV1“No guns, no body” and a cast of suspects: this acclaimed US drama knows how to set up a tale. And as a dollar bill changes hands in a struggling rust belt town divided by culture and class, secrets emerge, aided by John Carroll Lynch, Leslie Odom Jr, Nathaniel Martello-White and more.Hannah VerdierFilm choiceH Is for Hawk, out now, NetflixView image in fullscreen‘A perfectly evolved psychopath’ … H Is for Hawk on Netflix.Photograph: Roadside Attractions/Everett/ShutterstockGetting up close and personal with animals can be a life-affirming way of feeling at one with nature. It can also be a way of avoiding the messier everyday of being human. For Helen Macdonald (a febrile Claire Foy), in Philippa Lowthorpe’s adaptation of Macdonald’s bestselling memoir, it is the tug between the two that brings her world crashing down. After her beloved father (Brendan Gleeson) dies, Helen decides to train a goshawk (“a perfectly evolved psychopath,” her mentor warns) in memory of their shared love of the great outdoors. But confronting avian life red in tooth and claw isn’t the same as dealing with the complex emotions of grief. An arresting, affecting drama.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was scared I was going mad’: Meg Mason speaks to fellow authors about the parasocial relationships that begin on the page | Fiction | The Guardian
description: As a lonely teenager, the novels of Nancy Mitford offered the Sorrow and Bliss author a lifeline, and an imaginary friend. She explores why reading can create a particularly intense bond with a favourite writer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a lonely teenager, the novels of Nancy Mitford offered the Sorrow and Bliss author a lifeline, and an imaginary friend. She explores why reading can create a particularly intense bond with a favourite writer
Content: Meg Mason.Photograph: Anne PeetersView image in fullscreenMeg Mason.Photograph: Anne PeetersFiction‘I was scared I was going mad’: Meg Mason speaks to fellow authors about the parasocial relationships that begin on the pageAs a lonely teenager, the novels of Nancy Mitford offered the Sorrow and Bliss author a lifeline - and an imaginary friend. She explores why reading can create a particularly intense bond with a favourite writerMeg MasonSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer before university, my mother gave me a copy ofThe Pursuit of Love. We’d moved countries at the beginning of my A-levels and those months in between had been defined by a level of loneliness I had never known in my life. The sort of loneliness so acute and pervasive it feels like panic, and on top of all that, so shaming to be 17 with nowhere to go and nothing to do on a Saturday night.Growing up, my mother – a great reader – would say: “When you’ve got a book, you’ve got a friend,” which is why, presumably, I wasn’t a great reader. Then, I’d always had actual friends. And suddenly I didn’t and presumably that is why I accepted the Nancy Mitford paperback and started to read it.I loved it, immediately. Finished, I asked if there were others and could we get them. I loved them all, more and more with every rereading. There was so much humour, and such solace in sad parts. The novels were so populated, I found company in the characters, and eventually in the person of the author too, privately coming to believe that if I had ever met Nancy Mitford, we would have become friends.Although my loneliness ended when university began, Nancy remained with me – never as intensely, but always there, so that now, age 48, I still find it hard to believe she isn’t actually my friend.I never would have described this as a parasocial relationship, although that’s precisely what it is: “a connection that someone feels between themselves and a famous person they do not know”, as the Cambridge Dictionary defined it when they announced it as theirword of the year in 2025. To me, the term sounded creepy, an activity of the unhinged. But if it’s common enough to become a word of the year, does that mean everyone is going about life with an imaginary friend? And we readers, especially?double quotation markIs everyone going about life with an imaginary friend? And we readers, especially?Although current, nothing about the phenomenon is new, the term devised in the 50s by a pair of academics studying the curious connection watchers of television appeared to feel with characters. Unsurprisingly, it’s tricky to gather statistics on relationships that exist solely in the mind. Oneonline studya couple of years back suggested that “51% of Americans have likely been in parasocial relationships”, though “only 16% admit to it”.While I was writingSophie, Standing There, my novel about a parasocial relationship between a reader and an author (even writing, I resisted using the term until there was no way around it), my non-imaginary friend Cathy Rentzenbrink was at work onThe Agatha Christie Cure, her memoir published next month about returning to her most beloved author in the period following her divorce. Had she developed a parasocial connection with Christie while rereading every one of her novels, and now writing about the author’s life? Yes, Cathy said, insofar as: “I started talking to her and she was talking back. I am a bit embarrassed, not by the experience, which was wondrous, but by what people might say or how they might judge me. I was often scared I was going mad.”She wasn’t. Not according to Dr Georgia Carroll, a sociologist whose research is focused on parasocial relationships. “I think almost every single person has had one, whether it’s with Taylor Swift, or the millions of people who feel connected to Lewis Hamilton.” While there are commonalities to all – “the key is that the relationship will never become reciprocal” – there is, Carroll believes, a uniqueness to the reader-author version. “With books, it becomes a bit deeper, more often, because they hold such a place in the lives of big readers. Everybody has that favourite book that is so meaningful to them because the author captured something that makes us feel less alone.”View image in fullscreenNancy Mitford in 1970.Photograph: Reg Lancaster/GettyWhether readers are more inclined to loneliness (and it’s in lonely periods that parasocial relationships are most easily formed), our chosen pursuit is solitary, performed only in company with the author. “That one-to-one element is critical,” says Carroll. “The feeling that the author is talking only to you.”And there is a sense in which book-lovers are most primed for parasocial relationships by the very fact that novels are about imaginary relationships between invented people, and our skill in reading is suspending disbelief. “Readers, as opposed to watchers, have been trained to fill in the gaps,” says Rentzenbrink, “to convert sentences into multi-dimensional worlds.”“I think it’s all too easy for the lines to be blurred between a character we love, and the author who created that character,” agrees book blogger Tilly Fitzgerald. “If a character is warm and funny, and the kind of person we would choose to be friends with, we can often assume the author will be too.”double quotation markNow, putting together a picture of an author's life is the work of one evening in bed with your phoneOver a lifetime of reading, Barbara Trapido, author ofBrother of the More Famous Jack(the cult classic that has surely made her the object of many parasocial relationships), has formed many “deep and extended relationships with characters. For half a year, aged 17, I believed IwasHenry James’s Isabel Archer.” And there was a period, she says, “in which I found myself, doubtless through yearning, talking to Shakespeare, but all unawares. It’s massively exciting to have the privilege of talking to the dead.”Because, in the case of reading, it doesn’t actually matter if the author is alive. “In fact,” Rentzenbrink says, “it makes it a bit easier if they aren’t.” And in a way safer, because they do not change. The politics to one side, the intensity of fans’ anger towards JK Rowling is largely grief for a lost friendship, a version of: “I thought I knew you and I didn’t.”With a living author, the sense of truly knowing them has become much keener. It wasn’t that long ago you could read an author without ever discovering what they sounded or looked like. Now, putting together a picture of their life is the work of one evening in bed with your phone. And when it comes to the creation of a parasocial relationship, nothing is more potent than the podcast. “It feels more intimate, doesn’t it?” says Jack Edwards, of the hugely successful literary podcast,Inklings Book Club. “We bring the author’s voice into our homes, on to our morning commute, into our safe spaces,” – in my character Sophie’s case, it’s always in the bath – “so it’s a together-aloneness, where we have company in our ears, but otherwise feel unobserved.” It goes both ways, Edwards points out. “We invite authors into our homes, through the listening experience, but often they record from their own homes too.”Which brings up the other side. That is, how it feels to be an author in this moment. Certainly, readers can be passionate – I have seen Sorrow and Bliss tattoos, inspired bymy last novel– but no one I’ve met in real life has wanted anything more than to chat about books, or to tell me what my work meant to them, and how could I be other than glad about that? Likewise, Trapido says, “I’ve always liked readers coming up to say how much they like my books, though, oddly enough, they often apologise for approaching.”Feel a connection to a celebrity you don’t know? There’s a word for thatRead morePerhaps the whole thing is the author’s fault anyway, because what we are constantly trying to do is connect, and make you believe in our characters. So the idea that some made-up version of me as an author has provided company for someone who feels as unsurrounded as I did before university, or as Sophie does in my new novel – at no cost to myself – is extraordinary and a privilege. I’m grateful too that Nancy was there for me when I most needed her, and still is. Everyone says we read to know we’re not alone. But you could also say, we read and so we aren’t alone.Sophie, Standing There is published by Bloomsbury on 27 August. To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violence | Games | The Guardian
description: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards
Author: Jackson Ryan
Headline: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards
Content: A still from Halloween: The Game. The ability for players to smoke marijuana to detect an enemy has resulted in the game being banned in Australia.Photograph: IllfonicView image in fullscreenA still from Halloween: The Game.
