The ability for players to smoke marijuana to detect an enemy has resulted in the game being banned in Australia.Photograph: IllfonicGamesThe new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violenceAcademics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standardsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJackson RyanSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 21.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. The US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.But Australians will not be able to play Halloween, because it has been refused classification by the Australian Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders.In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that the Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of ComputerGames2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchiseRead more“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the boardwrote in a recent statement.In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game.The uproar has resurfaced longstanding grievances about how games are classified in Australia compared with film and television, and the inability for adults to access games widely available in other parts of the world.double quotation markCan we stop pretending that the way we classify games in Australia, in 2026, is appropriate for adults?Margaret Anderson, former director of the Classification BoardClaire Henry, an associate professor in screen at Flinders University and an Australian Research Council fellow, says the board enforced the guidelines correctly but the controversy around the decision highlights “a mismatch between the community standards and the classification standards”.The decision on Halloween: The Game follows several high-profile cases that have resulted in games such asState of Decay,Wasteland 3andSaints Row IVbanned in Australia for the same reason: incentivised drug use. All of these games were later reclassified after censoring aspects of their gameplay.View image in fullscreenSaints Row IV. The game was initially refused classification in Australia but was later released after a particular mission was removed.Photograph: Deep SilverDan Golding, a professor of media at Monash University, says that two assumptions have been baked into the classifying of games in Australia. “Games have always been regulated based on the assumption there is something more impactful aboutdoing,in a game, than there is aboutwatching,in a film,” he says.“A second assumption is that games are for kids – or at least the regulation system exists to protect kids.”Ron Curry has battled these assumptions in skirmishes with the Classification Board over his nearly two decades as CEO of the Interactive Games and Entertainment Association (IGEA). Alongside a dogged public campaign and a cadre of journalists, the IGEA helped introduce an R18+ category for video games in 2013, the absence of which had stopped several games being released in Australia before.After the R18+ classification was brought in, Curry noted the jobwas not finished– the trade-off for introducing the category was that video games were still seen as a distinct form of media, with greater risks attached.“It still very clearly said games are different to all other media, it’s more dangerous, and we need to treat it more carefully,” Curry says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSaints Row 4 refused classification in AustraliaRead moreInteractivity – thedoingGolding refers to – has always underlined this belief. The guidelines for games, introduced alongside the R18+ rating, state that “as a general rule computer games may have a higher impact than similarly themed depictions of the classifiable elements in film, and therefore greater potential for harm or detriment, particularly to minors”.Curry points tothe Australian government’s own research that hassuggested interactivity may not increase the impact of video games, particularly in regards to violent content, and there has been limited research on interactivity around drug use, sex, gambling and nudity.Margaret Anderson, a former director of the Classification Board, says the huge focus on interactivity in games drove her nuts during her seven years on the board. She points todecades of researchshowing games are predominantly played by adults.“Can we stop pretending that the way we classify games in this country, in 2026, is appropriate for adults? Because it’s not,” Anderson says.Academics have shown the current classification system isn’t just preventing access to games, however. Often, the standards are incoherent.Marcus Carter, founder of the Sydney Games and Play Lab at the University of Sydney, recently leda study– yet to be peer reviewed – that showed inconsistencies across the classifications of mobile games in the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. In 18 separate cases across the 31 top-grossing mobile games, four different age ratings were included for a single game.Carter describes the current system as “not fit for purpose”.The worry, for experts like Carter and Henry, is that the inconsistent standards have a negative impact on how the community views classifications and age ratings.“Inconsistencies can kind of undermine public confidence in the classification system,” says Henry. “It is a good system in many ways, and we’ve got to maintain that trust.”The Australian government isundertaking a review of the classification guidelineswith the aim of delivering a simpler, more consistent approach across films, games and publications. Among a raft of proposals – including introducing a PG13 rating and adjusting the MA15+ classification to MA16+ – one idea is to “remove the harsher judgement of video games’ interactivity”.IGEAandHenryhave made submissions to the review.In a statement to the Guardian,a spokesperson from the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts said: “The Australian Government is working to modernise the National Classification Scheme to ensure it remains aligned with community standards and helps Australians make informed decisions about what they read, watch and play. This work is ongoing.”Illfonic has shown no sign it will censor Halloween: The Game and have its classification reviewed in Australia. Illfonic and the game’s co-publisher Gun Interactive did not respond to requests for comment.Though the instances of Australia banning games have been rare occurrences, one future decision looms large: how will Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment in a franchise packed with sex, drugs and violence,be rated?For Anderson, the way forward is simple.“The foundational pillar of classification in Australia is that adults should be able to read, hear, see, play what they want,” she says. “Can we please respect that fact?”Explore more on these topicsGamesHalloween (2018)Horror filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Haribo Kimchi review – Korean snack bar serves lessons in belonging | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jaha Koo cooks up street-food treats for two lucky theatregoers as he reflects on how food preserves memory and cultural identity, with the help of a snail and an eel
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Jaha Koo cooks up street-food treats for two lucky theatregoers as he reflects on how food preserves memory and cultural identity, with the help of a snail and an eel
Content: A taste of South Korea … Jaha Koo.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA taste of South Korea … Jaha Koo.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHaribo Kimchi review – Korean snack bar serves lessons in belongingFestival theatre studio, EdinburghJaha Koo cooks up street-food treats for two lucky theatregoers as he reflects on how food preserves memory and cultural identity, with the help of a snail and an eelMark FisherSun 23 Aug 2026 06.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo get the measure of this slight but sweet one-man show, you need to listen to the singing snail. “In every soil grows a different version of you,” sings the animated creature in Korean, projected on a screen.It is echoing the sentiment just expressed by an eel: “My home has no location,” sings a fish that lives a life of transformation as it moves between saltwater and fresh.Their experience is one shared by performer Jaha Koo, who left his native South Korea for Europe 15 years ago and has the rootlessness of the displaced. His sense of alienation is exacerbated by the racism he encounters, notably the assistant who complains of a stench of garlic despite sitting behind a screen.That is a rare dark moment in a cheerful show, but the association with food is apt. Koo might be adrift in the world, but keeps his home with him via hisnational cuisine. Inviting two volunteers to join him at hispojangmacha, a street-food snack bar, he cooks up several courses as the show progresses: a cucumber starter, a kimchi pancake, a bowl of soup and a pudding flavoured with seagrass, mint and lime. They seem to enjoy it.View image in fullscreenScreen projections aid the storytelling in Haribo Kimchi.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianNot all his food-related memories are happy: after smelling the corpses lined up after theGwangju pro-democracy uprisingof 1980, Koo’s father could not bear the smell of fried chicken and retreated to the countryside to escape it.But for the most part, in Koo’s own production for Campo in Ghent, the performer reflects on a country that, like many others, finds community in food. It brings identity and salvation, not least the Haribo gummies that cheer him up away from home. Like the snail and the eel, they keep him company. Naturally, the Haribos get a song too.AtFestival theatre studio, Edinburgh, until 24 AugustAll our Edinburgh reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bebe Cave: Swoon review – dazzling portrait of marginalised muses and the male gaze | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Smart, slapstick and silly, this chaotic multicharacter comedy sends up the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
Author: Arusa Qureshi
Headline: Smart, slapstick and silly, this chaotic multicharacter comedy sends up the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
Content: The idea of the perfect woman involves her looking near death … Bebe Cave in Swoon.Photograph: Rebecca Nead-MenearView image in fullscreenThe idea of the perfect woman involves her looking near death … Bebe Cave in Swoon.Photograph: Rebecca Nead-MenearEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBebe Cave: Swoon review – dazzling portrait of marginalised muses and the male gazePleasance Dome, EdinburghSmart, slapstick and silly, this chaotic multicharacter comedy sends up the Pre-Raphaelite BrotherhoodArusa QureshiSun 23 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of the most revered works of art across history feature women as their primary focus. But though they might appear as favoured subjects, so often these women are relegated to the margins, their stories untold as they remain silent and often sexualised via the male gaze.In her new multicharacter comedy Swoon, Bebe Cave interrogates the role of the muse and what it means to be seen yet never heard. We initially meet Cave as Elizabeth Siddal – or Lizzie – who was immortalised as Ophelia by John Everett Millais in the mid 19th century, also becoming a popular model for several otherpre-Raphaeliteartists.With her comically excessive scouse accent and world-weary exasperation, she is the poster child for being sad and sexy, her story underlining the dichotomy between the elevated status of the muse and their simultaneously poor treatment by artists. The narrative, however, centres on the fictional Bertrude, Lizzie’s sister, who is desperate to be noticed and included by the pretentious Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, whose idea of the perfect woman involves her looking near death.View image in fullscreenAmping up the absurdity … Bebe Cave.Photograph: Rebecca Nead-MenearSwoon sees Cave take on numerous characters at breakneck speed, with appearances from a lanky redheaded mannequin, gloriously baffling dance sequences and casual pop culture references throughout. Cave emits a chaotic energy in her portrayal of the brotherhood and the many characters in their orbit, with her delightfully janky costumes and props and a Millais-coded set design amping up the absurdity at every turn.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreAs Dante Gabriel Rossetti, she is the ultimate hipster bro, a printed Carhartt logo stuck to her top hat adding an excellent touch in the depiction of his obnoxious faux-trendiness. The men’s nonchalant misogyny and their lack of care towards women is accentuated by Cave through their cringey edgelord behaviour.Giving us a Victorian-era Tyra Banks as well as the Brontë sisters, Swoon is a highly impressive and creative feat of physical comedy, with an intelligent throughline that never takes away from the more slapstick and silly elements. The show has a wealth of jokes that rely on the audience having some knowledge of art history, but even without this, the message is clear: ridiculous men with pompous attitudes are forever contributing to the erasure of women.They may live eternally in the art itself, but Cave argues that muses like Lizzie deserve more than just being nameless subjects. And in this, Swoon works to dismantle the illusion of impossible beauty standards set and romanticised by clueless men.AtPleasance Dome, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalTheatreThe pre-RaphaelitesPaintingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: This Black August, Americans will study, meditate, fast, exercise – and read – for Black liberation | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: Organizations across the country traditionally use the month as a means of activation for local communities
Author: Adria R Walker
Headline: Organizations across the country traditionally use the month as a means of activation for local communities
Content: Mourners give the Black Panther salute as the body of George Jackson is carried from St Augustine's Episcopal church in Oakland, California, on 28 August 1971.Photograph: Robert Klein/APView image in fullscreenMourners give the Black Panther salute as the body of George Jackson is carried from St Augustine's Episcopal church in Oakland, California, on 28 August 1971.Photograph: Robert Klein/APGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Black US cultureThis Black August, Americans will study, meditate, fast, exercise – and read – for Black liberationOrganizations across the country traditionally use the month as a means of activation for local communitiesAdria R WalkerSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the 1960s and 1970s, California was brimming with radical energy and potential, which also meant it was brimming with extreme backlash. The Black Panthers, a revolutionary Black political activist organization founded in response to police brutality, were organizing members at the same time Ronald Reagan, then the California governor and the future US president, and others were working torepress the groupand its growing political influence.At the same time, several young men, some incarcerated atSan Quentin prison, and some elsewhere in the California prison system, wereunder attack, beingassaulted and murderedby theAryan Brotherhood, a white supremacist group, and sympathetic guards. Some of the men – WL Nolen; George Jackson, a field marshal of the Black Panther party who also founded a prison chapter of the organization; and others – decided they needed to band together to defend themselves and formed the Black Guerrilla Family (BGF), a Marxist-Leninist prison gang.View image in fullscreenGeorge Jackson’s casket, draped in a Black Panther flag, is carried from St Augustine’s Episcopal church in Oakland, California, on 28 August 1971.Photograph: APMany of the early members of the BGF, most barely in their 20s, would not live to see the 1980s: Nolen was killed, along with two others, by San Quentin prison guards on 13 January 1970,George JacksonwaskilledinSan Quentin prisonon 21 August 1971; George’s brother, Jonathan Jackson, was killed on 7 August 1970; and Khatari Gaulden waskilledin San Quentin prison on 1 August 1978.“As a result of these deaths, the group known as Black Guerrilla Family decided they needed to commemorate the deaths of their comrades Jonathan, George and Khatari, and they began the process of deciding how they were going to do so,” said Jalil Muntaqim, a community organizer and former Black Liberation Army (BLA) member. He was convicted and imprisoned for several decades for the murder of two New York police department officers. “They began organizing what was called Black August,” Muntaqim said.Since its creation, Black August has spread beyond prison walls and is commemorated both by people who are and are not incarcerated today. True to its roots, people study, meditate and hone their activism during the month. It is a time when people push for the release of Black political and revolutionary leaders, many of whom are now in their 70s and 80s, from prison.Today, organizations across the country use the month as a means of activation for their local communities. Each year in Tallahassee, Florida, the Tallahassee Dream Defenders host aBlack August showcase.Black August in the Park, held annually in Durham, North Carolina, blends music, dancing and film screenings with educational opportunities. In Oakland, California, theBlack August Arc of Liberation Commemorationhonors the legacy of Black August through art. Using the tenets of the original Black August commemoration, the Brooklyn-basedFree Black Women’s Librarycreated a challenge to engage readers, along with hosting events throughout the month of August.What happens when the US declares war on your parents? The Black Panther cubs knowRead moreThe historian and author Gerald Horne said that “there’s a striking confluence that occurs in August”. It’s when, on 1 August, many Caribbean nations celebrate Emancipation Day; when, on 11 August, the Watts uprising began; when, on 21 August, Nat Turner’s rebellion began; and when, on 23 August, the Haitian revolution began, but it’s also the birth month of pan-Africanist leader Marcus Garvey, Black Panther Fred Hampton and Black liberationist Chokwe Lumumba.“It’s important for us to understand that Black August does not come out of a vacuum. It comes out of a movement, out of a determination of people trying to defend themselves against harm and the reality of the US penal slave system,” Muntaqim said.BGF members looked at the month of August, noted its almost divine confluence of births, deaths and events that are significant to Black history and Black liberation, and decided that the month needed particular acknowledgement.View image in fullscreenBlack August-Los Angeles, by Donald ‘C-Note’ Hooker, 2016.Photograph: Donald ‘C-Note’ Hooker“They evolved a concept of study, exercise and fasting for the month of August, and by virtue of them promoting Black August, it has now become a national and an international institution,” Muntaqim said. “People are to fast, they are to exercise. They are also to study and reflect, meditate. The primary principle of Black August and the golden objective is to restore our capacity for our humanity, and our ability to resist systems of white supremacy, racial capitalism, colonialism, neocolonialism and imperialism.”The commemoration remains “a way to talk about freeing Black political prisoners generally”, Horne, the author and historian, said. Several Black Panthers or other members of Black radical organizations who, despite now being in their 70s and 80s and, in many cases, in failing health, are still in prison, including Mumia Abu-Jamal, Thomas “Tahaka” Gaither and Veronza Bowers Jr. Many others have died in prison within the last several years.“You’re protesting injustice when you protest the fact that people like Mumia [Abu-Jamal] are still behind bars,” Horne said. “By protesting injustice, you’re also protesting the spread of injustice. In other words, ultimately, it’s an act of self-preservation because if you allow injustice to fester, it can obviously spread right to your front door.”It’s also an opportunity for international solidarity.“Black August is truly important because it creates a foundational basis for our resistance to other people’s resistance and in foreign people around the world, we are resisting,” Muntaqim said. “That’s the reason why we have to have international solidarity and build our relationship with others around the world … Black August is one of the areas which we can show or prove our capacity to resist.”Each year, people across the country and world use Black August as a time to be intentional about engaging with Black radical literature. They study Black precolonial history and learn about slave rebellions and the ongoing fight for liberation. Here are some texts to read this Black August:Crusade for Justice: The Autobiography of Ida BWellsby Ida B WellsThe Destruction of Black Civilization: Great Issues of a Race from 4500 BCto 2000 ADby Chancellor WilliamsBlack Reconstruction in America, 1860-1880by WE Burghardt Du BoisHave Black Lives Ever Mattered?by Mumia Abu-Jamalskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNegroesWith Gunsby Robert F WilliamsA Fighting Dream: The Political Writings of Claudia Jonesby Claudia JonesHow Europe Underdeveloped Africaby Walter RodneyBlack Skin, White Masksby Frantz FanonHarlem Shadows: Poemsby Claude McKayQueen Mother: Black Nationalism, Reparations, and the Untold Story of Audley Mooreby Ashley D FarmerThe Counter-Revolution of 1776: Slave Resistance and the Origins of the United States of Americaby Gerald HorneFree the Land: The Republic of New Afrika and the Pursuit of a Black Nation-Stateby Edward OnaciSoledad Brother: The Prison Letters of George Jacksonby George JacksonAnarchist Panther: The Selected Writings of Ashanti OAlstonby Ashanti Omowali AlstonWe Are Our Own Liberators: Selected Prison Writingsby Jalil MuntaqimMississippi, Conflict and Change: A New Editionby James W Loewen, Byron D’Andra Orey and Charles SallisGolden Gulag: Prisons, Surplus, Crisis, and Opposition in Globalizing Californiaby Ruth Wilson GilmoreWe Paved the Way: Black Women and the Charleston Hospital Workers’ Campaignby O Jennifer Dixon-McKnightResisting State Violence: Radicalism, Gender, and Race in USCultureby Joy JamesExplore more on these topicsBlack US cultureHistoryRaceUS prisonsUS policingActivismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect zaru soba, or cold soba noodles – recipe | Noodles | The Guardian
description: Hot days call for cool dinners, and these are Japan’s nutty, salty and sweet solution. Fiery or pickled accompaniments optional
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Hot days call for cool dinners, and these are Japan’s nutty, salty and sweet solution. Fiery or pickled accompaniments optional
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfectzaru soba.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfectzaru soba.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.How to cook the perfect ...NoodlesHow to make the perfect zaru soba, or cold soba noodles – recipeHot days call for cool dinners, and these are Japan’s nutty, salty and sweet solution. Fiery or pickled accompaniments optionalFelicity CloakeSun 23 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlthough every culture craves something different in hot weather – chilled beetroot soup in Lithuania, coolingbuttermilk drinksin India,gazpachoin Spain – what many of these dishes have in common is a certain soothing silkiness as they slide down the throat, plus a decent helping of salt. Japan’szaru soba, whichNamiko Hirasawa Chenof Just One Cookbook describes as her family’s “go-to meal when the summer heat and humidity soar”, is no exception. Cold, slippery noodles paired with a savoury dipping sauce, it’s a simple, satisfying dish that’s ready in 15 minutes, and can be accessorised with crunchy salads, sweet seafood or creamy tofu sides for something more substantial. Traditionally served on a bamboo mat, orzaru, to allow the noodles to drain, you can get away without one at home (though lose the seaweed and you can call itmori sobainstead), this is definitely one to stick in your summer repertoire alongside the chilled soups, watermelon salads and cucumber sandwiches.The noodlesZaru soba isn’t the only chilled noodle dish that Japan slurps in summer –Emiko Davies favours her mother’ssomen(delicate wheat-flour strands), whileShota Nakajima makes a case forhiyashi chuka, a Chinese-inspired ramen salad. Sadly, though, spindly somen and fresh ramen are trickier to source in the UK than buckwheat soba, which can be found in many larger supermarkets.In fact,Yumiko Maehashi of RecipeTin Japanreckons that these noodles’ nutty flavour is best enjoyed cold: “I read in a Japanese soba article that some soba fanatics would not consider the soba in hot soup as ‘soba’.” Not all, however, are created equal, as Maehashi goes on to explain: “Some soba brands indicate the ratio of buckwheat and wheat flours mixed in the soba noodles. The more buckwheat flour, the more flavour and the more expensive … It is really your preference as to what sort of soba noodles are the best, but, in general, the more expensive dried soba noodles cook to al dente better.” If you’d like to keep this dish gluten-free, you’ll need to look for 100% buckwheat noodles (and a gluten-free Japanese soy sauce – Kikkoman makes one), but, otherwise, it’s up to you. Buckwheat can, after all, be an acquired taste, especially in such a simple dish.The noodles are cooked without salt, I suspect to facilitate the contrast with the dipping sauce. Swirling them around the pan for the first 15 or so seconds, as Maehashi suggests, is a helpful tip to ensure that the strands don’t clump together. It’s also vital to rinse them well afterwards, to quickly cool down the noodles before they overcook, and to wash off some of the starch that will otherwise turn those lovely, silky noodles into a sticky bird’s nest (trust me on this). Chen dunks hers in iced water, too, but I don’t find that this step makes much of a difference texture-wise. Then again, neither do I notice that doing so causes the “noodles to ‘tighten’ up too quickly, losing their texture and flavour”, asLisa Kitahara at Okonomi Kitchenclaims, but I’ll concede I’m no soba expert.Once cooled, the soba are best consumed immediately, but if you find they’ve started to tangle, give them a rinse under cold water to separate the strands, then drain them well again afterwards. Traditionally, soba are served on a flat bamboo straining mat called azaru, but as long as you toss them well, a less picturesque plate or bowl is fine.The sauceThe proper way to eat zaru soba, according to Maehashi, is to “pick up a few strands of noodles and dip only the bottom half of them into the dipping sauce by simply lowering the chopsticks. Many people drop all the noodles they just picked up into the dipping sauce,” she adds, “but this is not a real gourmet way of eating buckwheat noodles. By dipping only part of the soba noodles in, you can taste the flavour of the noodles and enjoy it better.” So that’s you told.As only a little of the accompanyingmentsuyusauce gilds each helping of noodles, it has to be intense in flavour, hence the principal ingredients: salty soy sauce, mirin (a sweet rice wine; alcohol-free alternatives are available), umami-rich seaweed and dried, smoked tuna flakes. Maehashi points out that you can substitute ready-made dashi stock, easily found in any Japanese specialist store, for the kombu and katsuobushi element of things; indeed, you can even buymentsuyu in bottles, if you prefer, but it’s so easy to make that it won’t save you much time.Chen, andchef Aya Nishimura in her book, Japanese Food Made Easy, both add sake as well, which, though not mandatory, does give their sauces an interesting complexity that proves very popular with my testers (save yourself some money and go for a cooking sake, unless you’re planning to drink the rest of the bottle). We also enjoy the brown sugar that Nishimura and chef Maori Murota include, the latter in her bookTokyo Cult Recipes. Feel free to leave it out if you prefer; you can always stir some in at the end if you decide the sauce needs some sweetness. (Equally, Chen explains, if the sauce is too salty for your taste, you can dilute it with iced water.) Nishimura sticks in a couple of shiitake mushrooms too; I find them a bit overwhelming, but it does strike me that if you don’t eat fish, you might like to substitute these for the tuna flakes.The only small faff with this recipe is thinking ahead to ensure the sauce is cold before you eat, which is why it’s worth making several batches of it in hot weather; once strained, it keeps well in the fridge. I’d recommend keeping the kombu and tuna in for a few hours, as Murota seems to suggest, to extract as much flavour as possible. And don’t discard them once you separate the two, either; they can be saved and used to makefurikake rice seasoning.Chef Masaki Sugisaki of Dinings SW3in London, meanwhile, advises that, “once you have finished the noodles, heat the reserved noodle cooking water and add it to the dipping sauce. It is traditional to drink this as a soup, because the water contains nourishing minerals.”The accompanimentsZaru soba becomes nori soba with the addition of some shredded nori, those roasted laver seaweed sheets used to wrap some sushi rolls. This, along with fiery wasabi and spring onions, are the most common accompaniments in the recipes I try. Murota recommends daikon and garlic chive or the white part of a leek, rather than spring onions, and she and Nishimura include grated ginger too. All of these, along with the ground toasted sesame seeds that add an interesting additional texture to Nishimura’s dish, are possibilities. In fact, in the privacy of your own home, add whatever you want, but do bear in mind that the pleasure of this dish is its simplicity – silky noodles and salty broth – so try to avoid the temptation to load it up like a salad before you’ve even tried it.Perfect zaru sobaWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook10 minInfuse30 minChill2 hr+Serves22 x 75g bunches of soba noodles1 piece nori(optional)2 spring onions, or garlic chive leavesWasabi, fresh or pasteFor the sauce5cm x 5cm strip kombu4 tbsp Japanese soy sauce4 tbsp mirin2 tbsp sake(optional; if not using, add 2 tbsp extra water)1 tsp brown sugar5g katsuobushi (bonito) flakesPut the kombu and 150ml cold water in a small saucepan and leave to sit for half an hour.Add all the remaining sauce ingredients, bar the katsuobushi.View image in fullscreenSlowly bring to a boil, then turn off the heat, add the katsuobushi, leave to cool, then chill for a few hours, and preferably overnight.View image in fullscreenBring a wide pan of unsalted water to a boil. Add the noodles and stir for a few seconds to ensure they don’t clump together.View image in fullscreenCook according to the packet instructions (usually about five minutes) until very slightly al dente.Scoop the noodles into a sieve (save the cooking water) and rinse under cold water to cool completely, tossing them with your fingers to separate the strands. Shake the sieve a few times to remove as much water as possible.View image in fullscreenStrain the sauce (you can save the kombu and katsuobushi to makefurikake). Cut the nori into thin strips, finely chop the spring onion and grate the wasabi, if necessary.Serve the sauce in individual bowls with the noodles (on bamboo mats, if you have them) and accompaniments on the side for dipping. Once the noodles are finished, add cooking water to the remaining sauce to taste, to make a broth, and drink.Zaru soba: when did you discover this deliciously cooling noodle dish, where can you find the best, and what do you like to serve it with?Explore more on these topicsNoodlesHow to cook the perfect ...FoodJapanese food and drinkMain courseSouprecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘When I make a sale, I’ll sing a high note’: a day in the life of an opera singing car salesman | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Andrew Hiers is trying to start his own opera company. Until then, he’s serenading the parking lot
Author: Jaya Saxena
Headline: Andrew Hiers is trying to start his own opera company. Until then, he’s serenading the parking lot
Content: Andrew Hiers is both an opera singer and a car salesman, and his viral videos are all part of a plan to bring opera to his community in Florida.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/aahrealbassbaritoneView image in fullscreenAndrew Hiers is both an opera singer and a car salesman, and his viral videos are all part of a plan to bring opera to his community in Florida.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/aahrealbassbaritoneA day in the lifeWell actually‘When I make a sale, I’ll sing a high note’: a day in the life of an opera singing car salesmanAndrew Hiers is trying to start his own opera company. Until then, he’s serenading the parking lotJaya SaxenaSun 23 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew Hiers, 38, is an opera singer – a bass-baritone – and a car salesman in Cocoa, Florida. You might think these professions have nothing to do with each other, but hislibrettos about carsor to customershave gone viral– all part of a larger plan to bring opera to the local community.What time did you wake up?Today, I woke up a little bit earlier than usual, about 6.30. We have an old man cat; he’s 18 years old, and lately he forgets when feeding time is. At about 4.30, he’ll start yelling.I also returned an email to a young man finishing up his conducting degree. We’re trying to start our own opera company – I want something that’s going to be self-sustaining and generate revenue, whereas a lot of opera companies are based on donations and grants.What are your lunch plans?Because it’s a long day, I did bring some frozen stuff I can heat up. The other day, a customer I was taking on a test drive said, “Oh, I’m taking you to lunch with some friends,” which is not typical. One of them had seen my story, and he wanted to take my picture.When do you find time to make your videos?When the service people go home, that’s when a lot of my big videos have been shot in the store – I’ll bust out a few high notes. Or when I make a sale, I’ll sing a high note; those [videos] really have been doing well.What time do you normally go to sleep? Do you have any particular sleep routine?I’m a midnight, 1 o’clock person. I need to be better about it. They always say you should take 20 minutes before sleep to detox, but I want to maximize my me time. When my partner’s in town – she’s also an opera singer, actually a pretty famous opera singer [Chelsea Lehnea] – she tries to get me in bed closer to 11pm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy living situation is a bit unique. I live in an RV. When my partner and I met, it was right before the pandemic, and we quarantined together. After living with my parents for six months in West Palm Beach, she said: “I’m getting an RV. I’m going to renovate it. You can come with me or not.”I live in my college roommate’s front yard. She has a wonderful tub. Many nights, I’ll go over there and take a bath with Epsom salts, because my aching joints need it. I messed up my knee years ago – the day before my first opera, actually – I tore my ACL, so I’ve never done an opera on two good knees.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyA day in the lifeFloridaOperafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I tested the viral Shark CryoGlow LED face mask 100 times – it’s not right for everyone | Skincare | The Guardian
description: Brilliant for managing breakouts and refreshing puffy eyes, but after months of treatments, is Shark’s light therapy device the one our writer would buy now?
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: Brilliant for managing breakouts and refreshing puffy eyes, but after months of treatments, is Shark’s light therapy device the one our writer would buy now?
Content: Face time: ‘If my younger self got wind I was strapping on a glowing mask every day, she would die laughing.’Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFace time: ‘If my younger self got wind I was strapping on a glowing mask every day, she would die laughing.’Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSkincareReviewI tested the viral Shark CryoGlow LED face mask 100 times – it’s not right for everyoneBrilliant for managing breakouts and refreshing puffy eyes, but after months of treatments, is Shark’s light therapy device the one our writer would buy now?The best LED face masksSarah MatthewsSun 23 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf all theLED masksI’ve tested, the Shark CryoGlow feels like the most heavily marketed. Touted as a one-stop shop for anti-ageing, blemish-busting and undereye cooling, it’s trickled its way into countless influencer morning routines and post-work wind-downs, slowly but surely filling up my social media timeline.As an acne-prone woman whose work life revolves around beauty tech, the adverts are well placed. But that doesn’t negate the fact that, to the average consumer, LED therapy still reeks of pseudoscience. If my younger self got wind that I was strapping a glowing mask to my face every day, she would die laughing.Thankfully, I’ve spent months researching LED masks and have found that red-light therapy is backed by scientific researchdating to the 1990s. This includes studies onskin rejuvenation,wound healingandanti-ageing.I’ve had this mask for almost two years and have completed more than 100 light therapy treatments in that time. That makes this the most thoroughly tested product I’ve ever reviewed, and there’s a reason it became such a mainstay in my skincare routine. Here’s my full verdict on the CryoGlow, and why I’ve recently jumped ship in favour of a competitor.View at SharkNinjaView at John LewisHow I testedView image in fullscreenGlow with the flow: the mask’s blue light is meant to kill acne-causing bacteria.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianI’ve tested 14 other options in my quest to find thebest LED mask– which isn’t just about staring at your skin in the mirror and waiting for changes. For each LED mask I test, I consider how comfortable it is to wear for daily treatments, whether the eye guards block light effectively, as well as the number and brightness of the LEDs. I’m also looking for simple controls.To test the mask’s effectiveness, I noted the appearance, feel and texture of my skin before and after two months of daily treatments. I tried all the settings, including the undereye cooling, for at least four nights each, then chose my favourite setting for the rest of the test.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenThe right wavelength? The mask offers Better Ageing, Blemish Repair, Skin Sustain and Under-Eye Revive modes.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianView at SharkNinjaView at John LewisMany will be familiar with Shark’svacuum cleanersand hair care tools, but it hasn’t been in the skincare game for long. The 2024 CryoGlow was its first foray, followed by the 2025FacialPro Glow, a hydro and temperature therapy tool. While the FacialPro Glow came with a laundry list of usage warnings and a high risk of user error, the CryoGlow’s LED therapy is far less likely to go wrong.In LED therapy, each wavelength of light penetrates different levels of the skin, which can trigger specific natural processes. The CryoGlow has 160 LEDs that shine across three wavelengths: red light to help stimulate skin healing and collagen production; near-infrared light, which penetrates deeper into the skin; and blue light, which reduces acne-causing bacteria on the skin’s surface. It’s worth noting that blue light can cause hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones, so it should be used with caution.The wavelengths are arranged into three pre-programmed LED settings, starting with a six-minute anti-ageing setting, which combines red and near-infrared light. The Blemish Repair mode takes eight minutes and begins with blue and near-infrared light, followed by red light, which Shark says helps heal breakouts faster. After six to eight treatments, Shark recommends continuing with Skin Sustain, which combines all the light types at once in a four-minute treatment.The CryoGlow is also the only LED mask to have cooling pads under the eyes, which help to depuff the area. Cooling treatments alone can last from five to 15 minutes or can be used alongside the LED treatments. In each case, there are three temperature levels.The mask costs £299.99 at full price (from £245.32at the time of writing), which puts it firmly in the middle of the LED mask market. Cheaper masks, such as the £119Silk’n 100, offer a range of colours, but no infrared and tend not to be arranged into preset treatments, or have any extras such as undereye cooling. Conversely, more expensive masks can have brighter lights and deeper-penetrating near-infrared lights. The £499.99CurrentBody Multi Light Therapy maskis a fantastic example of this.Shark CryoGlow specificationsPrice:£299.99Recommended use:one treatment dailySettings:Better Ageing, Blemish Repair, Skin Sustain, undereye coolingTreatment time:four to eight minutes (LED), or five to 15 minutes (cooling)Suitable for:all skin types (excludingcertain skin conditions); darker skin tones should use caution with Blemish Repair modeBattery life:seven to 17 treatments, depending on cooling pad useCharging time:three hoursContents:Shark CryoGlow mask, clip-on undereye adjusters, USB-C charging cable and plugWhat we loveView image in fullscreenSkin Sustain mode did exactly what it promised, maintaining our tester’s calm, clear skin.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianAs an acne-prone person, I benefited most from the Blemish Repair mode. Unlike cheaper masks, which use blue light alone, the preset treatment combining blue and red light may bemore effective at treating acne, and I’ve found that to be true in my tests. The red light offers a gentler treatment because ithelps promote wound healing and calm inflammation, reducing the appearance of post-acne red marks. It’s far more convenient to have this as a preset treatment than to keep switching between different colours. After eight weeks of treatments, I noticed far fewer breakouts, and any that did pop up healed far quicker – a few days rather than a week without the treatment.After eight weeks, as Shark recommends, I switched to using the four-minute Skin Sustain mode. That treatment did exactly what it said: maintain my calm, clear skin until the next hormonal breakout reared its head. Thankfully, it was easy to switch back to the blemish treatment on those occasions.In my week testing the Better Ageing setting, I noticed my skin was more even, with less pigmentation. And while I don’t always get puffy undereyes, I enjoyed using the cooling pads during hay fever season. It’s not a cure for hay fever, but a quick cooling session soothed the area and left it feeling far more comfortable. While I could get similar results from a cold compress stored in the fridge, the electric Peltier coolers meant the pads stayed cold for the duration, rather than warming up on contact with the skin.That said, using the cooling pads drained the battery far faster than when they weren’t being used. When I tested the battery life using LED therapy alone, I was able to complete 17 treatments before the mask needed recharging. But when I switched the cooling on to full whack, the mask conked out after seven. That’s a dramatic drop-off. Most LED masks I’ve tested have run out of charge after about 10 days, though, so I think weekly charging is reasonable considering the cooling power on offer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor safety, the mask dims when removed from the face, and proximity sensors brighten the lights as soon as the mask is on your face. When the mask is fitted correctly, the eyes are well shielded from the light.Thanks to its sturdy plastic build, the mask weighs 537g, which means it’s heavier than flexible silicone masks. To combat this, there is comfortable padding at the forehead, nose and brow bone, which is where most of the weight sits. The straps can also be adjusted around and over the head, so there’s enough flexibility to get a good fit if you’re sitting upright.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenThe undereye cooling pads can be noisy and distracting during treatment.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianSadly, the main gripe I have with the Shark CryoGlow is one of its key selling points. Although I enjoy the calming effect of the undereye coolers, I found the weight of the mask made them dig into the delicate skin in that area. Whether I used the clip-on adjusters or not, I couldn’t bear lying down in the mask, as it was too heavy. The cooling pad positioning also meant the undereyes didn’t get any LED treatment.Another frustration was that the cooling pads have fans that create a constant whirring sound, which is noisy and distracting during treatment. The coolers can be deactivated by turning the dial on the controller, but reactivating them is just as easy. I’ve accidentally knocked the dial countless times, causing the cooling fans to roar into action. Even when switched off immediately, they take a minute or so to quieten down again.View image in fullscreenScroll call: the controller earns plaudits for ease of use.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianThat’s a shame, since the controller is generally well designed; the scroll wheel and buttons make it easy to browse the settings, and the clip is helpful, if a little insecure. If Shark could change the cooling controls to a button, that would improve the design.While the CryoGlow’s Better Ageing mode is great for early signs of ageing, it doesn’t have the most deeply penetrating wavelength – deep near-infrared – for more powerful anti-ageing. Deep near-infrared is becoming more common among new releases, although they tend to cost more. However, theSilk’n LED face mask ProI tested has deep near-infrared and costs just £265 at full price. Of course, the LED industry is growing at a rate of knots, so it’s hard for Shark to keep up with all the latest features, but I’m surprised that its newest release, theShark CryoGlow Plus, hasn’t added this (although battery life and LED coverage have improved).Warranty and repairsThe device is guaranteed for two years if you register your device online within 28 days. This covers the cost of a repair or replacement mask if you have any problems during that time. Shark also offerstroubleshooting advice online, or you can contact its customer service helpline (0800 862 0453).Coincidentally, I tested this repairs service earlier this year when my sister bought a faulty CryoGlow mask at Christmas. After complaining, she had a new mask sent to her within a week (albeit in a different colour due to stock levels).Should I buy the Shark CryoGlow LED mask?If you want an effective LED mask that can treat multiple skin concerns at once, without adding extra light settings that aren’t as well-researched, then yes. And if puffy undereyes are a concern, you’ll be able to treat those as well.The mask has given me good results, with daily breakouts minimised and unavoidable hormonal breakouts lasting less time than before. I found that the red light settings helped maintain a more even skin tone and a brighter complexion overall. And, notwithstanding its weight, its plastic build feels much sturdier than many silicone options.I hate that the cooling patches cover the undereye, though. If you want an LED mask you can lie down in like a lizard in the sun, this weighty mask isn’t for you. Equally, if loud whirring noises in your ears are likely to annoy you, I’d steer clear. You’d be better off investing in a soft silicone mask such as theCurrentBody Multi Light Therapy mask– my new favourite overall. It may cost more, but it’s lighter, more comfortable and has more penetrating deep near-infrared light.View at SharkNinjaView at John LewisFor more, readthe best LED face masks that are worth the hypeand ourCurrentBody Multi Light Therapy LED mask reviewSarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)Explore more on these topicsSkincareThe FilterBeautyGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Café Clement, London WC2: ‘Turns out it’s really rather good’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: I am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, especially when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in Tuscany
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: I am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, especially when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in Tuscany
Content: Café Clement, London WC2: ‘Sell your grandmother for a terrace table.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenCafé Clement, London WC2: ‘Sell your grandmother for a terrace table.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The Guardian.Grace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewCafé Clement, London WC2: ‘Turns out it’s really rather good’ – restaurant reviewI am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, especially when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in TuscanyGrace DentSun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCafé Clement, the all-day restaurant inside Nick Jones’ new St Clement Hotel at 180 The Thames in central London, opened with a bang in June and immediately rocketed to the top of every “sell your grandmother for a terrace table” list in London. Which isn’tthatmuch of a surprise, seeing as Jones,founder of Soho House, is the master of restaurant rumpus.Within days,Stanley Tucci,Nick Grimshawand full-length-trouser-phobic heart-throbPaul Mescalwere all there, tucking intooeufs mayonnaiseand lobster omelettes while politely ignoring the fact that the place was still, in many ways, a building site. The hotel itself isn’t due to open fully until early autumn, when a rooftop restaurant,Lunette, will also arrive with some of London’s most wondrous views andFlorence Knightat the helm. Still, Café Clement opened to frothy praise, and I am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in Tuscany and, frankly, lunch is not free.View image in fullscreen‘Stunning’: Café Clement’s cheese soufflé.Café Clement is elegant but not overdone: white linen, vintageCassina chairs. The staff, of whom there appear to be about 345, are a joy: everyone seems to have been hired for their personality and for having the chops to nail a busy service. There’s an open kitchen behind ornate glass screens, a south-facing terrace that gives itself to debauchery and a garden out the back. The menu, which is that of a broadly European, fancy, all-day bistro, offers the likes of spatchcocked chicken with speck and green bean vinaigrette, Dorset crab with marinated tomatoes and aïoli, and hearty meat and fish casseroles. There are pastas and grills, plus chocolatey, tarty things on the pudding menu.As with most central London celebrity brasseries, the food offering here is designed to mollify and comfort: steak haché with crinkle-cut chips, roast duck with dripping potatoes, with cosmos on the cocktail menu and a hulking sharing chocolate mousse that will soothe any recent knock-back for a starring role. And if anyone can keep all of this classy, it’s chefDanny Bohan, who spent 20-odd years atthe River Cafe, most recently as head chef, working alongside Rose Gray and Ruth Rogers, both of them names that make foodies genuflect. A reader told me recently that his life’s ambition was to eat at the River Cafe, where starters run to £51, pastas to £46 and mains to £69. Unfortunately, his partner misunderstood the assignment entirely and booked the now defunct and unmissedRainforest Café in Piccadillyinstead. Here’s hoping said errant partner finds out about Café Clement and tries to make amends by booking a table, because it turns out that it’s really rather good.View image in fullscreen‘Sweet and sharp in exactly the right proportions’: Café Clement’s sea bass carpaccio.Café Clement’s food offering could be merely passable and many would turn a blind eye, but it’s pleasing and careful in equal measure. A plate of eggs mayonnaise arrives jammy and generously stuffed, the mayo earthy and mustardy without ever tipping into sickly. The eggs are served starkly – there’s no trout roe, no caviar – and they are all the better for it. You get the sense that this is a kitchen that wants to spend money on exceptional produce, rather than on garnishes that may well end up in the bin. The cheese soufflé is stunning: upright, luscious, deeply cheesy. A sharply pickly, well-seasoned steak tartare comes free-form on the plate, and is served withcartadi musicaSardinian flatbread. Sea bass carpaccio is simply and beautifully arranged, all sweet and sharp in exactly the right proportions. A side of summer beetroots at £7 is, quite frankly, gorgeous: sweet, plump, properly baked, buttery, and made me wonder why baked beets aren’t on every side menu going.View image in fullscreenCafé Clement’s hazlenut and raspberry tart.Photograph: Amy Heycock/The GuardianNot everything lands, however. The fish casserole is thin and pale, a bouillabaisse in search of a meaning: some mussels, a piece of fish, not a lot else. Definitely good for those on a diet, though. A side of crinkles, or retro potato wedges, meanwhile, isn’t really worth the carbs. The £18 chocolate mousse for two, on the other hand, turns up with the energy of an unstructured brownie and the ability to put you on your back with a sugar high. Neither of those things is a quibble. A fresh, wobbly slice of custard tart is delightful, and comes with a mush of sweet strawberries and more custard.Café Clement quietly surpasses expectations, and I’d go back any day. It is fun, joyous and well thought out. As this stretch of the Thames around180 The Strandfinally starts to flourish, it will become even more useful and ridiculously difficult to get into. Come for the celeb rumpus, and, if none of them is there, stay for theoeufs mayonnaise.Café ClementSt Clement, 180 The Thames, 12 Temple Place, London WC2, 020-4632 6660. Open all week, 7am-11pm (9pm Sun). From about £60 a head for three courses, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Quench your thirst! 20 perfect spritzes and shandies to try now – from kumquat to portergaff | Food | The Guardian
description: Whether you love a traditional spritz or tend towards a wilder libation, this August there are bubbly and sophisticated drinks to suit every taste
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: Whether you love a traditional spritz or tend towards a wilder libation, this August there are bubbly and sophisticated drinks to suit every taste
Content: Fresh and floral … a Hugo spritz.Photograph: 5PH/AlamyView image in fullscreenFresh and floral … a Hugo spritz.Photograph: 5PH/AlamyFoodQuench your thirst! 20 perfect spritzes and shandies to try now – from kumquat to portergaffWhether you love a traditional spritz or tend towards a wilder libation, this August there are bubbly and sophisticated drinks to suit every tasteRachel DixonSun 23 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis summer, UK web searches for “Hugo spritz”, an elderflower-flavoured aperitif, overtook searches for “Aperol spritz” for the first time. As the spritz craze shows no sign of slowing down, pub chains are taking wild liberties, calling anything fizzy and served in a large glass over ice a spritz – and charging £10-plus for it. Echo Falls blue raspberry spritz? Pink gin spritz (Slug & Lettuce)? Raspberry vodka and honey spritz (Young’s)? Malibu cranberry spritz (Stonegate)?Mamma mia!Traditionally, the spritz is an Italian cocktail made from prosecco, a bitter aperitif or liqueur, and a splash of soda water to keep things steady. While Venetian bartenders are more likely to judge it by eye, there is a simple 3-2-1 formula for making a spritz at home: three parts prosecco, two parts liqueur and one part soda water. I’ve gone with 75ml/50ml/25ml – keep the same ratios to make a smaller (60ml/40ml/20ml) or larger (90ml/60ml/30ml) drink. Of course, you can then adjust it to make it stronger or weaker (I have been known to leave out the soda …).If wine-based cocktails aren’t to your taste, shandy is also showing signs of a resurgence – Ocado sales have increased 40% year on year, and the craft brand Shandy Shack is now stocked in M&S. Being half beer, half soft drink, it is another summery thirst-quencher that is easy to make at home and (in theory) shouldn’t get you too sloshed.So, here are 20 simple spritzes and shandies. Save your Malibu for a piña colada.View image in fullscreen‘All-conquering’ … an Aperol spritz.Photograph: David Cabrera Navarro/AlamyFive bittersweet spritzesAll recipes make one drink. Pour the liquids into a large glass with ice, stir briefly and garnish.Select spritzThe bittersweet aperitif Select (17.5% ABV) was created in Venice in 1920, and lo, the original spritz (AKA spritz Veneziano) was born. Select contains 30 herbs and botanicals, most noticeably rhubarb roots.75ml prosecco50ml Select25ml soda waterGreen olive, to garnishCampari spritzMy personal favourite. Bitter Campari (25%) was invented near Milan in 1860 from a still-secret blend of herbs, spices and fruit peels; the spritz version came later.75ml prosecco50ml Campari25ml soda waterSlice of orange, to garnishAperol spritzAll-conquering Aperol (11%) was created in Padua in 1919 from a mix of herbs, roots and fruits. It is sweeter and less alcoholic than most similar bittersweet liqueurs.75ml prosecco50ml Aperol25ml soda waterSlice of orange, to garnishCynar spritzArtichoke-based, herbal Cynar (16.5%), also from Padua, was first made in 1952.75ml prosecco50mlCynar25ml soda waterTwist of lemon or grapefruit peel, to garnishVermouth spritzSweet red vermouth (15-18%), a fortified wine, emerged in Turin in the late 18th century; dry white vermouth appeared in Chambéry, France, a couple of decades later. Either can be used in a spritz, or mixed with tonic water.75ml prosecco50ml red or white vermouth25ml soda waterSlice of orange (red) or lemon (white), to garnishFive alternative spritzesHugo spritzThe fresh and floral hugo is a recent addition to the spritz canon. It is said to have been invented in a bar in Naturno, northern Italy, in 2005. The original recipe used lemon balm syrup, which was replaced by more widely available elderflower cordial. Today, it is more common to use elderflower liqueur, such as the French St-Germain (20%). Some add a shot of gin for an extra kick.75ml prosecco50ml elderflower liqueur25ml gin (optional)25ml soda waterFresh mint, to garnishLimoncello spritzA light, zesty citrus spritz made from limoncello (26-30%), a lemon-flavoured liqueur first produced around 1900 in Naples, the Amalfi coast and Sicily.75ml prosecco50ml limoncello25ml soda waterSlice of lemon and sprig of mint or thyme, to garnishView image in fullscreenZesty and light … a limoncello spritz.Photograph: Maryna Voronova/AlamyItalicus spritzAnother newer spritz, made from the bergamot-flavoured Italicus Rosolio di Bergamotto (20%), which has been produced near Turin since 2016.75ml prosecco50ml Italicus25ml soda waterGreen olive, to garnishSarti spritzCasa Sarti, a liqueur-maker, was founded in Bologna in 1885, but Sarti Rosa (14%) was only launched in 2023. It makes a sweet, almost tropical spritz flavoured with blood orange, mango and passionfruit.75ml prosecco50ml Sarti Rosa25ml soda waterSlice of lime, to garnishAmarettospritzAlmond-flavoured amaretto (21-28%), a sweet liqueur from Saronno in Lombardy, has got in on the spritz action. It’s a good option for chillier days.75ml prosecco50ml amaretto25ml soda waterSlice of lemon and a cocktail cherry, to garnishThree non-Italian spritzesLillet spritzMaison Lillet was founded in Podensac, Bordeaux, in 1872. Today, Lillet – an aromatised wine – comes in red, white and rosé versions. Like vermouth, any can be used in a spritz or mixed with tonic.75ml prosecco50ml Lillet Blanc, Rouge or Rosé25ml soda waterSlice of lemon (Blanc), orange (Rouge) or grapefruit (Rosé), to garnishView image in fullscreenThere is a simple 3-2-1 formula for making a spritz.Photograph: FG Trade/Getty ImagesKir spritzCrème de cassis (15-20%), a blackcurrant liqueur, first appeared in Burgundy in 1841. It’s best known as a component of kir (mixed with white wine) and kir royal (mixed with champagne), but also works well in a spritz.75ml prosecco50ml crème de cassis25ml soda waterBlackcurrants and a sprig of thyme, to garnishKumquat spritzKumquats were introduced to Corfu in 1846 and have been turned into liqueur (20-25%) since the 1920s. Today, the kumquat spritz is the island’s bright orange alternative to Aperol.75ml prosecco50ml kumquat liqueur (or orange liqueur)25ml soda water (or ginger beer, which ispopular in Corfu)Kumquat (or slice of orange), to garnishSeven shandiesShandies couldn’t be any easier to make – they are a 50:50 ratio of beer and mixer (adjust to taste). I’ve gone for 220ml, half a standard UK beer can. Use a chilled glass, pour the soft drink in first, then slowly add the beer.Classic lager shandyTry cloudy or still lemonade to mix things up.220ml lemonade200mllagerView image in fullscreenShandies are back and more fun than ever.Photograph: Sergio Amiti/Getty ImagesShandygaffThe original British shandy, which dates back to 1853. You could also try it with root beer as the mixer.220ml ginger beer or ginger ale220ml ale or bitterRadlerPopular in Germany and Austria, in lemon and grapefruit flavours.220ml pink grapefruit soda220ml lagerRussA drink particularly associated with Bavaria, Germany.200mllemonade220ml wheat beerFruit shandyTry rose or raspberry lemonade, blood orange or lime soda, or elderflower presse …220ml fruit soda220ml pale aleCola shandyYes, it’s a thing – it’s known as beer-cola in France, mazout in Belgium and diesel in Germany.220ml cola220ml lagerPortergaffThe beer writerSophie Atherton also recommendspairing porter with raspberry lemonade, and stout with cream soda.220ml lemonade or ginger beer220ml porter or stoutExplore more on these topicsFoodCocktailsAlcoholfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A childhood sexual abuse allegation has rocked our family – what should we do?  | Family | The Guardian
description: Make the victim feel safe and able to talk at their own pace, and consider any danger the perpetrator currently presents to younger members of the family
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Make the victim feel safe and able to talk at their own pace, and consider any danger the perpetrator currently presents to younger members of the family
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyA childhood sexual abuse allegation has rocked our family – what should we do?Make the victim feel safe and able to talk at their own pace, and consider any danger the perpetrator currently presents to younger members of the familyAnnalisa BarbieriSun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA young adult woman in our family has recently shared that her older male cousin once touched her inappropriately when she was aged six and he was aged 12. This happened 18 years ago. Then a second incident allegedly occurred eight years later.She shared the story with her parents this year and the information was then shared withher cousin and other family members.He stated that he cannot recall either incident.The young woman’s parents have raised whetherher cousin is a now a threat to young children in the family. Theparents were both victims of sexual abuse when they were children, which adds to the horror.The story has completely shattered the entire wider family, which was once close. The young woman said she does not want an investigation. She has been encouraged to engage with counselling but has so far declined.Her cousin is accessing psychological support following mental health issues.The whole family is appalledby the situation, the main concern being the young woman’ssafety.Can you please advise on how wesupport them both– and help to repair the relationships. Or is this how it will be?It’s excellent you are trying to move forward and not do as many do and try to sweep sexual abuse against a child under the carpet. I need to make it clear that any sexual behaviour towards a child is illegal and incredibly harmful.I spoke to Rachel Haynes, head of young people’s services at theLucy Faithfull Foundationabout your letter. She recognised this was a “complex situation” and had real empathy for you and your family.“First and foremost is to think about the safety, physical and emotional, of the young woman. What’s important in these situations is to take things at her pace,” she said. “Often when people have experienced sexual harm, agency and choice has been taken away.”People must not say the survivorhasto report the perpetrator, which heaps all sorts of responsibilities on them and repeats taking away that agency. “Positioning her at the centre of this,” said Haynes, “is important. Giving her safe places to talk and mirroring her language can help her feel heard.”We also must think about the potential for further risk with any young people in the older male cousin’s orbit. You didn’t say much more about him. Given the young woman’s parents’ history of being abused, I wonder who else has been sexually abused in the family.There was a significant gap in ages between the male relative and the young woman – a “significant power difference” as Haynes put it. A huge proportion (30-50%) of child sexual abuse happens between children. “There’s an assumption,” explained Haynes, “that harm displayed between children is less harmful and that’s not the case. Sexual harm of any form is incredibly damaging and can have lasting impact.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy partner’s mother dominates him and it makes me feel helpless | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moreThere’s no getting around that this will affect your family, but this can be managed by what happens next. Haynes recommended you contact the Lucy Faithfull Foundation’sStop It Now helplineor theNational Association for People Abused in Childhood(details below). Stop It Now can help you and your family come up with a “family safety plan” where you talk around the risks involved and think through areas such as whether the man should have unsupervised contact with children in the family. “It’s not about demonising him,” explained Haynes, “but about keeping people safe.”The helpline would also talk the woman through what would happen if she ever does decide to report it to the police. Separately they can help the man, too.Perhaps someone in the family could take a lead role in organising this. But it’s vital no one takes the power away from the young woman involved.Names have been changedEvery week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is availablehere.Comments on this piece are pre-moderated to ensure the discussion remains on the topics raised by the article. Please be aware that there may be a short delay in comments appearing on the site.In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. (The National Association for People Abused in Childhood)offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800, orBraveheartson 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contactBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helplines International.Explore more on these topicsFamilyAsk Annalisa BarbierifeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My best ever British holiday: ‘I’ve travelled further, at greater expense, and had nothing like as much fun’ | United Kingdom holidays | The Guardian
description: Five travel writers share their favourite holidays at home, from gravel biking in Scotland and a steam train ride in Yorkshire to rowing all the way from Oxford to London
Author: Max Benato
Headline: Five travel writers share their favourite holidays at home, from gravel biking in Scotland and a steam train ride in Yorkshire to rowing all the way from Oxford to London
Content: Marcel Theroux (right) with James and Tom on their Thames boat trip.Photograph: James Bedford/jamesbedford.comView image in fullscreenMarcel Theroux (right) with James and Tom on their Thames boat trip.Photograph: James Bedford/jamesbedford.comGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.United Kingdom holidaysMy best ever British holiday: ‘I’ve travelled further, at greater expense, and had nothing like as much fun’Five travel writers share their favourite holidays at home, from gravel biking in Scotland and a steam train ride in Yorkshire to rowing all the way from Oxford to LondonMax Benato, Kirsten Henton,Jill Mead,Marcel Theroux,Andy PietrasikSun 23 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree men in a boat on the ThamesOne of my best UK holidays was the week I spent in June 2013 rowing from Oxford to London with two friends, James and Tom.We hired the boat from a company calledThames Skiff Hirethat mainly caters to people recreating the fictional adventure of the characters in Jerome K Jerome’s Three Men in a Boat.Our boat – Ewen – was a 26ft, 130-year-old mahogany skiff. It came with two pairs of oars, a rudder, a cooking stove, a boat hook, and iron hoops that supported a green canvas roof over the hull.After an hour’s briefing at a slipway by Donnington Bridge, we were off, piloting the boat 80 or so miles downstream to London. That June was blustery and wet. The first day was deceptively fine, but on the second, we got soaked on the stretch of water between Abingdon and Day’s Lock, and came close to packing it in.Even with the current helping us, the miles ahead seemed like folly. It’s not generally remembered that Jerome K Jerome’s Three Men in a Boat ends in disappointment and recrimination as the companions abandon their sodden skiff atThe Swanin Pangbourne.But we kept going. And, over the subsequent days, the weather improved, we got better at rowing and it turned into an extraordinary and memorable adventure.double quotation markIt always felt as if we were very far from the daily grind. There were stretches of extraordinary tranquillityLooking back, the trip appears to have been packed with incident. We visited lovely riverside pubs, brewed tea on uninhabited midstream islands, and popped into a meditation centre run by an ascetic Hindu sect. We passed Medmenham Abbey, the headquarters ofFrancis Dashwood’s Hellfire Club; Monkey Island, where the doomed romance inRebecca West’s The Return of the Soldierunfolds; and we moored for lunch one day at the luxurious faux-gothic hotelOakley Court, immortalised as Frank-N-Furter’s castle in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Logistically, the trip was never entirely straightforward. Although the Thames skiff was designed to be slept in, it was not big enough for three and the rules around wild camping made things more complicated. I also remember feeling a certain anxiety when mooring the boat to go to the pub. We had been instructed to hammer iron spikes into the riverbank and fasten the skiff to them. But it always seemed weird to walk away from this precious antique and assume it would be there when we got back.View image in fullscreenThe trio hired a 130-year-old mahogany skiff.Photograph: James Bedford/jamesbedford.comNegotiating the locks that regulate the water level of the river was also tricky. Someone had to remain in the skiff with a boat hook and keep it from bumping against the sides as the water poured out of the sluices. And, of course, rowing that distance, even with the current, requires a certain stick-to-it-ness.Paradoxically, the minor hardships of the trip probably made it more relaxing than a holiday whose explicit goal is relaxation. The overall pace was slow and reflective. And even within commuting distance of our own beds, it always felt as if we were very far from the daily grind. There were stretches of extraordinary tranquillity, deep silences, wonderful birdlife; I still remember the flash of a kingfisher in the willows outside Abingdon.Other river-users took kindly to us and our venerable skiff. One evening, we were invited for drinks onboard a beautiful narrowboat whose owner we met as we were queueing at a lock.Our final destination was Walton-on-Thames, but by the time we reached it, we were enjoying ourselves so much we pushed on to Hampton Court before turning the boat round and heading back upriver to return the skiff.It’s a trip I’ve always meant to repeat. I’ve travelled much further, at much greater expense and had nothing like as much fun.Marcel TherouxA birthday break in the TrossachsView image in fullscreenGravel biking in the Trossachs“Gravelfoyle,” my cycle-mad partner, Gary, replied instantly when asked where he’d like to go for his birthday. Gravelfoyle is the nickname of the village of Aberfoyle – gateway to the Trossachs, about 50 miles north-west of Edinburgh, and even closer to Glasgow – which claims to have “the UK’s finest gravel riding” and the waymarked trails to prove it.Growing up in Edinburgh, I spent many happy summers camping in the Cairngorms and roving around Perthshire. This instilled a habit of going north rather than west, so I didn’t know Scotland’s first national park,Loch Lomond and the Trossachs, as well.Off we set, bikes strapped to the car, passing Falkirk’s Kelpies, whose steel heads reared up alongside the M9, imposing Stirling Castle and the Mordor-esqueWallace Monumentin the distance. The drive was only 75 minutes, but we stopped en route atThe Smiddy farm shopin Blair Drummond (close to thesafari parkmy brother and I went to as kids) to pick up cheese and chorizo scotch eggs, “the best thing we sell”, according to the butcher.double quotation markThe glamping pod felt like the most decadent way to enjoy the outdoors, especially once the fire pit was roaring and fizz was in hand.I’d booked a snug-looking glamping pod on theCardross Estatenear Port of Menteith, not far from Aberfoyle. Tucked away down a single-track road flanked by farmland, where kites soar overhead, it’s a slick operation, from the easy self-check-in to the trolleys for wheeling stuff from the car park. Inside the curved, wooden pod was a sofa, pull-down double bed, shower and fridge, with picture windows framing fields speckled with cattle and crops rolling towards Ben Lomond. We could have chosen one of the estate’s self-catering cottages or a B&B stay in Cardross House, but the pod felt like the most decadent way to enjoy the outdoors, especially once the fire pit was roaring and fizz was in hand.View image in fullscreenKirsten Henton and her partner Gary try to avoid the midges.Photograph: Kirsten HentonLater that day, we embarked on our first ride, the 18.2-mile (29.2km) Lomond View, one of three Gravelfoyle routes plotted for gravel biking, and a wet and muddy affair after recent rain.
