Afterwards, atAberfoyle Bike Co(where you can hire bikes if you don’t bring your own), the owner, Liam, was ready with a hose and hot drinks.The next day, we hiked out of the nearby town of Callander on the 3.5-mile (5.3km) circular Bracklinn Falls hiking route. Crossing the bridge over the thundering waterfall, we pressed on through thick forest before returning to baguettes oozing generous fillings atMhor Bread. The afternoon’s downpour gave us a great excuse to nest in our cosy pod, read and, in my case, nap – the indulgence!That evening, the sun sprang loose, and we chinked glasses in the flower-strewn garden of Scottish chef Nick Nairn’s namesake restaurant,Nick’s at Port of Menteith. Swallows and housemartins swooped as we ate fish and chips and seafood linguine.Over three days, we biked and hiked various routes alongside lochs and through yawning, forest-clad valleys, ate fabulous, locally produced food, and soaked up the nurturing goodness of being immersed in the wilderness of the national park.Kirsten HentonAt the edge of north WalesView image in fullscreenBwa Gwyn arch at Rhoscolyn on Holy Island, Ynys Môn (Anglesey).Photograph: Andy PietrasikI’ve lost count of the number of times I’ve passed through Ynys Môn (Anglesey) over the years, but until recently I’d never actually been there. Ghosting through the darkness to catch the night ferry from Holyhead to Dublin, I had no idea what the island looked like until our daughter suggested an outing while we were visiting her at her student digs in Bangor, across the Menai Strait.That first time, she took us to Newborough Forest, a nature reserve on the south-west coast of the island made up of Corsican pines, sand dunes and a sweep of beach that offers panoramic views of the peaks of Eryri (Snowdonia) across the bay. We spent the afternoon walking over to the small tidal island of Ynys Llanddwyn, with its lighthouse and the ruined remains of Saint Dwynwen’s church. Saint Dwynwen is the Welsh patron saint of lovers, the equivalent of Saint Valentine. It was love at first sight for us, and we hatched a plan to come back for a longer visit.double quotation markI rued the fact that I had rattled through this glorious little island on the boat train on so many occasions,  without ever having spent any time hereOn that next visit, we rented a cottage with floor-to-ceiling windows that framed the mountains on the road out of Llanfair – or Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch to give it its proper majestic name – well, how could we not? What we discovered on that stay pretty much chimed with what I had read in HV Morton’s book In Search of Wales, published in 1932: “The long roads run through flat, green country, linking quiet, stone-built little market towns together.”But it’s at the edges that Ynys Môn comes into its own. On the first day, we walked theWales Coast Pathalong the cliffs at Rhoscolyn on Ynys Gybi (Holy Island) in the north – an island off an island with dramatic sea arches – and enjoyed a feeling of apartness, of almost floating out to sea.View image in fullscreenHeading through the sand dunes to Newborough beach in the south-west of the island.Photograph: Andy PietrasikOn another day, we parked up at the beach at Rhosneigr and again followed the signs for the coast path, walking through the marram grass and gorse on the dunes until we found a sheltered cove to go swimming. Then we drove across the island that at one time was called Môn, Mam Cymru (Anglesey, the Mother of Wales) because it was said to grow all the corn needed to feed the country, to Red Wharf Bay and another sweeping beach at the bottom of a single-track lane. There was no corn on the menu at the Boathouse cafe, but we made do with crab meat crumpets and mussels.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeafing through HV Morton’s book back at the cottage that night, I came across a line that made me rue the fact that I had rattled through this glorious little island on the boat train on so many occasions, simply seeing it as an embarkation point without ever having had the imagination to jump off and spend a bit of time here: “Holyhead is an excellent place for a holiday … you have bathing, fine cliff scenery, and all round you is excellent flat walking country with a supreme view of the whole Snowdon range.”Andy PietrasikNorth Yorkshire with 42 palsView image in fullscreenNorth Yorkshire Moors Railway steam engine on its way to Whitby.Photograph: David Lyons/AlamyTwelve years ago, I was sitting in my son Ned’s primary school playground when I said to my friend Vicky, “I’m thinking of taking a few friends up to Yorkshire.”“I’m in,” she said.Word got out, and before I knew it 42 of us were heading to lovelyCote Ghyll Mill, on the edge of the pretty village of Osmotherley. It was a youth hostel in those days, before its recent transformation into a B&B. Ned and I made a giant Welcome to Yorkshire banner and Blu-Tacked handwritten names on to the bedroom doors.None of us realised that week would become our June tradition, until Covid brought it to a halt.Brilliantly, my mum and dad took charge one day, leading us on a six-mile circular walk from Grosmont through the fairytale hamlet of Beck Hole, a centre for the traditional game of quoits, and back across the North York Moors.I remember Mum, ever the feeder in our family, opening the boot of their car to reveal her homemade fruit cake alongside a stack of enormous sandwiches they had collected fromDanby Bakery. Dad brought a few short thumbsticks (traditional walking sticks) he’d made for the kids from hazel branches. Florence, now 19, still has hers, and Julie, her mum, now uses it to reach an awkward light switch.double quotation markThe Birch Hall Inn doubles as a sweet shop and we came away clutching paper bags of lemon sherbets, cola cubes and pear dropsHalfway round was Dad’s favourite pub, theBirch Hall Inn, where his drink of choice was always the same: a bitter shandy. The pub doubles as a sweet shop and we came away clutching paper bags of lemon sherbets, cola cubes and pear drops, all bought by the ounce, while Ned carefully chose Barratt’s liquorice sticks for his grandad, as is tradition.Part of our walk crossed theNorth Yorkshire Moors Railwayline to Whitby, and, after watching a train steaming past us, we all wanted to take a ride. It is a magical way to see the moors. Every carriage told its own story. Couples were more romantic, kids chatted around the tables, and happy heads hung out of the windows to catch the smell of coal and steam. Eleven-year-old Eleanor caught far too much coal dust in her eye and ended up in A&E in Northallerton. Thankfully, she was fine.In Whitby, Ned’s pals buried him in the sand on Tate Hill beach. Although we brushed him down and emptied his shoes, he still left a little trail of Whitby all the way back to the station and on to the train.View image in fullscreenJill Mead with her son Ned and her parents outside the Birch Hall Inn in Beck Hole, near Goathland.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianOur trip wouldn’t have been complete without a visit to my own boozer of choice, theSun Inn, or Spout House, in Bilsdale. Its infamous cricket field, with a dramatic slope where fielders on the boundary can disappear from view, is where my dad and brother played. Spike W, AKA Prince Harry, is also recorded in the score book.My old primary school friend Audrey is the landlady now. I used to ride her ponies, her dad was the village milkman, and she somehow makes everyone who walks through the door feel as if they’ve come home.Audrey laid on a domino tournament and the most amazing Yorkshire platter, with cakes worthy of victory at any country show. Competition was fierce, with some local diehard domino players, mainly farmers, joining in. Harriet, aged just six, beat the lot of them. She burst into tears, while her mum, Steph, cried with laughter.This year, I casually asked Ned, now 21, “Do you think anyone might fancy going back to Yorkshire?”“Absolutely, Mum,” he replied.So we’re going back to Cote Ghyll Mill this month.I’ve dug out the original Welcome to Yorkshire banner and Harriet, now 18, is fiercely ready to defend her domino title.Jill MeadA quick dip into BristolView image in fullscreenGuests at the Lido Townhouse in Bristol have access to the restored Victorian poolTravelling by train from Kent to Bristol on one of the hottest days of the year might have been pretty close to madness. In sweltering heat and amid cancellations and delays, I arrived in the city hot, broken and miserable. Less than an hour later, I was gliding through the water at the city’s lido, smugly thanking myself for booking what may be one of the best summer city hotels in the country.I was in Bristol for the opening of an exhibition –Polly Braden: Against the Tide– at the brilliantArnolfini arts centre, which seemed the perfect excuse to visit a city that had somehow eluded me. The Arnolfini is a leading hub for the contemporary arts, housed in a 19th-century warehouse on Narrow Quay beside the harbour, a vibrant area packed with restaurants, cafes and bars, as well as some of the city’s leading tourist attractions, including the aquarium and Brunel’s SS Great Britain.double quotation markAfter my 9.30pm swim I sat in my robe at the bar nursing a glass of amaroMy base was theLido Townhouse, a six-bedroom hotel in a Georgian building that opened in 2024 in the city’s sought-after Clifton neighbourhood. Each of the rooms has been done out simply but with fabulous taste, featuring colourful throws, sparkling white bedlinen and jauntily tiled bathrooms.The real attraction isthe lidoitself, which dates back to Victorian times and has been restored after falling into disrepair. Open year-round, with the water heated to 20-24C, the pool is flanked by old-fashioned changing cabins on one side and a bar and restaurant on the other, with windows and a terrace that look out over the action. Booking directly with the hotel grants you full access to the lido, which is just a few steps across a (very quiet) road in the hotel’s robes and slippers. In 24 hours, I managed to squeeze in three swims, including one at 9.30pm (it closes at 10pm), emerging to sit in my robe at the bar nursing a glass of amaro. Breakfast the next day out on the deck was equally enjoyable, with coffee and a generous plate of Turkish eggs and coffee.A colleague and I paid £210 for two double rooms and a shared bathroom on the top floor of the hotel, which, with unlimited swims thrown in and 10% off our food bill, seemed like an excellent deal. The harbour is a 25-minute stroll from the hotel along shop-lined Georgian streets, past picturesque College Green and the cathedral. So, though it was a lightning visit, the city showed its best side. A return trip is on the cards.Max BenatoExplore more on these topicsUnited Kingdom holidaysFamily holidaysFamilyEngland holidaysScotland holidaysWales holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Aardman’​s Peter Lord and David Sproxton: ‘At the Oscars, I went to the gents and had a pee with Jack Nicholson!’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The ​s​tudio’s co-founders on ​accidentally creating Morph, not wanting a yacht in the Maldives and being each other’s best ally
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The ​s​tudio’s co-founders on ​accidentally creating Morph, not wanting a yacht in the Maldives and being each other’s best ally
Content: FlashbackFamilyAardman’​s Peter Lord and David Sproxton: ‘At the Oscars, I went to the gents and had a pee with Jack Nicholson!’The ​s​tudio’s co-founders on ​accidentally creating Morph, not wanting a yacht in the Maldives and being each other’s best allyHarriet GibsoneSun 23 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAardman’s Peter Lord and David Sproxton in 2006 and 2026, with their puppets of Fowler and Babs from Chicken Run, and MorphAardman’s Peter Lord and David Sproxton in 2006 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian. Styling: Andie Redman. Archive photograph: Aardman AnimationsPeter Lord and David Sproxton are the founders ofAardmanAnimations. The pair began animating as teenagers, selling their first short – starring a superhero called Aardman – to the BBC’s Vision On in 1972. In 1977, they created Morph for the children’s programme Take Hart. The studio’s breakthrough into adult audiences came via Channel 4’s Conversation Pieces series, and its animators, including a young Nick Park, went on to make Wallace & Gromit, whose films have won multiple Academy Awards. Aardman became employee-owned in 2018, with Lord and Sproxton transferring majority ownership to staff to safeguard the company’s independence. They were knighted earlier this year.Peter (on left)We’re sitting there smiling happily and in front of us are some puppets, because that’s what we’re famous for. In this case, Fowler and Babs from Chicken Run, and Morph.In 2006, we were in between productions – we had finished Chicken Run and the next was Flushed Away and Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit. I was going to California quite a lot to jolly the production along. While it was exciting to be in Hollywood, we never aspired to be part of it when we started Aardman.I was born in Bristol, but when I was nine my parents moved to Sydney, Australia. As a small, not very sporty boy, I found the school system there fairly terrifying. Then, when I was 12, we ended up in suburban Surrey. My new school was a very old-fashioned place where teachers wore gowns. On my first day, there was only one spare seat in the class. It was next to Sproxton, brackets, DA. By chance, we also got off at the same train stop, which was Walton-on-Thames.double quotation markMy car is 20 years old. Dave’s was even older when it finally packed up. Money has never been the motive. It’s always been to make a communityOver the years, we got closer. I liked that he was very different from me. I was very arty, and David extremely practical – good with his hands and able to understand how to build things. The turning point was when David’s father got a camera. We would sit around David’s kitchen table and work away on ideas.During our university holidays we would meet up and think of ideas for animations. Dave would create sets and props, and I’d make a puppet. It was a partnership of mutual interdependence.We created Morph accidentally. It was just a lump of Plasticine that turned into a little person and then developed over time as a character, which is where the fun lies. After a few years, we got the gig to do The Amazing Adventures of Morph – 26 five-minute episodes. When we found out, it was one of those fabulous high-five moments – not that we would ever have high-fived. But making children’s TV was the sum of our ambition and we were thrilled.Lena Headey looks back: ‘I told Harvey Weinstein where to go. A decade of possibilities disappeared’Read moreOver the years, disagreements would flare up, inevitably because it’s quite stressful. But mostly it has gone smoothly, partly because we both feel the same about the really important things: how you treat your people. It sounds cheesy, but we’re not in it for the money, and never have been. I’m not saying we haven’t made money. We have. I’m very happy. But we didn’t want a yacht in the Maldives. My car is 20 years old. Dave’s was even older when it finally packed up. Money has never been the motive. It’s always been to make a community.Dave was the best man at my wedding, his brother was the photographer and his father was the vicar. Perhaps because of his father’s background, Dave is a fantastically ethical person. He has a very strong sense of what is right and is extremely unselfish. In comparison, I seem possibly venal. If a project comes up that we could take on, he’s always looking to share it with somebody else.Faced with all the questions, the challenges of life and of running a company and of creative decisions, we’ve become each other’s best ally against the world.David (right)We took this photo when our CBEs were announced in 2006. I had bought the shirt in the late 90s from somewhere like Benetton and thought it was jolly, so it became my uniform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat year was a busy period for us, with significant business changes, lots of ideas and films we wanted to make. Animation was in the ascendancy.Peter and I went to a state-run grammar school in Woking. He was left-handed, I was right-handed, so we didn’t have much space between us. I noticed he was always doing figurative drawings in his notebook. He also had a very strong Australian accent. It was quite hard for me to actually work out what his surname was.As we got to know each other, we discovered that both our fathers worked for the BBC: his dad was in the sales side, and my dad was a religious programmes producer. Both our mums taught art, so there was a curious commonality there.I was better on the organisational side, and Pete had the more imaginative stuff covered. We also had shared beliefs and motives. My father was an ordained Congregational minister, so there was a strong value system in place. That we were both being brought up in the 60s and early 70s was important, too. There was an optimistic creative dynamic to the Beatles period, the youth revolution, the happy hippy stuff. The world was our oyster.double quotation markI am always asking myself: how do we make this stuff from his imagination actually happen?For the first six years, I was running around like a wotsit. Eventually, we built up a team of skilled people. When Creature Comforts won an Oscar [in 1991, for best animated short], it was a huge moment, because the Brits didn’t get many Oscars in those days. The ceremony in LA went on for five hours back then, so there were lots of ad breaks. I remember going to the gents during one break and turning around, thinking, “My God, I’m having a pee with Jack Nicholson.”When we did the deal with DreamWorks for Chicken Run, the question was: how do we divide our forces? I had broadly said to Pete and Nick [Park], “You go and direct Chicken Run and I’ll sort out everything else.” In retrospect, that might have been a dumb thing to say, because it took me out of the day-to-day film production side. I stepped back from doing the camera work – the shooting and the directing – and ended up doing more management and overseeing. I missed being on the studio floor. Did I tell Pete? Probably not at the time. It was the right thing to do, and I was doing it for all the right reasons. Even if I would visit the studio and gnash my teeth, thinking, “God, I wish I was doing that, rather than sitting in finance meetings.”Outside work we have supported one another, too. We were both deeply affected as our parents got older and eventually popped their clogs. Pete ended up with three kids, and I suppose that’s where our social time began to divide up a bit. I guess if I’d had kids, too, we would have done a lot more together. But that wasn’t to be.Pete is a natural storyteller and is an inspiration to others, often just by his presence. He’s not the best of timekeepers, but that’s always been part of his makeup and is not unusual for someone so creative. He has got an incredible mind, and I am always asking myself: how do we make this stuff from his imagination actually happen? Really, that question is at the core of everything that I do.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackPhotographyAardmanWallace & GromitAnimation on TVTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: Is it inevitable that consumerism will literally fill up the planet? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers whether there is sufficient global physical capacity for all our discarded and worn-out purchases
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers whether there is sufficient global physical capacity for all our discarded and worn-out purchases
Content: The end of stuff … the 2008 film Wall-E, about a lone garbage-picking robot on a future, uninhabitable Earth.Photograph: Disney/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenThe end of stuff … the 2008 film Wall-E, about a lone garbage-picking robot on a future, uninhabitable Earth.Photograph: Disney/Sportsphoto/AllstarNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: Is it inevitable that consumerism will literally fill up the planet?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers whether there is sufficient global physical capacity for all our discarded and worn-out purchasesThis week’s question:If all car tyres were filled with CO2, would this cut atmospheric carbon significantly?Sun 23 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf consumer capitalism continues at its current rate, will we reach a point at which there is literally no space left on Earth for all the stuff that has been created?Alex Robinson, Alnwick, NorthumberlandSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyWhen we’re full up here, we can send all our crap to the moon. I believe some people have already started.BobAggIt’s not inevitable if we keep recycling with fervour and keep buying in secondhand shops.RP Orlando, by emailNo. Within 100 years the world’s population will have reduced by 95%. The causes will be war, famine, plague and pestilence and our new shinier curses. The survivors will consume very little of anything.Alan Webb, by emailIt will probably go into the holes left from open-cast mining and in 5m or 6m years’ time, it will be a layer in the geology for Cockroach sapiens to marvel at, from “when monkeys ruled the Earth”.JoninBomoIf we run out of space on Earth for all the stuff that has been created, we can just order a new one on Amazon.Sagarmatha1953Stuff we make is not going to “fill” the planet, because everything that goes to make more stuff is made from the other stuff we dig out from the ground. What we might do is convert everything that was seen as raw materials when we got here into new stuff that nobody needs, wants or really knows how to dispose of. That new stuff could fill the holes we made digging out the stuff to make it. It’s not going to weigh much more or occupy a lot more space than what we started with – but it could be practically useless. We might use up all of what was previously raw materials, and from the processing leave enough toxic residue and pollutants to make human life on Earth near impossible.leadballoonJared Diamond’s Collapseexamines previous civilisations that collapsed, why, and the archaeological evidence that sheds light on the consequences. In all cases the cause was one or more of the following: climate change, interruption of trade routes, war or disease. In all of the cases, there was evidence of cannibalism. James Lovelock (of Gaia fame) opined that our current trajectory would result in our species being reduced “to a few breeding pairs in the Arctic where the climate remains tolerable”.Our global society will inevitably end. There will be far fewer of us, and our lives will be far harder, than now. We will consume less because there will be less to consume. But the world won’t end. When most of us are gone, the planet and its ecosphere will recover. It will take hundreds of years, but the future of the planet is assured. Ours, not so much.View image in fullscreenUltimate recycling … Charlton Heston and Edward G Robinson in Soylent Green.Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyIt’s also worth mentioning Make Room! Make Room! by Harry Harrison, made into a film,Soylent Green, starring Charlton Heston. It describes a world overrun with people, the only food available being soylent green biscuits provided by the government, purportedly made from soya beans and lentils. But soylent green isn’t made from pulses, but from people. Recycling taken to an extreme.rumblestripsIn reply: Something like a million years ago we were reduced to a thousand or so breeders; it took millennia before we got going again. Some species bounce back, others don’t, but we’re probably the first ones endangered because we did bounce back.jno50No, the Earth won’t ever get over-full of manufactured items, and storage space is not really the problem. It’s much more serious.Unsustainable consumption, in all its many forms, is the issue here, under every political and economic system. Consumer capitalism is very much part of the problem, but it runs much deeper.One group has calculated an “Earth overshoot day”, currently 30 July, a date in the year by which we have used more ecological resources and services than the Earth can naturally regenerate. The UN reckons that if we can move that date back by “just” five or six days each year we would be back in equilibrium by about 2050.NickEMThanks to the purchasing activities of Mrs N, our house ran out of space years ago. That has not stopped her. This whole consumerism thing is beyond my understanding. I assume that acquiring “stuff” must meet some deep need in those afflicted, but have they no regard for anyone else?And why? Something to do with dopamine? Whatever the answer, the planet and those on it will inevitably pay a very heavy price.neepheidView image in fullscreenDoes society train us to be compulsive buyers?Photograph: Posed by model; Luis Alvarez/Getty ImagesThere’s been a hypothesis floating around, which might be based on Marx, that the constant purchasing of stuff nobody wants or needs is something society trains into us from babyhood. We are receptive to it because we’re so alienated. There’s a hole in our middle that we don’t know how to fill. For shopping addicts, the act of purchasing makes us feel meaningful and connected. My own theory is that once we buy the stuff, we felt compelled to hoard it, because throwing it away would expose the truth: we buy for the sake of buying. Buying makes us feel good.krokodilFind a place to store your waste plastics where they won’t degrade, they’re a good carbon store.VraiconHumans seem to be hardwired to self-destruct. I think we might well have been created as a joke, and I don’t mean in the biblical sense.poorprintsView image in fullscreen‘It worked beautifully for some time, until another portal appeared …’Illustration: Rost-9D/Getty ImagesThere was a science fiction story about a portal that opened up, leading one way to another universe/dimension. What would the people of Earth immediately think of using it for: shovelling our garbage into it. Truckloads were driving up from all four corners of the world, and it worked beautifully for some time, until another portal appeared, and the garbage began arriving back.RegoriThe habitability of the planet will collapse long before we run out of room to store shit we bought on the interwebs. This is likely to depress Amazon’s sales – you would think they would care more about it.View image in fullscreenA crowd in Milan … the global human population is projected to peak by 2084.Photograph: Marco Bottigelli/Getty ImagesThe numbers: the land area of the Earth is about 57m sq miles (149m sq km). World population ispredicted by the UN to peak at around 10 billion, in 2084. If we decide to divide up the land equally (very unlikely), everyone gets around 14,000 sq metres, which is a square 120 metres on a side. And if you do manage to fill up your plot, you can always go upwards.SemiFunctionalWhat we’re going to end up with is an endless, lifeless desert of crumbled concrete and little pieces of UV-degraded plastic.BrianO_BlivionNo one else watchedWall-E?LintHumanCapitalism’s need for constant growth depends on the exploitation of two things: the environment and human labour.Fortunately, or unfortunately, both will have collapsed due to other factors before it’s impossible to set foot on anything but waste.getomovInfinite production growth is impossible on our finite planet.thevicaragecatView image in fullscreenHannah Ritchie, the author of Not the End of the World: How We Can Be the First Generation to Build a Sustainable Planet.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianNo, not in any foreseeable future. Not even in the right ballpark. For example,Hannah Ritchiecalculates thatall the world’s plastic could be disposed ofin landfill in a layer 10 metres deep, 30 metres below the surface in an area of 1,800 sq km. The land surface area of the world is 148,900,000 sq km.This does not imply that there are not important issues with pollution and waste management that must be dealt with.quokkaZUnbridled consumerism is already taking a terrible toll on our mental and physical wellbeing and nature as well. It’s time to rethink the concept of consumerism to halt going backwards progressively.macmccarthy999How to declutter your home planet?EddieChorepostI don’t think it will come to that. The question of where we will put all our stuff in the future assumes a continuation or acceleration of our current lives: holidays, homes, celebrations and everyday acquisition.For decades, I’ve been anticipating a global calamity that will put a stop to our thoughtlessness and leave those who survive to share the remains. In such a world, random items would gain special status.In George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four salvaged objects like a blank book, a lipstick and a ticking clock become symbolic of subversion in a dystopian future. And in Graham Oakley’s Henry’s Quest (1986) people repurpose the debris of a long-past industrial society to recreate an Arthurian one.WoollyAphidIn reply: Advocating for better waste management and recycling is more likely to lead to better outcomes than anticipating global calamity.quokkaZThe laws of physics prevent adding new stuff. We’re making new stuff from old stuff. Plastics from oil, disposable Ikea furniture from wood pulp and plastics, SUVs from iron ore and plastics, phones from silicon, silicates and plastics.As long as we make stuff that lasts, and it can either be recycled or composted when no longer needed, the world won’t fill up with our stuff.TopGyreA lot of stuff is really cheap now in comparison with previous times. In the 80s a decent TV would sell at £300-plus, maybe two or three grand in today’s money. Nobody would have had things like leaf blowers for their garden but they’re pretty inexpensive now.PeteTheBeatView image in fullscreenCarbon recycling … composting can help.Photograph: El Casanelles/Getty Images; posed by a modelWe need to overhaul education. Learn about sustainability, learn how to cook from scratch, gardening, learn how to budget so at 1am we are not sending another £40 to Jeff Bezos for stuff we probably don’t need; nutrition, stuff like sewing, basic car repairs. Too many people give up on something that can be repaired and just buy new.Stop, even on these pages showing off new gadgets or the latest fashions. Buy some good clothes and wear them whenever and for ever-ish.Global population predictions offer ‘hopeful sign’ for planet, UN saysRead moreI think someone will come up with a solution that maybe lets every piece of crap become some sort of power source in the future. We have a long way to go.catchytitledIn reply: Yep, the inability to sew was a great eye-openener for me. A (female) friend who, at the time, was about 30 years old, asked me for a special favour – to resew a button that had fallen off. What! Really? But basic car repairs? Oh I wish. Modern cars are all but impossible to do anything yourself. Even changing blown bulbs is now made way too awkward.lucyfamNobody wants to talk about overpopulation. I thought England and Wales was cramped in the 80s (56 million) but we’ve managed to add another third to that figure, on a small island. But politicians are desperate for the next generation to pay their bills, growth is always the mantra but misses the big picture completely.boliPeople used to burn their rubbish. If they ran low on coke or coal they burnt what they had. TVs were repaired and sold secondhand.In future, we will mine landfill for resources. It will be filthy work – people do that across many countries where we export our rubbish. Better that we upcycle and grow everything we can, compost and use grey water – and get science-based solutions.confusedofenglandView image in fullscreen‘They took all the trees’ … Joni Mitchell performing in California in 1974.Photograph: Larry Hulst/Getty ImagesWe’ve all seen a stretch limousine, one of the most cheap, ridiculous, pompous, and unnecessary wastes of human endeavour. This isn’t a stretch planet, and it’s already full.There was a point when Joni Mitchell was singing about a “tree museum”, and [paradise turned into] “a parking lot”, this has now been trumped by an almost limitless factory making Ikea cupboards.Growth? Which growth is that then? When the fields are brown, and the trees are burned.bricklayersoptionExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesRecyclingOverconsumptionWasteLandfillPollutionEthical and green livingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Landslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government says | Guinea | The Guardian
description: Dump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African state
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African state
Content: Residents and rescuers search for bodies in the dump site in Conakry on 23 August.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenResidents and rescuers search for bodies in the dump site in Conakry on 23 August.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesGuineaLandslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government saysDump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African stateReutersSun 23 Aug 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA ⁠landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to ⁠collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks.The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of WestAfrica.The landslide took ​place at about 2am (3am UK time) ‌in the Gbessia commune ‌of Conakry, according to a government statement.The death toll was 30, with six ‌people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I ‌have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite ​reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a ⁠World Bank report published in April.On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara​, announced ​that the government was closing ​the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to ​be relocated outside Conakry.The prime ‌minister, Amadou Oury ​Bah, visited ​the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.Explore more on these topicsGuineaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war | Canada | The Guardian
description: PM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressors
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: PM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressors
Content: The US president, Donald Trump, and Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, have each blamed the opposite side for the breakdown in negotiations.Photograph: Saul Loeb,dave Chan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US president, Donald Trump, and Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, have each blamed the opposite side for the breakdown in negotiations.Photograph: Saul Loeb,dave Chan/AFP/Getty ImagesCanada‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade warPM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressorsThe lesson from Canada’s collapsed trade talks with the US: negotiation may be futileLauren AlmeidaSun 23 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has hit back at Canada after a breakdown in negotiationsplunged the two countries into a trade war.In his first public comments since negotiations collapsed on Friday in Washington, the US president wrote on social media: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!”“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” he added. “No more!!!”His comments came after the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods, whileMark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar”.The US tariffs came into force on Saturday, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Trade experts have predicted that the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the biggest impact is expected to be political, triggering fresh tension between the neighbours.View image in fullscreenCanadian trade minister Dominic LeBlanc, left, and US trade representative Jamieson Greer speak to reporters in Washington DC on Friday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockBoth sides blamed the other for the breakdown in talks on Friday. Carney told Canadian journalists that the country was “at war” over trade with the US, after Trump “miscalculated” by escalating his tariff attack.“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Ottawa. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”Against the wind: despite Trump’s attacks, unions are fighting for good US clean energy jobsRead moreJamieson Greer, the US trade representative, has said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. He told Fox & Friends Weekend: “We’ve said enough and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.”Dan Kelly, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, estimated that 40% of small Canadian exporters will be directly hit by the US tariffs, and that nearly one-third expect their revenues will drop by 50% or more as a result.The escalation was also met with anger by Democrat lawmakers and governors from US states that border Canada including Minnesota, New York and Washington.New York governor Kathy Hochul posted on X: “Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That’s Trump’s economic policy in a nutshell.”Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar, said the new tariffs meant “higher costs for small businesses, farmers, and all Minnesota families.”She wrote on X: “Canada is Minnesota’s #1 trading partner. Minnesotans are paying for Trump’s chaos.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCarney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England,was elected as Canada’s prime minister last yearafter campaigning to lead a fightback against Trump, who has suggested he wants to make Canada a 51st state with “economic force”.Carney’s “dollar for dollar” tariffs are expected to take effect from 8 September, with new levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The escalation has also called into question the future of the North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico, known as USMCA.The pact, which was signed by Trump during his first term, governs about $2tn annually in goods and services between the three countries. Trumprefused to renew the USMCA this summerafter Canada and Mexico formally requested for it to be renewed for another 16 years.When asked how the US-Canadian collapse in trade talks would affect the USMCA, Carney said it was “certainly not good news”.Increasingly aggressive rhetoric and trade policy from the Trump administration has damaged US-Canadian relations, with tourism also suffering – there was a21% drop in Canadians entering New York state in 2025and 3mn fewer visits compared with the previous year.Furthermore, a petition to expel the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, from the country has gathered around 248,000 signatures since late July, according tothe Associated Press.This year apoll by Globe and Mail newspaperfound that only 9% of Canadians agreed that the US was a “trustworthy ally”, and that 51% of those polled had cancelled American trips in reaction to comments by Trump.Explore more on these topicsCanadaDonald TrumpMark CarneyTariffsUS foreign policyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: The lesson from Canada’s collapsed trade talks with the US: negotiation may be futile | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Breakdown shows Washington now prioritises its own interests over any semblance of shared economic ground
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Breakdown shows Washington now prioritises its own interests over any semblance of shared economic ground
Content: Donald Trump and Mark Carney. The US and Canada are now in a deepening trade war after weeks of urgent talks fell apart.Composite: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Mark Carney. The US and Canada are now in a deepening trade war after weeks of urgent talks fell apart.Composite: Dylan Martinez/ReutersTrump tariffsAnalysisThe lesson from Canada’s collapsed trade talks with the US: negotiation may be futileOlivia BowdenBreakdown shows Washington now prioritises its own interests over any semblance of shared economic ground‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade warSun 23 Aug 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTShareThe calamitous collapse of trade negotiations betweenCanadaand the United States is a warning to nations worldwide that pursuing any kind of dialogue with the current US administration is doomed at the outset, according to observers who say this recent episode indicates seeking a fair deal is futile.Andrea Lawlor, an associate professor of political science at McMaster University in Ontario, said: “No matter the closeness of the historical relationship, the American administration has signalled that it now prioritises its interests above those of some sort of global economic coordination or harmony.“It feels like these talks ‘failed’. However, I’m not sure there was really a success to be had.”The two countries are now in a deepening trade war after weeks of urgent talks fell apart shortly before the 12am EST (5am BST) deadline on Saturday, when the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods.A defiant Mark Carney said on Saturday that he had rejected the deal because of last-minute US demands that would haveundermined Canada’s sovereignty. The Canadian prime minister said: “They asked too much and they offered too little … you’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked.” He promised to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar”.Donald Trump had initially announced the tariffs on 20 July,saying Canada had unfairly discriminated against American businesses.The core example provided by the White House is Canada’s bans on the sale of US alcohol in eight of its 10 provinces and all three territories. The removal of US spirits, wine and beer from shelves came into effect after Trump’s first round of tariffs, slapped on Canada in early 2025.The breakdown of talks came as a shock. Trump had claimed on Tuesday that a three-day extension would be applied to the tariff deadline, as an agreement was all but signed. On Wednesday, he told reporters that a “very fair deal for both” sides had been ironed out.But as details of the agreement began to leak to Canadian media, there was growing alarm that Carney and his negotiators were conceding too much in exchange for lower tariffs on steel, aluminium and cars.The premier of Manitoba, Wab Kinew, and his Nova Scotia counterpart, Tim Houston, confirmed this week that Carney had asked the provinces to return US alcohol to shelves in order to seal the trade deal.Kinew told reporters he believed Canada “should fight” Trump instead, and that “you can’t get a good deal with a bad person”. He encouraged Canadians to avoid buying US alcohol, even if the premiers agreed to put it back on shelves.Fears of capitulating to Trump also emerged in a high-level briefing call held by Canada’s ambassador to the US, Mark Wiseman, with the Canada-US trade council.Sources told theCanadian Broadcasting Corporationthat Canada’s former chief trade negotiator Steve Verheul had warned in the call that concessions now would only lead to further demands from the Americans down the road.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJD Vance the US vice-president,was also recordedat a private event, seemingly mocking Carney for standing down on “a lot of issues” as the trade negotiations were occurring.Instead, Carney took the dramatic decision to bring his negotiators home to Ottawa, with no further meetings planned – and to launch a barrage of criticism against Trump, who in turn accused Canada of wanting “the benefits of being a state, without being one”.Goods covered by the swingeing US import taxes include everything from anoraks to Christmas ornaments.Lawlor suggested Canada would soon be back at the negotiating table, given the likely economic impact of the tariffs. But she said any negotiation with the Trump administration should be understood as prone to disintegrate at a moment’s notice.She said: “We are very much in a state of constant flux, where even where negotiations do produce agreements, these should not be viewed as eternally binding.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaMark CarneyDonald TrumpAmericasTariffsEconomicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: The new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violence | Games | The Guardian
description: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards
Author: Jackson Ryan
Headline: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards
Content: A still from Halloween: The Game. The ability for players to smoke marijuana to detect an enemy has resulted in the game being banned in Australia.Photograph: IllfonicView image in fullscreenA still from Halloween: The Game. The ability for players to smoke marijuana to detect an enemy has resulted in the game being banned in Australia.Photograph: IllfonicGamesThe new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violenceAcademics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standardsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJackson RyanSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 21.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. The US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.But Australians will not be able to play Halloween, because it has been refused classification by the Australian Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders.In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that the Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of ComputerGames2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchiseRead more“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the boardwrote in a recent statement.In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game.The uproar has resurfaced longstanding grievances about how games are classified in Australia compared with film and television, and the inability for adults to access games widely available in other parts of the world.double quotation markCan we stop pretending that the way we classify games in Australia, in 2026, is appropriate for adults?Margaret Anderson, former director of the Classification BoardClaire Henry, an associate professor in screen at Flinders University and an Australian Research Council fellow, says the board enforced the guidelines correctly but the controversy around the decision highlights “a mismatch between the community standards and the classification standards”.The decision on Halloween: The Game follows several high-profile cases that have resulted in games such asState of Decay,Wasteland 3andSaints Row IVbanned in Australia for the same reason: incentivised drug use. All of these games were later reclassified after censoring aspects of their gameplay.View image in fullscreenSaints Row IV. The game was initially refused classification in Australia but was later released after a particular mission was removed.Photograph: Deep SilverDan Golding, a professor of media at Monash University, says that two assumptions have been baked into the classifying of games in Australia. “Games have always been regulated based on the assumption there is something more impactful aboutdoing,in a game, than there is aboutwatching,in a film,” he says.“A second assumption is that games are for kids – or at least the regulation system exists to protect kids.”Ron Curry has battled these assumptions in skirmishes with the Classification Board over his nearly two decades as CEO of the Interactive Games and Entertainment Association (IGEA). Alongside a dogged public campaign and a cadre of journalists, the IGEA helped introduce an R18+ category for video games in 2013, the absence of which had stopped several games being released in Australia before.After the R18+ classification was brought in, Curry noted the jobwas not finished– the trade-off for introducing the category was that video games were still seen as a distinct form of media, with greater risks attached.“It still very clearly said games are different to all other media, it’s more dangerous, and we need to treat it more carefully,” Curry says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSaints Row 4 refused classification in AustraliaRead moreInteractivity – thedoingGolding refers to – has always underlined this belief. The guidelines for games, introduced alongside the R18+ rating, state that “as a general rule computer games may have a higher impact than similarly themed depictions of the classifiable elements in film, and therefore greater potential for harm or detriment, particularly to minors”.Curry points tothe Australian government’s own research that hassuggested interactivity may not increase the impact of video games, particularly in regards to violent content, and there has been limited research on interactivity around drug use, sex, gambling and nudity.Margaret Anderson, a former director of the Classification Board, says the huge focus on interactivity in games drove her nuts during her seven years on the board. She points todecades of researchshowing games are predominantly played by adults.“Can we stop pretending that the way we classify games in this country, in 2026, is appropriate for adults? Because it’s not,” Anderson says.Academics have shown the current classification system isn’t just preventing access to games, however. Often, the standards are incoherent.Marcus Carter, founder of the Sydney Games and Play Lab at the University of Sydney, recently leda study– yet to be peer reviewed – that showed inconsistencies across the classifications of mobile games in the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. In 18 separate cases across the 31 top-grossing mobile games, four different age ratings were included for a single game.Carter describes the current system as “not fit for purpose”.The worry, for experts like Carter and Henry, is that the inconsistent standards have a negative impact on how the community views classifications and age ratings.“Inconsistencies can kind of undermine public confidence in the classification system,” says Henry. “It is a good system in many ways, and we’ve got to maintain that trust.”The Australian government isundertaking a review of the classification guidelineswith the aim of delivering a simpler, more consistent approach across films, games and publications. Among a raft of proposals – including introducing a PG13 rating and adjusting the MA15+ classification to MA16+ – one idea is to “remove the harsher judgement of video games’ interactivity”.IGEAandHenryhave made submissions to the review.In a statement to the Guardian,a spokesperson from the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts said: “The Australian Government is working to modernise the National Classification Scheme to ensure it remains aligned with community standards and helps Australians make informed decisions about what they read, watch and play. This work is ongoing.”Illfonic has shown no sign it will censor Halloween: The Game and have its classification reviewed in Australia. Illfonic and the game’s co-publisher Gun Interactive did not respond to requests for comment.Though the instances of Australia banning games have been rare occurrences, one future decision looms large: how will Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment in a franchise packed with sex, drugs and violence,be rated?For Anderson, the way forward is simple.“The foundational pillar of classification in Australia is that adults should be able to read, hear, see, play what they want,” she says. “Can we please respect that fact?”Explore more on these topicsGamesHalloween (2018)Horror filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s marine parks protect ‘places no one goes’ rather than fragile waters near the mainland, scientists say | Environment | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of experts write to environment minister calling for stronger protections for ‘unique and distinct’ marine ecosystems
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: Hundreds of experts write to environment minister calling for stronger protections for ‘unique and distinct’ marine ecosystems
Content: A weedy sea dragon in Port Botany off Sydney’s coast. A group of scientists are calling for Australia’s coastal marine ecosystems to be better protected, saying many highly protected zones are concentrated in remote waters.Photograph: DaveBluck/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenA weedy sea dragon in Port Botany off Sydney’s coast. A group of scientists are calling for Australia’s coastal marine ecosystems to be better protected, saying many highly protected zones are concentrated in remote waters.Photograph: DaveBluck/Getty Images/iStockphotoAustralian climate and environmental reportingEnvironmentAustralia’s marine parks protect ‘places no one goes’ rather than fragile waters near the mainland, scientists sayHundreds of experts write to environment minister calling for stronger protections for ‘unique and distinct’ marine ecosystemsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian government has been accused of leaving waters near the mainland largely unprotected by establishing the bulk of highly protected marine parks in remote areas.More than 270 leading marine scientists from 84 research institutes have written to the environment minister, Murray Watt, urging stronger protections for marine ecosystems, as aonce-in-a-decadereview of marine parks gets under way.The oceans and seas surrounding Australia and its territories areglobally remarkable, with tropical reefs to icy Antarctic shores, six Unesco world heritage areas and at least 33,000 marine species. But they also face compounding pressures due to climate-driven ocean warming, fishing and extractive industries, and expanding use.Fears of ‘catastrophic’ decline of giant Australian cuttlefish after only 44 counted in dive surveyRead moreProf Jessica Meeuwig, director of the Marine Futures Lab at the University of Western Australia and an author of the statement sent to Watt, said many species found in Australian waters existed nowhere else on the planet. “If we don’t protect them here, it’s not like we can expect somebody else to do the job, they’re lost for ever.”About a quarter of Australian waters are currently highly protected. But these “no take zones” were concentrated in remote offshore and territorial waters, with minimal coverage in the waters surrounding mainland Australia, the statement said.It called for “at least 30%” of every marine bioregion to be highly protected, with bans on industrial trawling, long lining and mining across all marine parks. The scientists said no current protections should be wound back.“In some of our regions, there’s only 1% to 7% of the oceans that are highly protected, and the rest is open slather,” Meeuwig said. These included marine regions off New South Wales, south-east Queensland, Western Australia, western South Australia and the Northern Territory.View image in fullscreenA cock-eyed squid (Histioteuthis miranda) at the Bremer marine park on the south coast of Western Australia.Photograph: Marine Futures LabProf David Booth, a marine ecologist at the University of Technology Sydney, said the temperate east region – one of five regions up for review – is “incredibly biodiverse”.“For instance, around Sydney, we’ve got six to seven hundred species of fish, which is way more than we should have based on our latitude, and a mix of tropical and temperate species,” he said.The region, which stretches from the Great Barrier Reef’s southern border to Bermagui on the south coast of NSW, features the East Australian Current and underwater seamounts and canyons.It is also a “hot spot” for climate-driven changes, he said, with temperate fish species – including many that people liked to eat –moving south, and added pressure from urbanisation, industry and fishing. “It’s an area of rapid change, with very little protection at the moment,” he said.Watt said the government was “well on the way to meeting the Albanese government’s commitment to highly protect 30% of Australia’s ocean by 2030”, and the proposed expansion of marine parks around Lord Howe and Norfolk islands would achieve the target ahead of time.The marine parks review would provide “further opportunities to better protect key ocean habitats”, he said, “while allowing for sustainable use and conservation”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAssociate professor Carissa Klein, director of the Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Science at the University of Queensland, said the current locations of highly protected areas were “biased towards places that no one goes”.“We’re not actually protecting the diversity of life that we have in the ocean,” she said. “Every bioregion is unique and distinct, and has different animals and plants. We want them to get to 30% of every one.“We want a representative network of protected areas all around Australia.”That would benefit fishers too, as well as boosting tourism and the environment, Meeuwig said. For example, 80% of the coral trout caught in areas open to fishing on the Great Barrier Reef were born in highly protected areas.The review was a “tremendous opportunity”, she said. “When Australia leads, it keeps the bar high. When we set the bar low, it gives permission to everybody else to do a bad job.“If Australia flounders at this opportunity, it will have ramifications across other places.”This article was updated on 24 August, 2026, to remove reference to coastal waters. Commonwealth waters start 6km offshore.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentAustralian climate and environmental reportingOceansMarine lifenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pent-up demand’: first home buyers chase more loans as property investors step back, data shows | Housing | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: New entrants the only cohort making more loan applications amid interest rate rises and tax changes, mortgage broker says
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Exclusive: New entrants the only cohort making more loan applications amid interest rate rises and tax changes, mortgage broker says
Content: First home buyers feel the sentiment has turned in their favour while investors feel it has swung against them, a property expert says.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenFirst home buyers feel the sentiment has turned in their favour while investors feel it has swung against them, a property expert says.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPHousing‘Pent-up demand’: first home buyers chase more loans as property investors step back, data showsExclusive:New entrants the only cohort making more loan applications amid interest rate rises and tax changes, mortgage broker saysFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst home buyers are still taking out a large number of loans, with government backing, even as investors step back from Australia’s property market.New entrants are now the only cohort applying for more loans than they were in June, according to new data from the mortgage broker network Loan Market.Home buying had slowed after interest rates rose three times and Labor abolished negative gearing for most investment purchases. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has saidthe reformswere meant to “level the playing field” for first home buyers.Loan Market reported first-timer applications dropped 3% in July then rose 10% into the first half of August on a weekly average basis. Applications from other owner-occupiers and investors were roughly steady in August compared to June.Home loan demand had been falling across the board by June, down 5.4% compared with the prior quarter, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.While the number of investor loans fell by 8.6%, the number of first-time buyer mortgages fell only 2.9% on a seasonally adjusted basis, the ABS reported.First home purchases were still higher in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory than the same time the year before. They rose to hit their highest level since 2021 in South Australia and Tasmania.Could you save money on your mortgage? As house prices cool and lender rivalry heats up, experts say Australians should askRead morePeter Esho, the chief executive of the property finance firm 13x, said new entrants to the market had become more visible in recent months.“First home buyers now feel like the sentiment has swung in their favour, and investors feel like the sentiment swung against them,” Esho said.“There’s been a lot of buyers on the sideline for a long time … so that pent-up demand is going to keep it for the next few years and policy is obviously a big driver.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailEsho said demand was concentrating on properties with prices close to the eligibility caps set by the government’s 5% deposit scheme.The program allows first-time buyers to borrow up to 95% of a property’s value and have the government guarantee the loan, waiving costly lenders’ mortgage insurance (LMI).House prices have fallen across Australia but properties eligible for the guarantee have had slower falls than homes outside the scheme, according to the data company Cotality.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionProperty price change graphHomes are eligible if they are below $1.5m in NSW cities, $1m for south-east Queensland, $950,000 for Melbourne and Geelong, $850,000 for Perth, $900,000 for Adelaide and $700,000 for Hobart. Labor expanded the scheme and scrapped income caps for applicants in October 2025.Housing Australia, which administers the 5% deposit scheme, found applicants typically saved more than $15,000 in LMI for the median deposit paid on the median home purchased under the scheme.More than 320,000 people have become homeowners under the scheme since it was established in 2020.The housing minister, Clare O’Neil, told Guardian Australia that scheme participants had collectively saved more than $2.5bn in LMI by the end of July.“We know that for too long the housing market has been stacked against young people and without this scheme many wouldn’t be able to enter the market at all,” O’Neil said.More than 5,000 new guarantees had been issued each month since February. Housing Australia said that slipped just below 5,000 in July, which was still more than had been issued in any month before Labor expanded the scheme.Australia’s leading LMI company Helia has estimated the scheme’s expansion cost it nearly $9m worth of first home buyer business in the first half of 2026. Its remaining customers were typically people buying above the price caps or from non-participating banks, a spokesperson said.ANZ, which began offering the 5% scheme in March, was the only big four bank to maintain a steady value of mortgage applications in the June quarter.The influx of first home buyers offset a drop in lending to other groups. Scheme participants now account for one in every 20 new loan applications at ANZ.Explore more on these topicsHousingAustralian economyBankingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Absurd’: children to see gambling logos on sports jerseys until 2032 in transition period condemned by Pocock | Gambling | The Guardian
description: Government says it hopes clubs will end jersey deals with wagering companies earlier, but calls it a commercial decision
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Government says it hopes clubs will end jersey deals with wagering companies earlier, but calls it a commercial decision
Content: Sydney Roosters have a longstanding jersey deal with UniBet. They are one of seven NRL clubs with gambling company logos on their jerseys.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenSydney Roosters have a longstanding jersey deal with UniBet. They are one of seven NRL clubs with gambling company logos on their jerseys.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPGambling‘Absurd’: children to see gambling logos on sports jerseys until 2032 in transition period condemned by PocockGovernment says it hopes clubs will end jersey deals with wagering companies earlier, but calls it a commercial decisionFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotandJosh ButlerSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChildren across Australia will continue to see gambling logos on professional sport jerseys until up to 2032 despitethe government’s pledgeto break the link between sport and wagering.The Albanese government has banned gambling company logos on jerseys but legislated a five-year transition period to allow clubs and bookmakers to adjust.The 2032 deadline has been criticised by public health experts, who question why the government recognised the logos as harmful but allowed them to remain for so long.David Pocock on the ‘real betrayal’ of Labor’s deal on gambling reforms - podcastRead moreThe grandfathering provisions mean a child in year 8 today could see gambling logos on a sports professional jersey until they finish school.The five-year window has been criticised by the crossbench senatorDavid Pocock, who called on clubs to end jersey sponsorships “at the earliest opportunity”.“We are in an absurd situation where by the time of the legislation’s three-year statutory review, jerseys may still have betting logos on them,” Pocock said.The Liberal MP Andrew Wallace, whocrossed the floor to vote against the bill, said five years was too generous and that he pushed his party room to accept a two-year deadline.“I thought that was an appropriate period to allow these sporting codes and clubs to find alternatives and to cease those gambling company connections,” Wallace said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWhen asked about the five-year window, the communications minister, Anika Wells, said one unnamed sports club had a jersey deal until 2031.Wells said she hoped clubs would end their jersey deals with wagering companies earlier, but stressed that was a commercial decision for clubs and not government.“In trying to strike a balance here between grandfathering existing arrangements and ensuring viability, that’s what we got to,” Wells told reporters.“That [2031 contract] is the most egregious one (…) but there’s plenty that are expiring this year, for example.”Seven NRL clubs have the wagering or lottery company logos on their jerseys, with several contracts running until at least the end of the 2028 season.Samantha Thomas, a public health expert specialising in gambling harm, said the five-year window meant it was “difficult to take the government seriously when it claims to be trying to break the nexus between gambling and sport”.“We should be really concerned about the government’s lack of urgency to protect kids from gambling marketing,” Thomas said.“The government has effectively said that they recognise that gambling sponsorship is harmful to children and then decided that it can continue for the next five years.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMartin Thomas from the Alliance forGamblingReform has also criticised the grandfathering provisions and said it “underscored how little a difference these compromised gambling reforms will make”.The Brisbane Broncos have a jersey deal with The Star until the end of next season, although the club is yet to reveal its 2027 shirt and is in discussions with the casino. The Star did not respond before deadline.The Penrith Panthers signed a jersey deal with Picklebet in 2025 that, according to the club, will last until“at least” the end of the 2027 season.Australians could soon be able to block all online gambling ads. But will the plan actually work?Read moreThe Newcastle Knights have a jersey deal with Palmerbet that reportedly runs until the end of 2028. The club declined to comment on the specifics of this deal.In 2024 the Gold Coast Titans signed a jersey deal with The Lottery Office, although this is exempt from the changes due to a carveout for domestic lotteries.The Dolphins have a jersey contract with the gambling company Betr, which merged with the existing shirt sponsor BlueBet in 2024.The West Tigers have a deal jersey deal with NextBet, which was previously known as Play Up. This long-running contract will expire before 2032.The Sydney Roosters extended a longstanding jersey deal with UniBet in July last year. The logo also features on jerseys worn by the club’s women’s team.A draft exposure of the bill circulated in late May did not include the 31 December 2031 deadline, with that date appearing to have been only confirmed when the legislation was finally introduced into parliament.In Australia,Gambling Help Onlineis available on 1800 858 858. TheNational Debt Helplineis at 1800 007 007. In the UK, support for problem gambling can be found via the NHSNational Problem Gambling Clinicon 020 7381 7722, orGamCareon 0808 8020 133. In the US, call theNational Council on Problem Gamblingon 1-800-MY-RESETExplore more on these topicsGamblingAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseLiberal partyDavid PococknewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to visit Ukraine with promise of boost for Kyiv’s long-range missiles | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: PM will use independence day trip to announce sharing of classified information about Storm Shadow components
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: PM will use independence day trip to announce sharing of classified information about Storm Shadow components
Content: Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelensky talking at HM Naval Base Portsmouth last month. Burnham’s visit to Kyiv on Monday will be his first as prime minister.Photograph: Jason Alden/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelensky talking at HM Naval Base Portsmouth last month. Burnham’s visit to Kyiv on Monday will be his first as prime minister.Photograph: Jason Alden/EPAForeign policyBurnham to visit Ukraine with promise of boost for Kyiv’s long-range missilesPM will use independence day trip to announce sharing of classified information about Storm Shadow componentsKiran Staceyin London andDan Sabbaghin DniproSun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 20.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain will boost Ukraine’s capacity to make its own long-range missiles,Andy Burnhamwill announce on Monday, as he travels to Kyiv for the country’s independence day on his first foreign visit as prime minister.Burnham will arrive in the Ukrainian capital on Monday morning at a crucial time in the war, with Kyiv braced for another wave of Russian missile attacks and the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, facing his most direct domestic challenge.The UK prime minister will use the trip to announce that the UK government will allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to helpUkrainebuild its own version.While the announcement will probably take years to have an impact on the war, it is likely to escalate tensions with Moscow at an already fraught moment in UK-Russian relations.Burnham said in a statement on Sunday night: “On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.“I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security.“The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war. In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine and deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”Burnham will announce in Kyiv that the UK will help France set up assembly lines in Ukraine for long-range missiles, which the French president, Emmanuel Macron, promised last month.Macron spoke to Zelenskyy on Saturday to promise to deliver separate interceptor missiles, which could help counter the recent barrage of high-speed Russian missile attacks on Kyiv.Meanwhile, European leaders have condemnedFriday’s drone attackon a busy shopping centre in central Ukraine, which killed 16 people in Zelenskyy’s home town of Kryvyi Rih.View image in fullscreenRescuers with a dog work at the site of a Russian drone attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih on Saturday.Photograph: Serhii Chalyi/ReutersThe Ukrainian military has run out of US-made Patriot interceptors, and the US president, Donald Trump,recently backtrackedon a promise to let Ukraine build its own.However, Zelenskyy said over the weekend he still wanted to buy more US-made Patriots, adding that Ukraine was happy to pay for them rather than receive them as military aid. “I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package,” he said. “The request from our air force is 360.”He added that he had reached an agreement with France on at least one air-defence system ​this year, and with ‌Germany on the supply of ​about 600 ​interceptors in 2027-28.Macronposted on Xon Saturday: “It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its skies and thwart this aggression … It is essential that all countries with capabilities at their disposal also join this effort.”The British announcement is a small step in a much larger and longer-term project that could lead to Ukraine making its own long-range versions of the Storm Shadow cruise missile in several years’ time.But the move is likely to trigger further criticism from Moscow at a time when tensions between the UK and Russia are already high.Last week,
