Russiaaccused the UKof deliberately escalating the conflict by allowing Ukraine to launch attacks with British-made drones, warning that the deeper Britain’s involvement, “the higher the price it will pay”.This weekend it emerged that Russia hadwithdrawn its ambassador in Londonwithout naming a replacement, prompting speculation it was downgrading its diplomatic presence in the UK.Burnham has insisted that Russian threats will not weaken British support for Ukraine,saying last week: “We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”The prime minister will on Monday use a meeting of the coalition of the willing, which comprises 34 countries that have promised to help secure Ukraine in the event of a peace deal with Russia, to underline that commitment.Holding election in wartime would risk destroying Ukraine, says ZelenskyyRead moreThe meeting will be co-chaired by Burnham and Macron, who will join remotely via video link. Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, will also take part in the call as the leaders discuss ways to help Ukraine repel the recent wave of long-distance attacks.While there, Burnham will attend independence day events, the details of which are being kept secret amid concerns of a major Russian attack, and receive an award in recognition of the UK’s support for Ukraine.Zelenskyy is facing the most concerted internal political challenge of his presidency after the call for an election by his former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.The Ukrainian president responded to Fedorov’s dramatic announcement for the first time this weekend, telling reporters on Saturday that holding elections, which have been suspended since the war began,risked splitting the country.“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” he said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” he added.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyAndy BurnhamUkraineRussiaLabourEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia withdraws ambassador to UK as Kremlin raises pressure over Ukraine support | Russia | The Guardian
description: Embassy in London says Andrey Kelin left last month after seven years in diplomatic post
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Embassy in London says Andrey Kelin left last month after seven years in diplomatic post
Content: Kelin’s name no longer appears on the ‘diplomatic list’ section of the website of the Russian embassy to the UK.Photograph: Jeff Overs/PAView image in fullscreenKelin’s name no longer appears on the ‘diplomatic list’ section of the website of the Russian embassy to the UK.Photograph: Jeff Overs/PARussiaRussia withdraws ambassador to UK as Kremlin raises pressure over Ukraine supportEmbassy in London says Andrey Kelin left last month after seven years in diplomatic postBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 06.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, it has emerged, as the Kremlin continues to try to put pressure on Britain over its support forUkraine.Andrey Kelin left last month after seven years in the diplomatic post, according to the Russian embassy in London.Tensions have since ratcheted up, with a warning by the embassy last week of “consequences”after it emergedBritain was supplying attack drones to Kyiv.Russia’s online list of “senior diplomatic staff” in the UK now includes only Vasily A Tsyganov, chargé d’affaires at the embassy.A gap between ambassadors was not unprecedented, said John Foreman, a former British defence attache in Moscow and Kyiv. But he said in a post on X: “The embassy’s strident ‘consequences’ statement this week and the huge deterioration of bilateral relations since 2018 and especially since the start of the war make me wonder if Moscow will permanently downgrade the relationship this time, by default by not replacing him.”A spokesperson for the embassy said the Kremlin had concluded Kelin’s diplomatic mission on 21 July. “As for the state of Russia-UK relations across all areas, they have deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level entirely on London’s initiative,” they added.A spokesperson told the Sunday Times Kelin had made efforts to preserve channels of communication with the UK and accused the government of choosing a “path of confrontation” with Russia.“He left Britain in the hope that a more constructive and respectful dialogue could eventually be restored, should the UK reconsider its policies towards our country,” they said, adding that the Kremlin had not yet put forward a replacement candidate.The embassy later issued a statement saying there was nothing in the comments to imply that Russia intended to downgrade diplomatic relations with the UK.​A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “This is a matter for the Russian ministry of foreign affairs. We have an ambassador and embassy in Moscow to engage and raise concerns with the Russian government.“We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine, which has the right to defend itself against Russia’s illegal and unprovoked invasion.”Shaun Pinner, a former British soldier who later fought alongside Ukrainian marines before he was captured and held for a time by Russian forces, said there would be arguments that Kelin’s exit had been a “dangerous erosion” of communication between Britain and Russia but he added that this had not been the case for some time in reality.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said: “If Moscow refuses to meaningfully engage, rebuffs attempts at communication and uses its diplomatic presence primarily to repeat Kremlin narratives, then we shouldn’t pretend we’re witnessing some functioning diplomatic relationship.”Kelin has repeated Kremlin narratives in interviews to British media in recent years. In one on Sky News in June, he said that Russia “cannot lose” the war in Ukraine. He joined the Soviet diplomatic service in 1979.Russia stepped up its rhetoric towards the UK last week after Ministry of Defence sources indicated a report that two drones made by British companies had been used by Ukraine’s military to attack targets inside Russia was true.The Russian embassy, seeking to maximise the impact of its remarks, added in a widely reported statement on Telegram: “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaVladimir PutinUkraineEuropeForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Holding election in wartime would risk destroying Ukraine, says Zelenskyy | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: President sharply criticises proposal, saying ‘elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine’
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: President sharply criticises proposal, saying ‘elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine’
Content: Zelenskyy during the national anthem at the start of a veterans forum in Kyiv on Saturday.Photograph: Ukrinform/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZelenskyy during the national anthem at the start of a veterans forum in Kyiv on Saturday.Photograph: Ukrinform/ShutterstockUkraineHolding election in wartime would risk destroying Ukraine, says ZelenskyyPresident sharply criticises proposal, saying ‘elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine’Dan Sabbaghin DniproSun 23 Aug 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has said holding elections in Ukraine during wartime would risk splitting the country at a time when Russia is amassing ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers.The Ukrainian president, responding for the first time toa demand made bythe sacked former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sharply criticised an idea that he said was impractical given Russia appeared to have no interest in a ceasefire.“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” Zelenskyy said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will splitUkraine,” he said, adding that his plan was to end the war and preserve Ukraine as an independent state.Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion byRussia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there had until recently been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while the war continued.That shifted when Fedorov, a popular ministerwho had been dismissed by Zelenskyy a month earlier, called for a fresh contest. It was the most open challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion.Zelenskyy said, according to a transcript from the briefing, that if Ukraine’s allies were to establish “specific conditions” under which elections could be safely, legitimately and democratically held in Ukraine, he would support them.It would require “the participation of the military, in frontline territories, abroad, where millions of our citizens have gone, fleeing the war” and a poll would have to take place safely “without strikes and shelling”, he said.Fedorov, he said, had moved from his post because had had overreached, trying to cover functions belonging to the military. He had been offered four alternative jobs in the government but declined all four, the president added. “I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” Zelenskyy said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.”Russia had a stockpile of 600-630 high-speed ballistic missiles, its most potent type of weapon, and was trying to build a little more than 100 more a month in the run-up to winter, Zelenskyy said. Its maximum production capacity was 1,300 a year, he added.Ballistic missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them.“I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our air force is 360,” Zelenskyy said. He acknowledged this was difficult given that only about 600 of the most capable PAC-3 interceptor missiles were made a year. He said he had reached an agreement with France on at least one SAMP/T air-defence system ​this year, and with ‌Germany on the supply of ​about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 ​interceptors in 2027--28.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US could help by supplying “some small percentage” of its stockpiles – about 5% to 10%, he added. Ukraine was willing to pay and it would mean the country “could get through the winter”, he said, calling on the US to make what would be “a very significant difference both in protecting lives and diplomatically”.Following a conversation with Zelenskyy on Saturday, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had agreed to strengthen French support for Ukraine, including through the delivery of interceptor missiles, without giving further details.Ukraine’s allies in the so-called coalition of the willing – an initiative led by France and Britain – will meet on Monday to look at how to ramp up pressure on Moscow to halt its invasion.Russia is seeking to build up forces for a renewed effort to capture the rest of the eastern Donetsk province it does not control by the end of the year, though Zelenskyy said he was confident Moscow would fail to capture the area, comprising principally the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.The president said he believed Russia would try to conscript a further 300,000 soldiers after the Russian parliamentary elections in September. It would be a “peripheral mobilisation” conducted away from Moscow, St Petersburg and other main cities in an effort to regain momentum in the almost deadlocked frontline, he said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyEuropeRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Pine-cone grenades and planet-baking carbon: the French fires 170 years in the making – a visual guide | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: An 1857 decree to drain swamps and plant a monoculture, detritus from the trees and global heating combined to produce the conditions for the Gironde inferno
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: An 1857 decree to drain swamps and plant a monoculture, detritus from the trees and global heating combined to produce the conditions for the Gironde inferno
Content: An image of a firefighting vehicle taking part in efforts to contain the Gironde fire, overlain with a map of the area burned. Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / EPA / Getty ImagesAn 1857 decree to drain swamps and plant a monoculture, detritus from the trees and global heating combined to produce the conditions for the Gironde infernoByAjit Niranjanwith graphics byLucy Swan,Harvey SymonsandPaul ScrutonSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ruinous fires that overran parts ofFrancethis summer have burned more land than ever recorded, forced more people from their homes than at any point since the second world war and caused what scientists suspect is the country’s first firestorm thundercloud. The smoke from France’s biggest inferno in nearly 80 years choked Limoges, a city 125 miles (200km) from the flames, with more toxic dust than Delhi residents inhaled on the city’s worst day of smog last year.The blaze that tore through forests outsideBordeauxin late July took just a few weeks to reforge France’s relationship with fire, but the conditions behind it were centuries in the making.In the 18th century, the coastal wetlands of south-western France were so swampy that shepherds used stilts to cross them in winter. When an 1857 decree from Napoleon III forced landowners to drain the marsh and populate it with maritime pines, the water-logged landscape was converted into Europe’s largest human-made forest. It has since become a regional economic engine running on timber that employs 30,000 people.Map of Landes de GascogneIt is also a firefighter’s nightmare. The pines that make up 90% of the trees in the Landes forest hold resin that burns like petrol, needles that carpet the ground with flammable material and cones that whiz in the wind like grenades, spreading flames across breaks in vegetation that should act as barriers. Without the diversity offered by broad-leafed species, which retain more moisture and have shady canopies that stop vegetation from drying, the dense monoculture can burn with fury when sparks catch.View image in fullscreenPine trees burn near Marcheprime outside  Bordeaux on 26 July.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APThat is what happened in 1949, when a blaze that began in a saw mill burned 50,000 hectares. Gorging on plentiful fuel and with few breaks to impede their spread, the flames killed 82 people, most of them volunteers racing to put out the fire. It remains Europe’s deadliest wildfire.Firefighting capacity has vastly improved since, but the potential for disaster has continued to increase. Humanity has fouled the atmosphere with 1.85tn tonnes of planet-baking carbon since the 1857 decree,warming Europeby 2.4C and increasing the risk of hot and dry extremes that were once unthinkable.Astrikingly wet winterin western Europe this year helped plants grow tall, only for relentless heatwaves to later strip them of moisture, creating a large fuel surplus for fires to devour. By mid-July, temperatures across France had reached record highs and soil moisture had fallen to record lows, setting the stage for the Gironde inferno.Chart showing record breaking heat and drought conditions in FranceNot long after noon on 22 July, after three straight weeks of more than 30C heat, smoke rose from the tightly packed pine stands near Saumos, a village 20 miles west of Bordeaux. The source of ignition is under investigation, but workers contracted by Enedis, a utility company that manages France’s electricity distribution, were active in the area and reported having sparked a fire with a faulty machine. The Bordeaux public prosecutor, which has identified the machine as its leading line of inquiry, did not respond to requests for comment. Enedis declined to answer specific questions because of the continuing investigation.‘We stared into an abyss’: the men and women battling France’s megafireRead moreMost wildfires are started by humans through actions such as dropping cigarette butts, failing to properly extinguish campfires or dispose of barbecues. Public awareness campaigns to discourage reckless behaviour are thought to have contributed to a fall in the number of fires in southern Europe since the 1980s but preventing arson is much harder. French police havearrestednearly 500 people on suspicion of starting fires since the start of the summer, about 70% of which are thought to have been deliberate.Once a fire has begun, it is weather and geography that dictate whether it will quickly wither or morph into a hellish blaze. Outside Saumos, it was immediately clear that firefighters were facing the latter. The fire engulfed several hundreds of hectares in a matter of hours and reached the outskirts of La Porge, which would lose one in 10 homes to the flames in the days that followed. Within 24 hours of the initial spark, southerly winds had pushed the fire’s southern front to Cap Ferret, an upmarket peninsula known as the Hamptons of France, nine miles away.mapHelping the fire’s rapid spread was its location in an area that had been flattened by a powerful storm in 1999 and then swiftly replanted, resulting in a uniform tree height that created a continuous fuel load. But the response in those crucial early hours has also been criticised. Local forestry workers told Le Monde that firefighters had rejected their recommendation to quickly set a controlled burn, while residents of La Porge claim resources were taken from their village to protect the wealthier Cap Ferret. The Gironde fire service, which did not respond to requests for comment, has said it had done all it could to stop the fire and rejected allegations that it abandoned La Porge.Bruno Lafon, the head of the regional forest fire prevention service, an association of forestry workers who work with firefighters to prevent blazes, said he could understand that volunteers who saw their livelihoods go up in flames wanted more help to have come. But, he said, the powerful combination of drought, heat and wind made the initial spread extremely hard to stop. “The men on the ground did what they could, though I think it would have taken a greater number of planes from the beginning,” he said. The French government has also been criticised because maintenance work meant only seven of its 12 water-bombing planes were available at the peak of the fire.View image in fullscreenWildfires evacuees at an exhibition centre in Bordeaux.Photograph: Alain Jocard/AFP/Getty ImagesAs the fire torched more land, authorities acted quickly to get people to safety. The firstevacuationsbegan on the afternoon of 22 July, when 100 residents of the north-eastern quarter of La Porge were taken to shelter in a community hall. Overnight, that number rose to more than 10,000, and just a few days later it had reached nearly 220,000. Across France and neighbouring Spain, which was also battling extreme wildfires, evacuation orders covered more than 300,000 people, a peacetime displacement unprecedented in Europe.Some residents returned to charred possessions, burnt-out homes and shells of cars, but the evacuations proved hugely successful. Not a single person died as a direct result of the Gironde fire, though four firefighters lost their lives tackling separate blazes across the country last month.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA resident of Le Porge inspects damage caused by the fire.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesAmong the evacuees was Hervé Jactel, a forest scientist at INRAE, a public research institute, who was forced to flee twice in two days. Watching Nasa maps with apprehension as the fire drew near, he lost a 20-year experiment investigating the diversity of forest trees as a result of burning biomass that jumped a cornfield. He said the fire had not come as a surprise.“From an ecological and forest management point of view, everything was in place to increase the risk of a very large fire,” he said. “Not only because of the climate, but because of the amount and homogeneity of the fuel.”Scientists suspect those conditions resulted in the extreme levels of energy that generated a firecloud, a powerful chimney of smoke stretching into the atmosphere that creates its own weather system. Known as apyrocumulonimbus cloud, it can spit lightning, and rain down burning embers that spark new blazes and spread the fire further. Nasa has described them as fire-breathing dragons.The true danger, however, lay not in the apocalyptic fire cloud but in the pollutants that it dispersed.mapStudies have foundwildfire smoketo be responsible for 1.5 million deaths around the world each year, making it one of the deadliest environmental threats to human health. Initially, much of the smoke blew straight out over the Atlantic Ocean, but a shift in wind direction caused it to choke Bordeaux, which was nervously watching the approaching inferno, before drifting over Angoulême and Limoges.It clogged the air with so much soot and ash that daily concentrations of airway-inflaming particles hit highs rarely seen, even in cities as polluted as Delhi.graphA shift in the weather helped firefighters halt the advance of the blaze at 42,000 hectares of burned area at the end of July. In the days since, they have continued to put out small flare-ups and smouldering “zombie fires” underground that they say could continue to return for months.Scientists fear for the forest’s short-term recovery. Fire can trigger outbreaks of bark beetles, which attack damaged trees and increase the fuel load for the next fire – a vicious cycle already well documented in California. The burned wood also attracts the invasive pine nematode, a microscopic worm that had arrived in south-west France in November. It blocks the flow of sap in trees, causing them to wilt and die within months.The greatest threats to the forest, however, are yet to come.Fire weatheris projected to become increasingly severe across Europe as carbon pollution continues to heat the planet. Without action to improve fire management, the burned area in Europeis predicted to rise by 39%even in a best-scenario scenario for cutting pollution. In a worst-case scenario, it could nearly triple.Experts have called for rapid cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and better management of the land, such as breaking up continuous tracts of forest and diversifying tree species.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceExtreme heatExtreme weatherAir pollutionPollutionnewsShareReuse this content

title: The ‘ordinary’ woman accused of assassinating a Russian commander in Crimea  | Russia | The Guardian
description: Friends close to Margarita Reutt are shocked she could allegedly plant bomb that killed Ukrainian defector Robert Shageev, while others recall a stubborn grit to see any plan through
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Friends close to Margarita Reutt are shocked she could allegedly plant bomb that killed Ukrainian defector Robert Shageev, while others recall a stubborn grit to see any plan through
Content: Margarita Reutt posted frequently online about health and animal rights.Photograph: VkontakteView image in fullscreenMargarita Reutt posted frequently online about health and animal rights.Photograph: VkontakteRussiaThe ‘ordinary’ woman accused of assassinating a Russian commander in CrimeaFriends close to Margarita Reutt are shocked she could allegedly plant bomb that killed Ukrainian defector Robert Shageev, while others recall a stubborn grit to see any plan throughPjotr SauerSun 23 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was just after dawn in Sevastopol when a powerful explosion tore through a quiet square in a residential district of the Russian-occupied Crimean port city.Hidden inside a rubbish bin, a bomb containing the equivalent of about 500g of TNT detonated on 13 August as Robert Shageev, the deputy commander of a Russian Black Sea fleet submarine brigade, walked past in naval uniform. He was killed on the spot.Within hours, investigators had a suspect. Police detained Margarita Reutt, a 32-year-old resident of Sochi, the Russian resort city about 300 miles across the Black Sea from Sevastopol.During a search, investigators said they had found a remote control they believed was used to detonate the bomb that killed Shageev, a former commander of Ukraine’s only submarine who switched allegiance to Russia in 2014 when Moscow annexed Crimea.According to the security service, she confessed to the attack and said that a handler linked to Ukrainian intelligence had promised her a large payment in cryptocurrency and documents that would allow her to leave Russia afterwards.View image in fullscreenFriends remember Margarita Reutt as warm and sociable, but also unusually drawn to adventure and risk.Photograph: VkontakteThe FSB also said Reutt showed no remorse.Those assertions could not be independently verified, and Russian security agencies have previously publicised purported confessions from detainees before their cases have reached court. But several people previously accused by Russia of carrying out similar attacks against military figures were later found by reporters to have been involved in the operations Moscow had accused them of conducting.What exactly drove Reutt to allegedly embark on such an audacious mission remains unclear. As with other cases involving accused Ukrainian intelligence operations, her trial is likely to take place behind closed doors, offering little opportunity for her to give her own account publicly.But interviews with a dozen friends and acquaintances, combined with an examination of years of her social media activity, offer a portrait of a determined and adventurous woman whose attitude towards her country appears to have hardened gradually, with signs of a more striking change emerging in the months leading up to the attack.“Rita believed that the country was going in the wrong direction,” said a longtime friend, using the diminutive form of her name. “But I am still shocked she went so far,” the friend added.View image in fullscreenAn examination of Margarita Reutt’s social media activity offers a portrait of a determined woman whose attitude towards her country appears to have gradually hardened.Photograph: VkontakteRussia quickly accused Reutt of carrying out the attack on the orders of Ukrainian intelligence. Kyiv has not commented on the bombing or Reutt’s alleged role in it.Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have been linked to a string of assassinations and attempted killings of senior Russian military officers whom Kyiv has accused of involvement in the invasion. Ukrainian officials have occasionally acknowledged involvement in such operations, but more often have remained silent.The attacks have involved an array of methods and recruits, from committed anti-Kremlin saboteurs to Russians promised large sums of money. In other cases, unsuspecting couriers and delivery workers have effectively been used as mules.Usually, little is known about those accused of carrying out such attacks or how they prepared for them. Some have managed to escape, or were never publicly identified by Russian authorities, while others were killed carrying out their operations.The swift capture and naming of Reutt, however, offers a rare opportunity to examine the journey of a Russian citizen accused of turning against her own country.Reutt, born Margarita Yakovleva, grew up in Yaroslavl, a city north-east of Moscow, where she took the surname of the grandmother who largely raised her after her parents divorced. Friends recalled a largely unremarkable childhood, remembering her as warm and sociable, but also unusually drawn to adventure and risk.“Margarita was fearless. She would climb trees, jump off cars, do things most boys were scared of,” recalled one friend from her childhood.That streak followed her to Novosibirsk, thousands of miles to the east, where she studied management and threw herself into university life. Reutt became a regular at a local parachuting club, with photographs showing her jumping from Soviet-era aircraft, often the only woman among groups of men in camouflage gear.She also won prizes in amateur go-karting competitions and took up water polo, becoming goalkeeper for the university team and quickly distinguishing herself despite being new to the sport. “Margarita was so talented and never afraid of the ball,” recalled her water polo coach at the time.There was little then to suggest hostility towards the Kremlin. In Novosibirsk, Reutt became a well-liked member of a patriotic volunteer group that searched for the remains of Soviet soldiers killed during the second world war, part of a nationwide movement dedicated to recovering and reburying the war dead.After graduating, Reutt moved south to Sochi, the Black Sea resort that became her home. She briefly tried her hand at running a travel agency before joining Vitauct in the early 2020s, an alternative medicine company specialising in longevity.“She was the most ordinary person,” said Gennadiy Garbuzov, the company’s founder, who struggled to reconcile the woman he knew with the allegations now facing her. “There was nothing to indicate she would do this. She must have fallen under someone’s influence.”On the surface, her online life was similarly unremarkable. She posted frequently about health and animal rights and took to Telegram forums to discuss alternative medicine.Reutt also travelled widely. Leaked records from travel databases seen by the Guardian and photographs posted online show frequent trips abroad, including to Turkey, Thailand and Sri Lanka, where she often shared photographs of herself in bikinis at beach resorts.View image in fullscreenMargarita Reutt on one of her frequent trips abroad in a picture shared online.Photograph: Vkontakte“Margarita just seemed to be living her life and had lots of plans for the future,” said another colleague at Vitauct.“She was good-looking and popular,” the colleague added.In October 2025, Reutt travelled to Minsk for her sister’s wedding. Photographs from the celebration show her smiling among relatives and catching the bridal bouquet. To one friend she painted an idyllic picture of her life in Sochi, traversing mountains, waterfalls and canyons. “You can explore endlessly here, everything is lush and green,” she wrote to the friend.But beneath that outwardly happy life, another side of Reutt was becoming visible. She increasingly expressed concerns about environmental problems plaguing Sochi, and started to become involved in local volunteer initiatives, friends said.After a large oil spill in the Black Sea in December 2024, whentwo Russian tankers were wreckedin a storm, Reutt travelled to Anapa to join volunteers cleaning mazut, a heavy fuel oil, from contaminated beaches.Exactly when dissatisfaction with her surroundings hardened into something more political is difficult to establish. Friends described a growing estrangement from Russia that deepened after the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.“The war came as a shock,” said one friend, who recalled Reutt becoming increasingly outspoken in public about the fighting in Ukraine. “I told her once to keep quiet, otherwise she would get us both into trouble,” the friend said.By July 2025, her anti-war feelings had spilt into public view. While travelling on a Samara-Adler train, Reutt was fined under Russia’s sweeping law against “discrediting” the armed forces after reportedly shouting “Serves you right, Russians!” when news broke of a Ukrainian drone strike on a railway station in the Rostov region.The following February, Reutt posted the results of a genetic test showing she was 98% Russian, adding a hashtag declaring that she was “ashamed to be Russian”.Yet to friends and acquaintances, Reutt appeared to carry on much as before. She picked up occasional jobs, appeared in video clips made by friends and continued to travel. As recently as March, photographs from a trip to Cuba showed her drinking from a coconut.View image in fullscreenMargarita Reutt on a beach in Cuba.Photograph: VkontakteIt was only in late spring, several people who knew her said, that her behaviour began to change in ways they struggled to understand at the time. “She became more withdrawn,” recalled one friend.Around the same time, a group of friends began planning a trip together for the autumn. Reutt declined to join them without much explanation – an unusual response from someone friends said could be counted on to say yes to a new adventure.Another friend remembered Reutt suddenly acquiring a second phone. “She bought this second phone in the spring. She explained that she needed it for work, but it didn’t really make sense to me at the time.”“Margarita was hiding something,” the friend added. “I thought maybe she had a new boyfriend.”By the summer, Reutt had begun spending more time in Crimea, the place where she would eventually be arrested. One acquaintance said she explained the trips to Crimea by saying she was scouting possible locations for video shoots, having recently begun appearing more frequently in music clips.What she was actually doing in Crimea – and when, if at all, she came into contact with Ukrainian intelligence – remains unknown.If Russia’s allegations that she was recruited by Ukraine are true, Reutt would join a growing group of Russian citizens accused of being enlisted by Ukrainian intelligence to carry out sabotage and assassinations deep behind the frontlines.Such recruits offer obvious advantages: they can move around Russia more freely, and attract less scrutiny than Ukrainian operatives, and they can reach targets far from the frontline without putting trained agents at risk. Women have featured prominently in several of the most high-profile operations, potentially attracting even less suspicion.For those close to Reutt, there is no easy explanation for how the woman they remember ended up accused of carrying out an assassination. But a friend of two decades recalled a stubborn determination to follow through on whatever she decided to do.“If she had a plan in mind, she would do it,” the friend said. “Even if it was something like this.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaCrimeaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran-linked hackers blamed for cyber-attack that shut down UK power plant | Iran | The Guardian
description: Incident marks apparent escalation by Tehran in its in retaliation against UK over allowing US to use British bases
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Incident marks apparent escalation by Tehran in its in retaliation against UK over allowing US to use British bases
Content: Richard Horne of the National Cyber Security Centre, who has said the systems behind the UK’s key services are increasingly being targeted.Photograph: CyberUK/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRichard Horne of the National Cyber Security Centre, who has said the systems behind the UK’s key services are increasingly being targeted.Photograph: CyberUK/Getty ImagesIranIran-linked hackers blamed for cyber-attack that shut down UK power plantIncident marks apparent escalation by Tehran in its in retaliation against UK over allowing US to use British basesBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 10.46 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 05.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHackers linked toIranhave been blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down.The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government, which said that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system.However, it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran after the UK said it had given permission for the US to launch “defensive” operations against Tehran from British bases.‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacksRead moreThe power plant was shut down for four days as a result of the attack last month, accordingto the Sunday Telegraph, which first reported it.A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This story refers to an incident impacting a small-scale energy generator, and at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system. The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards.”The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, is understood not to have received any reported outages from regulated operators of power stations.The Conservatives said the incident reflected a “new kind of warfare”, which meant Britain needed to prioritise “cheap, reliable energy”. “The world is getting more dangerous, which is why we need to prioritise our energy security,” said Claire Coutinho, the Conservative spokesperson on energy.“Leaving ourselves reliant on imports of gas and electricity and failing to build enough reliable gas or nuclear plants for backup at home, all leaves us more vulnerable.”Hostile states such as Russia, China and Iran are increasingly targeting systems behind the UK’s key services, according to a warning this year from Richard Horne, the NCSC’s chief executive.The government said last month the UK was “ready to defend itself” after Iran’s military warnedany bases being used by the US were “legitimate targets”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK ‘ready to defend itself’ after Iranian threat over US basesRead moreThe UK has allowed the US to launch so-called defensive operations from British bases hosting American planes since the start of its war on Iran but has refused to help in offensive operations. That policy has not been altered by the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who was notified last week that a decision had been made to extend the agreement with the US.Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said last month that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.Iran has been accused for years of carrying out cyber-attacks on various countries, including in relation to a massivepower outage in Turkey in 2015and several possible breaches of Israeli government websites in 2022.US government security agencies issued a warning earlier this year of cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure by hackers linked to the IRGC.The US has alleged that an Iran-affiliated group known as “CyberAv3ngers” carried out a campaign against it in 2023 that compromised at least 75 devices in multiple infrastructure sectors.Get in touchContact Ben Quinn about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Ben using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. When asked to choose a recipient please switch to the Journalists list and select Ben Quinn.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailben.quinn@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsIranCyberwarHackingMiddle East and north AfricaForeign policyMilitaryEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran’s foreign minister calls threat of new US economic sanctions ‘desperate’ | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Abbas Araghchi says country is unbowed but president Masoud Pezeshkian admits its people face ‘many problems’
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Abbas Araghchi says country is unbowed but president Masoud Pezeshkian admits its people face ‘many problems’
Content: A man in Tehran reads a copy of the Iranian daily newspaper Hamshahri with a cover story about US economic sanctions.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreenA man in Tehran reads a copy of the Iranian daily newspaper Hamshahri with a cover story about US economic sanctions.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAUS-Israel war on IranIran’s foreign minister calls threat of new US economic sanctions ‘desperate’Abbas Araghchi says country is unbowed but president Masoud Pezeshkian admits its people face ‘many problems’Sam Jonesand agenciesSun 23 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTFirst published on Sat 22 Aug 2026 23.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran’s foreign minister has dismissed the threat of a fresh round of US economic sanctions as a “desperate” ploy, even as its president acknowledged that the Iranian people are facing “many problems” amid Washington’s efforts to isolate and debilitate the country’s economy.Last week, Donald Trump announced anew campaign to increase the pressure on the Iranian economy, calling it “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country”. The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is expected to announce further punitive economic measures on Iran – which he has described as “the toughest sanctions in history” – on Monday.Iran-linked hackers blamed for cyber-attack that shut down UK power plantRead moreDespite the threats, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, insisted the country remained unbowed. “The fact that [US leaders] ‌have moved on from military operations … to bringing up the same old plans shows that they are desperate,” he said in a ‌video posted on Telegram on Sunday.“We have never been afraid. All of their actions – whether blockades or other military moves they have made – have failed, and this new issue of theirs will fail as well.”Araghchi urged Washington to speak to Iran respectfully to find “a ‌solution based on justice and honour.“His defiant message came hours after Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said Trump had thrust his country into “a full-scale economic, military and security war”.“I understand we have many problems in society right now. We are trying to prevent these as much as we can,” he said in a speech broadcast on state television. “We are striving with all our hearts to overcome inflation, livelihood problems, unemployment, and to secure the future of the people, so that they can live with dignity and pride.”The Iranian government has faced several waves of mass protest in recent years, often triggered by economic hardships, including inflation and exchange-rate swings leading to declining purchasing power. At the end of December last year, a protest movement initially sparked by the rising cost of livingturned into mass demonstrationsdenouncing those in power.View image in fullscreenProtesters on the streets of Tehran in January.Photograph: MAHSA/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty ImagesAuthorities reported more than 3,000 deaths during the unrest, accusing the US and Israel of orchestrating the violence. Foreign-based NGOs, however, said Iranian officials had launched an indiscriminate crackdown that left thousands dead.Persuasion, denial and bluster: Trump ‘stuck’ on Iran war ahead of electionsRead moreThe new leader of Iran’s top security body has warned its neighbours against joining new US efforts to squeeze Tehran’s economy, and threatened US commercial interests in the region, as Trump doubled down on his fanciful view that the strait of Hormuz was a new US territory.Mohsen Rezaei, the hardline leader of Iran’s supreme national security council, told state television that Iran would target oil-shipping routes out of the Gulf – alternatives to the strait of Hormuz – if its neighbours joined what he called the “economic war” waged by the US. Those neighbours would be “considered an enemy” and “we will target their interests”, he said.View image in fullscreenMasoud Pezeshkian and Mohsen Rezaei, right, at a memorial for Iran’s late supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in July.Photograph: Mohammed Salem/ReutersRezaei also claimed Iran had more cards to play in the war, saying it had “not yet attacked any American economic interests”. “So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the United States has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them,” he said in the interview, which was broadcast on Saturday.Trump’s efforts to finish the war he started along with Israel on 28 February have foundered after a ceasefire agreement signed in June collapsed, leaving Iran in control of the strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the conflict.Washington has called on other governments to join its efforts to isolate the Iranian economy, notably China, among Iran’s top strategic partners. However, Beijing has criticised the initiative, arguing that US sanctions will not resolve the conflict in the Middle East.View image in fullscreenA fruit and vegetable stall at a street market in Tehran on Saturday.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAOne of Iran’s main trading partners, the United Arab Emirates, announced on Tuesday last week it was suspending all trade and financial transactions with Tehran until further notice.The US treasury has for months been carrying out Operation Economic Fury, aiming to cut off Iran’s funding with targeted sanctions, while a naval blockade in the strait of Hormuz has sought to block Iranian oil exports that are vital in keeping the country’s economy afloat.The US president has in recent days repeatedly raised the concept of declaring the strait a US territory, sharing a map identifying it as such in a social media post on Saturday.Donald Trump’s post on Truth Social.Photograph: @realDonaldTrump/TruthSocialRezaei said in his interview that discussions continued with Iran’s cross-strait neighbour Oman over management of the waterway, and said fees would be imposed.The French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, are expected to discuss plans to develop alternative routes to the strait of Hormuz during the Saudi leader’s two-day visit to Paris that starts on Sunday. Proposals include increasing trade through Omani ports outside the Gulf, expanding or doubling pipelines in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere, and developing new rail links, officials told the Associated Press.France and Saudi Arabia have formed a taskforce on energy and logistics connections between the Middle East and Europe that is scheduled to meet at the ministerial level on Monday. The officials said the work would focus on identifying the most strategic projects, securing financing and establishing roles for French companies.With Agence France-Presse, Associated Press and ReutersExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranUS foreign policyTrump administrationMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to face pressure at Labour conference to recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide | Labour | The Guardian
description: Grassroots groups to urge PM to break with Starmer policy and impose full arms embargo on Israel
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Grassroots groups to urge PM to break with Starmer policy and impose full arms embargo on Israel
Content: Groups want Burnham to accept findings of UN commission of inquiry that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.Photograph: Hassan al-Jedi/APAImages/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGroups want Burnham to accept findings of UN commission of inquiry that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.Photograph: Hassan al-Jedi/APAImages/ShutterstockLabourBurnham to face pressure at Labour conference to recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocideGrassroots groups to urge PM to break with Starmer policy and impose full arms embargo on IsraelAletha AduPolitical correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 07.26 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrassroots Labour groups are gearing up for a conference showdown withAndy Burnhamover Gaza, as the party’s members seek to force the prime minister to recognise Israel’s actions as a genocide and impose a full arms embargo.Momentum, Labour & Palestine, the Campaign for Labour Party Democracy and Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) plan to ramp up pressure on Burnham before his firstLabour conferenceas prime minister next month.The groups are circulating a model motion for Labour members to submit to conference, demanding the government accepts the findings of a UN commission of inquiry thatIsraelhas committed genocide in Gaza, and to impose “comprehensive sanctions”, including a full arms embargo.The motion also demands that ministers impose comprehensive sanctions and ban trade that “aids or assists” Israel’s military actions in Gaza or its unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territories, including trade withIsraeli settlements.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has apologised for Labour’s handling of Gaza under Starmer.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBurnham’s refusal to use the term genocide has caused frustration among manyLabourMPs, not just those on the left of the party. Several MPs told the Guardian they welcomed Burnham’s apology, but wanted him to go further and explicitly “acknowledge Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide”.The prime minister hasapologised for the party’s handling of Gaza under Starmer’s leadership, saying Labour had “not got it right”.Weeks before he became prime minister,Burnham told the Guardian: “We’ve got to do more to put pressure on the Israeli government … let’s be honest, the UK was too slow to call for a ceasefire. And we must now do more to strengthen our approach.” But he stopped short of describing what was happening on the ground in Gaza as a genocide, saying that while there was “increasing evidence” of war crimes, it was for the international courts to make that ruling.The UK government has signalled that further measures against Israel could be coming. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said ministers would set out a “comprehensive set of measures” after Israel moved ahead with its controversial E1 settlement plans in the occupiedWest Bank.In the run-up to the 2025 party conference, Labour sought to rule out motions onPalestinebeing debated at the conference, which triggered accusations that the party was trying to stifle debate. About 30 motions about Palestine from local parties were struck off last September.But conference went against the then leadership and backed an emergency motionproposed bythe Unison union that the Labour government should “employ all means reasonably available to it to prevent the commission of genocide in Gaza” and “fully suspend the arms trade withIsraeland the UK-Israel trade and partnership agreement”.The Labour groups are seeking to force the issue back on the conference floor this year, presenting it as an early test of Burnham’s promise not to “stifle debate” within Labour. Momentum is launching a petition aimed at current and former Labour members and voters, urging the prime minister to stick to the position backed by delegates last year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenActivists protest against Israel’s actions in Gaza.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianHe is facing growing pressure beyond Labour’s left after more than 100 British and French former diplomatswrote to Burnham and Emmanuel Macron urging tough action against Israel, including suspending arms transfers and taking further trade measures. Emily Thornberry this week said Britain should ban imports from the occupied West Bank amid growing concern over Israeli settlement expansion.It comes as Labour is hoping to win back progressive voters who deserted the party under Starmer. Polling commissioned by PSC and Friends of the Earth this summer found 67% of voters who switched from Labour to the Greens citedPalestineas a factor in their decision to leave Labour.Sasha Das Gupta, co-chair of Momentum, said: “Burnham must not allow the same failures that alienated voters under Starmer to continue. He must listen to the majority of the labour movement and take decisive action onGaza.”Dan Iley-Williamson, a political organiser at the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, said: “Burnham’s apology for Labour’s previous stance on Palestine will mean nothing if his government doesn’t decisively break with Keir Starmer’s complicity in Israel’s crimes.“Burnham could use this Labour conference to show the country he will make this break with Starmer. If he doesn’t, he risks the same fate: plummeting support and a legacy of infamy.”Explore more on these topicsLabourAndy BurnhamLabour conferenceIsraelGazaPalestineWest BanknewsShareReuse this content

title: UK productivity growing faster than official figures suggest, thinktank finds | Productivity | The Guardian
description: Resolution Foundation suggests economy may finally be emerging from shadow of 2008 financial crisis
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Resolution Foundation suggests economy may finally be emerging from shadow of 2008 financial crisis
Content: Productivity measures the economic output produced by each worker, and is a crucial determinant of growth.Photograph: Matt Crossick/AlamyView image in fullscreenProductivity measures the economic output produced by each worker, and is a crucial determinant of growth.Photograph: Matt Crossick/AlamyProductivityUK productivity growing faster than official figures suggest, thinktank findsResolution Foundation suggests economy may finally be emerging from shadow of 2008 financial crisisHeather StewartEconomics editorSun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProductivity in the UK – a vital measure of economic health – is growing more strongly than official figures suggest, according to analysis from theResolution Foundation.The thinktank suggests the chancellor,John Healey, may have inherited an economy finally starting to emerge from the long shadow of the 2008 global financial crisis.Productivity measures the economic output produced by each worker, and is a crucial determinant of growth.The Resolution Foundation reconsiders the UK’s recent productivity record, using what it argues is a more accurate snapshot of the workforce than the widely criticisedlabour force survey.Simon Pittaway, the thinktank’s principal economist, said: “Britain’s dismal productivity record since the global financial crisis explains a lot of its economic stagnation and weak living standards growth.“But while official figures suggest that the output of workers has worsened further in the mid-2020s, our more accurate productivity measure suggests that it has been improving in recent years.”A positive new report raises the question: was Reeves undermined by dodgy data? | Heather StewartRead moreSome economists have argued the potential uptick in productivity has resulted from job cuts in relatively low-skilled sectors such as hospitality and retail, meaning the average worker has become more productive.However, the thinktank rejects that idea, pointing out that the share of the workforce employed in hospitality is no lower now than it was in the late 2010s, and only just below its post-pandemic peak.It also suggests the uptick cannot just be AI-related, as it is more widespread across different sectors of the UK economy.Pittaway said: “Some have suggested that recent productivity gains have been driven by an early AI boom, and workers leaving low-productivity sectors like retail and hospitality. But nether explanation is borne out by the data. Instead, the UK’s productivity recovery has been achieved by the same workers, doing the same jobs, and working in the same sectors.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Resolution Foundation’s report was the latest to paint a relatively optimistic picture of the economy, after official figures last week showed the UK was the joint fastest-growing economy in the G7 in the first half of 2026.John Van Reenen, Rachel Reeves’s former chief economic adviser,recently published a blogpostpointing to a similar productivity rethink by him and his colleagues at the London School of Economics.Economists at Morgan Stanley said in a recent research note that the UK was now in “an OK place”. In a note titled “The vibes they are a-changin’”, its chief UK economist, Bruna Skarica, pointed out that growth and inflation had been hit less hard than feared by the Iran war, and consumer confidence had reached a two-year high.Explore more on these topicsProductivityResolution FoundationThinktanksJohn HealeyLabourEconomic growth (GDP)EconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Government vows to make business rate valuations for pubs and hotels fairer | Business rates | The Guardian
description: Review will look at improving system for English and Welsh hospitality venues before next revaluation date in 2029
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Review will look at improving system for English and Welsh hospitality venues before next revaluation date in 2029
Content: Hospitality venues were hit by higher business rate bills this year after the end of pandemic-era relief and when new revaluations took effect.Photograph: william87/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenHospitality venues were hit by higher business rate bills this year after the end of pandemic-era relief and when new revaluations took effect.Photograph: william87/Getty Images/iStockphotoBusiness ratesGovernment vows to make business rate valuations for pubs and hotels fairerReview will look at improving system for English and Welsh hospitality venues before next revaluation date in 2029Lauren AlmeidaSun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government has promised that business rate valuations will be “made fairer” for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, asAndy Burnhamfaces growing calls to help the UK’s struggling hospitality sector.An independent review forEnglandand Wales will look at improving the system for hospitality venues, which were hit by higher business rate bills this year after the end of pandemic-era relief and when new revaluations took effect.It comes after Burnham announced last month that he would cut business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in Englandby 20%from April next year.The government has faced calls to reduce the tax burden on hospitality businesses, which have also struggled to cope with rising energy and food bills in recent years.The review, which will be led by Jerry Schurder, an independent business rates specialist, will report back to the Treasury by the end of March 2027. It will consider valuations before the next revaluation date in 2029. The rise in valuations this year will not be affected.James Murray, the financial secretary to the Treasury, said: “Pubs and hotels are vital for communities and bringing growth to every postcode,” adding that a “rethink of valuations” would help “build a fairer system for the future”.Allen Simpson, the chief executive of the trade bodyUKHospitality, said it was positive the government was looking seriously at the valuation methodology for pubs and hotels.“Business rates remain a significant burden for hospitality businesses, and the system needs to better reflect the trading realities for the sector,” he said.Emma McClarkin, the chief executive of theBritish Beer & Pub Association, said the review was “sorely needed and hugely welcome” as pubs had for years “paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open”.While cuts have been welcomed by business owners, the industry has repeatedly called for the reform of the whole business rates system. Estimates suggest thattwo pubs are closing a day across Britainthis year, hit by higher taxes, wages, energy and food costs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham is also facing calls to extend the business rates relief aimed at pubs, clubs and live music venues to bookshops. This month 234 independent booksellerssigned an open lettercalling on the prime minister to give bookshops the same consideration as other businesses that play a positive role in their communities.The government has suggested that it will reform business rates, including small business rates relief, at John Healey’s first budget on 28 October.Explore more on these topicsBusiness ratesPubsHotelsHospitality industryAndy BurnhamEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform says it would put foreign-born UK citizens lower on social housing list | Social housing | The Guardian
description: UK-born married couples under 35 with children would get priority under proposals to be outlined by Farage’s party
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: UK-born married couples under 35 with children would get priority under proposals to be outlined by Farage’s party
Content: Those born while their British parents were temporarily overseas would be exempted from the policy, Reform said.Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamyView image in fullscreenThose born while their British parents were temporarily overseas would be exempted from the policy, Reform said.Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamySocial housingReform says it would put foreign-born UK citizens lower on social housing listUK-born married couples under 35 with children would get priority under proposals to be outlined by Farage’s partyKiran StaceyPolicy editorSun 23 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish citizens who were born abroad would be made to wait longer for social housing under proposals to be announced byReform UKon Monday.Nigel Farage’s party will announce the policy at a press conference in London. Under the policy, people born in the UK and young married couples with children would be given priority for social housing.The party haspreviously saidit would ban foreign nationals from social housing, meaning the new policy specifically prioritises Britons born in the UK over those born overseas.Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, said in a statement: “There are now 1.3 million people waiting for social housing in Britain. The vast majority of them do not have jobs. In terms of the social houses we have, less than half of households are in work and over half a million social homes are currently occupied by foreign nationals.“Meanwhile, young British men and women, who are working hard, can’t afford to move out of their family home, and when they do often find themself sharing a house with strangers, with no realistic prospect of forming a family or getting on.“It is time for us to prioritise young British workers, and that is what our policy is about.”View image in fullscreenFarage had previously proposed to ban foreign nationals from social housing.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe party said some foreign-born Britons would be exempted from the new rules, including those born while their British parents were temporarily overseas. Officials said, however, the new rules would require legislation to avoid breaking existing laws.Under the terms of a previous announcement by Farage, foreign nationals would be barred from social housing, with those already in homes given three months to find private accommodation or face deportation.The new policy would give priority access to British-born people in employment and married couples under 35 with children.Tory plan to ban foreign nationals from social housing condemned as ‘divisive’Read moreThe party said veterans would also be given preferential treatment – though soldiers, veterans and their families are already given priority under existing government policy.Experts have said that prioritising people based on nationality, age and family status could punish some of the most vulnerable in society.Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Designed to stoke division, these plans will only serve to disrupt the lives of thousands of families, tear communities apart, and put even more people at risk of homelessness.“Putting nationality and employment ahead of housing need, and moving away from a system designed to prioritise people who are homeless or at urgent risk of homelessness, could leave even more families trapped in awful temporary accommodation for years on end. Not to mention putting those escaping domestic abuse and violence at serious risk of harm.”A Labour spokesperson said: “Illegal migrants, asylum seekers and migrants on student or work visas are not eligible for social housing. This policy would go after long-term UK residents that have contributed to our country but are not British citizens, including NHS staff.”Reform has also said it would build 50,000 socially affordable homes a year, a significant uplift on the18,000 the government has promised to buildon average each year for a decade.Labour’s plans are being financed by a £39bn affordable housing scheme, 60% of which is due to be allocated to social homes, which are the most heavily subsidised.Reform said its plans would be funded, with no extra borrowing or taxation required to pay for the additional homes. It did not give further details on where the money would come from.Explore more on these topicsSocial housingReform UKHousingCommunitiesHousing benefitImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Families release pictures of police officers killed in A66 crash in which five others died | North Yorkshire | The Guardian
description: Tributes paid to PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough whose vehicle was in a head-on collision with car travelling wrong way
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Tributes paid to PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough whose vehicle was in a head-on collision with car travelling wrong way
Content: PC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades, who died when a car going in the wrong direction hit a police car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.Composite: Cleveland Police/PAView image in fullscreenPC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades, who died when a car going in the wrong direction hit a police car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.Composite: Cleveland Police/PANorth YorkshireFamilies release pictures of police officers killed in A66 crash in which five others diedEmotional tributes paid to PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough whose vehicle was in a head-on collision with car travelling wrong wayMark BrownNorth of England correspondentSun 23 Aug 2026 15.55 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCleveland police have published photographs of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough who died when a car travelling the wrong way on the A66 crashed head-on into their police vehicle.Two 17-year-old boys were among the seven people who were killed in the incident on Teesside.Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak died when their Volkswagen Passat, believed to be using cloned plates, collided with a marked armed response vehicle early on Saturday near Middlesbrough.Blades, 37, and Clough, 38, of Cleveland police, who were also killed in the collision, had been driving in the correct direction. Tributes have been paid to the officers, with their chief constable, Victoria Fuller, describing them as “brave officers protecting our communities”.Clough’s family described him as “our hero with a fantastic sense of humour” and someone who “jumped into action whenever needed, and [was] willing to help anyone for any reason”.In a statement issued via Cleveland police, the family said Clough had “proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place. Always on public duty throughout his short life.“We as a family and Tom’s partner would like to express our sincere gratitude for the overwhelming support and condolences from friends, colleagues and the wider community.”Blades’ wife said the pain of losing him is “beyond words” and the family’s lives “will never be the same”.In a statement issued through the force, she said: “No words will ever feel like the right words to honour our Matt – my beloved husband, my best friend, and the most devoted father to our two young boys.“He was an adored son and brother, a perfect son-in-law, and the most fun uncle. He was loved beyond words by all his family and friends, and his loss has left a space that can never be filled.“He gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness.“The pain of losing him is beyond words, and our lives will never be the same. Neither will the love he gave us ever fade.“Our children will grow up knowing what an incredible father he was and will always be, and I will carry his love, his memory and everything we shared with me always.“He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family.”Blades’ wife, who has not been named, also expressed “deepest gratitude and heartfelt thanks” to the police and emergency services and concluded: “Forever loved. Forever missed. Forever our superhero.”A local football club, Seaton Carew FC, said Blades had recently joined as coach and was preparing for the season with the new under-sevens Seahawks team. “He was looking forward to being part of the team and, most importantly, to coaching his own son, who is going to be playing for the Seahawks this season,” the club said on social media.“Matty and his oldest son are much-loved members of our club and our U10 Lions football family. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Matty’s wife, his two boys, and all of his family and friends at this incredibly difficult and heartbreaking time.”View image in fullscreenThe five young people who were killed, clockwise from top left, Jacob Matusiak, Michael Robert Cahill, Makai Saddington, Cole Worthy and Theo Rae.Composite: FacebookView image in fullscreenFlowers left near the scene on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough.Photograph: Richard McCarthy/PAThe Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has opened an investigation into the circumstances leading to the crash at 3.39am in South Bank after a mandatory referral from Cleveland police.On Sunday the IOPC said initial inquiries showed the Passat had been pursued by police for just under seven minutes before it turned on to the A66 against the flow of traffic.At that point the pursuit was aborted, the IOPC said. “Approximately 10 seconds later, the Passat collided with another police vehicle which was not involved in the pursuit but in the area to assist in a search for the Passat believed to be using cloned plates that had activated an ANPR camera.”The IOPC director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, said: “Our thoughts continue to be with the family and friends and all those affected by yesterday’s collision. We recognise the devastating impact the incident has had on those in the force, and the wider policing community, and offer our condolences.”On Sunday, Anna Turley, the Home Office minister and local Redcar MP, said it was “devastating” to think about the grief of the families of everyone who lost their lives on Saturday morning. The whole community was “reeling”, she said.“All of us in the community here are sending our heartfelt thoughts and sympathies to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives so tragically.”“I do want to place on record my tribute to PC Blades and PC Clough. The bravery that we see from our police officers every day, every night is incredible. No one should not come home to their families at the end of their shift.”She also said it was important to thank the emergency service workers who had attended the scene during “a really horrific incident”.Security camera footage from local houses appeared to show the police pursuit moments before the fatal crash on the A66.Security camera footage appears to show police pursuit minutes before fatal A66 crashAndy Burnham said he was “devastated” to hear two police officers had lost their lives on duty, as well as five members of the public. The prime minister said: “My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland police. Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”Fuller said she and her deputy had on Saturday visited the families of the two officers to offer condolences and support.“This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” she said. “This loss is being felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies. These were brave officers, protecting our communities and serving our residents, who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift.”View image in fullscreenCleveland police chief constable Victoria Fuller said it was an ‘incredibly sad day’.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PALauren Somerville, the chair of Cleveland police federation, said the grief among officers was “all-consuming, overwhelming”. She said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland police family are feeling.”The Cleveland police and crime commissioner, Matt Storey, described the force as a “really tight-knit family” and said the deaths “will have a big impact on them”.The young men in the car were named by Cleveland police on Sunday afternoon. The force said family liaison officers were working with the families.This article was amended on 23 August 2026. An earlier version gave the age of Cole Robert Worthy as 16, based on initial information provided by Cleveland police. After publication, Cleveland police corrected this to 17.Explore more on these topicsNorth YorkshireMiddlesbroughNorth of EnglandEnglandPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Spying device detectors may give domestic abuse victims false sense of security, study finds | Domestic violence | The Guardian
description: Many tools fail to help victims find hidden cameras, microphones and trackers, leaving them at risk of ongoing surveillance
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Many tools fail to help victims find hidden cameras, microphones and trackers, leaving them at risk of ongoing surveillance
Content: Surveillance devices are often marketed as home security or pet tracking tools, but can be misused for spying.Photograph: Pau Barrena/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSurveillance devices are often marketed as home security or pet tracking tools, but can be misused for spying.Photograph: Pau Barrena/AFP/Getty ImagesDomestic violenceSpying device detectors may give domestic abuse victims false sense of security, study findsMany tools fail to help victims find hidden cameras, microphones and trackers, leaving them at risk of ongoing surveillancePriya BharadiaSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCommercial detectors intended to help domestic abuse victims find hidden spying devices may actually give them a false sense of security, a study has found.The consumer detection tools claim to identify hidden cameras, microphones or trackers through methods such as signal-strength readings, infrared lens detection and scanning for wifi or Bluetooth devices.However, researchers at University College London’s computer science department found that many detectorsfail to adequately help users identify hidden surveillance devices, giving them a false sense of security.“There’s quite a great disparity in the capabilities of the [spying] devices themselves and the tools that are available for detecting them,” said the lead author, Akhil Polamarasetty.The researchers said that if the detectors failed to find surveillance devices it meant victims continued to be spied on in their homes unaware.The researchers identified approximately 1,000 covert surveillance products and 500 detection tools sold in the UK through mainstream online platforms, such as Amazon, AliExpress and eBay.Hidden surveillance devices included small cameras or microphones concealed inside everyday household items such as USB chargers, plush toys and clocks.Often marketed as home security or pet tracking tools, the researchers and campaigners said the devices could be misused for spying and abuse.“These devices are so small, it doesn’t actually make sense for them to be used for home security purposes,” said Polamarasetty. “[They’re] essentially designed for spying on people.”The researchers asked 34 study participants to search for hidden surveillance devices on their own inside a simulated living room, and then to do the same again using detection tools. The latter showed only a marginal improvement: participants missed 67% of the hidden devices when searching on their own, compared with a 59% miss rate when using a detector.During the experiment, many participants reported difficulties in interpreting a detector’s readings.
