Other tools gave out false positives, causing anxiety in the participants, or missed surveillance objects entirely.“Most of the detectors on the market are not designed with the typical consumer in mind,” said Polamarasetty. “Many people do not necessarily understand the limitations of such detectors and risk misinterpreting the results.”He said many of the detection products were not built with at-risk users in mind, often emitting loud sounds that could alert the person spying on them. “They’re absolutely not safe to be used when you’re living with the perpetrator. The devices are not discreet enough.”The researchers made several recommendations for manufacturers of detection devices, including making user guidance clearer and communicating inconclusive readings.However, the authors noted these recommendations alone could not prevent tech-facilitated abuse, and the only real solution was to stop the sale of hidden spy devices.The co-author Dr Leonie Tanczer said: “Most technology is dual-use, and companies have a responsibility to think about how their products can be misused – at the design stage, rather than after the harms emerge.She added: “A camera in things like a showerhead or a plug – I just cannot really see a legitimate reason for that without the intention to monitor someone without their consent.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDomestic abuse law fails to recognise danger of tech abuse, Lords committee toldRead moreThe UK domestic abuse charity Refuge said it had seen a “notable rise” in victims reporting finding hidden microphones or cameras inside their homes. Its policy manager, Bo Bottomley, said: “What is especially worrying is how accessible and affordable these devices are, allowing more perpetrators to weaponise them as a form of control.“We urge the government to review how these products are designed, safety tested, marketed and sold, and to take swift regulatory action to mitigate the risk they pose to survivors,” Bottomley said.Amazon declined to comment. A spokesperson from eBay said the platform “prohibits the sale of many products that are used to transmit or receive signals or for covert surveillance, and all sellers are required to comply with our policies and applicable UK law.“After investigation, we’ve removed two of the three listings shared and we are committed to maintaining a safe and trusted marketplace for our buyers and sellers.”A spokesperson for the Home Office said: “We will not tolerate covert filming or the harassment of victims.“The government has committed to updating controlling and coercive behaviour guidance to reflect clearer recognition of technology-facilitated abuse and we’re making it an offence to take intimate images without consent, including by installing equipment such as cameras to enable people to do so.”AliExpress has been contacted for comment.In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsDomestic violenceSurveillancePrivacynewsShareReuse this content

title: Eight-year-old dies after contracting rare brain-eating amoeba in Louisiana | Louisiana | The Guardian
description: Lillian Smart of Ruston infected with fatal Naegleria fowleri, likely after swimming in Lake Claiborne, health officials say
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Lillian Smart of Ruston infected with fatal Naegleria fowleri, likely after swimming in Lake Claiborne, health officials say
Content: Lillian Smart, an eight-year-old girl from Ruston, Louisiana.Photograph: Love for Lillian Smart/FacebookView image in fullscreenLillian Smart, an eight-year-old girl from Ruston, Louisiana.Photograph: Love for Lillian Smart/FacebookLouisianaEight-year-old dies after contracting rare brain-eating amoeba in LouisianaLillian Smart of Ruston infected with fatalNaegleria fowleri, likely after swimming in Lake Claiborne, health officials sayMarina DunbarSun 23 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn eight-year-oldLouisianagirl has died after contracting a rare, typically fatal brain-eating amoeba after a swim in Lake Claiborne.Lillian Smart, of Ruston, died on Saturday, one day after celebrating her birthday, her family announced in a public Facebook post on the “Love for Lillian”page.“Last night Lillian ran from our arms to the arms of Jesus,” her family said in the post. “The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from. Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?”The Louisiana department of healthconfirmedon 19 August that a state resident had been infected withNaegleria fowleriand said the exposure most likely occurred while the person was swimming in Lake Claiborne in Claiborne parish. Family friends later identified Lillian as the infected resident, according to reports from several local media outlets.View image in fullscreenNaegleria fowleriinfections are extremely rare.Photograph: CDC/ReutersNaegleria fowleriinfections are almost always fatal.Lillian had been hospitalized since 15 August,KNOEreported. As her family faced the crisis, more than two dozen businesses in Ruston showed support and donated a portion of sales to the Smart family, according to the Facebook page.Naegleria fowleriinfections are extremely rare, with only a handful occurring inLouisianasince 2011.The amoeba flourishes in warm water and is most commonly found in southern states during the summer. Only about 180 cases have been identified in the US since 1937,according tothe Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.In 2023, an Arkansas child died aftercontractingNaegleria fowlerifrom a country club splash pad in the state capital of Little Rock.Naegleria fowlerican be found in warm freshwater across the country, including lakes, rivers and ponds. It is not found in salt water or in swimming pools that are properly maintained and chlorinated.Experts say the climate crisis iscausingthe amoeba to pop up in parts of the US where it isn’t typical, such as the north and west. It is likely to cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis, a brain infection that can develop when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain.People cannot become infected just by swallowing water containingNaegleria fowleri, and the infection does not spread from one person to another.Explore more on these topicsLouisianaInfectious diseasesChildrenHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fast-moving wildfire in Reno, Nevada, forces tens of thousands to evacuate homes | US wildfires | The Guardian
description: Human-caused Hawk fire covers more than 13,000 acres as blaze approaches University of Nevada campus in Reno
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Human-caused Hawk fire covers more than 13,000 acres as blaze approaches University of Nevada campus in Reno
Content: Hawk wildfire in Nevada forces evacuations and road closuresUS wildfiresFast-moving wildfire in Reno, Nevada, forces tens of thousands to evacuate homesHuman-caused Hawk fire covers more than 15,000 acres as blaze approaches University of Nevada campus in RenoMarina Dunbarand agenciesSun 23 Aug 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fast-movingNevadawildfireexploded to more than 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares) on Sunday, pushing from the Sierra foothills toward the center of Reno and urging nearly 90,000 residents to evacuate as flames threatened neighborhoods and reached the edge of the University of Nevada campus.The Hawk fire’s “GO NOW” evacuation zone had expanded to the edge of the university campus as strong, gusty winds, low humidity and dry vegetation fueled the blaze, according to Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue in Reno. Of those urged to evacuate, 42,000 were under strict orders. An additional 45,000 people were in the evacuation warning zone, and encouraged to leave now and be prepared to stay away for several days to clear the roads for first-responders.“If you have been told to evacuate, please don’t wait!” Hillary Schieve, Reno’s mayor, said in astatementposted on social media on Saturday night. “Structures have already been burned in this fire and your life is more important than a building. Evacuating before the fire arrives also allows our firefighters to focus their efforts on battling the blaze.”Firefighters sound alarm as US faces critical staffing shortage: ‘We don’t have enough people’Read moreAuthorities confirmed three civilians and three first responders had been injured in the fire and several structures have been destroyed. Officials said the fire was human-caused but did not provide additional details on how the fire was started, saying it was under investigation.Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe county and mobilized theNevadanational guard. Two helicopter crews were deployed to support aerial firefighting operations, while 60 troops were assigned to help police safeguard evacuated neighborhoods. However winds were whipping the flames, complicating the fight.“It was extremely confusing,” said Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff, describing how changing winds sent the flames in different directions.The fire had already proved to be a challenge on Saturday night, moving exceptionally fast, jumping over fire trucks and making it difficult for responders to get to hotspots while residents were trying to get out, Balaam said.The fire was so small on Saturday morning that it wasn’t even a concern, said Tyler Duvall, who went camping over the weekend. By the next day, his house was in the evacuation zone.“The wind really blew it up,” Duvall said.“Approximately 400 personnel are currently working on the incident, with resources coming together from local, state and federal agencies, including ground crews and air resources,” the Truckee Meadowsstatementsaid.The rapidly expanding fire was surrounded by neighborhoods, and nearly 10,000 homes and businesses in Washoe county were without power on Sunday. Portions of US Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed because of the fire.Reno has a population of more than 280,000 residents.View image in fullscreenFire crews and local agencies respond to a fast-moving wildfire on the dry hillsides outside Reno, Nevada, on Saturday.Photograph: Hale Irwin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockDavid Barb returned from a weekend hunting trip to find the fire had leveled his taxidermy shop, but his house nearby appeared to have been spared thanks to workers with a landscaping company who cut a fire break, he said. His wife was home when the fire started on the other side of the mountain and later evacuated to a friend’s house.“I’m kind of devastated, but thank God everyone’s safe,” he said on Sunday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWashoe county emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees, but said pets could not be brought there. Small and large animals were instead to be left at two other locations. Casinos in Reno offered discounts on hotel rooms to evacuees.At least 20road closureswere in effect as of Sunday afternoon.The University of Nevada’s Reno campus remained just outside the evacuation zone on Sunday morning. The university, which had an enrollment of about 24,000 students in fall 2025, said officials hadestablishedan emergency response plan should conditions change. The first day of classes at the university is 24 August. However, students who are new to the university were allowed to move in as early as 13 August.The Reno-Tahoe international airport also remained outside the evacuation zone, and commercial flights were unaffected on Sunday. The smaller Reno-Stead airport was closed to general aviation traffic because of the Hawk fire but remained open to firefighting aircraft.Authorities were also closely watching a county detention facility located several blocks from the outer edge of the evacuation warning area.“We have those inmates in mind and we are making sure that we have plans in place in case we may have to evacuate the facility,” said Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff.The Hawk fire comes just weeks after three wildfires fueled by dry and windy conditions north of Reno forced more than 13,000 residents from their homes earlier this month, according to the Nevada national guard.Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsUS wildfiresNevadaUS weatherWildfiresnewsShareReuse this content

title: Democrats incredulous over Hakeem Jeffries and Jared Kushner meeting  | Hakeem Jeffries | The Guardian
description: Critics include Senator Chris van Hollen, ex-aide to Obama Tommy Vietor and ex-Republican congressman Adam Kinzinger
Author: Sam Levine
Headline: Critics include Senator Chris van Hollen, ex-aide to Obama Tommy Vietor and ex-Republican congressman Adam Kinzinger
Content: Jared Kushner, left, and Representative Hakeem Jeffries.Composite: Shutterstock/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJared Kushner, left, and Representative Hakeem Jeffries.Composite: Shutterstock/Getty ImagesHakeem JeffriesDemocrats incredulous over Hakeem Jeffries and Jared Kushner meetingCritics include Senator Chris van Hollen, ex-aide to Obama Tommy Vietor and ex-Republican congressman Adam KinzingerSam LevineSun 23 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 12.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemocratsand otherDonald Trumpcritics reacted incredulously to aNew York Times reporton Sunday that House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries met with Jared Kushner, the president’s influential son-in-law, to discuss possible areas of collaboration.The reported meeting comes months ahead of the November midterm elections in which Democrats are favored to retake the US House, a development that would make Jeffries speaker. If they are in the majority, Democrats are expected to use their oversight power to aggressively investigate theTrump administration, including self-enrichment by the president and his family.There are longstanding conflict-of-interest concerns about the way Kushner has continued to make money from foreign nations as he works on foreign affairs, including conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza.Asked about the reported meeting, Jeffries said in a statement: “Throughout this Congress, Republicans have adopted a my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people. To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition.“The American people want bold change and that’s what HouseDemocratswill deliver. In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable. We are fighting for an affordable America. The question is whether Republicans will join us.”Nonetheless, among some who lamented the reported gathering was Tommy Vietor, previously an aide to former president Barack Obama and now a co-host of the left-leaning podcast Pod Save America.“Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way [Jeffries] should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas,” Vietorposted.In April, Democrats on the House judiciary committee opened an investigation into Kushner’s financial conflict of interest. The investigation is focused on the way Kushner’s private business has raised money from Gulf nations while Kushner served as a special envoy for peace for the government.“You cannot both be a diplomat and a financial pawn of the Saudi monarchy at the same time; you cannot faithfully represent the United States with billions of dollars in Saudi and Emirati cash burning a hole in every pocket of every suit you own,” Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee,wrote in an April letterto Kushner.The reaction to the meeting underscores the appetite that Democrats have to bring a no-holds barred approach to investigating Trump during the final two years of his second presidency, should they have the opportunity.Not all Democrats have taken such a pugilistic approach to Trump. The Michigan governor, Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat,for example, has takena more collaborative approach to working with Trump in his second term.Asked whether he supported the meeting during an interview onNBC’s Meet the Presson Sunday, Senator Chris van Hollen – a Maryland Democrat – said: “I’m in favor of people meeting with whoever they want to discuss ideas. But it’s one thing to have a meeting. It’s another thing to see something real come out of that.”Adam Kinzinger, a former Republican congressman from Illinois who is an outspoken Trump critic and served on a House committee that investigated the Capitol attack, posted in reference to the meeting, “Make this make sense,” while tagging Jeffries.Appearing on Sunday on Fox News, Mike Johnson, the US House speaker and a Louisiana Republican,assertedKushner was “not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House”.“I don’t know what that’s about,” Johnson said of Kushner’s reported meeting with Jeffries. “I know Jared has interests and lots of other things going on.”Explore more on these topicsHakeem JeffriesJared KushnerDemocratsUS politicsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tim Scott defends Darline Graham’s ‘national security is not my thing’ comment | South Carolina | The Guardian
description: Republican senator tries to assuage concerns but does not offer details of Graham’s national security experience
Author: Sam Levine
Headline: Republican senator tries to assuage concerns but does not offer details of Graham’s national security experience
Content: Donald Trump watches Senator Darline Graham speak at her campaign event at the Myrtle Beach convention center in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on  21 August 2026.Photograph: Mic Smith/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump watches Senator Darline Graham speak at her campaign event at the Myrtle Beach convention center in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on  21 August 2026.Photograph: Mic Smith/APSouth CarolinaTim Scott defends Darline Graham’s ‘national security is not my thing’ commentRepublican senator tries to assuage concerns but does not offer details of Graham’s national security experienceSam LevineSun 23 Aug 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTim Scott defended fellow USSouth CarolinaRepublican senator Darline Graham’s knowledge of national security issues ahead of their state’s runoff election on Tuesday.Graham, who was appointed to fill the Senate seat held by her brother Lindsey Graham after his sudden death in July, is in a Republican primary runoff againstSouth Carolinacongressman Ralph Norman. During a debate between the two on Tuesday night, Graham struggled to answer a question about US national security interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea.Lindsey Graham’s sister and fill-in senator says she’s ‘not that informed on national security’Read more“I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security,”she saidduring the debate. She added: “National security is not my thing.”Scott tried to assuage concerns about her experience on Sunday when he was asked about Graham’s qualifications – and whether a US senator should have an understanding of national security issues.“Well, the answer is yes. And she does,” he said during an interview onNBC’s Meet the Press.He went on to give an answer that did not detail any of her national security experience.“The question we’re asking ourselves today is whether or not she is prepared to serve in the United States Senate and represent the people of South Carolina on the issues that are germane to the moment, with all the issues of the moment,” he said. “And is she prepared to hit those issues? She hits those issues spot-on.”Graham held various public policy jobs in South Carolina – but never had run for or held public office before she was appointed to the Senate.Beside Scott, Donald Trump has endorsed Graham –and he traveled to South Carolinaon Friday to rally for her. The president also brushed off Graham’s answer on Friday.“I watched that,” he said. “I thought it was a very honest answer, actually.”Explore more on these topicsSouth CarolinaUS politicsRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war | Canada | The Guardian
description: PM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressors
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: PM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressors
Content: The US president, Donald Trump, and Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, have each blamed the opposite side for the breakdown in negotiations.Photograph: Saul Loeb,dave Chan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US president, Donald Trump, and Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, have each blamed the opposite side for the breakdown in negotiations.Photograph: Saul Loeb,dave Chan/AFP/Getty ImagesCanada‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade warPM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressorsThe lesson from Canada’s collapsed trade talks with the US: negotiation may be futileLauren AlmeidaSun 23 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTFirst published on Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has hit back at Canada after a breakdown in negotiationsplunged the two countries into a trade war.In his first public comments since negotiations collapsed on Friday in Washington, the US president wrote on social media: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!”“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” he added. “No more!!!”His comments came after the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods, whileMark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar”.The US tariffs came into force on Saturday, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Trade experts have predicted that the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the biggest impact is expected to be political, triggering fresh tension between the neighbours.View image in fullscreenCanadian trade minister Dominic LeBlanc, left, and US trade representative Jamieson Greer speak to reporters in Washington DC on Friday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockBoth sides blamed the other for the breakdown in talks on Friday. Carney told Canadian journalists that the country was “at war” over trade with the US, after Trump “miscalculated” by escalating his tariff attack.“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Ottawa. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”Against the wind: despite Trump’s attacks, unions are fighting for good US clean energy jobsRead moreJamieson Greer, the US trade representative, has said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. He told Fox & Friends Weekend: “We’ve said enough and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.”Dan Kelly, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, estimated that 40% of small Canadian exporters will be directly hit by the US tariffs, and that nearly one-third expect their revenues will drop by 50% or more as a result.The escalation was also met with anger by Democrat lawmakers and governors from US states that border Canada including Minnesota, New York and Washington.New York governor Kathy Hochul posted on X: “Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That’s Trump’s economic policy in a nutshell.”Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar, said the new tariffs meant “higher costs for small businesses, farmers, and all Minnesota families.”She wrote on X: “Canada is Minnesota’s #1 trading partner. Minnesotans are paying for Trump’s chaos.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCarney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England,was elected as Canada’s prime minister last yearafter campaigning to lead a fightback against Trump, who has suggested he wants to make Canada a 51st state with “economic force”.Carney’s “dollar for dollar” tariffs are expected to take effect from 8 September, with new levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The escalation has also called into question the future of the North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico, known as USMCA.The pact, which was signed by Trump during his first term, governs about $2tn annually in goods and services between the three countries. Trumprefused to renew the USMCA this summerafter Canada and Mexico formally requested for it to be renewed for another 16 years.When asked how the US-Canadian collapse in trade talks would affect the USMCA, Carney said it was “certainly not good news”.Increasingly aggressive rhetoric and trade policy from the Trump administration has damaged US-Canadian relations, with tourism also suffering – there was a21% drop in Canadians entering New York state in 2025and 3mn fewer visits compared with the previous year.Furthermore, a petition to expel the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, from the country has gathered around 248,000 signatures since late July, according tothe Associated Press.This year apoll by Globe and Mail newspaperfound that only 9% of Canadians agreed that the US was a “trustworthy ally”, and that 51% of those polled had cancelled American trips in reaction to comments by Trump.Explore more on these topicsCanadaDonald TrumpMark CarneyTariffsUS foreign policyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Is there a pending AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0 | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: Fears of a datacenter buildout debt crisis are exaggerated. The risks are different than in the past and they are recoverable
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: Fears of a datacenter buildout debt crisis are exaggerated. The risks are different than in the past and they are recoverable
Content: The Stargate AI datacenter in Abilene, Texas, on 24 September 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Stargate AI datacenter in Abilene, Texas, on 24 September 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Is there a pending AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0Gene MarksFears of a datacenter buildout debt crisis are exaggerated. The risks are different than in the past and they are recoverableSun 23 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTShareSome experts are warning of a looming “debt bomb” crisis because bigdatacenterbuilders such asMeta,Oracle,xAIandCoreWeaveare not only raising billions to construct these facilities but are also not recognizing these long-term debt obligations on their balance sheets.Should we be concerned? No. I know because I’ve seen this movie before.It works like this: Meta wants to build a datacenter to accommodate its growingAIand cloud computing needs. It forms a separate entity that’s not consolidated in its financials, which builds the datacenter. To fund this, the entity raises money from investors, banks and other financial firms (including some from Meta) that own the majority of the entity. There is a contract by which Meta has exclusive and full use of the datacenter once built. This way Meta gets its datacenter but most of the debt incurred to build it is not shown as a liability on its books.Gen Z calls it ‘loud budgeting’ – small business owners have been doing it for decades | Gene MarksRead moreThe worry comes from the enormous sums of money being plowed into these entities. TheFinancial Timesreported in December 2025 that tech companies had shifted more than $120bn of AI datacenter spending off their balance sheets through special-purpose vehicles and similar financing structures.Goldman Sachsestimates that hyperscalers could spend $5.3tn on AI and datacenters through 2030 and expects private markets to play an increasingly important role in financing that buildout.Skeptics are worried that these tech guys are pulling the wool over the public’s eyes and not properly disclosing the long-term impact of all this debt. They point toEnron, the energy firm that spectacularly failed in 2001, causing tens of billions of dollars of losses to its shareholders and contributing to a historic market meltdown.Fine. Scrutinize them. Read the footnotes. Argue about consolidation. But don’t call them Enron. Enron caused the Enron crash. It’s highly unlikely that fraud at that level is being perpetuated now by these companies.When I first started out in accounting back in the mid-1980s, my biggest client was a publicly held biotechnology firm calledCentocor, which, at the time, was developing drugs using a technology based on monoclonal-antibody treatment for various purposes including sepsis. To raise money, Centocor also did off-balance-sheet financing. The company formed limited partnerships in which it held a minority interest but the entity issued debt and took in investments from limited partners in order to fund the development of various drugs, which Centocor then had the exclusive right to use.In the 1980s and early 1990s, hundreds of millions of dollars were plowed into these partnerships. This was common practice in the biotechnology during that time.Did some of the drugs fail in clinical testing? Yes. But did this cause a stock market panic? No. Like with today’s datacenters, the risks were spread. During that time – before the Internet, SEC disclosures and 24/7 media scrutiny – the public little knew of these vehicles. The good news is that the accounting has evolved, although the economic idea has stayed the same – no debt was shown on Centocor’s balance sheet. Ultimately, this financing vehicle became more expensive and less popular because it was easier and more affordable to raise money other ways.The off-balance-sheet financing strategies today that are being used by big tech firms have different risks than what the biotech companies were doing when I was younger. Today, the disclosures required by companies doing this are significant. The scrutiny is intense. The investing public is smarter. Today’s risks are different and arguably more recoverable.In the 90s Centocor,Genentech,Amgen,Biogenand other companies like them were raising millions in partnerships that were developing products with a high probability of failure during clinical testing.Today’s investors are financing land, buildings, electrical infrastructure and computing equipment. A datacenter can disappoint financially, but it doesn’t disappear because a clinical trial fails. It’s whyJeff Bezoscalls AI an “industrial bubble”. Industrial bubbles leave things behind. Railways. Fiber-optic cable. Factories. And this time, datacenters.If this is a glut, it’s a strange one: developers increased North American capacity by 36% last year and vacancy still fell to a record 1.4%. According toCBRE’s North America Data Center Trends H2 2025 report, demand is outpacing supply in nearly every major market. Unlike the drug companies hoping for success, there’s a legitimate market need today for datacenters. AI isn’t going away.Microsoftestimates that only 17.8% of the world’s working-age population currently uses generative AI. If that’s anywhere near correct, we’re still much closer to the beginning of adoption than the end.Some of these investments will fail. Some lenders will lose money. Some datacenters will be worth less than their owners paid for them. But that’s exactly why these financing structures exist: to spread enormous capital requirements and risk among investors willing to take it. The obligations are disclosed, the assets are real and demand for computing capacity remains strong. That’s why I’m not losing sleep over big tech’s off-balance-sheet debt. I see financial engineering, yes. I don’t see a debt bomb.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Datacenters – USMetaAmazonJeff BezoscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pretty shambolic’: new EU border checks cause stress for UK travellers | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Britons report that EES digital entry and exit system has led to frustration, visa mix-ups and long queues
Author: Jane Clinton
Headline: Britons report that EES digital entry and exit system has led to frustration, visa mix-ups and long queues
Content: Automated EES kiosks at Madrid airport. The EU rejected calls to suspend the implementation of the scheme over the peak summer period.Photograph: Juan Medina/ReutersView image in fullscreenAutomated EES kiosks at Madrid airport. The EU rejected calls to suspend the implementation of the scheme over the peak summer period.Photograph: Juan Medina/ReutersTravel & leisure‘Pretty shambolic’: new EU border checks cause stress for UK travellersBritons report that EES digital entry and exit system has led to frustration, visa mix-ups and long queuesJane ClintonandRosie Peters-McDonaldSun 23 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn top of fears aboutextreme heatandpossible jet fuel shortages, Britons planning summer holidays in the EU this year had another thing to worry about – long queues and waiting times caused by the bloc’s new border checks.TheEU digital entry and exit system (EES), which requires non-EU citizens to register and be photographed and fingerprinted on arrival and departure from the Schengen zone, has been technically in full force since April afterlaunching last autumn, but has been beset by teething problems.Despite reports of passengersfacing three-hour delaysand missed connections, Brusselsrejected calls by airports and airlinesto suspend the implementation of the scheme over the peak summer period. However, border police have been allowed to relax requirements if queues become unmanageable under an opt-out that expires next month.What are the new EU border checks and how will they affect your summer holiday?Read moreThose who shared with the Guardian their experiences of the system since its introduction highlighted a range of problems and snags.‘We checked in to Europe, but the EES says we haven’t checked out’View image in fullscreenMartin in Silkeborg, Denmark, on a paddle steamer with his dog, Morris.Photograph: Martin/Guardian CommunityOne of the main purposes of the system is to track whether non-EU citizens have spent more than their permitted 90 days in the bloc in a rolling 180-day period.However, Martin Farrall, a retired university professor, says his EES record failed to record his exit from the Schengen zone and he had to chase the authorities to update it.In May, the 67-year-old and his wife arrived by ferry at Hoek van Holland at the start of their camping trip in Denmark, both with a full residency allowance.Martin says the Dutch border police enrolled them into EES “But no entry stamp was made on our passports,” he adds.“On 30 June, 55 days after entry, we returned to the UK on the Dunkerque-Dover ferry. The French border police asked us where and when we entered Schengen, and we were handed back our passports without an exit stamp.”Once home, Martin checked his residency tally and found that instead of having 35 days left it was rapidly diminishing.View image in fullscreenMartin on a forest walk in Denmark with Morris.Photograph: Martin/Guardian Community“It appeared that EES had not been updated to show I’d left the Schengen area,” says Martin, who lives in Warwickshire. He was concerned that he would be registered as an “overstayer” at risk of refusal of entry in future.He reported the error to the Directorate General for Foreign Nationals in France on 13 July but says he has not received a response..When Martin checked on his day allowance again on 7 August, the EES website said he had zero days left, but when he looked on 17 August it had updated.“The EES website now claims I have 34 days left to travel in the 180 window! When I checked my wife’s passport she apparently has 90 days left despite us both having the same travel to Schengen history. So God only knows what’s going on.“I wonder how many other people who were waved through because of the hold-ups may also be in the same position.”‘The system obviously wasn’t ready – it’s pretty shambolic’Nadia, from Greater Manchester, thinks the system is not “communicating with other member states”. She made two trips to Schengen areas this summer with very contrasting experiences.A trip to Tenerife in June was “quite straightforward”, but her experience in July at Frankfurt airport where she was picking up a connecting flight home, was much less so.View image in fullscreenNadia says she was not sure which queue she should join at Frankfurt airport.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters“The queue there was ridiculously long, and there was very limited information,” she says. “People were wandering around trying to work out where they needed to go.“I’m very well travelled and pretty confident, but even I was slightly unsure and was thinking, is there some other queue I should be joining? There was no one nearby to check with without losing your place.”Eventually, her passport was checked. “He didn’t actually take fingerprints then,” says Nadia, who is a solicitor. “I think the queue was so long they decided to dispense with that.“It’s the efficiency of the system I question and the fact that individual member states’ systems do not talk to one another. They shouldn’t need to get information again if you have already gone through.“It’s pretty shambolic, and I think people missing their flights because of it is just not acceptable, especially when there’s no recourse; it’s not your fault.”Nadia is also unhappy about having to give her fingerprints repeatedly. “I’ve done it in a few countries now, but it’s something I feel very strongly opposed to,” she says.“This is not in keeping with the intention of the scheme, which suggests that once registered, you should not have to keep re-entering your biometric data. You also wonder where the information is going – who’s seeing it, who else has access to it?”‘There should be clearer signage about exemptions’Evie, originally from Manchester but studying in Munich, says her student visa has caused EES confusion.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In Munich airport, there are TV screens which explain the function of EES as a system to register ‘visitors’. As I hold an extended-stay visa for the purpose of studying, I would not describe myself as a ‘visitor’ as I can stay in Germany for up to 12 months,” the 23-year-old says.She says that upon seeing she had a British passport, she was often directed toward the EES queue and had to explain her visa situation, after which she “was normally allowed to stand in the queue with everyone else”.Evie says this has happened “virtually every time” she has flown in and out of Germany – in December, January, February and April – and believes there should be better signposting to avoid mix-ups, especially given unreliable airport wifi makes accessing online information difficult.‘You could see people getting anxious’Kevin and his wife, Christine, travelled to Lanzarote in June but struggled to get the machine to register their details.“The arrivals hall was packed, but there were loads of machines,” the 75-year-old says. “Some were not working. I noticed people getting angry when their fingerprints would not enter. People started holding their fingers in different positions, and when that didn’t work, they would hit the glass harder.”View image in fullscreenKevin and Christine on holiday in Lanzarote in June 2026.Photograph: Kevin/Guardian CommunityHe says there was “not much assistance to be found” and when all attempts failed, people queued up to “have it done manually at the kiosk”.“You could see people getting anxious,” says Kevin, who lives with Christine, 73, in Merseyside. He says the machines eventually registered them both.The couple’s next trip is to Palma for a cruise, and they are bracing themselves for there to be issues. “We’ll be visiting different countries on the cruise,” Kevin says. “What happens then?”‘The fingerprinting system didn’t work for me’Martin, 68, a retired IT worker, said he and his wife struggled to operate the screen to register at Schiphol airport in the Netherlands.“The fingerprinting system didn’t work for me,” says Martin of their trip at the end of April. “My wife had similar issues with her 71-year-old hands. Older people with drier fingers have trouble with touch screens.”Eventually, Martin, who lives in Stockport, was sent to manual entry “where they forgot to stamp my passport”.“When exiting Dusseldorf, the Germans got a bit excited about that and asked how we got intoEurope,” he adds. “I just said the Dutch didn’t stamp our passports, and they accepted that.“The interface is poorly laid out and will confuse the less technical I have an IT background, and it feels like the system was not walked through enough times. It’s a mess. It also hasn’t been properly tested for older people.”View image in fullscreenTravellers have reported problems with operating the digital touchscreens and fingerprint scanners used by the EES system.Photograph: Hugh Williamson/Alamy‘My wife, being visually impaired, couldn’t find where to look’Ed Griffiths, 67, a retired IT specialist, says his wife has impaired vision and could not work the machine at Prague airport as they passed through last September as she was unable to read the instructions.“The photo/fingerprint machine failed for both of us, and we spent one hour 15 minutes standing in a slow queue of confused people waiting for staff to retry it, but my wife, being visually impaired, couldn’t find where to look, so they skipped the photo and she was waved through,” says Ed, who lives in Buckinghamshire. The delay meant their prebooked taxi nearly left without them.Then the couple were in Milan in March and Ed had to re-register despite already having done so in Prague.“The machine ignored my previous registration, my fingerprint was asked for and failed, I waited an hour in a queue for manual assistance retry,” he says. His wife, also 67, however, did manage registration and was waved through.More recently, in Vienna in May an officer supervised the booths for photos and fingerprints. Again, the system ignored his previous registration, but the couple got through in five minutes.“Twice we have been registered already, and it made no discernible difference,” Ed says. “We have not found assistance at machines, but at booths there has been some help.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsTravel & leisureEuropean UnionEuropeBrexitAirline industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Frustrated Lewis Hamilton claims Ferrari strategy cost him F1 Dutch GP podium | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Britain’s Lewis Hamilton said talks were needed at Ferrari as to why they delayed bringing teammate Charles Leclerc into the pits at the Dutch Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Britain’s Lewis Hamilton said talks were needed at Ferrari as to why they delayed bringing teammate Charles Leclerc into the pits at the Dutch Grand Prix
Content: Fourth-placed Lewis Hamilton reckoned he could have improved his finishing position if Ferrari had been more decisive.Photograph: Antonin Vincent/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFourth-placed Lewis Hamilton reckoned he could have improved his finishing position if Ferrari had been more decisive.Photograph: Antonin Vincent/DPPI/ShutterstockFormula One 2026Frustrated Lewis Hamilton claims Ferrari strategy cost him F1 Dutch GP podiumBriton says team too slow to pit Charles Leclerc‘It’s something that we need to discuss offline’Giles Richardsat ZandvoortSun 23 Aug 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has told his Ferrari team that they must up their game if he is to remain in the Formula One world championship fight after the British driver was angry with strategy calls atthe Dutch Grand Prix, comparing them unfavourably with the decisive way his former team ­Mercedes had acted.The race was won by McLaren’s Lando Norris from Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and George Russell. Hamilton was fourth but believed he might have had a shot of a podium hadFerrarimoved Charles Leclerc aside sooner when Hamilton, on a different tyre strategy, was quicker than his teammate.Lando Norris denies Antonelli in F1 Dutch GP after Verstappen crashes out of home raceRead more“Great way of wasting time, good job,” was his unusually blunt admonishment when Ferrari finally pitted Leclerc. In contrast Russell had been given swift instruction to move over for Antonelli in the final stages of the race when the Italian was similarly on much faster rubber.“I think what’s clear is I’m looking ahead and seeing Mercedes execute like that,” Hamilton said. “They’ve got the car, they’re fighting for the championship, in the lead and they did it straight away. Here, I’m sitting back, losing seconds. It’s something that we need to discuss offline.”Despite Antonelli finishing second he has extended his lead over Russell and Hamilton, who are now 59 points behind the Italian, and Hamilton was adamant that his team could not afford to drop any points.“Today was definitely frustrating for me,” he added. “I’m here to win and I really believe that this team can win. To win championships you have to pick up every point. The last few races have been difficult with penalties and today I lost several seconds behind Charles which I think ultimately would have made the difference at the end.“My goal is to try and lead this team to the championship and we’ve got some work to do for sure.”Mercedes’ quick intervention with team orders was questioned, not least by Russell at the time given he is also vying for the title, but the British driver accepted it had been the right call.“We’ve always said as a team, when we’re on different strategies, we’re never going to fight, that’s always just been our sort of rules,” he said. “Kimi was ahead of me anyway, so he deserved to finish ahead. When you’re in the race, you want to fight for every single position but with the pace, with a new tyre, he would have overtaken anyway. So it’s the right decision.”Toto Wolff maintained it had been a straightforward on the pit wall. “Team orders are always harsh from one drivers’ perspective but it is what we always discussed,” the Mercedes team principal said. “We are not losing time with each other if there are competitors breathing down our neck. Today wasn’t a difficult call.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026FerrariLewis HamiltonFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Start your engines! Trump completes fast and furious takeover of Washington with IndyCar race | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president, pushing on with Freedom 250 festivities, makes over nation’s capital for Trump rally on wheels
Author: David Smith
Headline: US president, pushing on with Freedom 250 festivities, makes over nation’s capital for Trump rally on wheels
Content: Donald Trump waves the green flag to start Sunday’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix race in Washington DC, alongside Melania Trump.Photograph: Doug Mills/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump waves the green flag to start Sunday’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix race in Washington DC, alongside Melania Trump.Photograph: Doug Mills/ReutersThe US politics sketchDonald TrumpStart your engines! Trump completes fast and furious takeover of Washington with IndyCar raceUS president, pushing on with Freedom 250 festivities, makes over nation’s capital for Trump rally on wheelsKyle Kirkwood wins Freedom 250 IndyCar race after Trump waves the green flagDavid Smithin WashingtonSun 23 Aug 2026 17.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe got the wrong end of the stick.Donald Trumpcouldn’t figure outhow to hold the green flag until his wife, Melania Trump, and Command Sgt Maj Matt Williams set him right. Then the US presidentwaved the flagfast and furious like an excited schoolboy. Theracewas under way – and his conquest of Washington DC was complete.Since returning to Washington, Trump hasdeployedthe national guard,wreckedthe Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool,demolishedthe East Wing of the White House andrunthe John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts into the ground. His faceadornsthe Department of Justice, and he still has grandplansfor a triumphal arch worthy of a Roman emperor.On Sunday he made the nation’s capital tremble with fast, flashy cars brazenly roaring around a 1.7-mile street circuit in IndyCar’sFreedom ⁠250 Grand Prix, the capstone of his Maga-flavoured celebration of the 250th anniversary of US independence.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump claims IndyCar had been trying to host a race in Washington ‘for 20 years’.Photograph: Allison Robbert/APWashington was not built for a Trump rally on wheels andhad to make accommodations, like a party host bracing for a noisy and obnoxious guest. More than 200 manhole covers were welded down around the course so they would not be sucked up by cars thundering over them. The National Gallery of Art studied how vibrations from the vehicles might affect its exhibits and shielded some outdoor sculptures.Indeed, as the vehicles whizzed by the National Archives, home to America’s desperately fragile founding documents, and the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum, whereNeil Armstrong’s spacesuitrequires constant vigilance, it was not hard to imagine anxious curators twitching at every rattle of crockery or spillage of tea.Controversy and a corporate spectacle under the Claw: Trump’s birthday fight night at the White HouseRead moreNot that the president seemed to be sweating it. While officially the Grand Prix was open to everyone – and DC’s Democratic mayor, Muriel Bowser, declared, “Drivers, to your cars!” – the event had a distinctly Trumpian flavour reminiscent of June’sUltimate Fighting Championship boutson the White House South Lawn.The UFC impresario Dana White,testosteroneavengerPete Hegsethand “human printer”Natalie Harp, who would wait for Trump as ardently as Penelope did for Odysseus, were among the guests. Democratic socialists were less in evidence. IndyCar is neitherWoke 1nor Woke 2.Wearing a dark blue suit, white shirt and red tie, Trump gave fist pumps and shook hands with the IndyCar drivers. They posed for photographers, Trump giving his signature thumbs up, as the sun gleamed off the US Capitol dome beyond.The president gave a perfunctory TV interview to the Fox network. Why was it important for him to bring IndyCars to the streets of DC? The reply was very Trumpian: “Well, Roger [Penske, a billionaire who owns the IndyCar series] told me they’ve beentrying to do it for 20 years, and he’d come down; I think he said he was down 211 times to try and get it done. And when he came to see Trump, it got done in about 15 minutes, and it’s turned out to be much bigger than we ever even thought possible.”View image in fullscreenTrump has inserted himself into UFC fights, the football World Cup final and the Patriot Games in recent months.Photograph: Mike Kropf/Getty ImagesTranslation: every previous administration and mayor thought this plan was madness, and told Penske where to go. Note also the characteristic reference to “Trump” in the third person, and the boast that only he could fix it, and in 15 minutes. (If only ending the Ukraine war were so easy.)A ceremonial trundleTrue to form, the president also bragged about the crowd size and, as he has done since UFC night, insisted that he knows better than the meteorologists. “You know, I was hearing about rain all week long. ‘It’s gonna rain, it’s gonna rain.’ I said: ‘No, it’s not.’ And this is as nice today as I’ve seen in Washington in a long time.”Trump climbed into his armoured limousine, the Beast, mounted with flags and flashing blue and red lights, andtrundled a ceremonial lapof the track. Was that Harp sprinting after him? Or hiding in the trunk? No, but we did get theQatari-gifted planethat Trump has used as Air Force One flying overhead, escorted by four fighter jets.View image in fullscreenMore than 200 manhole covers were welded down around the course in Washington DC.Photograph: Mike Kropf/Getty ImagesThen Christopher Macchio, one of Trump’s favourite singers, performed The Star-Spangled Banner as Trump saluted and Melania, wearing a white blouse, stood with hand on heart in the presidential box, a temporary white, air-conditioned structure with a clear front.A trained bald eagle was released near the start line, swooping and flying overhead before returning to its handler. There were flyovers of military aircraft including a B-2 stealth bomber. Officials paused air traffic at Washington’s Ronald Reagan ​National airport for three hours to ​accommodate them.It fell to another stalwart ally, interior secretary Doug Burgum, sporting sunglasses,to bellow: “Gentlemen, start your engines!”The race began, with drivers completing147 lapscovering roughly 250 miles (400km), and produced an American winner in Kyle Kirkwood.View image in fullscreenTrump’s limousine, mounted with flags and flashing blue and red lights, trundled a ceremonial lap of the track.Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesIt was the latest chapter of a sporting summer in which Trumpinsertedhimself into the UFC fights, thefootball World Cup finaland thePatriot Games, a cross between a game show and athletics meet for high schoolers.Never slow to demonstrate his fealty to Trump, Mike Johnson, the Republican speaker of the House of Representatives, told Fox News that he wants to bring the IndyCar Grand Prix back next year and make it an annual event.By then, one hopes, Trump will have figured out how to hold and wave a green flag. Or as they say inIran, a white flag.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThe US politics sketchIndycarWashington DCUS politicsUS sportsMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool’s Szoboszlai spot-on with late, late leveller to salvage point at Newcastle | Premier League | The Guardian
description: New head coaches Matthias Jaissle and Andoni Iraola shared the spoils after a late Liverpool penalty denied Newcastle victory in a 2-2 draw
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: New head coaches Matthias Jaissle and Andoni Iraola shared the spoils after a late Liverpool penalty denied Newcastle victory in a 2-2 draw
Content: Dominik Szoboszlai goads the Newcastle fans with his celebration after his superbly struck stoppage-time penalty.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersView image in fullscreenDominik Szoboszlai goads the Newcastle fans with his celebration after his superbly struck stoppage-time penalty.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersPremier LeagueLiverpool’s Szoboszlai spot-on with late, late leveller to salvage point at NewcastleLouise Taylorat St James' ParkSun 23 Aug 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 18.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore kick-off a banner was raised in the Gallowgate End inscribed with a quotation fromthe late Kevin Keegan. “I want people to dream about their football,” it read. “We should all be dreamers at heart.”Out on the pitch it swiftly became apparent that both Matthias Jaissle, Keegan’s latest successor in the Newcastle dugout, and Liverpool’s new manager Andoni Iraola are on individual missions to create forms of organised chaos capable of subjecting the best opponents to torrid nightmares.Iraola ‘wouldn’t have signed up for this result’ but relieved for Liverpool to earn pointRead moreDespite a few, ultimately forlorn, attempts to introduce semblances of control on the parts of the visiting playmaker Florian Wirtz and Newcastle’s elegant central midfielder Lewis Miley, this was sheer, unadulterated, mutual mayhem of the sort to make Iraola’s more purist Anfield predecessor Arne Slot wince.Along the way to a draw secured, perhaps slightly fortuitously, by Dominik Szoboszlai’s 99th-minute penalty for Liverpool, the returning former Newcastle striker Alexander Isak left minimal imprint on a match that had been supposed to be all about him. Instead Isak was upstaged by Jaissle’s forward William Osula.No sooner had the heartfelt tributes to Keegan, a player and manager adored by both clubs, been completed it very quickly became apparent that Jérémy Jacquet and Virgil van Dijk had no answers to Osula as the young Dane turned and accelerated towards goal following Ryan Gravenberch’s inexplicable surrender of possession.The stage was set for this most unpredictable of strikers to spot Anthony Elanga, then in the process of leaving Milos Kerkez for dust down the right, slide a pass in the winger’s direction and watch as, a steadying touch later, Elanga’s shot flashed beyond Alisson’s reach.Only five minutes had passed, Jaissle’s tenure as Newcastle’s manager was off to perfect start and already Iraola looked distinctly stressed.His defence did not convince, with Kerkez finding few answers to Elanga. Like Jaissle, Iraola is a high priest of pressing but Liverpool’s best hope here seemed to be to retain possession, impose their technical superiority and out-pass Newcastle.Significantly their best moments coincided largely with those albeit sporadic occasions when Wirtz –who would be withdrawn midway through the second half – managed to get on the ball and began unnerving a Newcastle side supposedly in the throes of a dramatic transition.It is only three weeks sinceJaissle succeeded Eddie Howebut the former Al-Ahli manager has certainly succeeded in not merely re-energising a mentally jaded team but sharpening a swarm pressing game that had become more than a little half hearted and untidy. “The manager is top,” said Elanga. “Playing for him is fun.”Given that Jaissle has inherited a team shorn of last season’s luminaries – Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães – this achievement was all the more impressive. The 38-year-old German trusted 18-year-old Sean Steur, recently arrived from Ajax, alongside Miley in the key holding roles in his 4-2-3-1 system and for long periods they held their own.View image in fullscreenNewcastle and Liverpool fans pay tribute to Kevin Keegan, who died last month. Keegan played for both clubs and managed Newcastle.Photograph: Newcastle United/Getty ImagesBehind them, Malick Thiaw and Sven Botman excelled in central defence while Amar Dedic shone at right-back following his £30m move from Benfica.There are ways to leave a football club but the route Isak chose – mounting a one-man strike before forcing a record £125m move to Liverpool last summer – ensured he was greeted by chants of “rat, rat, rat,” as he alighted from the visiting team bus.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf Isak seemed quite unconcerned – he grinned broadly in the face of some further sustained hostility before kick-off – the Sweden striker added to Iraola’s problems by miscuing his sole chance of an alarmingly anonymous afternoon. Instead it was a forward facing an uncertain future at Anfield who kept Liverpool in it. When Jaissle’s midfield inexplicably stood off him Cody Gakpo’s first time shot from outside the area defied Lukas Hornicek.View image in fullscreenJoe Willock’s superb finish, found despite the attentions of several Liverpool players, had looked like being the winning goal.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersWith Osula now limping, on came Joe Willock for Newcastle leaving the impressive Yoane Wissa – arguably man of the match – to shift from the No 10 to No 9 role. Willock is reportedly close to joining Besiktas but delighted in immediately offering a reminder of his enduring worth on Tyneside.When Wissa, rather wonderfully, dodged three supposed markers his ensuing pass to Willock was superbly calibrated and the latter returned the compliment by curling a shot past Alisson and in off a post. Tellingly, Willock was mobbed by every outfield teammate with Nick Woltemade and his fellow home substitutes racing the length of the pitch to congratulate him.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Low on creativity, Liverpool seemed beaten until deep in injury time the substitute Victor Muñoz was felled when the otherwise convincing Newcastle left-back Lewis Hall rather unluckily caught his knee in the penalty area.All that remained was for Szoboszlai to lash his ensuing penalty high into the roof of the net and level a game as swashbuckling as anything even Keegan might have conjured.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueNewcastle UnitedLiverpoolmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Hull punished United defence in victory but Carrick’s attack is bigger area of concern  | Hull City | The Guardian
description: Manchester United again struggled against a back five as the promoted hosts exploited a set-piece weakness
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: Manchester United again struggled against a back five as the promoted hosts exploited a set-piece weakness
Content: A dejected Matheus Cunha (right) of Manchester United during their defeat at Hull.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA dejected Matheus Cunha (right) of Manchester United during their defeat at Hull.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesHull CityAnalysisHull punished United defence in victory but Carrick’s attack is bigger area of concernAndrew BeasleyManchester United again struggled against a back five as the promoted hosts exploited a set-piece weaknessSun 23 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 14.21 EDTShareHull scored nine league goals from set plays last season, the joint-fewest in the Championship. Yet two in 21 minutes earned them avictory over Manchester Unitedon Saturday.It was a disastrous start to the campaign for the visitors. While Michael Carrick said before the gameit would not be easy, he would not have expected victory being so straightforward for Hull. It was a match United simply had to win given the gulf in resources and expectation. Opta rated their chance of victory at 68.9% before kick-off.Carrick tells Manchester United to keep calm and carry on after Hull humblingRead moreUnited’s inability to deal with Oli McBurnie as the target man was painful to watch. Their slack defending on the set pieces from which Hull scored will also draw focus. Their attacking should be the greatest concern, though.A glance at expected goal numbers can paint a false impression. Hull generated 1.01 expected goals to United’s 1.83, so did the visitors deserve to win? The issue is the breakdown of chances that contributed to the total. United had 21 shots, 16 of which were worth less than 0.1 expected goals.This was a theme last season, albeit less obvious when they performed well under Carrick. United’s open-play shots were worth an average of 0.104 expected goals in 2025-26, the third worst rate among teams that finished in the top half of the Premier League. Against Hull, this figure was just 0.087.Not until the 78th minute did a notable opportunity fall to a player they would hope to have one, as Bryan Mbeumo received a through ball from Matheus Cunha. Before that, their highest-value chances fell to Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui. The former has experience as a winger, and started in the attacking midfield trio in United’s 4-2-3-1 formation, but the duo have just 16 top-flight goals between them. They are not reliable chance converters.Chart showing the worst 10 teams for expected goals per open play shot in the 2025-26 Premier LeagueMarcus Rashford is far stronger. He should take Dorgu’s berth in the long term, assuming he remains with the club. His natural attacking instincts may have aided in the creation of better chances in the first half. Regardless, it was alarming how hard United found it to fashion valuable opportunities against a club that conceded the second-most expected goals in the 2025-26 Championship.Hull’s manager, Sergej Jakirovic, used a back five. He deployed three centre-backs on 10 occasions last season, notably in victories in the playoff semi-final second leg against Millwall and the final against Middlesbrough.Chart showing the expected goal value of shots in Hull 2‑0 Manchester UnitedIt worked against United, with the extra bodies at the back able to crowd out attackers. Opta’s shot map showed Hull conceded eight efforts in the “danger zone” – the centre of the penalty area that covers the width of the six-yard box out to the 18-yard line. Five of the eight were headers, which are harder to convert, leaving little else of note. Space in the most valuable real estate came at a premium at the MKM Stadium and United were unable to penetrate it.This structure has caused United problems before. They have now won only one of their last six league matches against teams that started with a back three or five. Leeds won 2-1 at Old Trafford in April with a 3-4-3 formation and used the same system to draw 1-1 two weeks ago in a pre-season friendly. Milan employed the same framework when beating United 4-2 in their final warm-up game.“We got beat, we’re hurt and it’s not a nice feeling. It doesn’t mean it’s going to change the whole direction of how we’re going as a team or as a football club,”Carrick said. As sensible a long-term approach as that may be, United’s attack needs work.Explore more on these topicsHull CityManchester UnitedanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Teófimo López outpoints Rolly Romero to win title in third weight class | Teófimo López | The Guardian
description: López captures WBA welterweight title by majority decision in Las Vegas as former champion Romero condemns result as a ‘robbery’
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: López captures WBA welterweight title by majority decision in Las Vegas as former champion Romero condemns result as a ‘robbery’
Content: Rolando Romero (left) tries to evade a punch from Teófimo López on Saturday night in Las Vegas.Photograph: John Locher/APView image in fullscreenRolando Romero (left) tries to evade a punch from Teófimo López on Saturday night in Las Vegas.Photograph: John Locher/APTeófimo LópezTeófimo López outpoints Rolly Romero to win title in third weight classLópez wins majority decision to claim WBA crownRomero brands judges’ verdict a ‘robbery’New champion adds to previous 135lb, 140lb beltsGuardian sportSun 23 Aug 2026 04.32 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeófimo López became a three-division world champion on Saturday night, winning a 12-round majority decision over Rolando ‘Rolly’ Romero to claim the WBA welterweight title at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas.López prevailed by scores of 115-113 and 116-112, while the third judge saw the fight even at 114-114. Romero, making the first defense of his titlewon against Ryan Garcia 15 months ago, disputed the result in the immediate aftermath.“When I heard 114-114 I knew it was a robbery,” Romero said. “I got hit with two punches the whole fight that barely grazed me. I was never in any trouble.”The victory gave López a world title at 147lb after previous championship reigns at lightweight and junior welterweight.López largely controlled the fight behind his jab and movement, keeping the heavier-handed Romero from consistently closing the distance. According to Compubox’s punch statistics, López landed 124 punches to Romero’s 73, including a career-high 62 jabs.Romero’s best stretch came in the fifth round, when he opened a cut above López’s right eye and followed with a left hook and looping right hand that hurt the challenger. Romero pressed forward as López bled heavily, but the 29-year-old weathered the attack and recovered before the end of the round.“He hit me with a shot that woke me up,” López said. “I was just buzzed. I got right back to it. I stayed cool, calm and collected.”View image in fullscreenBoth fighters raise their arms in victory after the final bell.Photograph: Mikael Ona/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockLópez regained control over the middle and later rounds, using his footwork to stay outside Romero’s range while scoring with single punches and combinations. The 30-year-old struggled to sustain his offense and reached double figures in punches landed in only the fifth round.Romero produced another late opening in the 11th, catching López with a left hook that knocked him off balance. Neither fighter was able to establish a decisive advantage in a closely contested final round before the bout went to the scorecards.The win completed a rapid return to championship status for López, only seven months after Shakur Stevensoncomprehensively outpointed himby identical scores of 119-109. López had described that defeat as “the best thing that could have happened to us”, saying it helped realign him with his father and trainer, Teófimo López Sr.“If you lost and you come back, then you never lost, because you’re a winner,” López said. “I’m a true example of what winning is. It’s about not giving up.”López said afterward that he was ready to move on to his next challenge.“I just had to stay busy and keep my range against a strong puncher,” he said. “I’m just looking forward to the next thing.”Explore more on these topicsTeófimo LópezBoxingUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Browns QB Deshaun Watson laments ‘disrespectful’ booing by team’s own fans  | Cleveland Browns | The Guardian
description: Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson has called the booing he heard from the team’s own fans during Saturday’s home loss to Buffalo ‘personal’
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson has called the booing he heard from the team’s own fans during Saturday’s home loss to Buffalo ‘personal’
Content: Deshaun Watson has endured an unsuccessful spell in Cleveland.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APView image in fullscreenDeshaun Watson has endured an unsuccessful spell in Cleveland.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APCleveland BrownsBrowns QB Deshaun Watson laments ‘disrespectful’ booing by team’s own fansPlayer booed during team’s preseason loss to BillsQB has battled injuries during time in ClevelandWatson was suspended over sexual assault allegationsGuardian sportand agenciesSat 22 Aug 2026 20.46 EDTLast modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 20.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrowns quarterback Deshaun Watson has called the booing he heard from the team’s own fans during Saturday’s home loss to Buffalo “disrespectful” and “personal.”Watson, whohas a complicated relationship with Cleveland fansbecause of injuries, off-field issues – including an NFL suspension in 2022 – and a massive, $230m contract, was booed repeatedly during the second half of the 31-7 loss to the Bills.Watsonwas just 5 of 12 passing for 36 yardsand threw an interception during the preseason defeat. He came off the bench in place of Shedeur Sanders, who is competing with Watson for the starting job. Browns head coach Todd Monken has yet to decide which QB will start the season opener in Jacksonville on 13 September.The Browns’ sad and seedy Deshaun Watson era nears its predictable endpointRead moreIn 2022, the Browns sent a package that included three first-round picks to the Houston Texans in exchange for the quarterback, who had been accused of sexual assaultby dozens of women. The Browns then rewarded Watson, at the time one of the best quarterbacks in the league,with a $230m fully guaranteed contract. Watson never faced criminal charges over the sexual assault allegations but the NFL suspended him for 11 games of the 2022 season after its own investigation.Cleveland’s faith in Watson has not been rewarded. He is yet to complete a full season with the Browns due to injury and suspension and has consistently been one of the worst quarterbacks in the league in QBR. He has thrown 19 touchdowns and 12 interceptions in his four seasons with the Browns (20 quarterbacks threw more than 19 touchdowns in the 2025 NFL season alone). They have played just one postseason game since his arrival, which they lost, despite boasting one of the best defenses in the league. Watson missed that game through injury.Saturday’s game was his first at home sincehe tore his achilles tendon in October 2024, when some Browns fans cheered him sustaining a potential career-ending injury.“It has nothing to do about the performance,” Watson said of the boos. “It’s a little bit personal. I think that’s a disrespectful thing. I’m going to keep whatever I feel with me and my family internally on how I feel about that. Just move on.”Watson hasn’t forgotten the cheers that greeted his injury in 2024.“Last time I played on this field, I tore my achilles and that same fanbase, they cheered when I got hurt,” Watson said. “So what does that have to do with anything about performance? When a person gets hurt, especially for your own city and they cheer.”Watson said he’s not sure if he can win back Browns fans.“When I’m in public, no one’s mentioned anything,” he said. “Because this is social media, players can’t respond back. And then in the stadium, players can’t respond back. So I get it. I understand it. So it is what it is.“It’s a mental battle every day. I feel like I get more love in road games than I do home games. So if it is my spot and he [Monken] does make me the (starter), maybe it’s 17 away games then.”Last year, Brownsco-owner Jimmy Haslam admittedhis team’s decision to acquire Deshaun Watson has been a “big swing and miss”.Explore more on these topicsCleveland BrownsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ceferin brands Infantino’s failed World Cup plan as ‘even worse than the Super League’ | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Aleksander Ceferin, the Uefa president, has said Gianni Infantino’s attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup was ‘even worse than the Super League’
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Aleksander Ceferin, the Uefa president, has said Gianni Infantino’s attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup was ‘even worse than the Super League’
Content: Aleksander Ceferin (left) is keeping up the pressure on Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenAleksander Ceferin (left) is keeping up the pressure on Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAUefaCeferin brands Infantino’s failed World Cup plan as ‘even worse than the Super League’Fifa president will face opponent if he seeks re-electionCeferin: ‘We stopped another try to steal the sport’Nick AmesSun 23 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has described Gianni Infantino’s doomed attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup as “even worse than the Super League plan” and warned his embattledFifacounterpart that he will face an opponent if he runs for re-election next March.Ceferin has led Uefa’s firm collective stance against the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, which was shelved amid widespread opposition at the start of August. Uefa are pushing for Infantino to quit, also drawing on support from Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, and are yet to drop a threat to boycott Fifa competitions while talks are under way with Concacaf toset up a combined Nations League tournament.Infantino angers Concacaf nations by hijacking meeting in CaribbeanRead moreIn an interview with the podcastThe Rest is Politics: Leading, Ceferin denounced Infantino’s project as more damaging than the breakaway Super League that was shelved in 2021 after large-scale protests. “I think this plan is even worse than the Super League plan,” he said. “In the first case, super-important clubs wanted to do their own league, which is wrong and would destroy football. But in this case, football would be literally sold.“I’m absolutely sure that the [FFE] plan is dead. For me, the most important thing is that we stopped another try to sell the sport. It’s hard to imagine what kind of people would sell the sport that belongs to everyone.”Earlier this month it was reported that Infantino had held talks aboutrunning the Super League under Fifa branding. Ceferin is confident that any revival of that plan would be decades away. “It might happen in 20 years, you never know, but for now we cooperate with everyone in a great way. I’m sure it cannot happen in the next 10 years,” he said.Infantino spent much of the weekendcourting support from Concacaf membersat a meeting in the Dominican Republic, infuriating many of those present.
