title: The new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violence | Games | The Guardian
description: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards
Author: Jackson Ryan
Headline: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards
Content: A still from Halloween: The Game. The ability for players to smoke marijuana to detect an enemy has resulted in the game being banned in Australia.Photograph: IllfonicView image in fullscreenA still from Halloween: The Game. The ability for players to smoke marijuana to detect an enemy has resulted in the game being banned in Australia.Photograph: IllfonicGamesThe new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violenceAcademics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standardsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJackson RyanSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 21.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. The US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.But Australians will not be able to play Halloween, because it has been refused classification by the Australian Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders.In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that the Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of ComputerGames2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchiseRead more“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the boardwrote in a recent statement.In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game.The uproar has resurfaced longstanding grievances about how games are classified in Australia compared with film and television, and the inability for adults to access games widely available in other parts of the world.double quotation markCan we stop pretending that the way we classify games in Australia, in 2026, is appropriate for adults?Margaret Anderson, former director of the Classification BoardClaire Henry, an associate professor in screen at Flinders University and an Australian Research Council fellow, says the board enforced the guidelines correctly but the controversy around the decision highlights “a mismatch between the community standards and the classification standards”.The decision on Halloween: The Game follows several high-profile cases that have resulted in games such asState of Decay,Wasteland 3andSaints Row IVbanned in Australia for the same reason: incentivised drug use. All of these games were later reclassified after censoring aspects of their gameplay.View image in fullscreenSaints Row IV. The game was initially refused classification in Australia but was later released after a particular mission was removed.Photograph: Deep SilverDan Golding, a professor of media at Monash University, says that two assumptions have been baked into the classifying of games in Australia. “Games have always been regulated based on the assumption there is something more impactful aboutdoing,in a game, than there is aboutwatching,in a film,” he says.“A second assumption is that games are for kids – or at least the regulation system exists to protect kids.”Ron Curry has battled these assumptions in skirmishes with the Classification Board over his nearly two decades as CEO of the Interactive Games and Entertainment Association (IGEA). Alongside a dogged public campaign and a cadre of journalists, the IGEA helped introduce an R18+ category for video games in 2013, the absence of which had stopped several games being released in Australia before.After the R18+ classification was brought in, Curry noted the jobwas not finished– the trade-off for introducing the category was that video games were still seen as a distinct form of media, with greater risks attached.“It still very clearly said games are different to all other media, it’s more dangerous, and we need to treat it more carefully,” Curry says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSaints Row 4 refused classification in AustraliaRead moreInteractivity – thedoingGolding refers to – has always underlined this belief. The guidelines for games, introduced alongside the R18+ rating, state that “as a general rule computer games may have a higher impact than similarly themed depictions of the classifiable elements in film, and therefore greater potential for harm or detriment, particularly to minors”.Curry points tothe Australian government’s own research that hassuggested interactivity may not increase the impact of video games, particularly in regards to violent content, and there has been limited research on interactivity around drug use, sex, gambling and nudity.Margaret Anderson, a former director of the Classification Board, says the huge focus on interactivity in games drove her nuts during her seven years on the board. She points todecades of researchshowing games are predominantly played by adults.“Can we stop pretending that the way we classify games in this country, in 2026, is appropriate for adults? Because it’s not,” Anderson says.Academics have shown the current classification system isn’t just preventing access to games, however. Often, the standards are incoherent.Marcus Carter, founder of the Sydney Games and Play Lab at the University of Sydney, recently leda study– yet to be peer reviewed – that showed inconsistencies across the classifications of mobile games in the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. In 18 separate cases across the 31 top-grossing mobile games, four different age ratings were included for a single game.Carter describes the current system as “not fit for purpose”.The worry, for experts like Carter and Henry, is that the inconsistent standards have a negative impact on how the community views classifications and age ratings.“Inconsistencies can kind of undermine public confidence in the classification system,” says Henry. “It is a good system in many ways, and we’ve got to maintain that trust.”The Australian government isundertaking a review of the classification guidelineswith the aim of delivering a simpler, more consistent approach across films, games and publications. Among a raft of proposals – including introducing a PG13 rating and adjusting the MA15+ classification to MA16+ – one idea is to “remove the harsher judgement of video games’ interactivity”.IGEAandHenryhave made submissions to the review.In a statement to the Guardian,a spokesperson from the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts said: “The Australian Government is working to modernise the National Classification Scheme to ensure it remains aligned with community standards and helps Australians make informed decisions about what they read, watch and play. This work is ongoing.”Illfonic has shown no sign it will censor Halloween: The Game and have its classification reviewed in Australia. Illfonic and the game’s co-publisher Gun Interactive did not respond to requests for comment.Though the instances of Australia banning games have been rare occurrences, one future decision looms large: how will Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment in a franchise packed with sex, drugs and violence,be rated?For Anderson, the way forward is simple.“The foundational pillar of classification in Australia is that adults should be able to read, hear, see, play what they want,” she says. “Can we please respect that fact?”Explore more on these topicsGamesHalloween (2018)Horror filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaning | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Capitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spice
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Capitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spice
Content: ‘Our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionHalloweenStores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaningDave SchillingCapitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spiceSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTShareHappy spooky season, everyone! Get those jack-o’-lanterns out, becauseHalloweenis just around the corner!Just kidding, no, it’s not.It’s August, for God’s sake. Every day, I wake up to 90F weather – my skin moist with sweat and my eyelids stuck together. I can’t drink coffee on my porch without being consumed by an army of voracious mosquitoes that seem to find my blood to be the most delicious of all.And it’s not just Los Angeles that’s withering under a summer of discontent. Theeast coast heatwavesare piling up, sending millions of young people to the absolute last place they want to be:an air-conditioned movie theater. But you want to tell me it’s fine to be putting out Halloween decorations? If I don’t store my giant bag of fun-size Twix in a standup freezer, the whole damn thing will melt into chocolate soup. (Don’t even get me started on recent claims you shouldeat soup when it’s hotoutside. It’d rather slurp up my own sweat from a bowl.)Halloween is no ungodly American import – just ask the medieval monks and nuns who marketed it | Michael CarterRead moreWhy am I fuming about this? Even though I love Halloween, I’m mad because our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun. In August. I find all of that unacceptable. It feels like a violation of the natural order, a realignment of one of the few glorious constants left in the world. I yearn to go back to the tidy order of holidays, where no two ever cross paths. At most, Halloween celebrations should start in late September. Not a month after Independence Day. I fear those days are done, that our world has irrevocably changed and I need to start getting ready to give in to the new normal.I first became aware of Halloween’s creep into the summer during a recent sundries run at Target. There arecostumes, life-size skeletons, treats and various decorationson offer in-store. I’ve seen massive candy bags positioned to move at CVS. There’s even a smattering of greeting cards, which I find doubly frustrating, as I’ve never in my life considered buying someone a card for Halloween, a holiday that most adults spend binge drinking or squeezing into provocative outfits. What does a Halloween greeting card even say? “I Boo-lieve You Should Get an Uber Home”? “Have a Spooktacular One-Night Stand With Your Marginally Attractive Co-Worker”?On that Target outing, my friend Halle (an admitted Halloween pervert) bought a miniature cauldron from the growing, metastasizing spooky section. I asked what she expected to do with such a trivial piece of merchandise. “Maybe I can put my keys or some change in here.” For two months? Then what? Do you sayBack to the closet with youand wait another nine months before getting your coin cauldron out again?double quotation markIf the data says we want Halloween in the heat, then data shall be respected and worshipped. Who am I to argue with hard numbers?I know there are people with boxes and boxes of festive decorations who swap them out season after season. Christmas ends, but Easter is just around the corner. Once that’s done, you chuck the bunny rabbits and start bedazzling your home with American flags to prep for the Fourth of July. Now I’m seeing the insidious truth: we aren’t far off from that Fourth-to-Halloween corridor shrinking even further. I see a world in which witches, demons and vampires slowly start bleeding into our patriotic revelries. It’ll get to the point where some of us might start thinking Frankenstein’s monster fought at the battle of Yorktown.One day, we’ll all just celebrate whichever holidays we want, whenever we feel like it. As the climate crisis renders the idea of distinct seasons and unique weather conditions a relic of a bygone era, why wouldn’t we just all live our own little celebratory truths? Even if my local store isn’t carrying Halloween decorations, I could feasibly buy them year-round on Amazon – my mailbox jammed up with boxes of plastic fangs, fake blood and green grease paint. If it never gets cold again, then Halloween can be whenever. Though I suppose the lifestyle I’m describing already has a name and it’s “being goth”.It could be that our society is naturally evolving to be unbound by passé limitations such as “calendars” and “nature”. Instead of using holidays to mark the phases of the harvest or cycles of the moon (boring), they can be dictated by big data (chill and modern). Surely retailers around the country have statistics that point to consumers having a hankering for Halloween by August. Otherwise, why would Target be hawking rubber bats or decorative ghosts right now? We’re giving ourselves over to analytics in almost every other sector of our lives. Why not holidays?From bone-dry to soaked to the bone, welcome to the age of climate whiplash | Aditya ChakraborttyRead moreIf the data says we want Halloween in the heat, then data shall be respected and worshipped. Who am I to argue with hard numbers? If the sun’s always shining, the grass is consistently brown and the acrid bite of wildfire smoke is clogging our lungs, the average human being might not be able to differentiate between the phases of our natural world. The only way for me to not continue to rage against this phenomenon is to surrender to capitalism completely. Instead of putting my finger out and seeing which way the wind blows, I just have to pop into Target to know what season it is.The cognitive dissonance I might feel carrying my friend’s cauldron to my car in August is something my son might never feel. Time passes under the pall of climate control and fluorescent lighting. Our lives are measured by the movement of currency undulating and cresting like waves in the ocean. As this existentially crippling revelation washes over me, I take comfort in one thing:Soon, sooner than you think, it will be pumpkin spice season.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsHalloweenOpinionClimate crisisUS weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: Jumpy bond markets make it clear: Trump risks driving US into debt crisis | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm bond markets is a sign of weakness not strength
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm bond markets is a sign of weakness not strength
Content: Donald Trump and Scott Bessent.  Bessent’s panicky intervention last week smacked of rising anxiety about how markets now view the US fiscal position.Photograph: Al Drago/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Scott Bessent.  Bessent’s panicky intervention last week smacked of rising anxiety about how markets now view the US fiscal position.Photograph: Al Drago/EPAEconomics viewpointUS economyJumpy bond markets make it clear: Trump risks driving US into debt crisisHeather StewartTreasury secretary Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm bond markets is a sign of weakness not strengthSun 23 Aug 2026 06.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTShare“Look, there’s nothing magic about that $40tn number,” the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, told CNBC insouciantly last week, as the country’s debt mountain surpassed another bleak record.Yet Bessent’s decision to intervene in government bond markets in an effort to combat soaring yields belied his studied calm in TV interviews – and reignited fears the US may be on the road to a debt crisis.Half a lifetime ago, in 1992, Bessent cut his teeth in markets shorting the pound alongside George Soros in the chaos that led up to Black Wednesday, when the UK plunged out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.Why is the Trump administration causing turmoil in the bond markets? | Richard PartingtonRead moreToday he is on the other side of the tussle between policymakers and markets. When the US Treasury intervened tohelp prop up the Japanese yenearlier this month – crucially by selling euros, not the US dollar – it was widely read as a sign of weakness.Japan is a mega holder of US treasuries, and it looked as though theTrump administrationwas fretting that Tokyo might be preparing to dump a chunk of them to buy yen – potentially pushing up the yield, or interest rate.The US Treasury’s announcement that Japan would in future be able to use a little-known facility called the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility, effectively to borrow against its treasury holdings without having to sell them, was read as another sign of concern.As the economist Barry Eichengreenwrote in the FT at the time: “The bottom line is that Washington, fearing the consequences for US financial markets, is reluctant to see foreign central banks use their dollar reserves. This is telling us that the dollar is not the attractive reserve currency it once was.”In last week’s fresh intervention Bessent promised todouble the rateat which the Treasury woul buy up the longest-dated bonds – hoping to massage the yield downwards.It was the clearest sign yet of anxiety in Washington about a sell-off that has pushed up yields on 30-year government bonds to levels last seen before the global financial crisis in 2008.There are several, overlapping reasons for the bond market sell-off. One is inflation. Treasuries, which pay a fixed amount each year, are in part a bet on the future value of money – with higher inflation eroding the real value of those payments.With the Iran conflict slipping towards a forever war, keeping oil prices elevated, and amid concerns about the newFederal Reservechair Kevin Warsh’s willingness to raise interest rates, investors are fretting more about future inflation.Another reason lies in the extraordinary AI investment boom. Tech giants have been funding the buildout of vast datacentres by issuing a wall of corporate debt.Debt issuance by the “hyperscaler” AI companies is already $219bn (£160.5bn) so far this year,according to analysis by JP Morgan– potentially offering investors an alternative to treasuries and crowding out public debt.Third, and most worrying, is the gnawing sense that despite continued robust economic growth, the US is not the rock-solid creditor it once was.US public debt has exploded in recent years, smashing through every forecast. It lurched higher after the financial crisis and took another leg up during the Covid pandemic. It has continued to surge in Donald Trump’s second term, as tax cuts have been unmatched either by tariff revenue – some of which is now being repaid – or by spending cuts from Elon Musk’s short-lived Department of Government Efficiency.Without radical policy change, for which there seems little appetite on Capitol Hill, the independent Congressional Budget Office expects US government debt to rise from 100% of GDP today to 175% in 30 years’ time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, with his unwinnable war in the Middle East, capricious tariff regime andpenchant for self-enrichment on an epic scale, Trump is turning the US into an increasingly unpredictable player in the global economy. Instead of the guarantor of rules-based markets and open global trade routes, the US has become a source of uncertainty and chaos.As Adam Posen of the Peterson Institute for InternationalEconomicsput it in a recent piece: “The entire world is now doing business, investing, and trying to make a living in the post-American world economy.”Chart which forecasts US government debt rising to 175.1% by 2056The withdrawal was largely a deliberate decision by Trump’s Maga crew, who felt the US was shouldering too many of the running costs of the geopolitical order.Yet it was partly this role as the anchor of the global economy, with treasuries the quintessential safe haven asset, that prevented the logic of runaway deficits and spiralling debt from hitting home.By contrast, Bessent’s panicky intervention last week smacked of rising anxiety about how markets now view the US fiscal position.Far from drawing a line under the bond rout, 30-year yields were rising again by Friday afternoon, while at the same time the dollar was sliding fast – a cursed correlation more often associated with emerging economies.Bessent seemed to be signalling a willingness to step in again, if 30-year yields are pulled too far above 5%. As the financial commentator Stephen Innes put it: “Once traders think they have identified a policy pain threshold, they tend to come back and test whether it is real.”Warsh will have his moment in the spotlight at the Jackson Hole central bankers’ conference this week, but the risks are clearly growing of a self-inflicted bond market crisis – with consequences that would ripple out far beyond the US.Explore more on these topicsUS economyEconomics viewpointBondsEconomicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationGlobal economyFederal ReservecommentShareReuse this content

title: Surviving desire: what Buddhist thought teaches us about our war on want | Nadine Levy | The Guardian
description: The work is less about fighting what we feel, and more about meeting desire with curiosity, integrity and wisdom
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The work is less about fighting what we feel, and more about meeting desire with curiosity, integrity and wisdom
Content: ‘We live in a culture adept at stimulating desire while simultaneously encouraging us to distrust it,’ writes Nadine Levy.Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘We live in a culture adept at stimulating desire while simultaneously encouraging us to distrust it,’ writes Nadine Levy.Illustration: Guardian DesignMaking sense of itBuddhismSurviving desire: what Buddhist thought teaches us about our war on wantNadine LevyThe work is less about fighting what we feel, and more about meeting desire with curiosity, integrity and wisdomSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.02 EDTShareWhen I was a kid, I had a designated “junk food drawer”. I remember a particular kind of joy in choosing what I felt like eating: chips, chocolate, biscuits. I would saunter into the kitchen, choose my poison and kick back on the couch.These were simpler times.Perhaps you are raising an eyebrow. Such parenting might seem laissez-faire, irresponsible even. But this small act shaped my relationship to my body and its needs. Hunger was to be listened to, not feared or repressed. “When you are hungry, eat,” my mum would chime.I recognise the privilege of growing up in a home where food was abundant and the fact that I could usually stop when I had enough (a capacity I have since, ironically, lost). Yet, as an adolescent, I was struck by how often food became a site of negotiation and tension in other families. For many, food represents a source of profound struggle, bound up with shame, discipline and judgment.The idea of sin can cause shame and trauma. But what if it’s used as a cue to act? | Jackie BaileyRead moreOf course I didn’t get away scot-free. If food wasn’t a struggle for me as a child, other desires were – the desire for rest, pleasure, recognition.This is a strange moment in the history of desire. Digital platforms and their algorithms increasingly anticipate our desires, sometimes even before we register them ourselves. Do you need an app that tells you to drink water before you feel thirsty? Maybe you do!What’s more, we live in a culture adept at stimulating desire while simultaneously encouraging us to distrust it. We are sold viral food trends, alongside GLP-1 medications that can suppress appetite and, for some, calm the “food noise”.But what is the actual problem here? Do we desire too much, or too little? Or is there a more interesting question at play?It may come as a surprise to some, but Buddhism doesnot proposethat we eradicate desire altogether. Rather, it asks us to look closely at the ways desire arises; how it feels, what shapes it and where it leads.The heart communicates through its wanting – through its pulling, beckoning and reaching. We begin by respecting this dynamic. Bowing to it. And giving it enough space to reveal itself on its own terms. With time, we develop trust in our own discernment and capacity to move with wanting, rather than being trapped by its demands.Not all wanting is thesame. Some forms of desire entangle us; others support our flourishing.A useful Buddhist concept here istaṇhā, the Pali word for craving or thirst. This is wanting with a particular flavour: sticky, insistent, difficult to release. We crave something, get it, and sooner or later we want it again. The object of our yearning fails to live up to what we had subtly imagined, and the experience of satisfaction itself fades, giving way to more wanting.In fact, I am likely ensnared right now, as I reach for my third cup of coffee.The problem is not necessarily the coffee itself but ourgraspingat the idea of it and the promise it carries. Like a dog with a bone, we can’t loosen our grip.In Buddhist thought, desire can also take a wise andwholesomeform, an aspiration or intention to care, to grow, to practise non-harm, and to minimise suffering and confusion. And then there are very practical desires and instincts, like the need to eat, rest, move, connect. They are to be noticed and responded to wisely and compassionately.And this is where matters get interesting. Rather than immediately gratifying or repressing desire, we can learn to get to know its different faces, textures and patterns of movement.What sits behind the urge, or the pining? And how does it move in the body?Mary Oliver, the late American poet, famously implores “You only have to let the soft animal of your body … love what it loves”. For me, there is something in this line that opens the possibility of lingering in the wanting, allowing it to unfurl, refraining from extinguishing it through immediate gratification.When the Buddha taught mindfulness, he instructed his disciples to know the body in the body. The body is where instinct, sensation and craving can be known and felt directly. With tenderness and presence, we might notice the visceral tug of wanting and how it is linked to the future it imagines.And here is another twist: sometimes our desires are too small. What we think we want is a second sandwich, but what may lie beneath the wanting is broader, bolder. We want freedom, peace, a sense of completeness. In Buddhist terms, such aspirations find a rightful place in the spiritual path; it would be hard to sustain spiritual practice without them.An act of kindness, or mitzvah, teaches us to be part of something bigger than ourselves | Nomi KaltmannRead moreThere is no war on wanting. The work is less about fighting what we feel, and more about meeting desire with curiosity, integrity and wisdom. We take a breath and feel the sensations in the chest, the throat, the jaw; we watch the fantasies, the pleading and the magical thinking. There is no rush. Desire has a life cycle of its own.We notice the desires that make us contract and quicken, and those that make us feel spacious, connected and aligned with the heart of things.As an adult, I still have my hands in the junk food drawer. But the difference, perhaps, is I can see desire for what it is: a powerful intersection of body, evolution, memory, imagination and culture, something that is much bigger than me.Wanting need not be pushed aside, nor automatically followed.Instead, I imagine my late grandmother asking: “Are you hungry or do you want a cuddle?”Both!“Why don’t I fetch you a snack and a blanket and we can rest here together?”Dr Nadine Levy is a senior lecturer at theNan Tien Institute. She coordinates its health and social wellbeing program and the graduate certificate in applied mindfulnessExplore more on these topicsBuddhismMaking sense of itReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Walking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of England | John Harris | The Guardian
description: The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we should, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we should, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionHostelsWalking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of EnglandJohn HarrisThe landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we shouldSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.06 EDTShareAfortnight or so ago, my two teenage kids and I set out on a three-night visit to the Peak District where temperatures were hovering at a comparatively tepid 28C. We stayed at a youth hostel – more of which in a moment – and began the trip with the 20-minute ascent ofMam Tor, a modest peak that pulls in both dedicated ramblers who then yomp along the ridge beyond, and newbies who mostly want to get to the top and immerse themselves in the jaw-dropping view.The next bit might sound self-parodically Guardian-esque, but what the hell: in its own way, the most striking sight was the diversity of the scores of people rambling up, down and along. Women in their 20s wearing hijabs picnicked on giant rocks, while multiracial gaggles of young men attempted to race to the top; solo and shirtless white fitness freaks and retirement-age dog walkers took their places alongside them. With plenty of justification, country walking has long been typified as one of the most monoculturally white pursuits there is. But here – presumably because of the relatively close proximity of Manchester and Sheffield – things looked different.The scenes didn’t quite suggest Britain in microcosm, but they weren’t far off. I began to wonder, in fact, whether I was witnessing the (extremely) belated next emancipatory phase of a story that began with themass trespassat the nearby Kinder Scout in 1932, led by the Jewish anti-fascist Benny Rothman: the protest in which hundreds of men and women defied the law to walk on privately owned Derbyshire hills and moorland. Five of them received prison sentences, but the way was thereby opened to the creation of the UK’s first national parks.The latter-day people and organisations working tomake walking more inclusive– in response to national statistics that remain depressing, and often in the face of straight-up prejudice – surely deserve as much praise as Rothman and his comrades.Black Girls Hikewas founded in 2019 by the brilliant Mancunian Rhiane Fatinikun, aimed at creating “a safe space for Black women to explore the outdoors … challenging the status quo”. Soon after, the Coventry-based rambler Haroon Mota startedMuslim Hikers, and began group walks just over a year later. In the same city, Cherelle Harding createdSteppers UK, intended to “normalise black and brown faces in outdoor spaces and create a community of outdoor enthusiasts”.All this reflects aspects of our culture and politics that can be fascinating and inspiring – and, on the other side of some modern political and cultural divides, very unsettling. If he were to visit the Peak District, Nigel Farage would presumably get no further than his chosen pub. But his vision of bucolic England is symbolised by the outfit he tends to wear when he wants to accuse the supposed metropolitan elite of neglecting the countryside, usually by turning up at one of those faux – or not so faux –fox hunts. We all know the drill: flat cap, Barbour jacket, wellies, fag and pint. The cosplay is replete with meaning, and not just in its embodiment of what a cultural-studies specialist might call white rurality. Look, for example, at the terrible twist Farage and his political allies got their collective knickers in over theNational Trust’s driveto be open about some of its properties’ links to colonialism and slavery, and the same organisation’scampaigning to protect the environment.Further to the right, somewhere in the heart of every nativist lurk darkly romanticised visions of the British landscape – think of what is meant by that toxic phrase “blood and soil”. Last year, news broke about two wooded stretches of land in mid-Walesbeing bought by the Woodlander Initiative, a scheme led by the far-right activist Simon Birkett. He has links to Patriotic Alternative, reckoned to be the UK’s largest fascist organisation. The people involved were never going to be interested in urban land: to the fascist mind, the countryside, as opposed to the cosmopolitan and decadent stereotypical city (think about the far right’s constant demonisation of London), represents notions of racial purity and noble simplicity. From some far-right activists, there was sympathetic talk in response about “indigenous heartlands – places for our people”.The upshot of all this is obvious: the UK’s rural expanses can be as toxified and contested as any other aspect of our national life, and without wanting to sound too dour – walking is meant to be fun, after all – we need to actively promote the idea that the countryside belongs to all of us. To do so is to deprive the assortment of opportunists and hate-mongers who span the hard and far right of any idea that the British landscape and its romance and mythology might be theirs to monopolise.There is another, much more benign and everyday obstacle to maximising access to green spaces. In many places, hotels and hospitality increasingly embody a different kind of exclusivity: the upgrading of pubs and hotels to boutique, gastro-centric establishments with sky-high prices. Those charged on such platforms as Airbnb are part of the same problem. So if your ambitions extend further than a day trip and such luxury is beyond your budget, where can you stay?Part of the answer lies with the Youth Hostels Association (YHA) of England and Wales (the equivalent north of the border is Hostelling Scotland) and its network of places to eat, sleep and socialise. But the pandemic caused the YHA an incomeloss of £40min the first year alone, and in March last year, it said that its energy costs had quadrupled. In 2023, it had about 150 hostels; to date, it has announced the sale or closure of 29. Eight are now run as hostels thanks to a YHA franchising scheme, and there are similar hopes for at least one of my threatened favourites: Bellever on Dartmoor, one of the most idyllic places I have ever spent the night.But here is the crucial point: the YHA runsa programmethat provides fully or “partly funded stays at youth hostels for young people and families facing significant challenges” (including young carers, and those involved in refugee and migrant groups), and a scheme calledNo Child Left Behindthat helps to ensure that financial hardship does not stop kids going on residential school trips. It is an organisation that should be expanding, not shrinking.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving come down off Mam Tor, I drove the half hour back to where we were staying: Hartington Hall, a 17th-century manor house owned and run by the YHA. As we were having dinner, I noticeda plaquefixed to the wall, presumably dating from the distant days (the YHA was founded in 1930) when guests were obliged to muck in with the chores rather than sample the £14 burger-and-beer meal deal. “This youth hostel,” it said, “is one of many, both in this country and abroad, where young people, regardless of race or creed, may spend the night. The buildings are diverse in character but they have a common purpose: to help all, especially young people of limited means, to a greater knowledge, love and care for the countryside.”How, then, to preserve as many hostels as possible, bring in more young people and make those words real? An injection of cash from big-spending philanthropists? A modest tourist tax on hotels and short-let accommodation? Or the kind of relative loose change that could presumably be found by the departments for Food and Rural Affairs, Education, Culture, Media and Sport, or all three? Some parts of the British landscape are starting to undergo what seems to be an overdue and very welcome social change, but it needs the kind of support that comes in the form of bunk-beds and brickwork. In a country whose divisions are constantly inflamed and hyped up by demagogic chancers, that challenge is a lot more urgent than it might seem.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHostelsOpinionPeak District holidaysWalkingHobbiesHealth & wellbeingRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: When I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinised | Sanghmitra Singh | The Guardian
description: The city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendliness, says human rights lawyer and farmer Sanghmitra Singh
Author: Sanghmitra Singh
Headline: The city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendliness, says human rights lawyer and farmer Sanghmitra Singh
Content: An anti-racism demonstration in Glasgow, 13 June 2026.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn anti-racism demonstration in Glasgow, 13 June 2026.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionScotlandWhen I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinisedSanghmitra SinghThe city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendlinessSun 23 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 05.11 EDTShareScottish people have always been known for their friendliness. “We’re not like the south of us,” they say, referring to England. The official slogan of Scotland’s largest city, “People make Glasgow”, appears everywhere – on T-shirts, buildings, bus stops and mugs. And when I first moved to Scotland from India in 2018, I was immediately welcomed by kind strangers and helpful neighbours. People showed curiosity, rather than intrusiveness. They respected queues; told me I fit right in. Music, art and cultural events were considered inclusive spaces in the city, with calls for diversity, creativity, inclusion – all the good things.As an outsider, this was a dream come true: to be myself, to be alone, to have brotherhood and a community. It was life-changing. I could do whatever I wanted, wear whatever I wanted, walk by myself at night, even. That is a luxury, especially for a woman. But something has changed, particularly after Covid, a global recession and years of austerity. Now, I watch the steady rise of far-right, fringe violence and I feel a special scrutiny upon me.In June, we saw disorder and racists assaults in Glasgow as hundreds of masked protesters marched through the streets. Asian business owners were harassed and people were attacked – according to the police – “because of the colour of their skin”. Later that month, a man wascharged with attempted murderafter allegedly attacking men leaving a mosque in Edinburgh. A video appeared to show him shouting that he was “protecting the country”. In July, a delivery driverwas assaultedafter anti-immigration protesters, many of them masked, some shouting racist abuse, once again “rampaged” through Glasgow. We have seenmosques defacedwith “hate graffiti” – one is attacked in Britainevery five days, according to new data. We’ve heard a speaker at a protest outside an asylum hotel in Falkirk calling for a crowd to “keep Britain white”. There have been activists outside the Scottish parliamentstaging fascist-style demonstrations. It goes to show top-down propaganda funnels to real-life incidents.I feel this increasing hostility personally, too. Strangers point-blank question me about my nationality, accent, religion or clothes. A stranger once told me that my accent was weird. Anacquaintance said immigrants were taking away jobs from locals, after I told them I was struggling to find work despite being qualified. People jump queues and are quickly confrontational. The “outsiders” that Glasgow loved and accepted have seemingly become the subject of derision and suspicion.I find people staring at me, head to toe, for an uncomfortably long time. A customer in a Govan pub casually remarked aloud that immigrants are criminals and that we “need to go back”. An old lady on a bus interrupted me and my very white, very British husband to tell us to stop talking the way we were talking. Was it because we’re clearly an interracial couple? Is it because we categorically don’t sound like the locals? I’ll never know, but it’s gnawing now at the back of my mind when it never would have a few short years ago.Colleagues who have been here since the 1980s and earlier tell me that racist violence has happened inScotlandbefore, but this time it feels different. We’re afraid to step out now. There’s a clear, marked shift in our levels of nervousness. It is certainly more imminent, more immediate – closer to home.I blame a combination of factors for this unsettling change: the high cost of living, the worsening climate crisis and the rightwing agenda of some of the mainstream media have all increased resentment and suspicion of one’s neighbours. Then, during the Covid-19 pandemic, many people felt that they had been left alone. That the state wasn’t taking care of them as a democracy is supposed to do.Even a global health emergency, it seemed, couldn’t make for a better world. Instead of a fairer, more equal or accessible society, we haveextreme wealth inequalitythat is persistent and increasing. And it doesn’t help thatinflammatory posts are favouredby social-media algorithms. All of this creates a tinderbox in which people of colour understandably feel afraid.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform’s toxic thinking has infected Scottish politics – this week’s Holyrood elections will tell us how badly | Jasmeen KanwalRead moreMany places, including Leith and Glasgow, held anti-racist, pro-immigrant, pro-humanity rallies days after the racist incidents occurred. People carried signs reading: “Racism is weird, have you tried hobbies?”; “Migrants make the NHS”; “Hate has no home”. They made passionate speeches about standing up to bigotry. But is that enough? While it was heartwarming to see thousands of people come out, uniting for diversity, inclusion and multiculturalism, it won’t stop agrowing hatred and fearof people like me. And so every time I’m out in public now, my stress levels go up. Am I safe alone? What is my exit strategy? Can I even afford to be angry? Others feel it, too.I understand why many British people feel overlooked and badly done by – it’s true thatBritain is unequaland unfair. But I wish that the media would not validate people’s inherent biases and misconceptions, nor politicians legitimise their worst sentiments by calling for reactions like “pure, cold rage”. It is easy to whip up hatred between neighbours, but systematic hatred and divisiveness can take decades to undo. The only individuals who benefit from scapegoating are the powerful.We have to say “no” to this normalisation of bigotry, violence and othering. We have to focus on the living conditions and inequality we all share. We need to remember we have more in common with each other than with any billionaire. We must remember that the real blame lies with the system that wants us divided. Talk to real people who look and sound different from you. You’ll realise we’re all humans. We can do better than this.Sanghmitra Singh is a human rights lawyer and a writerThis article is published as part of a partnership with Pass the Mic, which works to amplify the expertise of women of colourDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsScotlandOpinionRaceFar rightWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘The country of my birth has lost its heart’: Miriam Margolyes on how to fix broken Britain | Miriam Margolyes | The Guardian
description: At 85, the actor has lived through much political upheaval. But, she writes, today’s hostile times feel like ‘the worst yet’. She reflects on her journey from teenage Tory to full-throated leftist – and says there’s still time to save the nation from the bad guys
Author: Miriam Margolyes
Headline: At 85, the actor has lived through much political upheaval. But, she writes, today’s hostile times feel like ‘the worst yet’. She reflects on her journey from teenage Tory to full-throated leftist – and says there’s still time to save the nation from the bad guys
Content: Miriam Margolyes: ‘It feels as though the country of my birth has lost its heart. How did we get here?’Photograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMiriam Margolyes: ‘It feels as though the country of my birth has lost its heart. How did we get here?’Photograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianMiriam Margolyes‘The country of my birth has lost its heart’: Miriam Margolyes on how to fix broken BritainAt 85, the actor has lived through much political upheaval. But, she writes, today’s hostile times feel like ‘the worst yet’. She reflects on her journey from teenage Tory to full-throated leftist – and says there’s still time to save the nation from the bad guysSun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfunny thing happened on the way to 2026: I got old and the world turned nasty. It happened very quickly and it’s to do with politics (the world) and pelvic floor weakness (mine). It’s strange being this old. Sometimes when I look in the mirror, it’s a shock to see wrinkles and grey hair, because inside I am still that naughty Oxford High School girl, risking detention just for the joy of entertaining her friends. People assume that with great age comes great wisdom, but actually we remain who we have always been, only more so, and we need to make our peace with that and with each other.The Britain I grew up in, though – that feels almost unrecognisable, and everyone I speak to says the same thing. The historian Eric Hobsbawm, whom I knew and loved, argued that people invent the past they want for their own purposes – that the real past was quite different: “Today is the great age of historical mythology.” He’s right, but that past is still the safe haven I’d like to return to. People feel adrift, they don’t understand or feel a connection to the place they thought they knew.Now at 85, I look around at my remaining friends and at my unique relationship with a woman of different qualities but luckily the same politics. In many ways I’m having the time of my life: I’ve never been richer or more in demand. And yet my heart is heavy with foreboding …My postwar generation lived through the rise and fall of many things: the Berlin Wall, Winston Churchill, the European Union, the NHS, the Beatles, Profumo, Elizabeth II, the Great Train Robbery, the pill, the IRA, Margaret Thatcher, the Falklands war, Black Monday and Grenfell, heart transplants, driverless cars, Brexit, the Covid-19 pandemic. But this feels the worst time yet.The things we took for granted – free speech, the Post Office, our local bank, even the home telephone – are disappearing. The US is an enemy. Evil oligarchs and their influence stalk the world, my world, your world. In recent times, thearchbishop of Canterbury resignedand north London Jews are afraid to wear a Magen David (Shield or Star of David) necklace outside their homes for fear of being attacked. You’re brave to open your mouth these days. Indeed, many have demanded I keep mine shut. But I can’t. The present has become threatening, hostile and unwelcoming to us – much as our shores must feel to asylum seekers, as they scramble for a foothold in our United Kingdom. It also feels as though the country of my birth has lost its heart. How did we get here?Now, I’m not usually one to tell jokes. Like my farts, my humour is largely unscripted. I love making people laugh, but at heart I’m a serious person, not just a funny little wobbly thing. I’m not a fan of jokes at the expense of others, those that are trite and mean and racist. But I’ve discovered that, in terms of the relationships and tensions between our nations, sometimes jokes go straight to the jugular.An Englishman is driving down a country road in Wales and realises he’s lost his way. He spots a localand pulls up alongside.“Dai! Dai!” he calls out in a lordly English accent,“which way is it to Cardiff ?” The Welshman eyes him up and down:“Just a minute now, how did you know my name was Dai?” The Englishman says,“I guessed, man! I guessed!”“Well, better guess your way to bloody Cardiff then, hadn’t you!”An Irishman, a Scotsman, a Welshman and an Englishman are on a plane which is going down and there is only one parachute. The Scotsman says,“Scotland will remember me,” and jumps out to his death. The Welshman says,“Wales will remember me,” and jumpsto his death. The Irishman says,“Ireland will remember me,” and pushes the Englishman out of the plane.I don’t think the English understand why their Welsh, Scottish and Irish neighbours loathe them so much. Like the Englishman in the first joke, they’re rather baffled by the hostility, while prolonging it with their arrogant attitudes. This behaviour is, of course, not isolated to them. It turns out that we Brits are even less popular abroad than we are with each other. The history of the British Isles is full of painful moments and terrible decisions. And we need to face those. It’s much easier to look away from bad things that happened and, as with a fart, hope no one noticed. (Spoiler: everyone noticed.) Like every multinational corporation, Great Britain plc has done a lot of harm in its long life. The choice of red to represent the British empire on the global map feels entirely apt. Take these unloving nicknames that zoom in on our annoyingness, inability to wear suncream and/or stop swearing:BrittunculiThis one’s the oldest: it was found on a tablet at the Roman fort of Vindolanda on Hadrian’s Wall, a Latin term showing exasperation and meaning “wretched little Brits”.PomsThis is what the Australians and New Zealanders call us. There are various theories: the late journalist Alan Whicker said “Pom” was short for pomegranate, the bright red colour a new arrival turns in the sun down under. Others claim that Pommie is really “POME”, which stands for prisoner of mother England, and thus the British convicts who were transported to Botany Bay.Rooinekor“redneck”The Boer nickname for the pale Brits, dangerously sunburnt again. Afrikaners of old had a ruder nickname for us, though –soutpiel(“salty penis”) – meaning that the Brits had one foot back home, the other in South Africa, so their penises were left to dangle in the salty ocean.LimeysThe American term, originating in the 1850s as “lime-juicer”, from the Royal Navy practice of adding lemon or lime juice to British sailors’ daily ration to ward off the scurvy that made all their teeth fall out.InselaffenTranslating as “island monkeys”, this is the Germans’ contemptuous nickname, supposedly dating back to Darwin’s theories of evolution.Les rosbifs“Roast beefs”; this French take is based on our fondness for a traditional Sunday roast. Historically they also called us “les goddams”, which originated in the hundred years war, referring to the typically potty-mouthed English soldiers. (So that’s where I got it from!) More recently, British tourists have been called “les fuckoffs”. Très charmant!My point is, history has always been the propaganda of the victors, but it can lead you astray. So why not try listening to the other side of the story? Don’t fall for your own hype. It all seems heroic if you turn it into a monologue about why you were right all along, instead of facing the painful bits from which there’s no way you can come out well.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jay Brooks/The Guardiandouble quotation markIt’s that rule of polite society again: one mustn’t rock the boat, ruffle feathers or put anyone’s nose out of joint. How absurd. Facts are factsOur British history needs to reflect our mother tongue, which is a patchwork of words gathered from the different tribes and peoples who’ve made these islands home. There’s room for everyone: we all bring something to the table, whether invader or inhabitant. The French word for a fanlight or transom window is vasistas and comes from the seven years war, when the German soldiers were baffled by the newfangled windows they saw in French houses and kept asking “Was ist das?” The French word is a joke, a snooty echo of the German reactions, but it stuck.People are always trying to fix language, but it remains on the move. The Normans tried to make England French; the English tried to ban the native Irish, Welsh and Scottish languages for “the greater common good” and then later to replace regional dialect and accents with received pronunciation. What idiots! Not only did they not succeed, but our shared language has ended up all the richer. If you can’t beat ’em, join ’em.Now I know many of my opinions – particularly those on politics, Palestine and Potter (Harry) – have provoked outrage. But I can’t help it – I believe in telling the truth, even if it’s my truth. In this, again, I realise I do not fit the English stereotype. The English excel at obfuscation, you see; they are masters at avoiding the truth. It’s that rule of polite society again: one mustn’t rock the boat, ruffle feathers or put anyone’s nose out of joint. How absurd. Facts are facts.My advice? If you believe someone is a liar, stay away from them. All around us, our politicians, news outlets and the media – the very people we are supposed to trust – are caught up in a relentless and divisive campaign of fearmongering and misinformation. Now it feels more crucial than ever to think for ourselves, debunk the deceits and sort the sheep from the goats.Mummy used to say “speak as you find”, and I think that’s an excellent way of sorting out decent folk from the vile. What unites us is far greater than what divides. Don’t be afraid to learn from everything wrong in our past – and there is a lot wrong in our past – let’s just do it better in the future.Ibet you didn’t know I was once a Tory candidate. But unlike most of the former Conservatives who have swelled the ranks of the current Deform party, I have grown into maturity and swung left. My campaign was in May 1955: I was 14 and in the upper fourth at Oxford High School. A general election was being held in the country, and we decided to hold one at school. Of course I was a Conservative: my parents had always been Tories – it was all I knew. They both worshipped Winston Churchill and credited him with having saved the United Kingdom from the Nazis. For Mummy, being Tory was a key part of her upwardly mobile climb, and so it was for my father, who, despite being a passionate supporter of the newly created NHS, could not imagine following Labour. They were delighted to hear I was the Tory candidate. We don’t remember who dared to stand against me in our form, or what my policies and promises were at the hustings – I was an old-school Tory and definitely pro capital punishment, so I dread to think – but I carried the day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLawrence Turner, the Tory who won the Oxford constituency when I won the upper fourth, went on to vote in favour of the Suez invasion, spend more than he earned and finally go bankrupt. Rather sweetly, one of his last parliamentary activities was presenting a petition to preserve the copyright of the words of WS Gilbert, one half of the prolific theatrical partnership Gilbert and Sullivan who created the comic operas that were the ironic soundtrack to the burgeoning British empire. Turner proved ineffectual again: he was not “the very model of a modern major-general” or even of a modern member of parliament, and copyright expired in 1961.Right seemed self-evidently right until I was assailed on two respectable fronts. After my election success, the father of my best chum from those days, Biddy Peppin, insisted I was invited to tea. He was that unusual thing, a leftwing bank manager, and his chosen task was to turn my path into a socialist future. And then another friend, Liz Hodgkin, also invited me for dinner. The Hodgkins were academic royalty – Liz’s mother Dorothy was later to win a Nobel prize – but they were committed socialists, too. You know how sometimes you can fall in love with a whole family? Well, I did. Their dinner guests were all communists and convinced Marxists (oh, that I had the courage to be a Marxist now, but that Putin, he puts me right off) and were winsome, hugely entertaining and great storytellers. Previously I had thought of communists as grim and humourless but boy, was I wrong. And so, eventually, this lady was for turning. I made a U-turn in the direction of sanity and humanity, and have never looked back. My parents were surprised and shocked by my new politics. But had they lived to experience the full horror of the last 14 years of Conservative reign under Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss and finally Sunak, I hope they, too, would have seen the light and embraced the left.The rise of the far right in Britain today can be traced back to a daft dyke. It depresses me to share that one of my fellow lesbians could be so silly, but the truth must be faced, and in 1923, Rotha Lintorn-Orman founded the first British fascist movement. In 1895 she was born in Kensington (where else?!) into enormous wealth. Obviously liking uniforms and women – and women in uniforms – she and a close chum originally wanted to join the Boy Scouts, but the Scouts wouldn’t have them. When the first world war broke out, she served as an ambulance driver, and was decorated for valour.After the war, Lintorn-Orman, a passionate admirer of Mussolini, formed the British Fascisti. But other, more extreme fascist societies proliferated and soon Lintorn-Orman and her cronies were outflanked. She descended into alcoholism and drug addiction, indulging in “drunken orgies and undesirable practices”, and her organisation died. But fascism would live on – from Oswald Mosley and his Blackshirts right through to Tommy Robinson.View image in fullscreenSet design: Victoria Twyman. Hair and makeup: Alice Theobald at Arlington Artists using Charlotte Tilbury and Living Proof. Stylist: Charlotte Gornall. All clothes, Margolyes’ own.Photograph: Jay Brooks/The Guardiandouble quotation markWhile the bad guys seem to be winning everywhere, I’m not giving up – and neither should youNow I’m old, I understand that older people like things “the way they were”. Me, too: I hate upgrades – be it in computers, in phones, in style, in my neighbours. I want what I had. And so, change (which the politicians tell us we want), I actively don’t want. Change makes me feel powerless and then I get angry and look for someone to blame. At least I know enough not to blame immigrants and asylum seekers. The mess the country’s in has got nothing to do with them, but too many of us have been bamboozled into thinking it has.I grew up knowing I’d receive a fine education and would get a job when I left university (which was free in 1963). Fascism had had its day, we thought. More than 70 million people had died to secure our freedom. But now racism was impossible to ignore, as one by one the last vestiges of the Empire started claiming their independence. The Windrush generation came to Britain – at the government of the time’s invitation – to staff our new welfare state, believing they were wanted and would be appreciated for leaving their homes and families, but finding the promised motherland felt harsh, hostile and unwelcoming.Taking advantage of this highly charged political climate, a new British fascist party – the National Front – was born in early 1967. The next year Enoch Powell, Conservative MP for Wolverhampton South West, made his “Rivers of Blood” speech. He posed as a brave visionary; perhaps he even believed that he was giving voice to the displaced white community of the Midlands who felt crowded out by Black and Asian immigrants.I knew straight away what Powell wanted to achieve with the speech: to fan the flames of public dissent. His Oxford education, classical training and powers of oratory served him well. He saw the race card as the way to obtain power. It still is.Today, a nasty little turd is floating about in our polluted waters. It has many names; one sticks out more than the others. A public schoolboy, posing as “one of the lads”; someone who thought it was funny to hiss at Jewish boys just after the second world war; someone who was given £5m to keep himself safe; someone who got German citizenship legally for his sons (his ex-wife is German) so Brexit disadvantages don’t inconvenience those close to him. There is a widespread fear that Farage (AKA the Odious Niggle) could succeed to the leadership; the kingdom is teetering on the brink of annihilation. But it’s not too late. After all, it is not the lie that passeth through the mind but the lie that sinketh in and settleth in it that doth the hurt. (Thanks, Francis Bacon.) While the bad guys seem to be winning everywhere, I’m not giving up – and neither should you.Exhausted by but addicted to doomscrolling, sliding from one terrifying headline to another, it’s easy to forget we are all in the same unsteady boat, north or south, young or old, lower, middle and even upper class, ignoring the culprits hiding in plain sight. It’snotthe foreigners, legal or illegal, who are pissing on us; it’s the billionaires who own the media and the internet and can pay the debts of the political parties they want to control, and fuck the rest of us. Well, I’m not putting up with it any longer. And neither need you. Let’s have a laugh. It’s the antidote (and all the ammunition) we need to those arseholes who forget that Britain was great before they were born – we can see right through them.Never forget that laughter is a good medicine, ridicule and satire can change minds, and there’s always sex. Mind you, it’s a while since I enjoyed the full-throated variety, but I know it’s out there.I refuse to be cut off from the wealth of possibilities that Britain and Ireland offer. Let’s live, have fun, learn new tastes, new words, new mastications. Build bridges, cross chasms. And before we go to the moon again, let’s reap the benefits strangers in our midst offer. It’s not their fault that things are tough. It’s ours. This is my middle finger to naysayers, Nigel Farage and everyone who says “whatever”. It’s time to be Great Britain again – or at least Better Britain. Steady the Buffs andonwards!This is an edited extract from Miriam’s Full English by Miriam Margolyes, published by John Murray on 3 September at £25.
