title: ‘So many people say things about my appearance – it’s not normal’: Jorja Smith on burnout, body-shaming and finding freedom | Jorja Smith | The Guardian
description: Being recognised by the Brits, Grammys and Drake made the singer one of British music’s most famous names – and also left her exhausted. Now, after decompressing in her home town she returns with a record made for raving
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Being recognised by the Brits, Grammys and Drake made the singer one of British music’s most famous names – and also left her exhausted. Now, after decompressing in her home town she returns with a record made for raving
Content: Jorja Smith … ‘I just love dancing. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m out.’Photograph: Ivor Lawson-AdamahView image in fullscreenJorja Smith … ‘I just love dancing. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m out.’Photograph: Ivor Lawson-AdamahJorja SmithInterview‘So many people say things about my appearance – it’s not normal’: Jorja Smith on burnout, body-shaming and finding freedomEmma LoffhagenBeing recognised by the Brits, Grammys and Drake made the singer one of British music’s most famous names – and also left her exhausted. Now, after decompressing in her home town she returns with a record made for ravingSun 23 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a sticky, sweltering July afternoon, and I have accidentally found myself at a wake withJorja Smith. I’m told that the pub where we have met, in the leafiest part of leafy south-west London, is usually a safe bet for an inconspicuous table. But today, sweaty black suits carrying pints drift between tables, and long queues snake round the bar.Dressed in a simple tank top, bare-faced with her hair scraped back, Smith is waiting for me when I arrive. “I’ve been waiting for my drink for ages,” she says. “But I feel bad saying anything because, you know …”The sombre mood doesn’t last long – in large part because Smith is effortlessly funny. When her alcohol-free sparkling wine finally arrives, she takes one sip, pauses for the waitress to disappear, then winces theatrically. “Oh,” she says. “That’s not good.” Every time we dissolve into laughter, I glance around guiltily, like we’re schoolgirls trying not to get caught talking at the back of assembly.It’s hard to imagine a less appropriate setting in which to discuss an album made for sunburnt block parties and 2am raves. What Are the Odds, the 29-year-old’s third album, released this week, is a certified, old-fashioned ass-shaker. Made with Richard Isong – the London producer better known as P2J, whose credits include Beyoncé, Burna Boy and Tems – and featuring the likes of Wizkid and Devlin, it is a vibrant collage of Black British dance music, weaving together UK garage, funky house, 2-step and Afrobeats, into a 12-track collection that pulsates from top to bottom.double quotation markI went straight to my label and said: ‘I think this is an album, not an EP. This is serious.’ I am so excited about itWhile dance music has always been threaded through Smith’s catalogue, usually in the form of a summer single – On My Mind in 2017, Little Things in 2023 – she is better known for her introspective, soulful R&B, as epitomised by her 2016 breakout single Blue Lights (whichNME praised as“a fantastically introspective and clever piece of songwriting”, and hadcritics declaring her Amy Winehouse’s successor). This is the first time she has committed fully to the dancefloor.“I just love dancing,” Smith shrugs. “I like going out to listen to music, a lot of my friends are DJs. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m outside.”The genesis of this album was different to her previous records. Her Mercury prize-nominated debut album, Lost & Found, emerged because she felt it was time to make an album. Its successor, Falling Or Flying, arrived because she felt she “needed” a second one. What Are the Odds was made almost accidentally, which is perhaps why it feels so light on its feet.After making the effervescent club single Little Things with P2J, the pair initially planned to write a dance EP. But the songs kept coming, and the project outgrew itself. “We went through nine songs in the first two days,” Smith says, her eyes widening again at the memory. “I turned up to the studio and he’d made all this music from our conversations. I left and went straight to my label and said: ‘I think this is an album, not an EP. This is serious.’ I’m so excited about it.”View image in fullscreenOdds on … Jorja Smith.Photograph: Ivor Lawson-AdamahThe album may be created for the dancefloor, but its emotional resonance remains unmistakably Smith. For Life mourns losing a friend to addiction; Young Heart is a love letter to Smith’s younger self; The Way It Was meditates on the end of a friendship. “If you just sang the songs with keys or piano,” she says, “they’d all probably be quite sad.”It is tempting to read What Are the Odds as a comeback album. In the weeks before its release, various headlines have announced Smith’s “return”. When I begin to ask her about this supposed break, she cuts in incredulously. “People keep saying, ‘Oh, you’re back!’ What do you mean, back? I’ve been on tour since 2017. When people say that, I’m like … [you should] check my calendar! People are likely talking about a ‘comeback’,” she says, “because I’m back on social media. I take breaks, and I’m not always out at events and things.”It’s an astute observation, and one that cuts to the heart of Smith’s unconventional relationship with celebrity. Since Blue Lights announced her arrival as an 18-year-old in 2016, she has become one of British music’s defining voices: a Mercury and Grammy nominee, double Brit award winner, and a featured artist capable of surfacing everywhere from Drake’s More Life to Burna Boy’s African Giant. Yet, she has never cultivated the kind of omnipresent celebrity that feels almost compulsory in the social media age, where visibility seems synonymous with existence. There are no carefully choreographed glimpses into her morning routine, no sense that her life exists to be consumed. Smith has clearly never been especially interested in that side of the bargain.“I never wanted to be famous,” she says. “I’ve always been quite private. I just wanted to put music out as a teenager and see what happened. I feel really lucky that I’ve got such an amazing fanbase and people really show me love, but fame was never the goal.”The tension, of course, is that success increasingly lives or dies by the algorithm. The defining British stars of recent years – PinkPantheress, Raye, Lola Young – have all been, in some part, forged in the fires of TikTok. Does Smith ever feel pressure to play that game? “Yeah definitely,” she says. “But, luckily, I’ve got a sick team, and we come up with ideas that we can do that are still me. I don’t want to be here doing trends – you’re not going to catch me doing TikTok dances or any of that stuff.”Her inclination to privacy also stems from growing up under an unusually unforgiving spotlight. Smith first found an audience by uploading covers to YouTube, recorded from her bedroom in Walsall. Aged 15, she signed with a manager, and began making regular trips to London for songwriting sessions. After finishing her A-levels, she moved to the capital full-time, working shifts in a cafe while trying to carve out a career in music.Blue Lights, which hauntingly paired Smith’s mellifluous voice with lyrics about police profiling and urban anxiety, landed on SoundCloud in 2016, instantly establishing her as one of the most compelling new voices in British music. The following year, Drake invited her on to his blockbuster playlist, More Life, exposing her to millions of listeners around the world.Alongside the acclaim, though, came another kind of attention. Almost overnight, Smith became a symbol of a modern beauty ideal, often uncomfortably sexualised before she had properly entered adulthood. For years, the conversation around Jorja Smith the musician existed alongside another conversation entirely, one that Smith had no control over: that of Jorja Smith the face, Jorja Smith the body. “It’s not normal,” she says, reflecting on that time. “Growing up and having so many people having something to say about your appearance.”The internet, as it tends to do, eventually turned. In the run-up to the release of Falling Or Flying in 2023, every online photo or video seemed to invite commentary on her weight. At one point, the phrase “Jorja Smith weight gain” trended on X for two days. It is something she brings up without prompting.View image in fullscreenJorja Smith picks up the Best British female solo artist award at the Brits in 2019.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImage“It was difficult. I’d be reading things like: ‘What happened to her?’ Or, ‘She’s let herself go.’” She trails off. “It really knocks your confidence.”On one occasion, she couldn’t resist replying. “Some blog page”– she waves away the name – “had put two photos side by side, like a before and after. I just commented: ‘What the hell, guys? I’m literally 18 in that picture. Why are you doing that?’” She shrugs. “People are so quick. They love you, then they hate you.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat made that period particularly disorientating, she says, was that the public narrative bore almost no resemblance to reality; at the very moment strangers were dissecting her body online, she felt healthier than ever.“I’d actually started eating properly,” she says. “Before that, I’d be so busy I’d skip meals, wake up late, I was running every day, obsessively. It was the first time I actually felt healthy, and then people wanted to criticise me? It was a proper headfuck because I was thinking: Wait … can I do anything right?”For a while, she stopped wanting to do photoshoots, or even go outside for fear of being photographed. “I sort of went into myself,” she says. “I felt like no one could really understand what I was going through.” Her coping mechanisms, she says, are to go for a walk or to the gym, though she catches herself revealing how fragile that equilibrium can still be.double quotation markI’m feeling the buzz of what London has to offer again, instead of feeling as if I have to wear armour all the timeSometimes she’ll still “see comments … and start thinking: Maybe they’re right?” She stops herself mid-thought. “Oh my God,” she says, laughing in disbelief. “Even me saying that now is crazy. Because they’re just random people!“But I have my days,” she continues. “I was talking to my mum about it the other day, and she was like: ‘At least they’re not saying you sound shit!’”One of the ways she’s protected herself is by stepping away from those online platforms. She no longer runs her own social media – her team posts on Instagram, and she only keeps the app to message artists and friends. She hasn’t been on X in years, and never goes looking for commentary about herself.Part of that self-reclamation meant physically removing herself, too. In 2023, after years in London, she moved back to Walsall – an unusual move for an artist at the height of their career. “I just needed a reset,” she says. “I thought: Let me move back home, touch some grass, see some trees.” London, she says, had become tangled up with the pressures of her career. This City, one of the tracks on What Are the Odds, explores her love-hate relationship with the capital. “Anything negative that happened, I kind of put London as the culprit,” she says. “I was like: ‘I hate this place. I need to get out.’” Distance has since softened London’s hard edges, and today, she divides her time between the West Midlands and the capital: “I’m feeling the buzz of what this place has to offer again, instead of feeling as if I have to wear armour all the time.”She is fiercely protective, too, of the place she comes from. In an industry so often centred on London, she is keen to keep reminding people that remarkable artists also emerge from elsewhere. “People forget I’m not from London,” she laughs. “And I’m not from Birmingham, either!” In September, Smith will return to Walsall for a home town show at Walsall Arena, a school turned community arts space she used to visit as a girl. Part of Spotify’s Hometown Billboard campaign, the bill doubles as a showcase of local talent: childhood friend Wesley Joseph, with whom she released the single July this year, supports, alongside the Blue Lights Choir she founded to create opportunities for young people in the town. “I hope it’s a moment that inspires the next generation to believe that big things really can come from Walsall,” she says.Jorja Smith review – mega-watt charisma powers ambitious new songsRead moreThese days, when she isn’t working, she is trying to build a life that exists beyond music. She walks, cooks and has rediscovered running. “I’ve signed up for the London marathon next year,” she says. “I wanted a goal, and I watched everyone finishing it this year and thought: That’s such a sick thing to do.”Despite her instinct to retreat from the spotlight, Smith is also consciously trying to step back into the world. Recently, she was on the phone with a friend back home when she mentioned turning down an invitation to a Vogue party. Her friend wouldn’t let it slide. “She was like, ‘Go! Not everyone gets invited to these things. You only live once. If you keep turning everything down, you’re going to be 70 and have zero stories of fun nights out because you never went anywhere!’” she laughs.Outside, the heat hasn’t lifted. Mourners are still in the beer garden. As she gets up to leave, Smith pulls a cap low over her face and slides on a pair of oversized sunglasses. Until that moment, it has been surprisingly easy to forget that she is famous at all.“It’s all about finding that balance,” she says, smiling as she stands. “But I’m feeling good. I’m starting to feel like my younger self again.”What Arethe Odds is out nowon FAMM.Jorja Smithperformsat Walsall Arena on 6 September.Explore more on these topicsJorja SmithDance musicR&BPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violence | Games | The Guardian
description: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards
Author: Jackson Ryan
Headline: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards
Content: A still from Halloween: The Game. The ability for players to smoke marijuana to detect an enemy has resulted in the game being banned in Australia.Photograph: IllfonicView image in fullscreenA still from Halloween: The Game. The ability for players to smoke marijuana to detect an enemy has resulted in the game being banned in Australia.Photograph: IllfonicGamesThe new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violenceAcademics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standardsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJackson RyanSun 23 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 21.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. The US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.But Australians will not be able to play Halloween, because it has been refused classification by the Australian Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders.In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that the Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of ComputerGames2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchiseRead more“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the boardwrote in a recent statement.In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game.The uproar has resurfaced longstanding grievances about how games are classified in Australia compared with film and television, and the inability for adults to access games widely available in other parts of the world.double quotation markCan we stop pretending that the way we classify games in Australia, in 2026, is appropriate for adults?Margaret Anderson, former director of the Classification BoardClaire Henry, an associate professor in screen at Flinders University and an Australian Research Council fellow, says the board enforced the guidelines correctly but the controversy around the decision highlights “a mismatch between the community standards and the classification standards”.The decision on Halloween: The Game follows several high-profile cases that have resulted in games such asState of Decay,Wasteland 3andSaints Row IVbanned in Australia for the same reason: incentivised drug use. All of these games were later reclassified after censoring aspects of their gameplay.View image in fullscreenSaints Row IV. The game was initially refused classification in Australia but was later released after a particular mission was removed.Photograph: Deep SilverDan Golding, a professor of media at Monash University, says that two assumptions have been baked into the classifying of games in Australia. “Games have always been regulated based on the assumption there is something more impactful aboutdoing,in a game, than there is aboutwatching,in a film,” he says.“A second assumption is that games are for kids – or at least the regulation system exists to protect kids.”Ron Curry has battled these assumptions in skirmishes with the Classification Board over his nearly two decades as CEO of the Interactive Games and Entertainment Association (IGEA). Alongside a dogged public campaign and a cadre of journalists, the IGEA helped introduce an R18+ category for video games in 2013, the absence of which had stopped several games being released in Australia before.After the R18+ classification was brought in, Curry noted the jobwas not finished– the trade-off for introducing the category was that video games were still seen as a distinct form of media, with greater risks attached.“It still very clearly said games are different to all other media, it’s more dangerous, and we need to treat it more carefully,” Curry says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSaints Row 4 refused classification in AustraliaRead moreInteractivity – thedoingGolding refers to – has always underlined this belief. The guidelines for games, introduced alongside the R18+ rating, state that “as a general rule computer games may have a higher impact than similarly themed depictions of the classifiable elements in film, and therefore greater potential for harm or detriment, particularly to minors”.Curry points tothe Australian government’s own research that hassuggested interactivity may not increase the impact of video games, particularly in regards to violent content, and there has been limited research on interactivity around drug use, sex, gambling and nudity.Margaret Anderson, a former director of the Classification Board, says the huge focus on interactivity in games drove her nuts during her seven years on the board. She points todecades of researchshowing games are predominantly played by adults.“Can we stop pretending that the way we classify games in this country, in 2026, is appropriate for adults? Because it’s not,” Anderson says.Academics have shown the current classification system isn’t just preventing access to games, however. Often, the standards are incoherent.Marcus Carter, founder of the Sydney Games and Play Lab at the University of Sydney, recently leda study– yet to be peer reviewed – that showed inconsistencies across the classifications of mobile games in the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. In 18 separate cases across the 31 top-grossing mobile games, four different age ratings were included for a single game.Carter describes the current system as “not fit for purpose”.The worry, for experts like Carter and Henry, is that the inconsistent standards have a negative impact on how the community views classifications and age ratings.“Inconsistencies can kind of undermine public confidence in the classification system,” says Henry. “It is a good system in many ways, and we’ve got to maintain that trust.”The Australian government isundertaking a review of the classification guidelineswith the aim of delivering a simpler, more consistent approach across films, games and publications. Among a raft of proposals – including introducing a PG13 rating and adjusting the MA15+ classification to MA16+ – one idea is to “remove the harsher judgement of video games’ interactivity”.IGEAandHenryhave made submissions to the review.In a statement to the Guardian,a spokesperson from the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts said: “The Australian Government is working to modernise the National Classification Scheme to ensure it remains aligned with community standards and helps Australians make informed decisions about what they read, watch and play. This work is ongoing.”Illfonic has shown no sign it will censor Halloween: The Game and have its classification reviewed in Australia. Illfonic and the game’s co-publisher Gun Interactive did not respond to requests for comment.Though the instances of Australia banning games have been rare occurrences, one future decision looms large: how will Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment in a franchise packed with sex, drugs and violence,be rated?For Anderson, the way forward is simple.“The foundational pillar of classification in Australia is that adults should be able to read, hear, see, play what they want,” she says. “Can we please respect that fact?”Explore more on these topicsGamesHalloween (2018)Horror filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: As You Like It review – French aristocratic trappings bring fresh comedy to Arden | Theatre | The Guardian
description: In a lively and deftly designed production, gowns and wigs fit for Versailles give way to plainer disguises as banished courtiers pursue happiness in the country
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: In a lively and deftly designed production, gowns and wigs fit for Versailles give way to plainer disguises as banished courtiers pursue happiness in the country
Content: Pomp … Lola Shalam as Rosalind leads a courtly procession through the Globe crowd.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenPomp … Lola Shalam as Rosalind leads a courtly procession through the Globe crowd.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewAs You Like It review – French aristocratic trappings bring fresh comedy to ArdenShakespeare’s Globe, LondonIn a lively and deftly designed production, gowns and wigs fit for Versailles give way to plainer disguises as banished courtiers pursue happiness in the countryArifa AkbarSun 23 Aug 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a play that pivots around the liberating disguises inside Arden’s bucolia, this production of the Bard’s pastoral comedy begins the dress-up long before its characters enter the forest for their games on gender and identity.Duke Frederick’s court resembles that of Louis XVI’s Versailles, with flamboyant gesticulations that seem to belong to Molière. It is Shakespeare, but it could be a French period romp. Costumes become plainer and more earthy in Arden. Is there a suggestion that these characters live their courtly lives in a constant state of disguise?It is probably not as deep as that in Sean Holmes and Charlie Josephine’s production, which seems to lead with great comic merriment above all else. The costumes appear an aesthetic decision, reflecting the pomp of a court. Rosalind (Lola Shalam), and Celia (Gracie Oddie-James), dispose of their enormous wigs and bustles in the glade, Rosalind replacing them with simple yokel garb as Ganymede, Celia still flouncing in exaggerated Little Bo Peep costume as Aliena.Many aspects of this production soar high, including the comedy, sublimely eked by almost every character. Touchstone (Jonnie Broadbent, bare-chested with lacy ruff) is a comic highlight, Jaques’ (Katherine Pearce) “All the world’s a stage” speech is quietly moving and Shalam is a commanding Rosalind, full of charm and cheek.View image in fullscreenCharm and cheek … Shalam with Charlie Josephine as Orlando, right.Photograph: Marc BrennerClass delineations are made deftly through costume and accent but with no sense of overstatement. So Orlando (played by Josephine) has an estuary accent which points to his lowly position among his brothers and lack of schooling, while Rosalind and Celia look and sound aristocratic.The forest has a stripped-down nature, with whiteboard backdrops on to which trees are drawn, first bare-branched but slowly coloured in to bloom. Paul Wills’ set design provides so much of Arden’s magic, along with the folksy musical accompaniment to Shakespeare’s many songs composed by Katie Richardson. The occasional winding in of the audience feels clever too, including a sing-along.And yet you never feel Rosalind and Celia’s closeness; the two stand at opposite ends of the stage as Celia declares “thou and I am one” after Rosalind’s banishment by Duke Frederick (Colm Gormley), but with a conspicuous sense of courtly performance that undercuts earnestness or intimacy. Later on, you do not feel Orlando’s infatuated flutters for Rosalind as he nails his poetry to the trees. Josephine plays him flatly, with little variety, although their performance certainly amuses. Thankfully, Shalam carries their romance, managing to be both arch and excitable in her passion.And although the comedy entertains, it takes away the play’s subversive edges, from the same-sex infatuation between Orlando and Ganymede to the alternative model for living that Duke Senior (also Gormley) encapsulates, in exile, and which seems a little lost among the fun.The production occasionally seems unclear in its action, although, what you lose in narrative clarity you gain in hearty comic frolics. Its achievement is ultimately this, along with its originality, which works a transformative kind of magic in itself, turning a familiar drama into something weirdly fresh.At Shakespeare’s Globeuntil 25 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreShakespeare's GlobereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was scared I was going mad’: Meg Mason speaks to fellow authors about the parasocial relationships that begin on the page | Fiction | The Guardian
description: As a lonely teenager, the novels of Nancy Mitford offered the Sorrow and Bliss author a lifeline, and an imaginary friend. She explores why reading can create a particularly intense bond with a favourite writer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a lonely teenager, the novels of Nancy Mitford offered the Sorrow and Bliss author a lifeline, and an imaginary friend. She explores why reading can create a particularly intense bond with a favourite writer
Content: Meg Mason.Photograph: Anne PeetersView image in fullscreenMeg Mason.Photograph: Anne PeetersFiction‘I was scared I was going mad’: Meg Mason speaks to fellow authors about the parasocial relationships that begin on the pageAs a lonely teenager, the novels of Nancy Mitford offered the Sorrow and Bliss author a lifeline - and an imaginary friend. She explores why reading can create a particularly intense bond with a favourite writerMeg MasonSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer before university, my mother gave me a copy ofThe Pursuit of Love. We’d moved countries at the beginning of my A-levels and those months in between had been defined by a level of loneliness I had never known in my life. The sort of loneliness so acute and pervasive it feels like panic, and on top of all that, so shaming to be 17 with nowhere to go and nothing to do on a Saturday night.Growing up, my mother – a great reader – would say: “When you’ve got a book, you’ve got a friend,” which is why, presumably, I wasn’t a great reader. Then, I’d always had actual friends. And suddenly I didn’t and presumably that is why I accepted the Nancy Mitford paperback and started to read it.I loved it, immediately. Finished, I asked if there were others and could we get them. I loved them all, more and more with every rereading. There was so much humour, and such solace in sad parts. The novels were so populated, I found company in the characters, and eventually in the person of the author too, privately coming to believe that if I had ever met Nancy Mitford, we would have become friends.Although my loneliness ended when university began, Nancy remained with me – never as intensely, but always there, so that now, age 48, I still find it hard to believe she isn’t actually my friend.I never would have described this as a parasocial relationship, although that’s precisely what it is: “a connection that someone feels between themselves and a famous person they do not know”, as the Cambridge Dictionary defined it when they announced it as theirword of the year in 2025. To me, the term sounded creepy, an activity of the unhinged. But if it’s common enough to become a word of the year, does that mean everyone is going about life with an imaginary friend? And we readers, especially?double quotation markIs everyone going about life with an imaginary friend? And we readers, especially?Although current, nothing about the phenomenon is new, the term devised in the 50s by a pair of academics studying the curious connection watchers of television appeared to feel with characters. Unsurprisingly, it’s tricky to gather statistics on relationships that exist solely in the mind. Oneonline studya couple of years back suggested that “51% of Americans have likely been in parasocial relationships”, though “only 16% admit to it”.While I was writingSophie, Standing There, my novel about a parasocial relationship between a reader and an author (even writing, I resisted using the term until there was no way around it), my non-imaginary friend Cathy Rentzenbrink was at work onThe Agatha Christie Cure, her memoir published next month about returning to her most beloved author in the period following her divorce. Had she developed a parasocial connection with Christie while rereading every one of her novels, and now writing about the author’s life? Yes, Cathy said, insofar as: “I started talking to her and she was talking back. I am a bit embarrassed, not by the experience, which was wondrous, but by what people might say or how they might judge me. I was often scared I was going mad.”She wasn’t. Not according to Dr Georgia Carroll, a sociologist whose research is focused on parasocial relationships. “I think almost every single person has had one, whether it’s with Taylor Swift, or the millions of people who feel connected to Lewis Hamilton.” While there are commonalities to all – “the key is that the relationship will never become reciprocal” – there is, Carroll believes, a uniqueness to the reader-author version. “With books, it becomes a bit deeper, more often, because they hold such a place in the lives of big readers. Everybody has that favourite book that is so meaningful to them because the author captured something that makes us feel less alone.”View image in fullscreenNancy Mitford in 1970.Photograph: Reg Lancaster/GettyWhether readers are more inclined to loneliness (and it’s in lonely periods that parasocial relationships are most easily formed), our chosen pursuit is solitary, performed only in company with the author. “That one-to-one element is critical,” says Carroll. “The feeling that the author is talking only to you.”And there is a sense in which book-lovers are most primed for parasocial relationships by the very fact that novels are about imaginary relationships between invented people, and our skill in reading is suspending disbelief. “Readers, as opposed to watchers, have been trained to fill in the gaps,” says Rentzenbrink, “to convert sentences into multi-dimensional worlds.”“I think it’s all too easy for the lines to be blurred between a character we love, and the author who created that character,” agrees book blogger Tilly Fitzgerald. “If a character is warm and funny, and the kind of person we would choose to be friends with, we can often assume the author will be too.”double quotation markNow, putting together a picture of an author's life is the work of one evening in bed with your phoneOver a lifetime of reading, Barbara Trapido, author ofBrother of the More Famous Jack(the cult classic that has surely made her the object of many parasocial relationships), has formed many “deep and extended relationships with characters. For half a year, aged 17, I believed IwasHenry James’s Isabel Archer.” And there was a period, she says, “in which I found myself, doubtless through yearning, talking to Shakespeare, but all unawares. It’s massively exciting to have the privilege of talking to the dead.”Because, in the case of reading, it doesn’t actually matter if the author is alive. “In fact,” Rentzenbrink says, “it makes it a bit easier if they aren’t.” And in a way safer, because they do not change. The politics to one side, the intensity of fans’ anger towards JK Rowling is largely grief for a lost friendship, a version of: “I thought I knew you and I didn’t.”With a living author, the sense of truly knowing them has become much keener. It wasn’t that long ago you could read an author without ever discovering what they sounded or looked like. Now, putting together a picture of their life is the work of one evening in bed with your phone. And when it comes to the creation of a parasocial relationship, nothing is more potent than the podcast. “It feels more intimate, doesn’t it?” says Jack Edwards, of the hugely successful literary podcast,Inklings Book Club. “We bring the author’s voice into our homes, on to our morning commute, into our safe spaces,” – in my character Sophie’s case, it’s always in the bath – “so it’s a together-aloneness, where we have company in our ears, but otherwise feel unobserved.” It goes both ways, Edwards points out. “We invite authors into our homes, through the listening experience, but often they record from their own homes too.”Which brings up the other side. That is, how it feels to be an author in this moment. Certainly, readers can be passionate – I have seen Sorrow and Bliss tattoos, inspired bymy last novel– but no one I’ve met in real life has wanted anything more than to chat about books, or to tell me what my work meant to them, and how could I be other than glad about that? Likewise, Trapido says, “I’ve always liked readers coming up to say how much they like my books, though, oddly enough, they often apologise for approaching.”Feel a connection to a celebrity you don’t know? There’s a word for thatRead morePerhaps the whole thing is the author’s fault anyway, because what we are constantly trying to do is connect, and make you believe in our characters. So the idea that some made-up version of me as an author has provided company for someone who feels as unsurrounded as I did before university, or as Sophie does in my new novel – at no cost to myself – is extraordinary and a privilege. I’m grateful too that Nancy was there for me when I most needed her, and still is. Everyone says we read to know we’re not alone. But you could also say, we read and so we aren’t alone.Sophie, Standing There is published by Bloomsbury on 27 August. To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: A supreme being, the nearly naked show and politics with paws: Edinburgh fringe pick’n’mix | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: From Taiwanese steampunk dance to Australian climate comedy, here are 13 quick-fire fringe reviews
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: From Taiwanese steampunk dance to Australian climate comedy, here are 13 quick-fire fringe reviews
Content: What on earth … Anna Leong Brophy: Born Sexy Yesterday.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWhat on earth … Anna Leong Brophy: Born Sexy Yesterday.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026A supreme being, the nearly naked show and politics with paws: Edinburgh fringe pick’n’mixFrom Taiwanese steampunk dance to Australian climate comedy, here are 13 quick-fire fringe reviewsAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsBrian Logan,Lyndsey Winship,Arifa Akbar,Kate Wyver,Tim JonzeandChris WiegandSun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 04.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnna Leong Brophy: Born Sexy YesterdayFor new perspective on the strange ways we behave, we all know the thought experiment “if a visitor from space arrived on Earth, what would they think?” In Born Sexy Yesterday, Anna Leong Brophy plays a supreme being implanted into a grown woman’s body to experience life for the first time. Presenting like some sci-fi sex robot with the soul of a naive child, Brophy duly marries a man on the front row and settles down to a life of domestic drudgery. Until she discovers she has other settings, other brands of femininity available for her to try out … Thus begins a potent hour, not always hilarious but undeniably persuasive, protesting against the strictly circumscribed roles that women are allowed to play – particularly in the movies, as Brophy sardonically demonstrates. The supreme-being conceit dilutes a bit – but our host’s righteous indignation and strong performing chops make this a compelling hour.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustTaiwan Season: Under MaskSome of the best dancers I have seen at the fringe are from Mailantia Dance Company, led by choreographer Lai Yun-Chi, who has danced with Hofesh Shechter’s junior company in London. It is worth singling out Huang Hsiao-Wen, who moves with incredible flow and compelling presence. Under Mask is a quartet for dancers dressed in steampunk-style masks and painted faces – the theme of identity, masks and the roles we play don’t come through much more meaningfully than that, but the way they move with swagger and mystery is enough. The piece is inspired by Taiwanese temple rituals and has that feel of something ancient, mythical or spiritual, even when the movement recalls commercial pop. It also draws on martial arts, hip-hop and contemporary dance, and you can see hints of Indian classical dance, maybe even flamenco at one point. A choreographer to watch out for.LWAtAssembly @ Dance Baseuntil 30 AugustView image in fullscreenGreat fun … Lauryn Jenkins in Big Dog.Photograph: Danny KaanBig DogPromising young writer-actor Izzy Radford’s debut play, Seating Plan, was a romcom set at a birthday party. Now she has penned an exuberant satire about a group of true-crime podcasters. Directed by Zoë Templeman-Young, Radford stars alongside Lauryn Jenkins as a fellow podcaster and Tumba Katanda as a journalist and office newbie, with Eleanor Cross as a disgruntled listener. There are energetic performances across the board, but it verges on the chaotic at times and is overstuffed with ideas, wavering somewhere between a true-crime parody and a dark comedy in the vein ofSeverance, for its observations on managerial-level, white-collar tyranny and conformist office behaviour. Great fun to watch, even if it feels underdeveloped in this current state.AAAtGilded Balloon Patter Houseuntil 31 AugustRosalie Minnitt: Clementine 2“A single baguette is worth 1,000 francs – and a married one far more!” Inher smash-hit maiden show, Rosalie Minnitt’s Regency-era alter ego Clementine tried to find a husband. In its follow-up (and in a bid, jokes Minnitt, to pass the Bechdel test), our heroine makes for the big city, to get caught up in a revolution with a distinctly French flavour. And taking to the streets amid popular revolt could scarcely be more disorientating than Clementine 2, an absolute blizzard of character-comedy that confirms Minnitt as a writer/performer in the vanguard. Does it pack quite the punch of its predecessor? Perhaps the satirical bite of Clementine 1.0 is lacking. Is its plot throwaway bordering on incomprehensible? It is. But this adventure in self-realisation for our bumptious, puppyish heroine (befriending Dickensian pickpockets; orchestrating the regicide of the king; flirting shamelessly with the audience) makes up for that abundantly in chaos, silliness, smarts and Minnitt’s full-pelt approach to comic performance.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustView image in fullscreenFolky celebration … The Palestinian Circus: Step and a Half.Photograph: UnderbellyThe Palestinian Circus: Step and a Half“Hope is a daily choice,” says a voice at the opening of the Palestinian Circus’s Step and a Half. “As long as the heart continues to beat, we keep on moving.” The Palestinian Circus has been running for 20 years, teaching children across the region and spawning this collective of artists. Not all the acts are at the technical level you become accustomed to at the fringe, but that’s not to say there isn’t some great work on the trapeze, straps and silks, taking nosedives from the ceiling. There’s a street performer feel, with fire poi and one guy who seems a very average juggler and then turns out to be a demon on the diabolo. It’s all enveloped in a folky, celebratory atmosphere, with traditional dabke dancing, too. “Joy itself is an act of resistance,” they say. It’s an easy show to feel warm towards.LWAtUnderbelly’s Circus Hub on the Meadowsuntil 29 AugustAhir Shah: Golden“Three hundred people looking one way, and one person looking the other. How do I justify that?” So asks comedianAhir Shah, and his answer is: honesty, about where he’s at in his life right now. That’s a laudable principle, but the result in Golden suggests honesty isn’t always the best policy – or at least, not in this dosage. The show finds Shah 35 and married, so overworked and anxious about money he develops a severe allergic reaction to his own life. Pile on depression, autism, a fire in his parents’ house and the expounding of his pessimistic view of midlife stasis with no further possibility of personal growth, and you get a show that no amount of decent jokes (of which there aren’t quite enough) can jollify. What’s left is an hour with a man grappling with his own mordant worldview, towards a sunnier conclusion – and probably towards a show striking a better balance as it develops between dark humour and despondency.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustView image in fullscreen‘What my mum thinks all fringe theatre looks like’ … Fanny Bleach: The Nearly Naked Show.Photograph: Ray MaloneFanny Bleach: The Nearly Naked ShowThis is what my mum thinks all fringe theatre looks like. A skulking performer dressed as a many-eyed Ikea bag hag emerges from an overflowing bin to lip-sync with toothy aggression, before stripping down several layers and unhinging her jaw to scream into a microphone. From geordie clown Emma Crowley-Bennett, this is an irreverent cabaret “freak show” – but everyone else in the lineup has tapped out, leaving only nervous work experience kid Daniel to man the stage. Crowley-Bennett’s energy is high and her costumes and characters are inventively grotesque, with Ms One-Tit flashing us her single massive nipple, and a Prawn Star pulling out its dark vein to appease Daniel’s fishy fetish. But what might work as a subversive short slot in a more populated cabaret is dragged out, with not enough dramatic muscle to confidently pull us through. A show that’s yet to find its hairy green feet.KWAtAssembly Roxyuntil 30 AugustRosco McClelland: The BonesIt’s never a great sign when a comedian airs their difficulties deciding what their show should be about. Rosco McClelland settles on “pathological demand avoidance”, his own brand of stubbornness that resists anyone making demands on him. It provides a very tenuous frame for what is, in effect, several club-comedy routines strung together by the Glaswegian. When that’s the case – when your show isn’t really about anything – you’ve got to hit big joke-to-joke, and happily McClelland lands a few comic haymakers here. There’s some palate-cleansing material about Scotland’s World Cup (mis)adventure, and a dopey anecdote about “ladling piss from a dog”. Later, an argument with his wife about a picture posted on Facebook (and this oneisabout demand avoidance) ends with a very satisfying punchline, and his shaggy-dog story about a supposed cyborg nemesis stacks laugh upon ridiculous laugh.BLAtMonkey Barrel Comedy(Cabaret Voltaire)until 30 AugustView image in fullscreenTrapped in a novelty news story … Meet Mayor MaxMeet Mayor MaxFirstly: awwwww! If you love puppy pics – and what kind of heartless fringegoer doesn’t? – then Alex Robins will quickly have you eating out of the palm of his paw. When Robins is dressed in dog ears and yapping away, a PowerPoint presentation is always on hand to bring coos of affection. This one-man play tells the true story of Max, a golden retriever who becomes the mayor of the sleepy California town of Idyllwild. So beloved is Max to this community of artists and hippies that, when he dies, a second Max is installed, and then a third (Maximus Mighty-Dog Mueller III currently serves there with a lifetime term). The play is billed as a story of hope but it can feel like you’re trapped inside a novelty news story. Robins is an engaging performer with an unsettlingly messianic edge, but we’re left with too many unanswered questions: what happens after Idyllwild’s citizens start voting for Trump? How exactly did Robins extract himself from scientology? The ending – no doubt like lovely Max himself – needs a sharper bite.TJAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 31 AugustCrushHadsan Mohamud’s debut play, longlisted for the 2025 Tony Craze award, oozes charm. It is a kooky kind of meet-cute in a mental health clinic for people with eating disorders where two British Somali teenagers become friends. When Najma (played by Mohamud) spots Zak (Mohamed Hashi), she finds him pretentious. But they are drawn closer, slowly opening up to each other, in Alena Sahota’s production. Although full of painful truths and culture-specific reflections, it plays out haltingly and rather statically. The couple are sweet although the romance seems contrived. But it captures the insidious and insistent nature of eating disorders and we fear for the outcome of these teenagers in their rocky journeys towards healing.AAAtUnderbelly, Bristo Squareuntil 30 AugustView image in fullscreenToo hot to handle … Alex Hines and Sarah Stafford in BirdsBirdsJust sit back and enjoy the heat?Richard Tice should try telling that to this pair.House of Oz’s apocalyptic two-hander, created by Alex Hines and Sarah Stafford, opens with two toweringly beehived ladies of leisure, Shayna and Beverley, on deckchairs beneath the punishing sun. As the booze from the cooler slips down, they watch the birds above whose cackling cries and sharp talons they share – along with the instinct to beak into each other’s business. It can feel like a cheeky camp spin on Caryl Churchill’s Escaped Alone and the flights of fancy build in terrible rage until a rat-a-tat finale delivered almost at the pace of Beckett’s Not I. As their skin begins to peel and houses collapse into the ocean, in a luridly painted show that feels a little over-extended, you may need to lie down in a shady spot yourself.CWAtAssembly George Squareuntil 30 AugustBurger and a Pint: Treats for the SoulSketch duo Burger and a Pint (AKA James Trickey and Ted Milligan) won the Leicester Square Sketch Off in 2024 and arrive promising to explore “expectations of masculinity” in their debut fringe show. That promise is not fulfilled by a conventional and fairly slapdash offering with nothing to say about masculinity whatsoever – unless there’s deeper meaning sublimated in that Indiana Jones-alike sketch about having to amputate your penis to enter an ancient temple. That’s blokey par for the course in a show that reaches its nadir with a sketch in which a puppeteer must repeatedly insist that he doesn’t have sex with his puppets. There’s better stuff elsewhere: a choice Mastermind sketch; Dickens’ Fagin on Diary of a CEO. The between-scene banter, and the relationship it reveals, is unsurprising. Even allowing for tech difficulties at the performance I saw, it all feels a little underworked.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustJonathan Oldfield: Exquisite CorpseOldfield makes his solo debut this year but he’s been an unseen presence in recent hits, includingLorna Rose Treen’s workandJoe Kent-Walters’ debut as Frankie Monroe. This character-comedy effort is a real eye-catcher, similar to Treen’s in its array of apropos-of-nothing oddballs, yet with a flavour entirely its own. It derives from the kids’ doodling game sometimes called exquisite corpse, in which legs, torso and head, all drawn by different people, are united to create unlikely bodies. Oldfield plays it with his audience here, and feeds the results into his gallery of eccentric creations: an allotment gardener with a sideline in erotic dancing; a Blockbuster video clerk pining for a son. The linking narrative about Oldfield breaking his arm seven times, and how that led to an ambivalent relationship with his body, can feel tenuous – but this is a captivating hour on corporeal fragmentation and reassembly.BLAtPleasance Courtyarduntil 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsIn the UK,Beatcan be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In the US, theNational Eating Disorders Associationis on 800-931-2237. In Australia, theButterfly Foundationis at 1800 33 4673. title: When my husband died in a surfing accident, life as I knew it was destroyed. Ten years on, this is what I’ve learned about grief | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: One crashing wave on one single day changed everything for our family. How would I keep going?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: One crashing wave on one single day changed everything for our family. How would I keep going?
Content: ‘Grief is a sinkhole, opening up where real life once stood’: Hannah Richell at Tamarama beach.Photograph: David Maurice Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Grief is a sinkhole, opening up where real life once stood’: Hannah Richell at Tamarama beach.Photograph: David Maurice Smith/The GuardianAutobiography and memoirWhen my husband died in a surfing accident, life as I knew it was destroyed. Ten years on, this is what I’ve learned about griefOne crashing wave on one single day changed everything for our family. How would I keep going?Hannah RichellSun 23 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 17.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore they enter the water, surfers will study the ocean. They consider wind and tide conditions. They analyse currents and patterns, break points and swells. They try to read the waves. I have travelled across oceans and a day to sit here on Tamarama beach in Sydney on a high-tide weekday morning in 2024. A notebook and pen lie beside me on the sand as I, too, attempt to read the waves, to find meaning in their unfathomable churn.These past 10 years, this beach has loomed large in my mind. Even when absent, it’s as if my face has been turned to these waves and I have been buffeted, sometimes staggering, sometimes falling, always bracing for the next set to roll in. For I have learned that all it takes is one ocean, one day, to come along and knock you off your feet.Sydney, 2014It’s an ordinary Wednesday afternoon in Sydney, the first week of July, when two plainclothes police officers knock at our front door. I am not home to greet them. I am a few streets away, buried in my studio, wrestling with the tangled threads of a novel, when I receive a call from my husband’s PA.“I’ve had a call from a Bondi detective,” she tells me. “They were asking for your address. I can’t reach Matt.”I grab my laptop but leave everything else in place and try Matt’s number as I half-run, half-walk up the steep hill to our house. No answer. I call our childminder. “Weird question but has anyone come to the house?”“Yes,” she says. Her voice is different, strained.“Police?”“Yes.”The red front door to our tiny sandstone cottage is shut tight. Through the glass pane I see two figures in dark clothing standing in our living room. I fumble for my keys. The door opens and I cross the threshold.“Hannah Richell?” they ask. I guess I nod, and they introduce themselves as police detectives. One of them, I think, has tears in her eyes.I glance between them, my panic rising, until the more composed of the two comes right out with it. “I’m sorry to tell you your husband has been in a surfing accident.”“Is he OK?” I’m already running through childcare options to make a hospital dash.“I’m afraid he died.”I’m still in my coat and boots. My laptop bag hangs from my shoulder. I look down at the old wooden chest that stands in the front room, doubling as a coffee table, and notice an unfamiliar box of tissues sitting on its surface – a box of tissues I have not bought or placed there. A small part of my brain, one not yet numbed by shock and disbelief, registers that the police must have brought it. I look at the tissues, then back to the police. My bag slides from my shoulder to the floor.On the way to the morgue, I gaze out of the window. He is dead, I keep telling myself. You are going to view his body. But I don’t truly believe it. I will see the body and I will feel only relief, because of course it won’t be him. There is no way it can be him, my warm, vivid, drily funny, thoroughly alive husband. It will be another man, belonging to another family, who are at this very moment unaware of the tragedy that awaits them. I will leave the morgue dizzy with relief and return to the life I should be living.But it is him.And it isn’t.The body in the blue gown lying on the gurney belongs to my husband, but it isn’t my husband as I knew him. What lies before me is a stiff wax model of the man I love.Matt. But not Matt.It is the longest, shortest, most loving, most painful hour of my life. One hour alone, to kiss and caress him. To stroke his stubbled cheek and hold his hand and lay my head upon his chest and weep. Kissing his temples, I see the cuts on his face and a diamond crosshatch line of stitches across the back of his head from the autopsy. The sight of those stitches makes me reel. They have cut open his beautiful skull. The one I absent-mindedly caressed while reading on the sofa, the prickle of his shaved head under my fingers. The one my three-year-old daughter would stroke while high on his shoulders and proclaim “spiky” with a giggle. I try not to think about what else they have had to do to him.From our inauspicious beginning, when Matt joined the London publishing company to steal the promotion I had coveted, to a deep bond forged through travel, marriage and babies, I sit in this closed, quiet morgue and remember words written in my diary as our first new year together had raced towards us. “Don’t let him hurt me,” I had written, imploring an unseen, unknown power. I suppose I knew, even then, that a love like this could break my heart.View image in fullscreenHannah and Matt on their wedding day in 2007.Photograph: Hannah RichellWendy, a counsellor from the forensic science team, enters the room and sits quietly with me. “You’re very affectionate with him,” she says.“I thought his eyes were opening,” I tell her, knowing how crazy I sound for still wishing that they might.“That can happen,” she admits. “Muscles can relax.”“He smells different.”“They will have washed him,” she says.Though not as carefully as they’d intended, perhaps, for when I try to hold his stiff hand, grains of Tamarama sand fall from his palm into mine. They feel like a last gift: a piece of the country he loved so deeply. Precious. I want to scoop the sand up and take it home with me, carry the grains around in a locket, but they slip through my fingers and fall to the floor, disappearing with the sound of my crying and the last kiss I leave on his lips.Itext Adam, the friend who was with Matt when he died. “Hi, this is Hannah, Matt’s wife. Yesterday must have been terrible. Are you OK?” We tread carefully, cautiously polite, until Adam offers to come to our home and talk me through what happened. He is a virtual stranger at my front door, but the moment he steps over the threshold, I am with him. The connection feels instant and real. We sit for a couple of minutes on the sofa in our front room, but the kids are noisy in the background and the house feels claustrophobic and all wrong. “I need to get out of here. Can we get some air?”Adam looks relieved.We walk to the park and sit on the grass. It is strange but, out here, in the sunshine and clean air, I feel calmer. Adam’s presence is comforting, like a blanket, muffling me from the horror of the last few days. Slowly, he begins to tell me about the accident. He talks of their joy paddling out from Bronte beach, two work friends choosing to talk shop on their surfboards rather than over lunch in an overpriced restaurant. “Surely this must be the definition of success?” Adam had said.“Yep,” Matt had replied, and when Adam says it, he delivers it just as Matt would have. In that one word I can see Matt in his wetsuit, straddling his board, salt water in his stubble and a wide grin plastered across his face as he gazes towards the horizon.double quotation markHe must have had hope, until that last wave, rushing at him, pushing him forwards. The cliff rising upAdam tells me of the suddenly shifting tide conditions and of seeing Matt’s board come loose. He describes the rip, pulling Matt dangerously close to the rocky Tamarama headland. I sense his internal struggle as he relives the tragedy, and I sit quietly, listening.Adam’s explanation comes to its end. The swallows are dancing around us, twisting and looping over the grass. I lean back and close my eyes. For the very first time since I arrived home to find the police in my house, I feel my heartbeat begin to slow in my chest. It’s shock – madness – but for a moment it’s as if he is here with us. Three people, not two, Matt’s presence hovering lightly between us.“Have you talked to Wendy?” Adam asks.“Wendy at the morgue?”“She offers counselling. You might want to call her.”My mum appears at the far edge of the park with the kids. They have a soccer ball. I point them out and Adam sprints away to kick the ball back to my son. They play like any others in the park around them – a man and a boy kicking a ball back and forth across the grass – but watching them, I feel a deep pain radiate through my body for all that our children have lost.Grief is a sinkhole, opening up where real life once stood. A cavernous black void swallowing everything I hold dear. Life as we know it has been destroyed in a single day by one crashing wave. The world feels tilted. How to process the enormity of what has happened when everything shifts and moves around me?I visit Wendy for a counselling session. We sit opposite each other in a small windowless room, a box of tissues on a side table at the ready. I am getting used to their subtle placement. I never seem to be far away from a box of tissues these days.Wendy exhales and smiles her greeting. “Hello,” she says. There’s a stillness in the air between us as we regard each other and the threshold we sit upon. Her opening question is to ask how I feel about coming to see her. I think about this carefully, trying to identify the fizzing adrenaline rush inside of me. “Excited,” I reply, then worry she will think me unhinged.“And why is that?” she asks, her face unchanging.“Because this was the last place I saw Matt. It feels like I am returning to him … although I know I’m not,” I add, certain she must think me mad. “I guess I’m excited to talk about him. Glad to be doing something.”I feel that painful ache in my throat, of everything broken held so tightly. “I can’t bear this pain. I need to know how long it will feel like this. I miss him.” That’s all it takes for me to dissolve into tears.There is no judgment from Wendy. No rules. Nothing off limits in our roaming conversations. As I discover in the coming months, sitting in this room with this woman, there is never any judgment, only compassion and a kind ear. Wendy gives me a safe place to explore everything Matt is and was to me, a space where I can crack open the dark chrysalis of grief. I think about her job title. Forensic counsellor. I like that. She allows me to examine the substance of my grief. Not just the macro experience of loss but all the tiny micro details I need to pore over. And afterwards, when I step out through the sliding doors of that building, I feel a lightness in my body that wasn’t there on walking in.Days and months pass in lonely, blunt-edged monotony, a low, breathless panic beating in my chest. I try to return to my novel, but my brain is treacle. I don’t know if it’s single-parent exhaustion or grief, or if there is something physically wrong with me, but the focus required to plot fiction feels beyond me. I have no capacity for creativity or imagination. “No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear,” writes CS Lewis. I am so full of fear. For the future, for my children, that they’ll grow up holding only the faintest outline of their father.A friend tells me about “memory jars”, how they can help grieving children access happy memories and start conversations about their lost parent. We sit down with pens and paper, and begin to talk about the things we love and remember about Matt.View image in fullscreen‘He loved us … and we loved him’: Matt with his daughter, aged three, in May 2014, two months before he died.Photograph: Hannah RichellMy daughter remembers swooping and giggling with her dad on the round saucer swing in the park. My son recalls curling into the crook of Matt’s arm when he read him a bedtime story. I remember the special light that shone in Matt’s eyes whenever he stepped from the waves after an ocean swim. We all remember the unique kind of grumpy he could get when he was hungry. I write each memory down on a slip of paper before placing it into the jar.“Singing Frozen songs at the top of his voice in the car.”“He made the best yorkshire puddings.”“He loved us … and we loved him,” my daughter says.The kids, needing sudden escape from the emotion, race outside. I can hear them squealing and laughing in the courtyard, on the edge of meltdown. It is heartbreaking to reduce the love of your life and the father of your children to fragments of memories scrawled on to pieces of paper, but it feels important. They remind us that he existed and the love was real. I turn the jar under the light, scraps of folded paper trapped in glass. How can it ever be enough?It’s an early spring day when I take the kids to the beach, a gentle bay with a dappled park, a shark net and tapering cliffs that curve to embrace the thin crescent of sand. It has been chosen carefully. No surf. No swell. No obvious signs of danger. We lay our towels on the sand, unpack fruit and water, buckets and spades, before the kids make a break for freedom.“Wait! Sunscreen! Hats!”My son returns grudgingly and allows me to apply the necessary sunscreen, then turns and scampers along the shoreline, lost to the sensory experience of the gently lapping water. I see him stop, then run back. “I’ll put your suncream on, Mummy.” He looks worried, and I hate this new responsibility he bears.Friends arrive. We drink coffee and watch the children dig tunnels in the sand.Go for a swim, Han. It’ll do you good.I hear it just the way Matt used to say it – teasing, goading, slightly exasperated at my reluctance to hurl myself into the cold waves he loved. I study the water, gently undulating, turquoise. I haven’t been into the ocean since his accident, but the water looks enticing, hardly foreboding.Fine, I think. Have it your way.I wade out quickly, eager to get through the chill and minimise the onslaught of emotion before diving under, my body tightening at the sensation of being enveloped. Not thinking. Just doing. Losing myself in movement.A little way out, I stop and float on my back. Blue below me and blue above me. My skin has cooled enough to feel the water like an embrace. I let go and for a moment it’s as if I am not being held by the water but by Matt. I feel him, right there with me, the warmth and pressure of him, and it is the strangest, most unearthly feeling.View image in fullscreen‘I hope he knew we were with him, holding his hand’: with Matt …View image in fullscreen… and their children in 2012. Photographs: Hannah RichellSettled there, I find the perfect, fleeting glimpse of him from another time, another beach. Shaved head, broad shoulders tapering to a slim waist, feet planted in the sand and arms folded. He is sun-speckled and his beard – longer in the holidays – is salt-crusted and scratchy. I notice how, even in this memory, his eyes don’t leave the sea. Whenever I think of Matt by the ocean, it is always like this. Turned away from me, his gaze fixed on the waves he was so drawn to.More and more, I find myself thinking about Matt’s last moments. Not so much the actual sequence of events now, but the experience of them. The sensation. The decision, turning to paddle, feeling the wave lifting his board. The surge of the water. The snap of his leg rope, the surfboard going in one direction as the rip took him in the other. The wash of water. The scrape of rocks.I think he must have had hope; he was a hopeful man. The hope of pulling himself out. The hope of survival, until that last wave, rushing at him, pushing him forwards. The cliff rising up. A churn of salt and sunlight – a final letting go to blackness.I hope it was peaceful.I hope he didn’t know he was about to die.I hope he knew we were with him, holding his hand in that moment, loving him. Always.It is Wendy who tells me, nearly two years later, that an inquest will be held. She explains it is not about pointing fingers or finding fault, but to see if things could be done differently in the future. She adds, gently, that as Matt’s death was so high‑profile and in such a popular beauty spot, it is deemed to be “in the public interest”. Such a jarring phrase for something that feels so intensely private, but I nod. The last thing I could bear is for another family to endure a loss like ours and to know there was a chance it could have been prevented.For two days, over and over, the fast and treacherous chain of events leading to Matt’s death is relayed. The facts are given, all carefully gathered and noted by the coroner, until the last witness steps down from the box and the coroner closes the proceedings and withdraws to consider all the evidence.In the more peaceful days that follow, I retreat to the coast. I find myself thinking more and more about acceptance. The formal procedure seems to have lifted something in my being. I feel calmer and more balanced. I know he is gone. I know my life is transformed.double quotation markI know now that grief will never leave me. It will always be a part of me, just like the love it stems fromView image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Maurice Smith/The GuardianBut can there ever be a final stage to grief? I’m not sure there can. The pendulum keeps swinging back and forth, though with less sickening ferocity. And the pain still rises frequently, as consistently as the tides, the absence of Matt a deep ache. What feels different is how I hold myself, the pain more often tucked away inside, less obvious to others. The grief is a weight I hold almost sacred now, my body developing the muscle to carry it.I realise that I have been looking at the concept of acceptance all wrong. It is not about rightness. There will never be anything right about Matt’s death. No, acceptance is allowing it to be, whatever it is. A letting go of the need for things to be different. Acceptance is seeing a new path open up before you. Not the one you thought you’d be taking. Acceptance is seeing this new path winding ahead of you and finding the strength to put first one foot on it, then the other.Iready the house for sale, our belongings for the move ahead. Sifting through our life’s possessions is not an easy process, but it is the last hours in the house that are most painful. Wandering alone for the very last time, I revisit the empty rooms, my footsteps echoing strangely through the space. I look out at the Japanese maple we planted, new purple-green leaves shimmering in the morning light. I let my hand trail up the polished wooden banister, take the creaking steps to the first floor. It’s all so familiar – so touched by us. I know it almost as well as my own skin.I sit on the floor in my son’s room by the window and let the tears fall. I think of all the moments that have made up our lives here. Big and small. Joyful and painful. Through the windowpane I can see the spire of the church across the road. I remember noticing it the first time Matt and I looked around the house. I think of the number of times we tiptoed into this room to check on our sleeping boy. To retrieve a fallen toy. To tuck his small body beneath a sheet. Time breaks my heart. I wonder what of ourselves we will leave behind. A lost note, fallen down the back of the mantelpiece? A stray marble caught between the cracks of the floorboards? Or perhaps just the lingering of feeling – of lives bound by love and loss – of the simplicity of our everyday, echoing in these empty rooms.Our story here has ended.I thank the house. I lock the door. I leave.Tamarama, Sydney, 2024Golden hour is settling over Tamarama, the sun sliding low on to the hill behind the beach. I’ve been here a while, traversing a decade of grief, honouring and assessing the shifting weight of our loss. With time and patience, I have returned to writing, found solace in books and reading. Slowly, I have relearned the world, restitched my heart.Down at the tideline, I step into the shallows, the water washing the sand from my skin. It’s cold, but my feet are planted. Steady. I can breathe, my chest no longer tight and pained. These waves will not topple me today.‘Grief became my brand’: Freya Bromley on writing about personal tragedyRead moreI know now that grief will never leave me. It will always be a part of me, just like the love it stems from. The shift comes in wanting to embrace it – to own it. And in the embrace, in pulling it close and examining it, the grief has shifted from something ugly and unthinkable to something softer, more akin to love than pain. So when I hear a song on the radio that reminds me of Matt, I can smile now and offer up my silent thank you.The waves still come, yet we carry on, living lives illuminated by wonder and grief, the duet of both. I think of those on the path, a little behind me. Am I brave enough to share my writing in comfort and solidarity?The surfers are still out, straddling their boards as the waves barrel in, occasionally chasing one down to the shore. I know everything has its time and that one day I, too, shall be called upon to take my place in the lineup, but as I stand here in this golden hour, facing the horizon, thinking about this ocean and that day, and all the days that came before, and all the impossible, joyous, wretched, beautiful ones lived since, I feel only gratitude to be here, holding this love and this pain.You will survive your greatest loss.You will be altered, but you will survive.Listen to the breathings of your heart. They will show you the way.This is an edited extract from An Ocean and a Day by Hannah Richell, published by Bedford Square at £16.99 in the UK and by HarperCollins in Australia.
