title: ‘Dancing with Rylan made me feel arthritic’: Jeremy Vine’s honest playlist | Jeremy Vine | The Guardian
description: The presenter and journalist used the Psychedelic Furs to soothe teenage heartbreak and had a Damascene moment to Bowie, but which cheesy 70s ballad does he secretly adore?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The presenter and journalist used the Psychedelic Furs to soothe teenage heartbreak and had a Damascene moment to Bowie, but which cheesy 70s ballad does he secretly adore?
Content: Jeremy Vine … ‘Belinda Carlisle would have to tone it down a bit for my funeral.’Photograph: Ray Burmiston/BBCView image in fullscreenJeremy Vine … ‘Belinda Carlisle would have to tone it down a bit for my funeral.’Photograph: Ray Burmiston/BBCHonest playlistJeremy Vine‘Dancing with Rylan made me feel arthritic’: Jeremy Vine’s honest playlistThe presenter and journalist used the Psychedelic Furs to soothe teenage heartbreak and had a Damascene moment to Bowie, but which cheesy 70s ballad does he secretly adore?As told toRich PelleySun 23 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withI loved a fellow sixth-former, Sarah, at school. It was unrequited. She kissed me once at the end-of-term party. I came home at 5am and played Love My Way by the Psychedelic Furs 18 times in my bedroom as the sun came up and my adult life began.The song that is my karaoke go-toI once cleared a bar in the US by singing Losing My Religion by REM. I’m looking for another chance to let rip on it, although Stan by Eminem might be better. He sings one note, and it’s the only note I have.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toRuby, Don’t Take Your Love to Town by Kenny Rogers is just incredible. I love the image of the sun going down and the shadow on the wall. The narrator has been left paralysed by the Vietnam war and is begging her not to go out looking for someone else, while accepting he cannot give her what she needs.The best song to play at a partyI once danced with Rylan [Clark] to Shackles (Praise You) by Mary Mary. He has snake hips and I felt arthritic by the end. But I would go again if I had Rylan on hand.The song I can no longer listen toI must have played Big Yellow Taxi by Joni Mitchell 2,000 times. The line “they paved paradise and put up a parking lot” is far too similar to the story of human behaviour, which is sad.The song I secretly like but tell everyone I hateMandy by Barry Manilow is soppy, melodramatic, silly, and I absolutely love it. The key change towards the end is a car crash, but I don’t care.The song that changed my lifeI first heard Sound and Vision by David Bowie when I was 12. I thought it was so weird and brilliant that he doesn’t even start singing until halfway through. The opening lyrics “Blue, blue, electric blue …” are what awakened me.The song that makes me cryDiamonds & Rust by Joan Baez. It’s about the imbalance between her love for Bob Dylan and his for her, how much was lost between them, and how she understood that his greatness excused it all.The song I want played at my funeralHeaven Is a Place on Earth by Belinda Carlisle. She would have to sing it live for my friends and family. And tone it down a bit. Perhaps I’ll try to book her.BBCRadio 2in the Park is at City Park, Stirling, 11 & 13 September.Explore more on these topicsJeremy VineHonest playlistRadioRadio 2featuresShareReuse this content

title: Megasquirt: Fully Loaded review – how to combat existential angst? A comedy rave at an ungodly hour | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Ashley Blair and Drew Reilly send up gen Z anomie with hardcore ditties about awkward dinners, megachurches and centaur boyfriends
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Ashley Blair and Drew Reilly send up gen Z anomie with hardcore ditties about awkward dinners, megachurches and centaur boyfriends
Content: Garnished with silliness … Drew Reilly and Ashley Blair in Fully Loaded.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenGarnished with silliness … Drew Reilly and Ashley Blair in Fully Loaded.Photograph: Alex BrennerEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMegasquirt: Fully Loaded review – how to combat existential angst? A comedy rave at an ungodly hourUnderbelly, Cowgate, EdinburghAshley Blair and Drew Reilly send up gen Z anomie with hardcore ditties about awkward dinners, megachurches and centaur boyfriendsBrian LoganSun 23 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘How to feel whole in an empty world?” There are many possible answers to that question, and Megasquirt’s late-night comedy rave workshops a good few of them. But there’s probably no better way than putting on a banging show and performing it to an adoring audience of your peers – and that’s what Brooklyn imports Ashley Blair and Drew Reilly do in Fully Loaded, turning the Underbelly at some ungodly hour into a pulsating queer(ish) celebration-cum-sendup of gen Z anomie. “Everything is empty / Life is a hole / You gotta fill it up,” they sing, looking like refugees from Warhol’s Factory but delivering comedy that couldn’t be more now.View image in fullscreenCouldn’t be more now … Blair and Reilly in Fully Loaded.Photograph: Alex BrennerThe show starts as if we’re being seconded to a generational revolution, but it’s soon clear that this pair, bothSecond Cityalumni, are threats to nothing but your funny bone. Their premise is that life is void of meaning. We flash back to meet them as alienated schoolkids and one terrific sketch, a silly symphony of clinking cutlery andASMRtuts and sighs, imagines two parents at dinner, struggling to repress their mutual loathing. If this is our hosts’ generational inheritance, whynotlook for a better way of being? Like a romance with an inverted Centaur Boyfriend, the title of one daft ditty, or like forming a megachurch to start replenishing the spiritual chasm.There are first-base satirical sideswipes in that latter sketch, against Christian homophobia and the church’s obsession with sin. But Blair and Reilly’s satire is usually garnished with, or eclipsed by, silliness, as they belt out their songs about being bullied in bakeries, and “gooning in the DJ booth”. So much the funnier that these songs are tightly constructed, lyrically adroit and delivered with hardcore hyperpop attack.Only occasionally does the standard slip: the skit about straight female writers fetishising gay male sex is on point, but soon devolves into so-so smut. That’s not going to fill anyone’s gaping hole – but there’s lots here that will, as Megasquirt minister to our existential angst with whip-smart, high-energy comedy.AtUnderbelly, Cowgate, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)CabaretEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Haribo Kimchi review – Korean snack bar serves lessons in belonging | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jaha Koo cooks up street-food treats for two lucky theatregoers as he reflects on how food preserves memory and cultural identity, with the help of a snail and an eel
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Jaha Koo cooks up street-food treats for two lucky theatregoers as he reflects on how food preserves memory and cultural identity, with the help of a snail and an eel
Content: A taste of South Korea … Jaha Koo.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA taste of South Korea … Jaha Koo.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHaribo Kimchi review – Korean snack bar serves lessons in belongingFestival theatre studio, EdinburghJaha Koo cooks up street-food treats for two lucky theatregoers as he reflects on how food preserves memory and cultural identity, with the help of a snail and an eelMark FisherSun 23 Aug 2026 06.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo get the measure of this slight but sweet one-man show, you need to listen to the singing snail. “In every soil grows a different version of you,” sings the animated creature in Korean, projected on a screen.It is echoing the sentiment just expressed by an eel: “My home has no location,” sings a fish that lives a life of transformation as it moves between saltwater and fresh.Their experience is one shared by performer Jaha Koo, who left his native South Korea for Europe 15 years ago and has the rootlessness of the displaced. His sense of alienation is exacerbated by the racism he encounters, notably the assistant who complains of a stench of garlic despite sitting behind a screen.That is a rare dark moment in a cheerful show, but the association with food is apt. Koo might be adrift in the world, but keeps his home with him via hisnational cuisine. Inviting two volunteers to join him at hispojangmacha, a street-food snack bar, he cooks up several courses as the show progresses: a cucumber starter, a kimchi pancake, a bowl of soup and a pudding flavoured with seagrass, mint and lime. They seem to enjoy it.View image in fullscreenScreen projections aid the storytelling in Haribo Kimchi.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianNot all his food-related memories are happy: after smelling the corpses lined up after theGwangju pro-democracy uprisingof 1980, Koo’s father could not bear the smell of fried chicken and retreated to the countryside to escape it.But for the most part, in Koo’s own production for Campo in Ghent, the performer reflects on a country that, like many others, finds community in food. It brings identity and salvation, not least the Haribo gummies that cheer him up away from home. Like the snail and the eel, they keep him company. Naturally, the Haribos get a song too.AtFestival theatre studio, Edinburgh, until 24 AugustAll our Edinburgh reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Chineke!/ Heyward/ Angel Blue review – belated premiere for forgotten Black composer | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: A suite of reconstructed dance pieces from 1918 by Edmund Thornton Jenkins made a moving start to Chineke!’s Prom, where soprano Angel Blue sang Barber’s nostalgic Knoxville and Dvořák’s Symphony No 8 made a breathless finale
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: A suite of reconstructed dance pieces from 1918 by Edmund Thornton Jenkins made a moving start to Chineke!’s Prom, where soprano Angel Blue sang Barber’s nostalgic Knoxville and Dvořák’s Symphony No 8 made a breathless finale
Content: Gleaming tone … Angel Blue performs alongside conductor Jonathon Heyward and Chineke! Orchestra.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCView image in fullscreenGleaming tone … Angel Blue performs alongside conductor Jonathon Heyward and Chineke! Orchestra.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCProms 2026ReviewChineke!/ Heyward/ Angel Blue review – belated premiere for forgotten Black composerRoyal Albert Hall, LondonA suite of reconstructed dance pieces from 1918 by Edmund Thornton Jenkins made a moving start to Chineke!’s Prom, where soprano Angel Blue sang Barber’s nostalgic Knoxville and Dvořák’s Symphony No 8 made a breathless finaleErica JealSun 23 Aug 2026 09.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSlowly but surely, our perceptions of what a composer looked like in the early 20th century are widening.Chineke!’s ongoing mission to unearth music by forgotten Black composers here brought about the belated premiere of Ballet by Edmund Thornton Jenkins, its incomplete manuscript parts reconstructed by his great-nephewTuffus Zimbabwe.Growing up in Charleston, South Carolina, Jenkins died in Paris aged only 32, having made a name for himself as a rising composer and band leader. In between he studied at the Royal Academy of Music in London, where in 1918 he wrote his three-movement Ballet. It sounded persuasive here, as conducted by Jonathon Heyward. A substantial opening Processional, ominous then light-footed, gives way to a second movement beginning with a bubbling flute duet and a florid viola solo; together, these repeatedly show a gift for weaving together melody and countermelody. The flaw is in the finale, where the waltz that dominates the movement sounds unavoidably slender and staid next to the trumpet fanfare that announces it. Still, Jenkins rounds things off with an exuberant, uptempo ending.That was where the discoveries ended in this Prom – it was a pity that a song by Margaret Bonds had been quietly dropped from the programme. The rest of the first half was a showcase for the US soprano Angel Blue. In Barber’s Knoxville: Summer of 1915, the words of the poet James Agee didn’t always make it across the hall, but her gleaming tone, the childish innocence of her character and the music’s atmosphere of intense nostalgia certainly did.A change of frock later Blue returned to the stage, microphone in hand, and powered rather self-indulgently through four Great American Songbook standards. She relied a lot on charm, singing My Funny Valentine directly to the front rows, but these songs didn’t all get the vocal polish they deserve: in Puttin’ On the Ritz the high point was Richard Kelley’s trumpet solo.The whole orchestra, not least its versatile and superbly blended brass section, was on form in Dvořák’s Symphony No 8. Heyward shaped a performance full of momentum, setting electric tempos and driving the finale to its close with breathless excitement.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicChineke! OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a hit jumpy horror series returns with Dan Stevens  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Terror is a terrifying drama anthology. Plus, tissues at the ready for a super emotional finale of The Piano. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The Terror is a terrifying drama anthology. Plus, tissues at the ready for a super emotional finale of The Piano. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: The ambient hum of horror … The Terror: Devil in Silver on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Emily V Aragones/AMC/2025 AMC Film Holdings LLC. All Rights Reserved.View image in fullscreenThe ambient hum of horror … The Terror: Devil in Silver on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Emily V Aragones/AMC/2025 AMC Film Holdings LLC. All Rights Reserved.TV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a hit jumpy horror series returns with Dan StevensThe Terror is a terrifying drama anthology. Plus, tissues at the ready for a super emotional finale of The Piano. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Graeme Virtue,Hannah VerdierandSimon WardellSun 23 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Terror: Devil in Silver9pm, Sky Atlantic“We all got our demons, don’t we?” We certainly do, though it’s rare to see them manifest so vividly in a drama. This third standalone story in The Terror anthology series is set in an understaffed, underfunded and quite possibly cursed psychiatric hospital. Dan Stevens stars as Peter “Pepper” Coffin, who has been wrongfully committed to the institution and is forced to reckon with its tatty malevolence. We meet the patients in their past and present lives and connect them via the sinister Dr Walter (John Benjamin Hickey) who may just be the key to the whole mystery. It doesn’t lack jump-scares but also generates a subtler, more genuinely unsettling ambient hum of horror.Phil HarrisonViolent Earth6pm, Sky Nature“It was chewing up everything in its path!” So begins the first episode – about terrifying tornadoes – in an intense new series about the science behind natural disasters. It’s presented by actor Liev Schreiber, for reasons unknown, and features first-hand footage taken across the world, along with eyewitness accounts.Hollie RichardsonForce of Nature7pm, ITV1Extreme heat is tackled in this instalment of the series dramatising how the climate crisis affects animals, from increased drought to the rise of wildfires around the globe. That means a wombat in Australia, a leopard in Zambia and a kangaroo rat in Arizona all abruptly find themselves starring in their own mini disaster movies.Graeme VirtueMozart at the Proms8pm, BBC FourA pair of Wolfie’s crowd-pleasers for your delectation: the Third Horn Concerto, featuring star soloist Felix Klieser; plus his exuberant Symphony No 35, AKA the “Haffner”, whose first movement, Amadeus advised, should be “played with fire”. Also, pieces by Elgar, Britten and, making its Proms debut, Thea Musgrave’s Out of the Darkness concerto for bassoon.Ali CatterallThe Piano9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenShow time! … The Piano on Channel 4.Photograph: Channel 4 / Nic Serpell RandJamie asked Claudia to sing a few notes, which he then improvised from when he first played in the competition. Will he need her help again in the final? He plays on stage along with Grace, who lost all her fingers after meningitis, Harri, with his song inspired by his grandad, wildcard teen Sophie and “piano-breaker” Gabby.HROne Dollar11.20pm, ITV1“No guns, no body” and a cast of suspects: this acclaimed US drama knows how to set up a tale. And as a dollar bill changes hands in a struggling rust belt town divided by culture and class, secrets emerge, aided by John Carroll Lynch, Leslie Odom Jr, Nathaniel Martello-White and more.Hannah VerdierFilm choiceH Is for Hawk, out now, NetflixView image in fullscreen‘A perfectly evolved psychopath’ … H Is for Hawk on Netflix.Photograph: Roadside Attractions/Everett/ShutterstockGetting up close and personal with animals can be a life-affirming way of feeling at one with nature. It can also be a way of avoiding the messier everyday of being human. For Helen Macdonald (a febrile Claire Foy), in Philippa Lowthorpe’s adaptation of Macdonald’s bestselling memoir, it is the tug between the two that brings her world crashing down. After her beloved father (Brendan Gleeson) dies, Helen decides to train a goshawk (“a perfectly evolved psychopath,” her mentor warns) in memory of their shared love of the great outdoors. But confronting avian life red in tooth and claw isn’t the same as dealing with the complex emotions of grief. An arresting, affecting drama.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bebe Cave: Swoon review – dazzling portrait of marginalised muses and the male gaze | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Smart, slapstick and silly, this chaotic multicharacter comedy sends up the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
Author: Arusa Qureshi
Headline: Smart, slapstick and silly, this chaotic multicharacter comedy sends up the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
Content: The idea of the perfect woman involves her looking near death … Bebe Cave in Swoon.Photograph: Rebecca Nead-MenearView image in fullscreenThe idea of the perfect woman involves her looking near death … Bebe Cave in Swoon.Photograph: Rebecca Nead-MenearEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBebe Cave: Swoon review – dazzling portrait of marginalised muses and the male gazePleasance Dome, EdinburghSmart, slapstick and silly, this chaotic multicharacter comedy sends up the Pre-Raphaelite BrotherhoodArusa QureshiSun 23 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of the most revered works of art across history feature women as their primary focus. But though they might appear as favoured subjects, so often these women are relegated to the margins, their stories untold as they remain silent and often sexualised via the male gaze.In her new multicharacter comedy Swoon, Bebe Cave interrogates the role of the muse and what it means to be seen yet never heard. We initially meet Cave as Elizabeth Siddal – or Lizzie – who was immortalised as Ophelia by John Everett Millais in the mid 19th century, also becoming a popular model for several otherpre-Raphaeliteartists.With her comically excessive scouse accent and world-weary exasperation, she is the poster child for being sad and sexy, her story underlining the dichotomy between the elevated status of the muse and their simultaneously poor treatment by artists. The narrative, however, centres on the fictional Bertrude, Lizzie’s sister, who is desperate to be noticed and included by the pretentious Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, whose idea of the perfect woman involves her looking near death.View image in fullscreenAmping up the absurdity … Bebe Cave.Photograph: Rebecca Nead-MenearSwoon sees Cave take on numerous characters at breakneck speed, with appearances from a lanky redheaded mannequin, gloriously baffling dance sequences and casual pop culture references throughout. Cave emits a chaotic energy in her portrayal of the brotherhood and the many characters in their orbit, with her delightfully janky costumes and props and a Millais-coded set design amping up the absurdity at every turn.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreAs Dante Gabriel Rossetti, she is the ultimate hipster bro, a printed Carhartt logo stuck to her top hat adding an excellent touch in the depiction of his obnoxious faux-trendiness. The men’s nonchalant misogyny and their lack of care towards women is accentuated by Cave through their cringey edgelord behaviour.Giving us a Victorian-era Tyra Banks as well as the Brontë sisters, Swoon is a highly impressive and creative feat of physical comedy, with an intelligent throughline that never takes away from the more slapstick and silly elements. The show has a wealth of jokes that rely on the audience having some knowledge of art history, but even without this, the message is clear: ridiculous men with pompous attitudes are forever contributing to the erasure of women.They may live eternally in the art itself, but Cave argues that muses like Lizzie deserve more than just being nameless subjects. And in this, Swoon works to dismantle the illusion of impossible beauty standards set and romanticised by clueless men.AtPleasance Dome, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalTheatreThe pre-RaphaelitesPaintingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: My best ever British holiday: ‘I’ve travelled further, at greater expense, and had nothing like as much fun’ | United Kingdom holidays | The Guardian
description: Five travel writers share their favourite holidays at home, from gravel biking in Scotland and a steam train ride in Yorkshire to rowing all the way from Oxford to London
Author: Max Benato
Headline: Five travel writers share their favourite holidays at home, from gravel biking in Scotland and a steam train ride in Yorkshire to rowing all the way from Oxford to London
Content: Marcel Theroux (right) with James and Tom on their Thames boat trip.Photograph: James Bedford/jamesbedford.comView image in fullscreenMarcel Theroux (right) with James and Tom on their Thames boat trip.Photograph: James Bedford/jamesbedford.comGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.United Kingdom holidaysMy best ever British holiday: ‘I’ve travelled further, at greater expense, and had nothing like as much fun’Five travel writers share their favourite holidays at home, from gravel biking in Scotland and a steam train ride in Yorkshire to rowing all the way from Oxford to LondonMax Benato, Kirsten Henton,Jill Mead,Marcel Theroux,Andy PietrasikSun 23 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree men in a boat on the ThamesOne of my best UK holidays was the week I spent in June 2013 rowing from Oxford to London with two friends, James and Tom.We hired the boat from a company calledThames Skiff Hirethat mainly caters to people recreating the fictional adventure of the characters in Jerome K Jerome’s Three Men in a Boat.Our boat – Ewen – was a 26ft, 130-year-old mahogany skiff. It came with two pairs of oars, a rudder, a cooking stove, a boat hook, and iron hoops that supported a green canvas roof over the hull.After an hour’s briefing at a slipway by Donnington Bridge, we were off, piloting the boat 80 or so miles downstream to London. That June was blustery and wet. The first day was deceptively fine, but on the second, we got soaked on the stretch of water between Abingdon and Day’s Lock, and came close to packing it in.Even with the current helping us, the miles ahead seemed like folly. It’s not generally remembered that Jerome K Jerome’s Three Men in a Boat ends in disappointment and recrimination as the companions abandon their sodden skiff atThe Swanin Pangbourne.But we kept going. And, over the subsequent days, the weather improved, we got better at rowing and it turned into an extraordinary and memorable adventure.double quotation markIt always felt as if we were very far from the daily grind. There were stretches of extraordinary tranquillityLooking back, the trip appears to have been packed with incident. We visited lovely riverside pubs, brewed tea on uninhabited midstream islands, and popped into a meditation centre run by an ascetic Hindu sect. We passed Medmenham Abbey, the headquarters ofFrancis Dashwood’s Hellfire Club; Monkey Island, where the doomed romance inRebecca West’s The Return of the Soldierunfolds; and we moored for lunch one day at the luxurious faux-gothic hotelOakley Court, immortalised as Frank-N-Furter’s castle in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Logistically, the trip was never entirely straightforward. Although the Thames skiff was designed to be slept in, it was not big enough for three and the rules around wild camping made things more complicated. I also remember feeling a certain anxiety when mooring the boat to go to the pub. We had been instructed to hammer iron spikes into the riverbank and fasten the skiff to them. But it always seemed weird to walk away from this precious antique and assume it would be there when we got back.View image in fullscreenThe trio hired a 130-year-old mahogany skiff.Photograph: James Bedford/jamesbedford.comNegotiating the locks that regulate the water level of the river was also tricky. Someone had to remain in the skiff with a boat hook and keep it from bumping against the sides as the water poured out of the sluices. And, of course, rowing that distance, even with the current, requires a certain stick-to-it-ness.Paradoxically, the minor hardships of the trip probably made it more relaxing than a holiday whose explicit goal is relaxation. The overall pace was slow and reflective. And even within commuting distance of our own beds, it always felt as if we were very far from the daily grind. There were stretches of extraordinary tranquillity, deep silences, wonderful birdlife; I still remember the flash of a kingfisher in the willows outside Abingdon.Other river-users took kindly to us and our venerable skiff. One evening, we were invited for drinks onboard a beautiful narrowboat whose owner we met as we were queueing at a lock.Our final destination was Walton-on-Thames, but by the time we reached it, we were enjoying ourselves so much we pushed on to Hampton Court before turning the boat round and heading back upriver to return the skiff.It’s a trip I’ve always meant to repeat. I’ve travelled much further, at much greater expense and had nothing like as much fun.Marcel TherouxA birthday break in the TrossachsView image in fullscreenGravel biking in the Trossachs“Gravelfoyle,” my cycle-mad partner, Gary, replied instantly when asked where he’d like to go for his birthday. Gravelfoyle is the nickname of the village of Aberfoyle – gateway to the Trossachs, about 50 miles north-west of Edinburgh, and even closer to Glasgow – which claims to have “the UK’s finest gravel riding” and the waymarked trails to prove it.Growing up in Edinburgh, I spent many happy summers camping in the Cairngorms and roving around Perthshire. This instilled a habit of going north rather than west, so I didn’t know Scotland’s first national park,Loch Lomond and the Trossachs, as well.Off we set, bikes strapped to the car, passing Falkirk’s Kelpies, whose steel heads reared up alongside the M9, imposing Stirling Castle and the Mordor-esqueWallace Monumentin the distance. The drive was only 75 minutes, but we stopped en route atThe Smiddy farm shopin Blair Drummond (close to thesafari parkmy brother and I went to as kids) to pick up cheese and chorizo scotch eggs, “the best thing we sell”, according to the butcher.double quotation markThe glamping pod felt like the most decadent way to enjoy the outdoors, especially once the fire pit was roaring and fizz was in hand.I’d booked a snug-looking glamping pod on theCardross Estatenear Port of Menteith, not far from Aberfoyle. Tucked away down a single-track road flanked by farmland, where kites soar overhead, it’s a slick operation, from the easy self-check-in to the trolleys for wheeling stuff from the car park. Inside the curved, wooden pod was a sofa, pull-down double bed, shower and fridge, with picture windows framing fields speckled with cattle and crops rolling towards Ben Lomond. We could have chosen one of the estate’s self-catering cottages or a B&B stay in Cardross House, but the pod felt like the most decadent way to enjoy the outdoors, especially once the fire pit was roaring and fizz was in hand.View image in fullscreenKirsten Henton and her partner Gary try to avoid the midges.Photograph: Kirsten HentonLater that day, we embarked on our first ride, the 18.2-mile (29.2km) Lomond View, one of three Gravelfoyle routes plotted for gravel biking, and a wet and muddy affair after recent rain. Afterwards, atAberfoyle Bike Co(where you can hire bikes if you don’t bring your own), the owner, Liam, was ready with a hose and hot drinks.The next day, we hiked out of the nearby town of Callander on the 3.5-mile (5.3km) circular Bracklinn Falls hiking route. Crossing the bridge over the thundering waterfall, we pressed on through thick forest before returning to baguettes oozing generous fillings atMhor Bread. The afternoon’s downpour gave us a great excuse to nest in our cosy pod, read and, in my case, nap – the indulgence!That evening, the sun sprang loose, and we chinked glasses in the flower-strewn garden of Scottish chef Nick Nairn’s namesake restaurant,Nick’s at Port of Menteith. Swallows and housemartins swooped as we ate fish and chips and seafood linguine.Over three days, we biked and hiked various routes alongside lochs and through yawning, forest-clad valleys, ate fabulous, locally produced food, and soaked up the nurturing goodness of being immersed in the wilderness of the national park.Kirsten HentonAt the edge of north WalesView image in fullscreenBwa Gwyn arch at Rhoscolyn on Holy Island, Ynys Môn (Anglesey).Photograph: Andy PietrasikI’ve lost count of the number of times I’ve passed through Ynys Môn (Anglesey) over the years, but until recently I’d never actually been there. Ghosting through the darkness to catch the night ferry from Holyhead to Dublin, I had no idea what the island looked like until our daughter suggested an outing while we were visiting her at her student digs in Bangor, across the Menai Strait.That first time, she took us to Newborough Forest, a nature reserve on the south-west coast of the island made up of Corsican pines, sand dunes and a sweep of beach that offers panoramic views of the peaks of Eryri (Snowdonia) across the bay. We spent the afternoon walking over to the small tidal island of Ynys Llanddwyn, with its lighthouse and the ruined remains of Saint Dwynwen’s church. Saint Dwynwen is the Welsh patron saint of lovers, the equivalent of Saint Valentine. It was love at first sight for us, and we hatched a plan to come back for a longer visit.double quotation markI rued the fact that I had rattled through this glorious little island on the boat train on so many occasions,  without ever having spent any time hereOn that next visit, we rented a cottage with floor-to-ceiling windows that framed the mountains on the road out of Llanfair – or Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch to give it its proper majestic name – well, how could we not? What we discovered on that stay pretty much chimed with what I had read in HV Morton’s book In Search of Wales, published in 1932: “The long roads run through flat, green country, linking quiet, stone-built little market towns together.”But it’s at the edges that Ynys Môn comes into its own. On the first day, we walked theWales Coast Pathalong the cliffs at Rhoscolyn on Ynys Gybi (Holy Island) in the north – an island off an island with dramatic sea arches – and enjoyed a feeling of apartness, of almost floating out to sea.View image in fullscreenHeading through the sand dunes to Newborough beach in the south-west of the island.Photograph: Andy PietrasikOn another day, we parked up at the beach at Rhosneigr and again followed the signs for the coast path, walking through the marram grass and gorse on the dunes until we found a sheltered cove to go swimming. Then we drove across the island that at one time was called Môn, Mam Cymru (Anglesey, the Mother of Wales) because it was said to grow all the corn needed to feed the country, to Red Wharf Bay and another sweeping beach at the bottom of a single-track lane. There was no corn on the menu at the Boathouse cafe, but we made do with crab meat crumpets and mussels.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeafing through HV Morton’s book back at the cottage that night, I came across a line that made me rue the fact that I had rattled through this glorious little island on the boat train on so many occasions, simply seeing it as an embarkation point without ever having had the imagination to jump off and spend a bit of time here: “Holyhead is an excellent place for a holiday … you have bathing, fine cliff scenery, and all round you is excellent flat walking country with a supreme view of the whole Snowdon range.”Andy PietrasikNorth Yorkshire with 42 palsView image in fullscreenNorth Yorkshire Moors Railway steam engine on its way to Whitby.Photograph: David Lyons/AlamyTwelve years ago, I was sitting in my son Ned’s primary school playground when I said to my friend Vicky, “I’m thinking of taking a few friends up to Yorkshire.”“I’m in,” she said.Word got out, and before I knew it 42 of us were heading to lovelyCote Ghyll Mill, on the edge of the pretty village of Osmotherley. It was a youth hostel in those days, before its recent transformation into a B&B. Ned and I made a giant Welcome to Yorkshire banner and Blu-Tacked handwritten names on to the bedroom doors.None of us realised that week would become our June tradition, until Covid brought it to a halt.Brilliantly, my mum and dad took charge one day, leading us on a six-mile circular walk from Grosmont through the fairytale hamlet of Beck Hole, a centre for the traditional game of quoits, and back across the North York Moors.I remember Mum, ever the feeder in our family, opening the boot of their car to reveal her homemade fruit cake alongside a stack of enormous sandwiches they had collected fromDanby Bakery. Dad brought a few short thumbsticks (traditional walking sticks) he’d made for the kids from hazel branches. Florence, now 19, still has hers, and Julie, her mum, now uses it to reach an awkward light switch.double quotation markThe Birch Hall Inn doubles as a sweet shop and we came away clutching paper bags of lemon sherbets, cola cubes and pear dropsHalfway round was Dad’s favourite pub, theBirch Hall Inn, where his drink of choice was always the same: a bitter shandy. The pub doubles as a sweet shop and we came away clutching paper bags of lemon sherbets, cola cubes and pear drops, all bought by the ounce, while Ned carefully chose Barratt’s liquorice sticks for his grandad, as is tradition.Part of our walk crossed theNorth Yorkshire Moors Railwayline to Whitby, and, after watching a train steaming past us, we all wanted to take a ride. It is a magical way to see the moors. Every carriage told its own story. Couples were more romantic, kids chatted around the tables, and happy heads hung out of the windows to catch the smell of coal and steam. Eleven-year-old Eleanor caught far too much coal dust in her eye and ended up in A&E in Northallerton. Thankfully, she was fine.In Whitby, Ned’s pals buried him in the sand on Tate Hill beach. Although we brushed him down and emptied his shoes, he still left a little trail of Whitby all the way back to the station and on to the train.View image in fullscreenJill Mead with her son Ned and her parents outside the Birch Hall Inn in Beck Hole, near Goathland.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianOur trip wouldn’t have been complete without a visit to my own boozer of choice, theSun Inn, or Spout House, in Bilsdale. Its infamous cricket field, with a dramatic slope where fielders on the boundary can disappear from view, is where my dad and brother played. Spike W, AKA Prince Harry, is also recorded in the score book.My old primary school friend Audrey is the landlady now. I used to ride her ponies, her dad was the village milkman, and she somehow makes everyone who walks through the door feel as if they’ve come home.Audrey laid on a domino tournament and the most amazing Yorkshire platter, with cakes worthy of victory at any country show. Competition was fierce, with some local diehard domino players, mainly farmers, joining in. Harriet, aged just six, beat the lot of them. She burst into tears, while her mum, Steph, cried with laughter.This year, I casually asked Ned, now 21, “Do you think anyone might fancy going back to Yorkshire?”“Absolutely, Mum,” he replied.So we’re going back to Cote Ghyll Mill this month.I’ve dug out the original Welcome to Yorkshire banner and Harriet, now 18, is fiercely ready to defend her domino title.Jill MeadA quick dip into BristolView image in fullscreenGuests at the Lido Townhouse in Bristol have access to the restored Victorian poolTravelling by train from Kent to Bristol on one of the hottest days of the year might have been pretty close to madness. In sweltering heat and amid cancellations and delays, I arrived in the city hot, broken and miserable. Less than an hour later, I was gliding through the water at the city’s lido, smugly thanking myself for booking what may be one of the best summer city hotels in the country.I was in Bristol for the opening of an exhibition –Polly Braden: Against the Tide– at the brilliantArnolfini arts centre, which seemed the perfect excuse to visit a city that had somehow eluded me. The Arnolfini is a leading hub for the contemporary arts, housed in a 19th-century warehouse on Narrow Quay beside the harbour, a vibrant area packed with restaurants, cafes and bars, as well as some of the city’s leading tourist attractions, including the aquarium and Brunel’s SS Great Britain.double quotation markAfter my 9.30pm swim I sat in my robe at the bar nursing a glass of amaroMy base was theLido Townhouse, a six-bedroom hotel in a Georgian building that opened in 2024 in the city’s sought-after Clifton neighbourhood. Each of the rooms has been done out simply but with fabulous taste, featuring colourful throws, sparkling white bedlinen and jauntily tiled bathrooms.The real attraction isthe lidoitself, which dates back to Victorian times and has been restored after falling into disrepair. Open year-round, with the water heated to 20-24C, the pool is flanked by old-fashioned changing cabins on one side and a bar and restaurant on the other, with windows and a terrace that look out over the action. Booking directly with the hotel grants you full access to the lido, which is just a few steps across a (very quiet) road in the hotel’s robes and slippers. In 24 hours, I managed to squeeze in three swims, including one at 9.30pm (it closes at 10pm), emerging to sit in my robe at the bar nursing a glass of amaro. Breakfast the next day out on the deck was equally enjoyable, with coffee and a generous plate of Turkish eggs and coffee.A colleague and I paid £210 for two double rooms and a shared bathroom on the top floor of the hotel, which, with unlimited swims thrown in and 10% off our food bill, seemed like an excellent deal. The harbour is a 25-minute stroll from the hotel along shop-lined Georgian streets, past picturesque College Green and the cathedral. So, though it was a lightning visit, the city showed its best side. A return trip is on the cards.Max BenatoExplore more on these topicsUnited Kingdom holidaysFamily holidaysFamilyEngland holidaysScotland holidaysWales holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect zaru soba, or cold soba noodles – recipe | Noodles | The Guardian
description: Hot days call for cool dinners, and these are Japan’s nutty, salty and sweet solution. Fiery or pickled accompaniments optional
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Hot days call for cool dinners, and these are Japan’s nutty, salty and sweet solution. Fiery or pickled accompaniments optional
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfectzaru soba.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfectzaru soba.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.How to cook the perfect ...NoodlesHow to make the perfect zaru soba, or cold soba noodles – recipeHot days call for cool dinners, and these are Japan’s nutty, salty and sweet solution. Fiery or pickled accompaniments optionalFelicity CloakeSun 23 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlthough every culture craves something different in hot weather – chilled beetroot soup in Lithuania, coolingbuttermilk drinksin India,gazpachoin Spain – what many of these dishes have in common is a certain soothing silkiness as they slide down the throat, plus a decent helping of salt. Japan’szaru soba, whichNamiko Hirasawa Chenof Just One Cookbook describes as her family’s “go-to meal when the summer heat and humidity soar”, is no exception. Cold, slippery noodles paired with a savoury dipping sauce, it’s a simple, satisfying dish that’s ready in 15 minutes, and can be accessorised with crunchy salads, sweet seafood or creamy tofu sides for something more substantial. Traditionally served on a bamboo mat, orzaru, to allow the noodles to drain, you can get away without one at home (though lose the seaweed and you can call itmori sobainstead), this is definitely one to stick in your summer repertoire alongside the chilled soups, watermelon salads and cucumber sandwiches.The noodlesZaru soba isn’t the only chilled noodle dish that Japan slurps in summer –Emiko Davies favours her mother’ssomen(delicate wheat-flour strands), whileShota Nakajima makes a case forhiyashi chuka, a Chinese-inspired ramen salad. Sadly, though, spindly somen and fresh ramen are trickier to source in the UK than buckwheat soba, which can be found in many larger supermarkets.In fact,Yumiko Maehashi of RecipeTin Japanreckons that these noodles’ nutty flavour is best enjoyed cold: “I read in a Japanese soba article that some soba fanatics would not consider the soba in hot soup as ‘soba’.” Not all, however, are created equal, as Maehashi goes on to explain: “Some soba brands indicate the ratio of buckwheat and wheat flours mixed in the soba noodles. The more buckwheat flour, the more flavour and the more expensive … It is really your preference as to what sort of soba noodles are the best, but, in general, the more expensive dried soba noodles cook to al dente better.” If you’d like to keep this dish gluten-free, you’ll need to look for 100% buckwheat noodles (and a gluten-free Japanese soy sauce – Kikkoman makes one), but, otherwise, it’s up to you. Buckwheat can, after all, be an acquired taste, especially in such a simple dish.The noodles are cooked without salt, I suspect to facilitate the contrast with the dipping sauce. Swirling them around the pan for the first 15 or so seconds, as Maehashi suggests, is a helpful tip to ensure that the strands don’t clump together. It’s also vital to rinse them well afterwards, to quickly cool down the noodles before they overcook, and to wash off some of the starch that will otherwise turn those lovely, silky noodles into a sticky bird’s nest (trust me on this). Chen dunks hers in iced water, too, but I don’t find that this step makes much of a difference texture-wise. Then again, neither do I notice that doing so causes the “noodles to ‘tighten’ up too quickly, losing their texture and flavour”, asLisa Kitahara at Okonomi Kitchenclaims, but I’ll concede I’m no soba expert.Once cooled, the soba are best consumed immediately, but if you find they’ve started to tangle, give them a rinse under cold water to separate the strands, then drain them well again afterwards. Traditionally, soba are served on a flat bamboo straining mat called azaru, but as long as you toss them well, a less picturesque plate or bowl is fine.The sauceThe proper way to eat zaru soba, according to Maehashi, is to “pick up a few strands of noodles and dip only the bottom half of them into the dipping sauce by simply lowering the chopsticks. Many people drop all the noodles they just picked up into the dipping sauce,” she adds, “but this is not a real gourmet way of eating buckwheat noodles. By dipping only part of the soba noodles in, you can taste the flavour of the noodles and enjoy it better.” So that’s you told.As only a little of the accompanyingmentsuyusauce gilds each helping of noodles, it has to be intense in flavour, hence the principal ingredients: salty soy sauce, mirin (a sweet rice wine; alcohol-free alternatives are available), umami-rich seaweed and dried, smoked tuna flakes. Maehashi points out that you can substitute ready-made dashi stock, easily found in any Japanese specialist store, for the kombu and katsuobushi element of things; indeed, you can even buymentsuyu in bottles, if you prefer, but it’s so easy to make that it won’t save you much time.Chen, andchef Aya Nishimura in her book, Japanese Food Made Easy, both add sake as well, which, though not mandatory, does give their sauces an interesting complexity that proves very popular with my testers (save yourself some money and go for a cooking sake, unless you’re planning to drink the rest of the bottle). We also enjoy the brown sugar that Nishimura and chef Maori Murota include, the latter in her bookTokyo Cult Recipes. Feel free to leave it out if you prefer; you can always stir some in at the end if you decide the sauce needs some sweetness. (Equally, Chen explains, if the sauce is too salty for your taste, you can dilute it with iced water.) Nishimura sticks in a couple of shiitake mushrooms too; I find them a bit overwhelming, but it does strike me that if you don’t eat fish, you might like to substitute these for the tuna flakes.The only small faff with this recipe is thinking ahead to ensure the sauce is cold before you eat, which is why it’s worth making several batches of it in hot weather; once strained, it keeps well in the fridge. I’d recommend keeping the kombu and tuna in for a few hours, as Murota seems to suggest, to extract as much flavour as possible. And don’t discard them once you separate the two, either; they can be saved and used to makefurikake rice seasoning.Chef Masaki Sugisaki of Dinings SW3in London, meanwhile, advises that, “once you have finished the noodles, heat the reserved noodle cooking water and add it to the dipping sauce. It is traditional to drink this as a soup, because the water contains nourishing minerals.”The accompanimentsZaru soba becomes nori soba with the addition of some shredded nori, those roasted laver seaweed sheets used to wrap some sushi rolls. This, along with fiery wasabi and spring onions, are the most common accompaniments in the recipes I try. Murota recommends daikon and garlic chive or the white part of a leek, rather than spring onions, and she and Nishimura include grated ginger too. All of these, along with the ground toasted sesame seeds that add an interesting additional texture to Nishimura’s dish, are possibilities. In fact, in the privacy of your own home, add whatever you want, but do bear in mind that the pleasure of this dish is its simplicity – silky noodles and salty broth – so try to avoid the temptation to load it up like a salad before you’ve even tried it.Perfect zaru sobaWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook10 minInfuse30 minChill2 hr+Serves22 x 75g bunches of soba noodles1 piece nori(optional)2 spring onions, or garlic chive leavesWasabi, fresh or pasteFor the sauce5cm x 5cm strip kombu4 tbsp Japanese soy sauce4 tbsp mirin2 tbsp sake(optional; if not using, add 2 tbsp extra water)1 tsp brown sugar5g katsuobushi (bonito) flakesPut the kombu and 150ml cold water in a small saucepan and leave to sit for half an hour.Add all the remaining sauce ingredients, bar the katsuobushi.View image in fullscreenSlowly bring to a boil, then turn off the heat, add the katsuobushi, leave to cool, then chill for a few hours, and preferably overnight.View image in fullscreenBring a wide pan of unsalted water to a boil. Add the noodles and stir for a few seconds to ensure they don’t clump together.View image in fullscreenCook according to the packet instructions (usually about five minutes) until very slightly al dente.Scoop the noodles into a sieve (save the cooking water) and rinse under cold water to cool completely, tossing them with your fingers to separate the strands. Shake the sieve a few times to remove as much water as possible.View image in fullscreenStrain the sauce (you can save the kombu and katsuobushi to makefurikake). Cut the nori into thin strips, finely chop the spring onion and grate the wasabi, if necessary.Serve the sauce in individual bowls with the noodles (on bamboo mats, if you have them) and accompaniments on the side for dipping. Once the noodles are finished, add cooking water to the remaining sauce to taste, to make a broth, and drink.Zaru soba: when did you discover this deliciously cooling noodle dish, where can you find the best, and what do you like to serve it with?Explore more on these topicsNoodlesHow to cook the perfect ...FoodJapanese food and drinkMain courseSouprecipesShareReuse this content

title: Café Clement, London WC2: ‘Turns out it’s really rather good’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: I am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, especially when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in Tuscany
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: I am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, especially when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in Tuscany
Content: Café Clement, London WC2: ‘Sell your grandmother for a terrace table.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenCafé Clement, London WC2: ‘Sell your grandmother for a terrace table.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The Guardian.Grace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewCafé Clement, London WC2: ‘Turns out it’s really rather good’ – restaurant reviewI am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, especially when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in TuscanyGrace DentSun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCafé Clement, the all-day restaurant inside Nick Jones’ new St Clement Hotel at 180 The Thames in central London, opened with a bang in June and immediately rocketed to the top of every “sell your grandmother for a terrace table” list in London. Which isn’tthatmuch of a surprise, seeing as Jones,founder of Soho House, is the master of restaurant rumpus.Within days,Stanley Tucci,Nick Grimshawand full-length-trouser-phobic heart-throbPaul Mescalwere all there, tucking intooeufs mayonnaiseand lobster omelettes while politely ignoring the fact that the place was still, in many ways, a building site. The hotel itself isn’t due to open fully until early autumn, when a rooftop restaurant,Lunette, will also arrive with some of London’s most wondrous views andFlorence Knightat the helm. Still, Café Clement opened to frothy praise, and I am forever curious as to how these kind of sizzling places feel on a normal Tuesday two months in, when the celebrities are all off sunning their bottoms in Tuscany and, frankly, lunch is not free.View image in fullscreen‘Stunning’: Café Clement’s cheese soufflé.Café Clement is elegant but not overdone: white linen, vintageCassina chairs. The staff, of whom there appear to be about 345, are a joy: everyone seems to have been hired for their personality and for having the chops to nail a busy service. There’s an open kitchen behind ornate glass screens, a south-facing terrace that gives itself to debauchery and a garden out the back. The menu, which is that of a broadly European, fancy, all-day bistro, offers the likes of spatchcocked chicken with speck and green bean vinaigrette, Dorset crab with marinated tomatoes and aïoli, and hearty meat and fish casseroles. There are pastas and grills, plus chocolatey, tarty things on the pudding menu.As with most central London celebrity brasseries, the food offering here is designed to mollify and comfort: steak haché with crinkle-cut chips, roast duck with dripping potatoes, with cosmos on the cocktail menu and a hulking sharing chocolate mousse that will soothe any recent knock-back for a starring role. And if anyone can keep all of this classy, it’s chefDanny Bohan, who spent 20-odd years atthe River Cafe, most recently as head chef, working alongside Rose Gray and Ruth Rogers, both of them names that make foodies genuflect. A reader told me recently that his life’s ambition was to eat at the River Cafe, where starters run to £51, pastas to £46 and mains to £69. Unfortunately, his partner misunderstood the assignment entirely and booked the now defunct and unmissedRainforest Café in Piccadillyinstead. Here’s hoping said errant partner finds out about Café Clement and tries to make amends by booking a table, because it turns out that it’s really rather good.View image in fullscreen‘Sweet and sharp in exactly the right proportions’: Café Clement’s sea bass carpaccio.Café Clement’s food offering could be merely passable and many would turn a blind eye, but it’s pleasing and careful in equal measure. A plate of eggs mayonnaise arrives jammy and generously stuffed, the mayo earthy and mustardy without ever tipping into sickly. The eggs are served starkly – there’s no trout roe, no caviar – and they are all the better for it. You get the sense that this is a kitchen that wants to spend money on exceptional produce, rather than on garnishes that may well end up in the bin. The cheese soufflé is stunning: upright, luscious, deeply cheesy. A sharply pickly, well-seasoned steak tartare comes free-form on the plate, and is served withcartadi musicaSardinian flatbread. Sea bass carpaccio is simply and beautifully arranged, all sweet and sharp in exactly the right proportions. A side of summer beetroots at £7 is, quite frankly, gorgeous: sweet, plump, properly baked, buttery, and made me wonder why baked beets aren’t on every side menu going.View image in fullscreenCafé Clement’s hazlenut and raspberry tart.Photograph: Amy Heycock/The GuardianNot everything lands, however. The fish casserole is thin and pale, a bouillabaisse in search of a meaning: some mussels, a piece of fish, not a lot else. Definitely good for those on a diet, though. A side of crinkles, or retro potato wedges, meanwhile, isn’t really worth the carbs. The £18 chocolate mousse for two, on the other hand, turns up with the energy of an unstructured brownie and the ability to put you on your back with a sugar high. Neither of those things is a quibble. A fresh, wobbly slice of custard tart is delightful, and comes with a mush of sweet strawberries and more custard.Café Clement quietly surpasses expectations, and I’d go back any day. It is fun, joyous and well thought out. As this stretch of the Thames around180 The Strandfinally starts to flourish, it will become even more useful and ridiculously difficult to get into. Come for the celeb rumpus, and, if none of them is there, stay for theoeufs mayonnaise.Café ClementSt Clement, 180 The Thames, 12 Temple Place, London WC2, 020-4632 6660. Open all week, 7am-11pm (9pm Sun). From about £60 a head for three courses, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Quench your thirst! 20 perfect spritzes and shandies to try now – from kumquat to portergaff | Food | The Guardian
description: Whether you love a traditional spritz or tend towards a wilder libation, this August there are bubbly and sophisticated drinks to suit every taste
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: Whether you love a traditional spritz or tend towards a wilder libation, this August there are bubbly and sophisticated drinks to suit every taste
Content: Fresh and floral … a Hugo spritz.Photograph: 5PH/AlamyView image in fullscreenFresh and floral … a Hugo spritz.Photograph: 5PH/AlamyFoodQuench your thirst! 20 perfect spritzes and shandies to try now – from kumquat to portergaffWhether you love a traditional spritz or tend towards a wilder libation, this August there are bubbly and sophisticated drinks to suit every tasteRachel DixonSun 23 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis summer, UK web searches for “Hugo spritz”, an elderflower-flavoured aperitif, overtook searches for “Aperol spritz” for the first time. As the spritz craze shows no sign of slowing down, pub chains are taking wild liberties, calling anything fizzy and served in a large glass over ice a spritz – and charging £10-plus for it. Echo Falls blue raspberry spritz? Pink gin spritz (Slug & Lettuce)? Raspberry vodka and honey spritz (Young’s)? Malibu cranberry spritz (Stonegate)?Mamma mia!Traditionally, the spritz is an Italian cocktail made from prosecco, a bitter aperitif or liqueur, and a splash of soda water to keep things steady. While Venetian bartenders are more likely to judge it by eye, there is a simple 3-2-1 formula for making a spritz at home: three parts prosecco, two parts liqueur and one part soda water. I’ve gone with 75ml/50ml/25ml – keep the same ratios to make a smaller (60ml/40ml/20ml) or larger (90ml/60ml/30ml) drink. Of course, you can then adjust it to make it stronger or weaker (I have been known to leave out the soda …).If wine-based cocktails aren’t to your taste, shandy is also showing signs of a resurgence – Ocado sales have increased 40% year on year, and the craft brand Shandy Shack is now stocked in M&S. Being half beer, half soft drink, it is another summery thirst-quencher that is easy to make at home and (in theory) shouldn’t get you too sloshed.So, here are 20 simple spritzes and shandies. Save your Malibu for a piña colada.View image in fullscreen‘All-conquering’ … an Aperol spritz.Photograph: David Cabrera Navarro/AlamyFive bittersweet spritzesAll recipes make one drink.
